full_text:
Beck's stat line wasn't good in his debut game, but he showed one particular encouraging flash. The Cardinals have plenty of reasons to be patient. Mike Christy / Getty Images
GLENDALE, Ariz. — His first NFL start over, Carson Beck left his locker and walked around the room. The rookie quarterback started with the receivers, slapping hands. Then Beck made his way to the offensive line, greeting guards Isaac Seumalo and Isaiah Adams, and stopping to chat with Hayden Conner as the center returned from the shower.
Throughout another miserable season, one that has gone through two veteran quarterbacks and several roster-depleting injuries, the Arizona Cardinals have arrived at a place where the future trumps the present. After Sunday’s 34-6 loss to the Los Angeles Rams , coach Mike LaFleur said the team has seven more weeks of a “master evaluation” to see how this roster will look.
Less than two weeks before Thanksgiving, the 2026 third-round draft pick out of Miami is the only interesting storyline remaining for sinking Arizona, which dropped its 11th consecutive home game (dating to last season) and fell to 3-7. Is he the franchise quarterback this team desperately needs? Sunday marked the official start of discovery. Results were mixed.
“He did everything we asked him to do,” said LaFleur, placing blame on a “collection of errors” that prevented the Cardinals from finding an offensive rhythm. “All you ask these guys is to do their job. And I thought he did his job.”
Early in Sunday’s game, Beck said he looked across the line and saw Myles Garrett and Aaron Donald, destroyers who have built Hall of Fame careers harassing quarterbacks young and old. The rookie smiled and thought, “This is sick.” Here he was, living a dream that started during grade school, a starting quarterback in the NFL. Then reality hit.
Beck did not lead the Cardinals into the end zone. He threw two interceptions, although LaFleur said neither was the quarterback’s fault. Beck’s final numbers — 11 of 18 for 108 yards — were not good. The Cardinals ran 40 fewer plays than the Rams and only 12 in the second half. They secured six first downs. This was bad offensive football.
Yet one play was impressive enough to suspend judgment. If only to make everyone think …
On Arizona’s second possession, Beck faked a handoff to Tyler Allgeier and looked downfield. Leading up to Sunday’s game, tight end Trey McBride was asked what he liked about Beck, and McBride discussed the rookie’s intelligence and ambition, but three times in his answer he said the same phrase. He’s very talented . Beck showed as much here.
The 24-year-old lofted a perfect ball over the hands of Rams safety Quentin Lake, reaching Arizona receiver Devin Duvernay in stride, a gain of 31 yards. It was the Cardinals’ biggest play — they mustered only 123 yards all day — and it reflected the young quarterback’s potential.
“A phenomenal throw,” Duvernay said.
“Excellent,” LaFleur said.
“It makes it easy when the offensive line is standing up and I’m able to sit back there, and they did a great job on that play,” Beck said. “And, obviously, Duvernay was able to shake (the defender) out of his shoes a little bit and get open. That was definitely a big explosive. We just got to continue doing that.”
Carson Beck connects with Devin Duvernay for 31 yards 🎯
LARvsAZ on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/9Ct73g3Gwy
— NFL (@NFL) November 15, 2026
The full picture here will take time to develop, which is a silver lining of sorts. Fading in the NFC West, the Cardinals have nothing but time. Had Jacoby Brissett played better or Gardner Minshew stayed healthy, Beck likely would have remained sidelined until December. Instead, with the rookie forced into action, the Cardinals have a bigger window in which to evaluate. How Beck commands the offense. How he finishes drives. How he connects with teammates.
Advice to fans: Be patient. With a beat-up line and receivers who have spent most of this season on special teams or the practice squad, Beck doesn’t have much to work with beyond McBride. Progress likely will be best measured in moments. A few plays this week. A few more next week at Kansas City. Maybe enough to beat the New York Jets before Christmas.
This is not unusual. Few quarterbacks enter the league positioned for immediate success. In 2009, the quarterback opposite Beck on Sunday — the Rams’ Matthew Stafford, who began his career with the Detroit Lions — completed 16 of 37 for 205 yards with three interceptions in a loss to the New Orleans Saints. It’s a steep learning curve, especially for someone like Beck, who had not played since Arizona’s first preseason contest Aug. 6.
What stood out to receiver Simi Fehoko on Sunday was Beck’s confidence. He saw a quarterback who acted like he belonged, improvising when needed. “It’s pretty impressive to see,” Fehoko said. “But I think there are a lot of things that we can do to help him as an offense and as a staff to mitigate the mistakes. We really hurt ourselves in that aspect.”
With the Cardinals trailing 10-6 late in the second quarter, Beck threw a pass to Duvernay that the receiver mishandled. The ball bounced up and landed in the arms of Rams safety Kamren Kinchens, a turnover that changed the game. The Rams scored three plays later to take a 17-6 halftime lead. They then scored on their first third-quarter possession. Beck and the Cardinals never recovered.
“I felt comfortable,” Beck said. “I knew our plan. I felt like I was seeing it well. But when we have the plays, I got to make them. Especially against a good defense, you can’t afford to not make the big explosives, because those are game-shifters. And when you’re not able to do that, obviously, the game gets away from you.”

title: The Ravens say their mini-bye offered a ‘reset.' They had better be right With a competent QB and favorable schedule, Baltimore has a prime window to string together wins while waiting on Lamar Jackson’s return. Jeff Zrebiec 22

OWINGS MILLS, Md. — Coach Jesse Minter called the past week a “reset” for a reeling Baltimore Ravens team that badly needed one. A rewind would have been far more preferable, of course, but it wasn’t an option.

full_text:
With a competent QB and favorable schedule, coach Jesse Minter’s Ravens have a prime window to string together wins while waiting on Lamar Jackson’s return. Scott Taetsch / Getty Images
OWINGS MILLS, Md. — Coach Jesse Minter called the past week a “reset” for a reeling Baltimore Ravens team that badly needed one. A rewind would have been far more preferable, of course, but it wasn’t an option.
With 11 days between their humbling Week 9 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars and Monday’s primetime home game against the winless Los Angeles Chargers, the Ravens had a rare opportunity for extended self-evaluation.
For Minter and the coaching staff, it meant reexamining everything from personnel to play calling to practice habits. For the players, it meant much-needed time off and honest conversations about the two months ahead.
“Reset is a good word to use,” safety Kyle Hamilton said last week. “I think giving the coaches an opportunity to just take a step back and assess us just from a third-party perspective almost — what do we do well, what do we do poorly and ways that we can improve in certain areas of the game. I think they brought that to us this week. We have a good mindset, outlook and approach to this game.”
Yet, as Hamilton cautioned, “At the end of the day, it’s just all talk. I appreciate the coaches for the effort that they put in, but it’s up to us to go out there and have the result that we want on the field. We can talk all we want about whatever we’ve said and whatever we want to do, but we have to let it show on the field.”
Defensive coordinator Anthony Weaver put it even more succinctly.
“Winning doesn’t care about what you’re saying. It cares about what you’re doing.”
Monday starts a four-game stretch that might as well be the last stand for the 2026 Ravens. They are 4-5, losers of four straight contests (three by blowouts) and in last place in the AFC North. Still, they find themselves firmly in the wild-card mix.
To stay there, they almost certainly have to beat the 0-8 Chargers at M&T Bank Stadium, where a primetime television audience will get a glimpse of two of the NFL’s most disappointing teams. They then probably have to win at least two of the next three, which consist of trips to the Carolina Panthers (4-5) and Houston Texans (3-6), followed by a home game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers (3-6) after the bye week.
Hamilton didn’t want to use the word “desperate,” but if the Ravens falter Monday, any hope of a second-half surge into contention will be all but lost. They’d also deal with far more than the ignominy of losing to a winless team this late in the season.
They’d face weeks of playing out the string in front of a presumably half-empty home stadium. There would be several months of speculation about a pending roster teardown for a prideful franchise showing signs of losing its way.
They’d also all but ensure that star quarterback Lamar Jackson’s season is over. For all the talk about Jackson’s timetable to return from thumb surgery — the Ravens say it’s anywhere from six to 10 weeks — what purpose would it serve for Jackson to play again if the team is essentially out of the postseason picture?
“Win,” defensive lineman Nnamdi Madubuike said of the team’s message ahead of the Chargers game. “That’s Ravens history. That’s Ravens football — winning, defensive team, offensive execution and just winning games.”
The sense of urgency in Minter’s voice all week was palpable. There’s been an edginess to him since the putrid loss to Jacksonville that hadn’t necessarily been there up until this point in the season. That the Ravens are playing the Chargers, for whom Minter worked the past two years as defensive coordinator, surely has nothing to do with it.
“You are what your record says you are,” Minter said. “You are what the last time you played — that’s what you are. I think sometimes it’s easy for guys to be like, ‘Well, this, this (and) this,’ and you can spin almost every game and every situation back to some sort of positive thing. But if you really just say screw all that, and we’re going to look at this thing realistically, this is what we are right now. The only people that can do anything about it are us.”
The Ravens’ biggest change Monday night will be veteran Jacoby Brissett, who will become the team’s fourth starting quarterback this season. The recent trade acquisition has already earned widespread praise from his teammates and coaches for his leadership and preparation.
Whether personnel changes extend beyond signal-caller and the kicker — Riley Patterson will make his Baltimore debut Monday — remains to be seen. Minter didn’t rebuff a question early last week about potentially demoting or benching a few of his struggling veterans .
The most obvious change for the Ravens was how they practiced. Veterans who normally trickle onto the practice field for the early stages of practice hustled out of the building to make sure they were in line for the stretching/warm-up phase.
The early stages of practice were more up tempo and specialized, with the defensive backs running through agility ladders and defensive linemen using medicine balls. Coaches worked with players individually. Once practice started, the Ravens did more “best-on-best” work with the starting offense operating more than usual against the starting defense. Hamilton said “details” and the “littler things” were emphasized all week.
“We definitely tweaked some things,” right tackle Roger Rosengarten said. “I think change is good for this time. When our backs are against the wall, like we are right now, you have to change some things up. Me and the rest of the guys are all for it. It keeps the competitive spirit going up.”
It’s not just that the Ravens have been losing; they’ve struggled to remain competitive since Jackson went to the sideline in Week 8 in Buffalo and his backup, Tyler Huntley, ultimately joined him with a season-ending toe injury. Over the past three games, they’ve been outscored 104-43, as all their flaws have risen to the surface. They’ve looked like one of the league’s worst teams.
Getting embarrassed by the Jaguars might have felt like rock bottom for the Ravens. For many players, it felt like a continuation of a nearly month-long stretch of bad football.
“I don’t think it started last game,” Hamilton said. “I don’t think we ever felt really good, even at 4-1. I think we still felt like there was a lot to be desired, especially on the defensive side of the ball. Obviously, Lamar getting hurt doesn’t help, but I think we have more than enough pieces to be productive on both sides of the ball, special teams included.”
Hamilton then added, “We have Jacoby. He’s been great so far, and he’s looked great in practice. I’m excited to get him out there, too.”
Brissett went 4-16 as a starter over the past two seasons for the Arizona Cardinals, and he was benched in one of those four wins . Now the Ravens have turned to him to essentially save their season, or at least win enough games to still be in the playoff mix in mid-to-late December, when Jackson potentially could return.
It’s a lot to ask of a journeyman quarterback who is less than a month shy of his 34th birthday and who was benched in the middle of his last start. It sure beats the alternative, as the Chargers can attest, of having virtually no postseason shot at all.
The Ravens had better hope their reset results in a resurgence. The clock is ticking.
“I just feel like the team is refreshed, and I think that there’s just a focus on our identity and nothing else, and just what we want to be,” Minter said. “Obviously, we talk about it, and we want it to be really, really crystal clear to our guys of what we’re after in all three phases, but now (it’s time to) go out there and do that.”

title: Bills observations: Amani Hooker looks like an instant upgrade in win over Jets Hooker seized a starting role, T.J. Parker delivered two sacks and Christian Benford's injury could put Tre'Davious White back on the field. Joe Buscaglia 23

full_text:
Buffalo Bills safety Amani Hooker impressed in his debut Sunday against the New York Jets. Vincent Carchietta / Imagn Images
When the Buffalo Bills originally acquired Amani Hooker, the first thought was that they’d take a slow approach with their new safety, hoping he’d eventually become the full-time starter.
Most deadline acquisitions need time to learn the playbook and terminology before being thrust into an every-snap role. As the week went on, the signs began to add up that this wasn’t a typical deadline acquisition.
Bills head coach Joe Brady, defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard and general manager Brandon Beane lauded Hooker for his intelligence and adaptability, and his teammates said as much after just a few practices. By the end of the practice week, it was clear Hooker was in line for a huge role just four full days into his Bills tenure.
That’s what happened in Sunday’s 31-12 win over the New York Jets. Not only did Hooker take over as the starting safety next to Cole Bishop, but he also played every snap while the game was still relevant. He completely took the starting role from Damar Hamlin, reducing Hamlin to a dime-defense role as he subbed in for a linebacker, allowing Bishop to play the dime-backer role, usually next to middle linebacker Terrel Bernard. More than that, Hooker’s overall impact was a massive upgrade over what the Bills have had at safety all season.
Hooker was constantly around the ball and showed the versatility he demonstrated all year with the Tennessee Titans. He crashed down against the run and was a consistent tackler, rather than letting the play come to him.
In coverage, he took away space when receivers came near him in his zones, and above all else, he let Bishop be the chess piece the Bills wanted him to be without sacrificing too much on the back end. On top of that, Hooker was right in there for an interception on two occasions, showing his instincts when the ball is in the air.
Hooker will need to stack more games on top of his debut against a struggling Jets team, but there are plenty of signs for optimism with him in Jim Leonhard’s scheme.
Having Hooker as the starting safety on every snap wasn’t the only big change Sunday, though this one was more subtle, based on the Bills’ rotations and how they handled obvious passing downs.
Through the first eight games of the season, the Bills have followed a pretty standard formula with their edge rushers and the groupings they use on third downs. It usually meant Greg Rousseau and Bradley Chubb took the vast majority of snaps at outside linebacker throughout the game. Then, on obvious passing downs, they’d have Rousseau rush from the left side and Chubb from the right side; they’d sub in Michael Hoecht as an interior pass rusher and have him next to Ed Oliver or Deone Walker. All of that changed Sunday.
The outside linebackers went from a heavy emphasis on Rousseau and Chubb to a legitimate three-person timeshare. Though Rousseau and Chubb still played the most snaps, their percentages dropped a lot before garbage time hit. Until the Bills took a 31-12 lead in the fourth quarter, Rousseau’s playing time was unofficially at 67.2 percent, and Chubb’s was at 68.8 percent — both down quite a bit from when they were in the 80s for the first two months of the season.
The drop came because rookie TJ Parker saw his role grow considerably, taking 51.6 percent of the snaps up to that point. The Bills went from a total platoon change of Parker and Hoecht subbing in to just one of Rousseau or Chubb coming out for Parker.
That wasn’t the only change for Hoecht, whose defensive role was almost completely vanquished before garbage time. He was no longer part of the obvious pass-rush unit, as he had been all season. Rather than subbing in Hoecht, the Bills kept a second interior defensive lineman in to rush the passer with the outside linebackers. The Bills usually used Ed Oliver and Deone Walker on those reps, with T.J. Sanders occasionally filling in. They even had Rousseau and Parker rushing from the edges on one snap, with Chubb rushing from the inside next to Oliver. That grouping, given Parker’s uptick in snaps and two-sack performances, seems like one we could see more of.
This switch was necessary, as Hoecht had struggled to generate pressure all year. His 7.7 percent pressure rate through Week 9 ranked 139th out of 183 defenders with at least 100 pass-rush snaps, according to TruMedia. It is also well below Oliver (16.7 percent) and Walker (11.7 percent). Taking either of those two off the field for Hoecht actively worsened the Bills’ pass rush. They recognized this and made the change, and it seems like one that will stick when their rush group is healthy.
The Bills defense limited the Jets to 12 points, and while they again had to go up against a backup quarterback for most of the second half, it was another step in the right direction for that side of the ball. A lot of that has to do with how far the boundary cornerbacks have come since the season began. No. 1 cornerback Christian Benford had a couple of beats, but he was mostly a strength.
The problem, though, is that once again this season, Benford had to leave the game injured. Earlier in the year, a toe injury kept him out of a game. Last week, a wrist injury kept him from finishing against the Minnesota Vikings, and against the Jets, a groin injury ended Benford’s game early. The Bills have been fortunate that Benford hasn’t missed much time, but the one game he missed was against the New England Patriots — the Bills’ lone loss on the year, and the game that prompted the switch at cornerback from Maxwell Hairston to rookie Davison Igbinosun.
Any in-game rule-out puts the following week in jeopardy. If that’s the case, Igbinosun could be joined by the struggling Hairston in the lineup once again. However, this time around, there’s a key difference. Tre’Davious White is on the practice squad, and this is why the Bills brought him back in the first place. That’s also why they decided against going after another veteran cornerback in the trade market.
The Athletic caught up with White ahead of the Jets game, just a few weeks after his return to the Bills. He said he’s been pushing himself hard on the scout team, and he’s at the point where if they need him to play, he’s ready.
“Everybody’s been telling me I look good, so there it is. You know, I always leave it to my teammates and my peers,” the 31-year-old said. “I always say it like, ‘Hey, you see me out there and I look like I’m walking, just tell me to hang it up.’ And nobody told me to hang it up yet, Joe, so I’m good, man, I feel like I am good.”
White was a strength for the starting lineup down the stretch last season and into the playoffs, but he ultimately returned to the practice squad to help mentor Igbinosun and Hairston while trying to finish what he started in 2017.
“This ain’t have to be what it was; this is what I chose,” White said. “You know what I mean? I could have been anywhere else on a team, on a 53, playing right now, but I’m a Bill. … I mean, it’s bigger than me, man.”
“I know I can go out there and play right now. Movement good, body feels good, I know how I can play, but right now my role is to help the young guys out and to be that. But it’s hard, being that I just started every game last year, you know what I mean? And played good football. So it’s like, ‘ Ahh .’ But I’m going to trust the process, and I’m gonna be here to cheer the guys on. But as I’m doing it, I’m definitely preparing to play, too.”
If Benford has to miss any time, the Bills might need White to play as early as next week. And if it goes well enough, maybe even earn a bigger role as the year goes on.
Up next: The 8-1 Bills head back to Orchard Park to take on the rebuilding 1-8 Dolphins.

full_text:
The Bears have called Soldier Field home since 1971. In the coming weeks, fans could gain some clarity about where their next stadium will be built. Todd Rosenberg / Getty Images
The Chicago Bears’ quest for clarity in their bid for a new stadium has reached another defining stage. Beginning Tuesday, Illinois lawmakers will gather in Springfield for their fall veto session, an opening to pass legislation that could keep the team playing inside state lines while derailing a potential move to Indiana.
In the best-case scenario for the Bears, with three days of governing sessions this week plus three more Dec. 1-3, the state Senate and House of Representatives will push forward a bill that provides the team a framework for tax certainty and requested infrastructure aid to resume seriously pursuing its stadium project in Illinois.
The Bears’ desired project location in Illinois remains Arlington Heights, where the organization owns 326 acres of property on a site that has been pad-ready for some time and offers substantial space for both a stadium and a mixed-use development and entertainment district.
Will this stadium venture finally move ahead in Illinois? We’ll see. Shovels in the ground in 2027? Perhaps. But it’s worth emphasizing that this saga remains fluid — and has been for years.
Less than three months ago, Bears leadership emphasized the team was fixated on advancing its exploration of northwest Indiana for a potential new stadium. “Our sole focus at this point in time is working on a world-class stadium and mixed-use development in Hammond,” team president and CEO Kevin Warren said on Aug. 13.
But in recent months — with added push from NFL commissioner Roger Goodell — the organization has re-engaged with prominent Illinois lawmakers, including Gov. J.B. Pritzker, to keep that door open.
As this week’s veto session begins in Springfield, here are six questions worth considering.
There’s an argument to be made — and one the Bears will aggressively champion — that this could be Illinois’ last chance to figure something out. Deadline pressure? For real this time?
The Bears had hoped for more substantive momentum from Illinois’ spring legislative session and, at one point, vowed to make a final decision on their stadium site by late spring or early summer this year. That target period came and went, and still the organization finds itself in limbo.
What could set this veto session apart from last spring’s General Assembly activity, however, is the increased urgency and involvement of Pritzker. Fresh off his gubernatorial re-election, Pritzker has become more public about his desire to keep the Bears in Illinois — and increasingly active with attempts to do so. That includes his increased collaboration with Goodell, plus comments earlier this month reflecting hope that Springfield lawmakers can get something done.
“We want to make sure the legislation is ready for people to look at and maybe have some hearings during that first week and then hopefully get voted on during the second week of the veto (session),” Pritzker told reporters on Nov. 6.
Motivation for negotiation progress and a concrete solution seems evident in Pritzker, along with prominent legislative leaders like state representative Kam Buckner and state senator Bill Cunningham, who have been heavily involved in conversations with the Bears this year.
The Bears have repeatedly noted that their exploration of a potential stadium project in Hammond, Ind., has gained significant support from the state’s legislative bodies and Gov. Mike Braun. Last winter, Indiana lawmakers signed Senate Bill 27 into law, greenlighting the Northwest Indiana Stadium Authority, which would have the power to acquire land and publicly finance a Bears stadium in Hammond.
Since that progress was made across the state line — and despite the Bears’ assertions this summer that an Indiana stadium project had become the sole focus — the team has been waiting for a legislative response in Illinois that would provide incentive to remain in the state.
The Bears have remained consistent in establishing their biggest requests. Assistance with needed infrastructure improvements has been labeled a prerequisite. More significantly, the team has insisted that without significant tax certainty, the project can’t get off the ground.
The most significant pushback has come from Illinois politicians averse to providing a private business worth billions of dollars with a massive tax break. Additionally, many Chicago politicians have strongly opposed allowing the Bears to leave the city.
Pritzker has been emphatic in urging legislators to agree that now is the time to do something for the Bears. Will significant action follow?
Until new legislation is finalized in Illinois, the Bears’ exploration of a possible stadium project in Hammond remains on the table, with more favorable political and financial dynamics in place. However, the sites the team has been targeting near Wolf Lake have yet to be fully approved, even with legislation in place to facilitate a Bears move. Due diligence on the sites won’t last forever, though. At some point, the Indiana locations could also be ready for a stadium.
Certainly Indiana politicians will watch this Illinois veto session closely, hoping Lucy won’t pull the football away nine months after they celebrated the idea of the Bears moving to their state.
On Thursday, a team of developers showcased a $10 billion proposal for a Bears stadium south of downtown, on the Michael Reese Hospital site in Chicago’s Bronzeville neighborhood. However, it’s important to emphasize that it was a strategically timed pitch to the Bears — not in collaboration with the team. So while flashy renderings and a public presentation created new waves of attention, that was not a Bears-backed proposition.
Furthermore, given the urgency for the Bears and the NFL to finalize a decision on this stadium venture, introducing new proposals at this stage seems highly impractical, requiring costly, time-consuming research and due diligence that could extend the project timeline by many years.
In April 2025, Warren also said the Michael Reese Hospital site was too narrow for a new stadium. And that site never seemed to gain serious consideration from the Bears, who spent almost a year — starting in the spring of 2024 — exploring another potential Chicago project within the Museum Campus near Soldier Field.
When that city-based push hit a dead end, the Bears vowed in March 2025 to focus exclusively on Arlington Heights, where the team closed on the purchase of the property from the old Arlington Park racetrack two years earlier.
Then, additional snags in securing legislative support for the Arlington Heights project sent the team on its research trip to Indiana.
With the veto session approaching and Pritzker wanting to keep options open, speculation about potential sites around Chicago has returned to the news cycle.
The Municipal Stadium Authority Act — passed by the Illinois Senate in June but never voted on by the House — would open the door so that “any home-rule municipality with a population of 70,000 or more residents that is located in a county with a population of more than 3,000,000 residents may establish a municipal stadium authority.”
Chicago could, therefore, be an option for establishing a future stadium authority. But the Bears would have to choose where their stadium would be. And the team has been insistent that the lone Illinois-based site currently under consideration is in Arlington Heights.
Has anything changed with these new proposals, politics and finances to get something done in Chicago after the Bears spent a year working on a city-based project?
When Goodell recently joined Warren and Bears chairman George McCaskey in a meeting with select state lawmakers, including Pritzker, he did so to add weight and emphasize the urgency of reaching a resolution.
After that interaction, the Bears issued a statement…

full_text:
Joe Burrow continued his phenomenal season with four more touchdown passes in Sunday's win over the Steelers. Kareem Elgazzar / Associated Press
CINCINNATI — Joe Burrow threw for 302 yards. He added three touchdown passes and no interceptions. The lead stood at 21 against a division rival with one of the most fearsome defenses in football.
Chants echoed into the night above the whiteout crowd at Paycor Stadium.
By the time the roars of a 38-18 drubbing of the Steelers subsided, Burrow had racked up 409 yards with four touchdowns and no interceptions and stood on the sidelines with a smile and a hat, watching Joe Flacco finish off a division rival for the second consecutive AFC North game.
Nine weeks into the season, Burrow is halfway through his football masterpiece.
“It would be impossible to say anyone is playing better,” head coach Zac Taylor said. “I’m not watching every game, but I bet the people that aren’t talking about him aren’t watching our games, because if you are, it’s really hard to say that he is not the best player on planet Earth.”
Burrow accounted for four touchdowns for the fifth consecutive game. That tied 2004 Peyton Manning for the longest such streak.
His 74.7 completion percentage ranks second best (Drew Brees) in NFL history through nine games.
He’s now on pace for 5,279 yards and 51 touchdowns.
Burrow has connected with Ja’Marr Chase for 527 yards in the last three weeks. That’s good for the second-most receiving yards in a three-game span by any player in the last 10 years.
The Bengals have now scored at least 31 points in five straight games, tied for the longest streak in the last 10 years.
Elite quarterback play happens across this league every week. Josh Allen, Jordan Love and others have their arguments. What Burrow does to run one of the best individual units in the NFL can’t be denied at this point.
“I don’t know who else is in the convo, but he should be No. 1,” said tight end Drew Sample, who caught a touchdown Sunday.
No team puts more on their quarterback. The Bengals throw at a higher rate than any team in football. The running game has devolved into a changeup designed for efficiency and the periodic explosive.
In the dominant first half, Burrow threw 34 passes against just eight handoffs. Why would you run? It feels like lighting a play on fire.
No matter what a defense throws at Burrow, he rips off the answer.
Pittsburgh defensive coordinator Patrick Graham opted to bring blitzes on Burrow early, hoping to disrupt his rhythm and create pressures to rattle him.
Burrow responded by going a perfect 12 of 12 for 186 yards against blitzes, according to TruMedia.
Throwing the Steelers out of that philosophy, Graham reverted to dropping defenders into coverage, specifically in the red zone.
Burrow countered by twice holding the ball for at least six seconds while patiently waiting for a player to uncover for a touchdown. First, it was Sample racing to the front pylon, then Chase Brown darting across the end zone.
When the Steelers played off Brown, Burrow hit him crossing over the middle for a catch-and-run, 35-yard explosive or on a deep comeback near the sideline. When the coverage got tight on the outside, Burrow threw a dime over the top for 53 yards.
“He thought he overthrew me,” Brown said. “But he trusted me in that moment and got me the ball.”
When asked to drive the length of the field, Burrow did so with ease.  The Bengals started a drive at their own 22-yard line or worse five times. Those drives combined for 24 points.
“He’s just on it,” Taylor said. “I thought the protection was really good. There are some times that they are going to create some movement, but it’s blocked movement. I think Joe did an excellent job keeping his eyes down the field and finding guys for some big plays. Those guys made big plays and tremendous catches — all of those guys really. Everyone stepped up and made some plays for us. Obviously, (Burrow) sets the tone.”
Setting the tone doesn’t only happen on the field. In fact, that tone was on his mind in the hour after the Sunday night win.
Burrow didn’t decide to lean into the MVP chatter or stump for how this offense and this team belong in the greater NFL landscape.
No, he intentionally dampened the mood.
“It’s a long season ahead,” Burrow said. “We’ve just got to keep going. Nobody’s winning anything in Week 9, so we just have to keep getting better. Nobody is winning the division with seven wins. Nobody is making the playoffs with seven wins. And we’re certainly not satisfied.”
Only five weeks prior, following a loss to Jacksonville, Burrow pointed out after the loss to fall to 2-2, “This isn’t Armageddon.”
Understanding what tone his team needs after a dominating showing illustrates a keen sense of leadership.
It would have been easy for him to sit at the stage and wax poetic about his journey and an undeniably dominant level of play. He didn’t shy away when prodded, like when he was asked what type of quarterback he was on Sunday.
The scene set itself, really. “Redemption Song” played in the locker room, drowning out Burrow’s softer tone. A face of the franchise who has endured more than most over his seven NFL seasons, including missing out on the playoffs three years in a row and dealing with the often lonely, mental strain of rehabbing.
He calls Bob Marley’s hits “a good vibe,” which is why he chooses them.
The vibes are high in Cincinnati. Burrow is keeping the pedal down on a team that owns its best point differential through nine games this century. This passing game is chasing records and rewriting history every week.
Burrow finds himself in the middle of it.
That’s why the MVP chants offered a fitting backdrop to his big night.
Don’t expect him to lose focus now. He says they don’t faze him.
“Not in Week 9,” he said. “Not in Week 9.” So, when do they get serious? “We’ll see,” he said.
Everyone is seeing it now. Burrow is playing like an MVP and the case is impossible to deny. Sunday night solidified as much.
“This is why we do it,” Burrow said. “For big moments like that — Steelers, Aaron Rodgers, primetime, two 6-2 teams for sole possession of the division (lead). That’s what I love to do. That’s why I work so hard to put myself in a good position to play in games like that.”

full_text:
Deshaun Watson celebrates after the Browns' decisive fourth-quarter touchdown in Sunday's 27-24 victory against the Texans. Jason Miller / Getty Images
CLEVELAND — There once was a distinct roar on this soil on Sunday afternoons in the fall, and anyone who was around in 1980 can still describe it.
It was the collective cries of relief and exasperation when Brian Sipe threw to Ozzie Newsome in the end zone to beat the Pittsburgh Steelers, or when Sipe to Greg Pruitt on fourth down completed a fourth-quarter comeback to beat the New York Jets.
The waves of joy rolled out of the old stadium on the lake and down into the neighborhoods and through open windows as a whole city exhaled at once. Sipe was the MVP. The team lost and won games in ways that made grown men grip their recliners. The Kardiac Kids were formed.
Forty-three years later, the sound came back — albeit briefly — when Joe Flacco got off his couch and turned December into some version of a weekly parade. Photos went viral of Flacco at the local coffee shop in his Patagonia quarter-zip as delirious fans took turns buying his favorite morning drinks.
Now the Cleveland Browns are 6-4. Six wins, each one of them needing a fourth-quarter rescue mission after they’ve been outscored 78-13 in first quarters this year.
They trailed Houston 17-0 on Sunday and won 27-24. It was more of the same dreadful football for at least one half and the same magic beans and sorcery in the fourth quarter and especially the final minute. But 6-4 is 6-4, and if the NFL playoffs started today, the Browns would be participants.
So why does it all feel … so … muted?
People are watching. People still care, but the roar is a bit more guarded.
This team should be the reincarnation of those Kardiac Kids. They’re young. They don’t know what they don’t know, but they know enough to keep fighting no matter what.
The Muni Lot had rows of vacant parking spaces a few hours before kickoff, and the upper deck left plenty of empty seats exposed throughout the afternoon.
The windy, rainy weather certainly played a role, as did perhaps consecutive losses in the past two weeks. But the get-in price hovered around $20 before kickoff for a team very much in the playoff race. Some of the fans who did show up appeared to leave early when defeat looked inevitable in the fourth quarter. Even Browns coach Todd Monken noticed.
“It’s awesome for our players and for our fans. For our fans that stayed around,” Monken said before catching himself.
“I’m not trying to bash the fans,” he said a few moments later. “We’ve got the greatest fans in the world, and you could tell that. Early on, we deserved to get booed. We didn’t play very good. At the end, we deserved to get cheered. But at the end of the day, we need them. And they were big at the end of the game.”
These Browns are giving Cleveland the thing it has longed for. A franchise that notoriously found new ways to lose, couldn’t finish games, and couldn’t protect leads is resolving all of that, week after week, with a jarring regularity.
For years, Browns fans swore they didn’t care how their team won. They just wanted it to win.
Maybe it mattered after all.
Part of the explanation is in the numbers. The Browns have one of the most robust analytics departments in the league. That’s what makes all of this mildly hilarious.
The analytics say the Browns aren’t a good football team, and yet they keep winning. They have a minus-32 point differential, by far the worst of any team currently sitting in a playoff chair. The math projects them at four wins, not six. The offense ranks near the bottom in EPA per play and success rate.
Deshaun Watson still ranks in the bottom half of quarterbacks in EPA per dropback.
For years, the Browns have been guided by the data perhaps more than any other organization in the league, insisting that their fans believe in the numbers. Now the numbers say not to believe in the Browns, but they keep winning.
So when do the fans fall in love with this team? It hasn’t happened yet.
Flacco was a 38-year-old life preserver in a season that felt lost before his arrival. The Kardiac Kids had Sipe and a roster of endearing personalities.
This team has Watson and all the baggage he brings.
He can lead six game-winning drives and still not be the joyful revelation Flacco became overnight. The trade that brought Watson here divided the fanbase, and it still hasn’t healed. Beating his former team Sunday surely brought Watson special joy, despite the trade that brought him to Cleveland being a disaster up until a few weeks ago. Watson had never thrown for 300 yards for the Browns before this season, and now he’s done it in three straight games. He would seem a lock for Comeback Player of the Year, but no one in the league is ready for that awkward conversation.
Rooting for the Browns with Flacco felt simple. Watson has made it complicated regardless of how many fourth-quarter comebacks he generates.
The Kardiac Kids felt like the beginning of something great. Flacco’s arrival was a Hail Mary caught in the end zone.
What exactly is this team’s story?
They were booed at home again in the first half on Sunday and cheered in the second. They were lousy in the first half again and brilliant in the second.
Young players like Denzel Boston, K.C. Concepcion, Carson Schwesinger and Mason Graham deserve to know what Cleveland really looks like when the Browns are winning. The nicknames, the made-up songs like “ Ber-nie Ber-nie, ohhhhh yeah, how you can throw. Yeah yeah yeah yeah yeah yeah. Ber-nie Ber-nie, ohhh baby, Super Bowl. ”
Maybe a December playoff push breaks something open between this team and this city, but it hasn’t happened yet.
Browns fans have said for generations that all they ever wanted was a winner.
This season is showing how it might be a little more complicated than that.

full_text:
Dallas has allowed eight plays of 50 or more yards this season, most in the NFL. Stacy Revere / Getty Images
ARLINGTON, Texas — As bad as the Dallas Cowboys defense was all day, it had an opportunity to put a positive spin on things in the end. But that unit did what it’s done most of the season: played like one of the worst groups in the league when it mattered most.
With just under four minutes to go Sunday at AT&T Stadium, trailing the San Francisco 49ers by six, Dallas needed one stop. A three-and-out would’ve been ideal, but preventing another score was the biggest goal.
The next possession lasted two plays and ended with a 49ers touchdown.
On second-and-10, San Francisco quarterback Brock Purdy found a wide-open Christian McCaffrey for an easy 66-yard trip to the end zone. Dallas brought six defenders after Purdy, which left McCaffrey single covered by 37-year-old Von Miller. It was far from a fair fight against one of the NFL’s best offensive players.
And that wasn’t even the 49ers’ longest play in their 46-40 win. It wasn’t even McCaffrey’s longest gain — he also had a 74-yard touchdown reception. Wide receiver Deebo Samuel added a 70-yard rushing touchdown. Dallas’ defense now has given up eight plays of 50 or more yards this season, most in the NFL.
The 584 yards the Cowboys allowed Sunday is the most they’ve given up in any home game in franchise history, and the third most overall (the two performances higher on the list both happened in 2013).
“I thought the second half was unacceptable,” Cowboys coach Brian Schottenheimer said. “Tackling was atrocious, and we got to do a deep dive on the film and see why. You can’t give up three explosive plays of over 65 yards for touchdowns and expect to win in this league.”
As bad as the Cowboys’ defense has been the past two seasons, Sunday was the most frustrated Schottenheimer has been with the group; he seemed to get angrier as his 11-minute postgame news conference went along.
The Cowboys allowed 244 yards and 17 points in the first half. Over the final two quarters, those numbers climbed to 340 and 29, respectively.
“I haven’t been around a situation like this, where the defense was that poor in the second half,” Schottenheimer said. “Very disappointed, very frustrated. I thought the first half we did some really good things. It’s a very good (San Francisco) offense, right? But what got us in the second half was the tackling — or the lack of tackling. And you’ve got to get guys on the ground.
“And yeah, they’re good players, but at the end of the day, we tackled like s— in the second half.”
It didn’t help that the Cowboys, who are used to their fans taking over opposing teams’ stadiums, effectively played a road game Sunday because of all the 49ers fans that made the trip.
Schottenheimer said the crowd split had no impact on how the Cowboys played, but it was clearly noticeable before kickoff as boos for the home team and cheers for the visitors rang out.
“Anticipated it,” Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott said. “Tricked myself and told myself early on that the red was for my high school. At the end of the day, all I ask for is a great environment to play this game. And unfortunately, their fans were more present than ours. But it created a great atmosphere. So, we take the good out of it, one way or another.”
San Francisco coach Kyle Shanahan said his offense had prepared to use a silent cadence to deal with the crowd noise. By the end of the 49ers’ first drive, he realized it wasn’t needed.
“I’ve been in (this) stadium a bunch, just coaching in the NFC East for a while and stuff like that,” he added. “And for us not to have to use the silent cadence at all — I don’t think we did on third down — it was really cool. It makes a difference.”
Prescott and the Cowboys’ offense could’ve been better, too, but they played well enough to win. Star wide receiver George Pickens had his most impactful game of the season, catching 11 of 18 targets for 145 yards and three touchdowns. Each of Dallas’ top three wide receivers — Pickens, CeeDee Lamb and Ryan Flournoy — had a touchdown catch in the fourth quarter.
Prescott finished 30-for-51 passing for 343 yards, five touchdowns, one interception and a 103.6 passer rating.
Dallas has had one of the league’s best offenses over the past two years, Prescott has been healthy and the Cowboys have an 11-15-1 record to show for it. Their franchise quarterback was asked Sunday night if these results are starting to feel like “Groundhog Day.”
“No,” he said. “I really couldn’t even give you the ‘Groundhog Day’ analogy, to be honest. I still don’t even know what ‘Groundhog Day’ is. Don’t care for it. I control what I can control. I don’t give a damn if the groundhog comes up or not. It’s on me.”
It seems unrealistic to think these Cowboys can win anything of note without drastic defensive improvements. Ten games don’t exactly make for a small sample size. Why would anyone believe that defense is close to turning a corner?
Given how poorly things went a year ago, it’s also difficult to argue that bringing in a new defensive coordinator for the fifth consecutive season is the answer. But something has to change, and it doesn’t feel like a minor tweak will cut it.
Growing pains were to be expected in Christian Parker’s first season running the defense, but the results have fallen well short even of those tempered expectations.
“This is what it is — he’s a young coach that’s in his first year of coordinating, and basically, calling the plays,” said Cowboys owner Jerry Jones when asked after the game about Parker. “So, you would have to say that you would hope you could win games like the last (few) that we’ve lost.
“I’ll weigh his early times. I’ve been with teams that had some pretty good coordinators on defense that ended up winning Super Bowls.”
The 49ers are the NFC favorites to reach the Super Bowl this season. Their defense wasn’t great on Sunday, either, but they’ve found a way to win eight of their past nine games. The Cowboys’ defense makes you wonder if Dallas can get to eight wins by the end of the season.
When leaving the field, Schottenheimer usually walks with the players and coaches back to the locker room, past reporters. He didn’t take that path Sunday.
“I was pretty pissed off, to be honest with you,” he said. “I wanted to get in, collect my thoughts before I talked to the team. At the end of the day, (the Cowboys’ play) wasn’t good enough, so that’s why.
“There’s a lot of emotions. … This is a good football team that we played. They’re the best in the business. I feel confident that we can be in those games, but certainly we’ve got to find ways to win those games. And we didn’t do that. A tale of two halves.”

Broncos quarterback Bo Nix, ahead of his team’s Week 7 trip t
full_text:
Bo Nix threw five touchdowns against one interception in the three games before Denver’s bye. Todd Kirkland / Getty images
The Denver Broncos return from their bye Monday and begin preparations for Sunday’s home game against the Las Vegas Raiders. There are eight games left for Denver ahead of what the team hopes will be a long playoff run, so here are eight thoughts I have on the Broncos as the second half of their season approaches:
Broncos quarterback Bo Nix, ahead of his team’s Week 7 trip to play the Arizona Cardinals, pointed his arm upward at a 45-degree angle, his fingers jutting toward the cloudless Colorado sky.
“My training is going like this,” Nix said, the most important right arm in Denver creating an upward trajectory, “At the end of the day, it’s all about getting better.”
Nix’s comment came after a six-game start to 2026 that invited sharp criticism about the quarterback’s play at the beginning of his third NFL season, the one that could set him up for a major contract extension. The Broncos were 4-2 at that point, but Nix ranked No. 27 out of 33 qualified quarterbacks in expected points added per dropback and No. 32 in yards per attempt, ahead of only Tampa Bay Buccaneers undrafted free agent Jalon Daniels.
Nix appeared too tentative at times, particularly as it related to his willingness to turn up the field and run, a dangerous staple of his first two seasons in Denver. Nix reiterated ahead of that trip to Arizona, for perhaps the 53rd time, that there was nothing physically wrong with the right ankle upon which a surgeon operated twice this offseason. But he allowed that there was a mental component of recovering from those procedures — and the accompanying time off the field they necessitated — that he was still navigating. It was all normal, Nix contended, and part of a process that he believed would have him playing at his best by the time the Broncos entered the most important stretch of their season.
About a month later, Nix appears to be well along that path to his optimal quarterbacking self. He ranked No. 4 in EPA per dropback in the three weeks before Denver’s bye. He threw five touchdowns against one interception in that span and saw his yards per attempt leap from 5.1 to 6.9. He ran for nearly twice as many yards on his glorious, 62-yard touchdown burst against the Cardinals in Week 7 as he had in the previous six games.
Yes, a relenting schedule has helped. The Broncos faced a brutal six-game start, full of intimidating defenses and sharp coordinators. The Cardinals and Carolina Panthers are nobody’s idea of the units from Seattle or San Francisco. But there’s an eye-test component to this, too. Nix appeared far more comfortable in the three weeks preceding the bye. You could see that arrow he painted with his arm climbing up. That puts him in a strong spot as the Broncos return to action this week. Time will tell whether he can maintain that progress.
The outside world loudly suggested in the days leading to the NFL trade deadline that Denver needed to add a running back. It made sense. There appeared to be a number of available targets — from Indianapolis Colts star Jonathan Taylor to secondary options such as Breece Hall of the New York Jets — and the Broncos ranked No. 28 in the NFL in running back yards per rush (3.6). J.K. Dobbins, re-signed in the offseason on a contract that included $8 million in guarantees, was mired in the slowest start to a season in an NFL career that began in 2020.
Yet the Broncos have faith in their backfield, a confidence illustrated by their decision not to add to the position before the deadline. That’s not to say, of course, that Denver didn’t evaluate that market, but Broncos coach Sean Payton has continually voiced confidence in a backfield that has been led in snaps and carries the past three weeks by rookie Jonah Coleman. Dobbins has had fewer than eight carries in each of the past three games, and his four carries against the Panthers in Week 9 were his fewest in any game since his rookie year
Those numbers tell a clear story: The Broncos believe Coleman is their best chance right now at creating sustained success on the ground, and second-year player RJ Harvey figures to reclaim his role as the position’s top pass-catching weapon and change-of-pace threat when he returns from injured reserve, which can happen as soon as Week 13 against the Miami Dolphins.
Payton has been adamant that Dobbins nonetheless remains an important part of the equation. The Broncos could also get Tyler Badie back from IR in the coming weeks. They believe they have enough in the backfield going forward.
Payton during the bye week was blunt in his assessment as to why Denver struggled to run the ball against a Panthers team that hadn’t exactly been stout in that department entering the game.
“I’m watching the cutups of the game we just played,” the coach said during an interview with Fox Sports host Colin Cowherd, “and we didn’t block them very well. I’m just being honest. That has to improve.”
Payton said after the 26-21 victory in Carolina that it had taken time for the Broncos to adjust to the increased rate of odd fronts the Panthers used in their first game since the dismissal of defensive coordinator Ejiro Evero. Payton’s dive into the film, though, left him frustrated with the performance of the offensive line.
He then hinted that changes would be considered.
“We’ve got plenty of depth in the offensive line,” Payton said. “During this bye, we are going to look at all those little things closely.”
The assessment was open-ended enough to suggest the changes Denver makes could be to the specific run looks in the game plan, the blocks the team is calling or the players the Broncos are double-teaming. They could also be considering personnel changes to a starting five that has been on the field together, by and large, for the past three seasons.
Alex Palczewski, who signed a two-year extension this offseason, played half of last season at left guard after Ben Powers went down with a biceps injury. Palczewski also has experience at right tackle, where Mike McGlinchey has been the starter since 2023. If the Broncos are going to use their depth, Palczewski would likely be the first player who gets a chance to slot into the starting lineup.
Forget the four catches for 56 yards. Forget the 26-yard touchdown catch up the seam that proved to be the winning score. The larger takeaway from Pat Bryant’s return to the lineup against the Panthers after a four-game IR stint was that the second-year receiver makes Denver’s offense feel more capable and dangerous.
When isolating the five games the Broncos have played with Bryant on the field, the 2025 third-round pick ranks No. 2 in receptions (13) behind Jaylen Waddle and No. 2 in yards per catch (14.5) behind Troy Franklin. He is also the position’s leader this season in yards after catch per reception (5.8), and that brings an element that has allowed Nix to access the middle of the field on a number of route combinations when Bryant is involved.
Bryant was the standout of training camp for the Broncos’ offense, and he has continued to grow into a larger part of the attack with every game he plays. The big question is whether the Broncos can keep him on the field. He missed time at the end of last season because of concussions and missed the four games this season due to an ankle injury. He plays a physical style that makes him a versatile threat because of his ability to mix it up in the run game — thus helping Payton disguise his calls.
The flip side is that style has also made Bryant susceptible to big hits. The Broncos don’t want the young receiver to change the way he plays. His aggressiveness, physicality and fearlessness are what make him a valuable piece of Denver’s offense. It is also critical that the Broncos do what they can to ensure they have a healthy Bryant when the playoffs arrive.

full_text:
Blake Corum had the second 100-yard rushing game of his career in the Rams' win over the Cardinals. Mike Christy / Getty Images
GLENDALE, Ariz. — The Los Angeles Rams were stuck in a deja vu moment Sunday against the Arizona Cardinals, running into brick walls, throwing too much and falling behind.
And then everything changed. Because this team has changed ever since it hit rock bottom.
In classic Rams fashion, a late-half drive woke up something inside, even down to a third-string center and a third-string left guard, because they did what they couldn’t do the last time they faced these Cardinals and fell to 2-4.
They returned to the run earlier and stuck with it, pounding Blake Corum up the middle, with veteran linemen and tight ends straining for blocks and Corum using his trademark vision, cuts and speed to rip off chunk gains until the ball finally crossed the end zone.
One drive sprung the leak from which everything else flowed. Kam Kinchens intercepted a Carson Beck pass for an explosive return, the Rams dialed up a tunnel screen for a 22-yard touchdown to Xavier Smith and they poured it on from there to win 34-6 over the Cardinals for a fourth straight victory to get to 6-4.
“This is who we are,” right guard Kevin Dotson said earlier in the week of the run game.
Who they are now is not who they were the last time around.
Just one month ago, this Cardinals team came into SoFi Stadium and delivered the most humbling of defeats by playing keep-away, running with volume, blitzing Matthew Stafford into happy-feet plays and winning the special teams battle. An 18-16 loss had coach Sean McVay fuming after the game.
“We won’t win a game,” McVay said that day, “until we figure out how to not beat ourselves.”
The real tension was not that the Rams were 2-4. After all, they’ve started like this twice in the past three years under McVay and climbed out for 10-win seasons.
It was that their best players were dropping like flies, with Davante Adams, Poona Ford and Kobie Turner going on injured reserve. It was that they had a team with 11 captains and no identity on either side of the ball.
Everyone knew what this Rams team was supposed to be entering the season. But they hadn’t figured out who they needed to be through adversity and injuries.
“We had to look ourselves in the mirror: Who are we? What are we doing?” linebacker Omar Speights said. “We didn’t start the season how we expected to start. The Cardinals game and all of the other games and how they went, that whole first half of the season was a wake-up call.
“From that point on, not even just on defense, whether it was the way we were practicing or in meetings, everybody was just intentional, detailed and focused.”
The injuries are still crippling this team’s ceiling in some ways, notably in the passing game without Adams or Puka Nacua. But what the Rams have found on offense and defense is an identity.
On offense, it’s about running at high volume in a balanced rotation of Kyren Williams and Corum. The numbers keep bearing out the success in complementary ways, with Williams leading the NFL for a second straight year in rushing success, as defined by the yards expected to be gained by each down and distance; and Corum finding more yards than the Rams have blocked with his cuts and decisiveness, which have opened up four straight performances with at least 50 yards, 5.3 yards per carry and a rushing touchdown.
“There’s an identity,” McVay said of the run game. “We’ve had to do that, and today was really cool to be able to close the game out that way.”
The volume and efficiency in the run game have limited the risks that have led Stafford to 10 interceptions this season, opened the play-action game for easier one-on-one matchups for tertiary receiving options, diversified the personnel groupings, and brought the confidence and nasty demeanor out of an experienced offensive line that can now make an imprint.
On Sunday, that happened even with the Rams down to a third-string center and left guard.
“It was a game of, ‘We’re just going to beat you,'” Dotson said. “‘Do what you can. We’re not changing our play. You know what’s coming. Do it again. Do it again. We might add something in there just to keep you honest, but we’re going to do the same thing again.'”
What McVay is doing now is tailoring play calls and designs to the specific strengths of his individual pieces rather than forcing square pegs into round holes. That allowed a speedy Smith to slip under a screen against a blitz to take the ball 22 yards for a score and for Konata Mumpfield to zip up the sideline against man defense in a favorable matchup for 44 yards and for Tutu Atwell to win on a flag route against a backup nickel cornerback for 31 yards.
For as maligned and quiet as the Rams’ receiving room has been lately outside of Nacua, Sunday featured four different wideouts who each had a catch of 20 yards or more.
On defense, the identity comes in stopping the run as a unit to allow the superstar offseason additions to shine in pressurized situations. The Rams have found a way to do that over the past month even after losing Ford at nose tackle for the season, as they’ve held the past four opponents to an average of 51.5 rushing yards per game.
And when the Rams can take a lead, stop the run on early downs and force teams to throw, the monsters come out. Last week, Myles Garrett put on a show with three sacks and a forced fumble. This week, he didn’t factor into the box score while double-teamed and limited with his healing knee, but it opened the door for Aaron Donald to get his first 1.5 sacks of the season.
And with Trent McDuffie shutting down a team’s primary option — on Sunday, that was Cardinals tight end Trey McBride — quarterbacks are being pressured and forced to throw to defenders sitting and waiting to make plays, which led to interceptions from Kinchens and Wesley Bailey.
“When you get guys like Myles Garrett and Donald, you know where the protections are going to go, so we try to manipulate things,” safety and captain Quentin Lake said. “And when you have a guy like Trent McDuffie back there who can shut down one side of the field, and you can roll over the coverage because you know he’s going to dominate his one-on-one matchup. It allows us on defense to gain the numbers back and do a lot of different things that are great — do a lot of different stunts and do a lot of different coverages, knowing we have the personnel.”
Perhaps no stat defines who the Rams have become over the past month more than this: They have rushed for 654 yards and allowed 206 rushing yards.
Now, the model is enough to beat teams like the Las Vegas Raiders, Washington Commanders, Los Angeles Chargers and Cardinals, who combine for a 10-26-1 record. The rest of their opponents are a combined 34-23. That is where this team must return players such as Adams, Turner, Terrance Ferguson and eventually Nacua to evolve beyond winning on the ground.
But by then, the Rams could be looking for evolution rather than identity. Like with returning Garrett and McDuffie on defense, the offense could evolve from a high floor to scratching at a higher ceiling.
They’re not out of the woods and won’t be in any week this season. But unlike that dreadful day against the Cardinals a month ago, this is no longer a team wondering who it is.

summary:

The Athletic has live coverage of NFL Week 10 news and reactions .
If the first three quarters of the Minnesota Vikings’ 30-10 victory at Green Bay didn’t convince the purple masses that acquiring Kirk Cousins was the answer to their trade-deadline prayers, consider what happened early in the fourth.
Cousins completed passes to star receiver Justin Jefferson on five consec
full_text:
Kirk Cousins’ second stint with Minnesota is off to a great start, renewing the Vikings’ hope. Todd Rosenberg / Getty Images
The Athletic has live coverage of NFL Week 10 news and reactions .
If the first three quarters of the Minnesota Vikings’ 30-10 victory at Green Bay didn’t convince the purple masses that acquiring Kirk Cousins was the answer to their trade-deadline prayers, consider what happened early in the fourth.
Cousins completed passes to star receiver Justin Jefferson on five consecutive plays. Then, after a handoff, Cousins targeted Jefferson for yet another completion.
“I mean, that is just quality ball right there,” a coach from another team said. “Cousins wears the guy out. Jefferson is huffing and puffing. The kid takes himself out of the game. It’s like he had fallen out of shape because for two months, he’s been watching (Kyler) Murray scramble and (Carson Wentz) bounce it off the ground 5 yards in front of him. It’s funny, but it’s true.”
The Pick Six column for Week 10 ranks the NFL’s in-season trades by the immediate returns and the ripple effects, starting with the Vikings’ move to reunite Cousins with a team and fanbase that appreciates him like never before, even though Minnesota won Sunday the way it has won all season: by dominating on defense and special teams.
• Cousins and the top trade impacts • Tomlin Paradox remains for Steelers? • Mendoza, Beck thrown to the wolves? • Justin Herbert, meet Boomer Esiason • The Rams’ looming dilemma at WR • Two-minute drill: Browns beat Texans (and Vegas)
The Packers faced a choice after Cousins threw incomplete to Jefferson on third-and-8 from the Green Bay 23-yard line on Minnesota’s third drive. They could accept a 15-yard face mask penalty, betting their defense could force a longer field goal attempt by stopping Cousins on third-and-23. Or they could decline the penalty, conceding a 41-yard attempt.
Packers head coach Matt LaFleur had a rough day on offense, letting the play clock run while sticking with a deep passing game. That gave Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores time to configure his personnel before the snap, and time to disrupt the deep passing game. Jordan Love took eight sacks, giving him 12 in two games against the Vikings and 13 in eight against everyone else.
Despite all that, LaFleur had reason for accepting the face mask penalty on the Vikings’ third drive. His defense had ranked among the NFL’s best in recent weeks. Cousins had already taken a 9-yard sack.
Who could have known Cousins would find receiver Myles Price up the seam for a 38-yard touchdown? It was the first time in 50 career attempts that Cousins threw a scoring pass on third-and-20 or longer. It was exactly what the Vikings needed after suffering through one of the worst offensive performances in franchise history just six days prior.
“That ball he threw on that third-and-23, that’s as good of a Tier 1 throw as you will see in the NFL all year,” the coach said. “There is only one place he can put the ball, but he actually does one better. He back-shoulders it, twisting the receiver to keep him away from the corner.
“You have to be not afraid to make that throw — and remember, he spent two days game-planning for Seattle (while with the Raiders), flew in Tuesday night and had to switch gears.”
Cousins’ other touchdown was a work of art: a fake screen to his left, a spinning fake screen to his right and a very real timing strike over the middle to tight end Gavin Bartholomew.
“That is just pure veteran quarterback with a veteran play caller (head coach Kevin O’Connell) saying, ‘I see the game like you do,'” another coach said. “Now, Kirk tries throwing the thing when he gets sacked, and he gets saved from an interception by replay because his knee was barely down. And he hesitates against the rush, and can’t get the ball up and down when there is a half safety there ( resulting in an interception ).”
The Vikings’ offense wasn’t great Sunday (-1.5 EPA), but it was good enough to win big on the road with a dominating day from the defense (+13.7 EPA) and special teams (+7.9). Minnesota got even bigger contributions from those two phases against Tampa Bay in Week 3 but won that game by only a touchdown, 23-16.
Functional quarterback play gives the Vikings an opportunity to more accurately evaluate their roster and coaching staff, including O’Connell, whose reputation for maximizing quarterbacks has taken a hit through recent failures.
“He’s a quarterback whisperer, so why can’t he get Wentz to play better?” the coach asked rhetorically. “Because the guy is never playing good. Never.”
Functional quarterback play also makes the idea of this defense — clearly the best of Flores’ already impressive tenure — carrying the Vikings on a deep playoff run just a little bit more plausible.
“I’ve been watching the game for 25 years, and I get a headache watching those guys line up,” another coach said of the Vikings. “I get nervous watching on TV. My God, who’s coming? What are they doing? They are up in the A-gaps, then they are out, then they are back in the A-gaps, then the linebackers and DBs change positions, then (Andrew) Van Ginkel changes what foot is up in his stance multiple times . It’s ridiculous.”
The ripple effects of the Cousins trade are also being felt in Las Vegas, where Fernando Mendoza made his first start Sunday, struggling against Seattle’s defense in a 21-13 defeat (more on that in a bit).
There’s no break for Cousins and the Vikings, who travel to Mexico City to face the 49ers and their top-ranked offense in Week 11 as the race for the NFC’s top seed heats up. In the meantime, Minnesota fans can enjoy what is, so far, the most impactful trade of the season.
Seven other trades moving the needle:
• DT Jeffery Simmons from the Titans to the Bears: Simmons had 10 tackles, including two sacks and an additional tackle for loss, while playing 121 snaps in his first two games with the Bears. His downfield tackle in a 27-24 victory over Tampa Bay showcased an all-out playing style few men his size can match. It’s the type of move that elevates contenders.
• QB J.J. McCarthy from the Vikings to the Giants: No one should suggest the Giants have found their long-term starter, but after losing Jaxson Dart to a season-ending injury in Week 2, their chances of winning the NFC East appear higher with McCarthy than they were with Jameis Winston.
The Giants are 2-1 in McCarthy’s three starts and have a higher rate of explosive plays with him (15.1 percent) than with Dart (10.7) or Winston (8.5). That’s good value for a fifth-round pick, and great value if McCarthy revives his career over the season’s second half.
• S Amani Hooker from the Titans to the Bills: Hooker played all 73 defensive snaps in his Bills debut, a 31-12 victory over the Jets. He made seven tackles, including five short of the first-down marker, and broke up a pass while filling an obvious need in Buffalo.
• S Jessie Bates III from the Falcons to the Jaguars: Bates hasn’t even played for the Jaguars yet, but Atlanta seemed to miss him Sunday. The Chiefs’ Patrick Mahomes, who had completed zero passes on throws traveling at least 20 yards downfield over the previous four games, connected on four of them for 150 yards and three touchdowns Sunday.
“Sometimes those new guys that get in charge of teams can’t wait to collect draft picks and can’t wait to get their own people,” an exec said of the Falcons’ decision to move on from Bates. “It sounds like a great idea, but good luck finding Jessie Bates in the second or third round next year. If you do find him, it’s gonna take him a couple years, so you take a big step back.”
• WR Keenan Allen from the Colts to the 49ers: Allen made two third-down conversions against Dallas in his 49ers debut, catching five passes for 61 yards overall, both most among Niners wide receivers, on only 31 snaps (21 routes).
“Keenan is very well-rounded,” another exec said. “He can work the middle of the field.…

title: Remember those calls to bench Drake Maye? Now he's injured and Patriots need him badly The more we see of the Pats, the clearer it becomes that Maye was never really the big problem for what's currently a train wreck of a team. Steve Buckley 14

full_text:
Drake Maye is sacked by the Lions' Aidan Hutchinson early in the Patriots' 35-10 loss in Munich. Lennart Preiss / Associated Press
The Athletic has live coverage of NFL Week 10 news and reactions .
There was a time earlier this season when it was all the rage for Drake Maye supporters to put it out there that the third-year New England Patriots quarterback is still “on the ascendancy.”
Forget those three fourth-quarter interceptions in New England’s season-opening loss to the Seattle Seahawks, including an ill-advised toss into the end zone with 21 seconds remaining. Or the key fumble in the early stages of New England’s 35-6 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars, or the two interceptions that came later in that debacle. He’s only 24. Still growing as an NFL quarterback.
It’s just that Maye’s critics, you’ll remember, sailed right past all that by slamming down a gavel and ruling that the kid is not an “elite” quarterback, and never will be.
As is often the case, the truth is somewhere in the middle, with wild and unpredictable swings. Which brings us to the Patriots’ humiliating 35-10 loss to the Detroit Lions on Sunday in Munich, Germany. If you include their 45-27 loss to the Green Bay Packers on Nov. 8 at Gillette Stadium, this is the second straight effort by the Patriots in which that old line about how “the score doesn’t indicate how bad it was” has been dusted off and put into service. But with a twist: This time, the Patriots were reduced to soldiering on with Tommy DeVito as their quarterback. That’s because Maye never made it out of New England’s game-opening possession after suffering a right ankle injury while being sacked by the Lions’ Aidan Hutchinson. A team source confirmed to The Athletic ’s Chad Graff on Monday that Maye is expected to miss extended time with the injury .
While it’s hard to gather bipartisan support on anything these days, be it in politicking or playmaking, we can all agree that Sunday’s loss to the Lions shows the Patriots to be a train wreck of a football program when Maye isn’t behind center. OK, so even with Maye, they’ve struggled some. Let’s be grown-ups about this: We’ve seen Maye make great plays, even if we’ve seen too many occasions when he developed a hero complex and tried to make a great play that simply isn’t there. His throw into the end zone in the last seconds of the Seattle game, intercepted by Josh Jobe, is a very good example of a very bad decision.
But the more we see of this season, the clearer it becomes that Maye was never really the problem. Oh, he may have been a problem here and there, but never to the degree that he needed to be benched. You do remember when that was a thing, right? And it wasn’t just Tony from Dorchester calling in to the talk shows. No less an expert than Fox talking head Terry Bradshaw, a Hall of Fame quarterback with four Super Bowl rings, argued that benching Maye would help the kid regain his confidence.
No disrespect to DeVito, who did the best he could against the surging Lions under the circumstances (12-for-24 for 81 yards, four sacks and his first touchdown pass as a Patriot), but he wasn’t going to lead the Patriots to victory. Nor was Maye likely to win this game had he remained in the fray, except that at least he has a track record of doing more with less. He’s been doing it all season.
The Patriots have a banged-up running game, so Maye scrambles. Injuries have forced the Patriots to assemble a makeshift offensive line, which puts Maye in harm’s way. As for the collection of receivers the Patriots assembled for this season, one of them, A.J. Brown, has appeared in just four games. Sunday’s showcase game against the Lions was one of those, but he exited in the third quarter with a hamstring injury after making two receptions for 27 yards.
It helps that the Patriots have a bye week coming up. After that, they travel to Los Angeles to play the Chargers, who take an 0-8 record into their Week 10 “Monday Night Football” meeting against the Baltimore Ravens. Pats-Chargers gets a lot more complicated and uncertain if Maye is out.
That’s how dramatically, stunningly, this Patriots season has been knocked off its axis. Where once it was deemed acceptable to ponder a game or two without Maye, now there’s a very real fear that a game or two (or longer) without Maye could derail what’s left of the season.
