full_text:
Patriots quarterback Drake Maye was sacked on the final offensive play of the opening drive against the Lions, left the game and did not return. Doug Benc / Associated Press
In a brutal blow that seems likely to put an end to their path to the playoffs, New England Patriots do-it-all quarterback Drake Maye suffered a serious ankle injury in Sunday’s loss to the Lions in Munich and is expected to miss extended time, a team source confirmed to The Athletic .
Coach Mike Vrabel confirmed on Monday that Maye stayed behind in Germany for further evaluation and will undergo additional testing once he returns to the U.S. to help determine a better timeframe. There’s a chance Maye could miss the rest of the season, however, with the fear he could have suffered a fracture, according to a source, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss Maye’s medical situation.
It’s the latest gut punch in this cursed Patriots season after everything went so well a year ago during their run to the Super Bowl.
Now, they enter the bye week at 5-5. Their quarterback is likely to miss extended time. Their big offseason acquisition, A.J. Brown, has struggled when on the field and has rarely been on it due to three different injuries. And even cornerback Christian Gonzalez, the league’s highest-paid at the position, is routinely getting beat.
Before this injury, Maye had made 43 straight starts as he played in his third NFL season. He had been remarkably durable for a young quarterback who scrambles. But this changes the outlook of the rest of the season.
It leaves the Patriots facing a massive uphill climb to try to salvage a playoff berth, and more likely begins opening up questions about what the offseason will look like, how they can tinker their roster to better help Maye and improve the defense, and how high of a draft pick the Patriots might have in April.
Maye suffered the injury while being sacked by Aidan Hutchinson , who then suffered a serious injury of his own while celebrating the play. Referees determined that the sack didn’t meet the requirements to throw a flag for an improper hip drop tackle.
“I don’t think it was anything intentional,” Vrabel said of the sack that yielded Maye’s injury. “I’m sure that it wasn’t. That’s part of the game.”
The injury turns attention now to Tommy DeVito.
He came to the Patriots in via waivers in August of last year as a third-string option. But he impressed Josh McDaniels and offensive coaches with both the way he ran the scout team and his acumen in meeting rooms.
The Patriots came away from those initial months impressed, and signed DeVito to a two year, $4.4 million contract extension, elevating him to the backup role over Josh Dobbs. They did that with the belief that if DeVito had to step in for a few games, he could steady the ship in an uncertain time.
Well, that time has arrived.
While what the Patriots have said about DeVito behind the scenes is great, his first extended look of the season didn’t go well. Maye suffered his injury on the first drive Sunday and DeVito played the rest of the game. The offense cratered with DeVito in instead of Maye.
DeVito completed half of his 24 passes on Sunday for 81 yards with a touchdown and an interception. The hope is that with the full bye week to prepare, then a full week of practice reps with the starters, DeVito will play better.
“I’m going to continue the process I have been doing up to this point,” DeVito said after Sunday’s game of potentially taking over as the starter. “Something that as a two, as cliche as it sounds, you have to be prepared to be a starter. So just keep doing what I’m doing, keep my head down, and then if something like that were to happen, you would have the reps and practice and the walkthroughs and everything going forward, so just keep on preparing and on to the next.”
Maye’s injury is crushing for an offense that runs totally through him. It’s difficult to imagine — even with their next game against the winless Chargers after an extended break — how this Patriots offense will manage to pick up the pieces without their star quarterback.
Maye’s absence will also put more focus on the running game. The Patriots spent the offseason prioritizing that area. So far this season, it hasn’t worked.
But perhaps with a week off, McDaniels can tweak some of the run game plan and the team can get healthy at important spots. Fullback Reggie Gilliam returned from injury on Sunday, which should help that phase of the game. Rhamondre Stevenson played through a knee injury, but perhaps two weeks off helps him re-gain some explosiveness. Maybe a better run game sets up DeVito for more success as a game managing quarterback.
All of that is the more optimistic view.
But put most bluntly, Maye’s injury is a crushing blow, leaving the Patriots now without their best and most important player.
In a season where it seems like everything that could go wrong has gone wrong, it’s hard to think of more devastating news for the Patriots than this.

title: Eagles thoughts: Howie Roseman's bye week, from trading Jordan Davis to watching Miami-Duke Howie Roseman hugged Miami QB Darian Mensah at Duke-Miami. The Eagles have two first-round picks in 2027. How much should fans read into it? Zach Berman 8
summary:

The Philadelphia Eagles return from their bye week with unavoidable indications of a lost season.
They dealt a team captain at the trade deadline. They waived two veterans days later. They were flexed out of a nationally televised time slot. They are at least 1.5 games behind the next team in an NFC East
full_text:
Eagles general manager Howie Roseman added a 2027 first-round pick and a 2028 second-round pick by trading defensive tackle Jordan Davis to the Jacksonville Jaguars. Eric Hartline / Imagn Images
The Philadelphia Eagles return from their bye week with unavoidable indications of a lost season.
They dealt a team captain at the trade deadline. They waived two veterans days later. They were flexed out of a nationally televised time slot. They are at least 1.5 games behind the next team in an NFC East that would otherwise have been wide open.
The Eagles had an eventful idle week. Here are five Eagles thoughts on some of those events and their ramifications ahead of the back stretch of the schedule.
1. If you told me after the Week 9 loss to the New York Giants that the Eagles would finish the bye week with an extra first- and second-round pick, I would have asked if they traded Jalen Carter.
And if you said no, I would have wondered if they dealt Saquon Barkley and Zack Baun.
The fact that all three are still on the roster, and the Eagles added premium picks, makes it a successful trade deadline — even if dealing Jordan Davis was the Eagles’ only move. ( Cincinnati backing out of the Arnold Ebiketie deal is part of the reason for only one trade.)
The Eagles didn’t deal any expiring contracts. This was likely more indicative of the market than a sign of a delusional team.
Goedert’s contract complicated trade talks. Trading him would have triggered a full $18.3 million cap hit in 2027, raising the required compensation. The Eagles can instead split that charge over two years if he leaves via free agency.
I was surprised they didn’t move Riq Woolen. This might also be me inflating Woolen’s value compared to how the league apparently values him. The Eagles didn’t get swept off their feet by Woolen offers any more than the Seattle Seahawks at last year’s trade deadline. Woolen could have been valuable for a contender, but it’s worth remembering he’s been available via trade before. He signed a one-year contract with the Eagles when the free-agent market wasn’t as robust as he’d hoped.
The Davis trade was made, in part, because of Moro Ojomo’s value to the team. Trading Davis gave the Eagles more room to re-sign Ojomo (more on this below).
Getting a sixth-round pick from the Bengals for Ebiketie (plus a more favorable compensatory pick formula) would have been a boon. Understandably, they were miffed that the Bengals backed out. The Eagles started to move on from players with expiring contracts via the waiver wire later in the week. That shows there wasn’t much interest on the trade market.
I didn’t expect the Eagles to move Barkley and Baun, who are in line to be major contributors in 2027. The roster needs to improve if the Eagles expect to contend next year. Two first-round picks — including one likely to land in the top 10 — will help.
That was the headline of the bye week for the Eagles. It doesn’t change the fact that they’re 2-7. They must own that record. If they capitalize on these picks, it could help avoid 2-7 in the future.
2. The Eagles surrendered a valuable player and locker room figure in Davis. He helped bring the Eagles a championship, earned a lucrative contract extension, and was voted team captain. But Davis’ play this year (and how he’s been used) never matched that three-year, $78 million deal.
Davis was paid to be a disruptive pass rusher, not just a space-eating nose tackle. That hasn’t been the case this season. Davis has played only 10.9 percent of obvious passing downs this season, a decline from 20.5 percent last season. The Eagles needed an increase — not a decrease — to justify an extension at $26 million per year. That’s not the market rate for a run stuffer.
The tools have long tantalized, and perhaps the Jaguars use Davis as a three-down player, helping fortify the front of a Super Bowl contender. I respect that Jacksonville is going for it — opportunity is not a lengthy visitor, as the expression goes — but Davis’ usage in Philadelphia this season was reason alone to make him expendable. To get a massive return on top of it made the trade a no-brainer. It also made Ojomo a priority …
3. … Reports that the Eagles wouldn’t move Ojomo made little sense while both Davis and Carter were on the roster. It would have been difficult for the Eagles to keep three defensive tackles on big-money deals. This trade opens up a runway for Howie Roseman to re-sign Ojomo, who’s blossomed into a promising interior pass rusher.
Ojomo hasn’t shown it with sacks this season — and the sacks need to come — but the advanced pass-rushing data is encouraging. He leads the Eagles with 16 hurries and is tied for a team-high with 21 pressures. His pressure rate of 9.6 percent is down from 11.6 percent last season and 12.2 percent in 2024, but it’s still a strong rate for an interior rusher. His pressure rate and quarterback hit rate of 2.3 percent are both better than Carter and Davis.
He also has the type of football character and work ethic worthy of an investment, and would fit on even fronts if the Eagles changed defensive schemes.
The Eagles lost a respected locker-room figure with Davis’ departure, but I’d feel comfortable entrusting Ojomo with a bigger presence. He’s already called “Coach Mo” among the defensive linemen. The Eagles will have to pay a high price to keep him. It’s the type of move Roseman should feel comfortable making.
It might even take off some of the sting of losing Milton Williams two years ago.
4. The Eagles let go of two reserves who didn’t fit into their 2027 plans when they waived wide receiver Hollywood Brown and offensive tackle Fred Johnson on Friday. These transactions open roster spots and opportunities for other players.
With DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks set to return, Brown’s role was minimal. He never found his place after being signed, and Darius Cooper passed him on the depth chart.
Johnson has been the Eagles’ top reserve tackle since Lane Johnson’s retirement. But Markel Bell beat him out during the summer, and the Eagles could be better served evaluating practice squad offensive tackle Kiran Amegadjie (a 2024 third-round pick) or scouring practice squads elsewhere for developmental players.
I wonder if this is just the beginning of these types of moves. Jonathan Jones, Elijah Moore and Kenny Moore fit the profile of aging players unlikely to be part of the 2027 core. At 2-7, the Eagles must be realistic about this season. Friday’s moves indicate they already are.
5. The Eagles are on pace to land a top-10 pick. They also have a late first-round pick from the Davis trade. Most times when a team drafts in the top 10 for the first time in a few years, the quarterback conversation is unavoidable. Plenty of time remains for those debates.
Speculation grew louder when footage circulated Saturday of Roseman at the Miami-Duke game, embracing Hurricanes quarterback Darian Mensah ( No. 27 on Dane Brugler’s midseason draft rankings ). The thought was that Roseman spent his bye week scouting quarterbacks.
Philadelphia Eagles GM Howie Roseman a little pregame love for Canes QB Darian Mensah @WPLGLocal10 pic.twitter.com/QkhiiNuepN
— Kacy Hintz (@KacyHintz) November 14, 2026
This is where context is necessary. Roseman’s son goes to Duke and works with the Blue Devils’ football program. (Jaguars pass rusher Wesley Williams, who played at Duke, credited the younger Roseman for helping his development last season.) That should be understood before anyone gets too carried away.
Of course, the timing is convenient — any general manager would benefit from watching this year’s loaded Hurricanes roster — but I didn’t interpret this as intentional quarterback scouting. In fact, Brugler’s rankings are instructive. His top 10 includes two quarterbacks (Oklahoma State’s Drew Mestermaker at No. 4 and Notre Dame’s CJ Carr at No. 10), two edge rushers and one offensive tackle. If I had to guess today, I’d watch the line of scrimmage…

full_text:
Veteran quarterback Aaron Rodgers went 15-of-29 for 143 yards and a pair of touchdowns, most of that in garbage time, in Sunday's loss to the Bengals. Jeff Dean / Getty Images
CINCINNATI — The white rally towels twirled inside Paycor Stadium on Sunday night as a chant broke out among the fans. First, it was a small, almost unrecognizable smattering of cheers after Joe Burrow’s first touchdown pass to tight end Drew Sample. The roars grew when Burrow found running back Chase Brown in the end zone. By the time Burrow had tossed his third TD of the first half to build a three-score lead, the whiteout crowd was at full volume.
Burrow sure looked like it during a dominant 38-18 win over the Pittsburgh Steelers in which he racked up 409 passing yards and threw four touchdowns. Any team that steps into a stadium with a quarterback of this caliber better have one of two things: elite defensive backs to help suppress the scoring or dynamic offensive playmakers to stand toe-to-toe in a shootout. Pittsburgh is missing both parts of that equation.
If the last four games showed the Steelers’ strength in the trenches, the Bengals’ high-flying offense exposed Pittsburgh’s roster weaknesses that went unaddressed at Tuesday’s trade deadline. The Bengals (7-2) now sit alone atop the AFC North. Given Cincinnati’s soft second-half schedule, Pittsburgh could be looking up the rest of the season.
“We did not execute at a good enough level to win,” Steelers defensive tackle Cameron Heyward said. “Got to own it. It’s one game. I tip my cap to them. They did a really good job today. But man, we got our ass kicked today.”
To beat an MVP candidate at QB who is surrounded by an embarrassment of offensive riches takes outstanding personnel. Recognizing the unique challenge presented by the Bengals’ two-headed receiving monster of Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins, the Steelers drafted Joey Porter Jr. in 2023 specifically with this matchup in mind. Pittsburgh has not often missed the corner, who was dealt to the Dallas Cowboys amid a messy contract dispute. Sunday, Burrow often picked on Porter’s replacement: Asante Samuel Jr.
The Steelers’ 5-foot-10 defensive back allowed four catches on six targets in the first half alone. (Samuel also got away with what looked like a hold in the end zone and committed a costly defensive pass interference penalty on a deep shot to Chase). The Steelers pivoted to rookie Daylen Everette for part of the second half. When Samuel re-entered, Burrow went after him again and connected with Chase for a 43-yard reception. By the time it was over, Chase’s fingerprints were all over the game with 11 catches for 231 yards.
From a game-planning perspective, the Steelers came out with an aggressive approach with hopes of pressuring Burrow. The QB had the answers all night. He identified the blitzes early and got the ball out of his hand quickly to nullify the pass rush. In many cases, Burrow got to his checkdown. He connected with Brown eight times, including for two touchdowns, and found Samaje Perine for another four catches and 25 yards.
The Bengals’ improved offensive line also used seven-man protections to keep T.J. Watt and company from wrecking the game. As a result, Pittsburgh recorded only nine pressures, according to Pro Football Focus, and sacked Burrow once. Again, this underscores one of the issues with the way the defense is built. Rush and coverage have to work together in the NFL. Without the quality defensive backs to play man coverage, the Steelers have been almost forced into a zone-centric philosophy. Even when the secondary stood up, Burrow had far too much time to pick apart the defense or find escape lanes through the A and B gaps.
“They were just rolling,” inside linebacker Patrick Queen said. “We never stopped the bleeding.”
Meanwhile, on offense, the Steelers’ inability to jump-start a drive led to a massive disparity in time of possession, plays and yards. By the end of the first half, Burrow had thrown for more than 300 yards and three touchdowns, and the Steelers had produced just 40 total yards of offense.
Though Pittsburgh built an identity on the ground during its four-game winning streak (one that will be tested after starting left guard Mason McCormick sustained a serious ankle injury), the passing game continues to underwhelm. Beating press man coverage, in particular, has been Pittsburgh’s biggest glaring weakness, especially without Michael Pittman Jr. for the fifth game and Roman Wilson for the fourth game.
“They played a lot of man coverage,” Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers said. “We didn’t make them pay — at all.”
The Steelers tried to move DK Metcalf around the formation and into the slot to create advantageous matchups. Rodgers often looked for the Steelers’ WR1. Almost nothing worked until it was too late. The Steelers picked up just one first down over their first three series combined. Rodgers misfired on his first eight passes and didn’t complete a pass until less than five minutes remained in the first half. The veteran QB ended the day 15-of-29 for 143 yards and a pair of touchdowns, most of that in garbage time.
“We kind of shot ourselves in the foot with a couple plays,” Rodgers said. “Couldn’t get going. Didn’t hit any passes. … We just couldn’t get anything going on offense for a long time.”
The Steelers still sit squarely in playoff position. Over the stretch run, they’ll play just two teams with winning records. Plenty of winnable games remain, and the Steelers can continue to rely on their running game and defensive front seven to take care of business against subpar competition.
In that way, this isn’t the type of setback that should cause concern about the Steelers’ chances of making it into the playoffs. But Sunday’s result in a measuring-stick moment revealed cracks in the roster that are likely to be exposed again when Pittsburgh sees high-level quarterback play like the Buffalo Bills’ Josh Allen or the Jacksonville Jaguars’ Trevor Lawrence or a suffocating defense like that of the Denver Broncos. Yes, the Steelers can make the playoffs. But after the way this game unfolded, it’s fair to wonder whether we’ll see a similar outcome when the competition tests the weak links in the roster.
“The biggest thing is you come back to work, and you understand who you are as a person, who you are as a team, who you are as a defense,” Queen said. “Who are we going to be? Are we going to come back to work, get better, understand where we messed up? Or are we just going to let it snowball?”

full_text:
Jaxon Smith-Njigba had a season-high 171 yards receiving Sunday. John Locher / Imagn Images
LAS VEGAS — For the second time in three weeks, Jaxon Smith-Njigba disagreed with a pass interference penalty that negated a touchdown for the NFL’s leading receiver.
Smith-Njigba was plenty ticked and subsequently entered halftime of Sunday’s game against the Las Vegas Raiders with only one catch for 11 yards. The Seattle Seahawks trailed 10-7 going into the third quarter, too, and with a 1-4 record in the five games this year when they were behind at the break.
Midway through the third quarter, Smith-Njigba slipped on Allegiant Stadium’s grass while running a short route from the slot on a third-down play. Instead of the officials, this time it was the playing surface coming in between Smith-Njigba and quarterback Drew Lock.
Smith-Njigba rose to his feet, made a beeline downfield and hauled in a bomb from Lock before racing to the end zone for a 71-yard touchdown as part of a 171-yard performance in Seattle’s 21-13 win .
“Got my eyes back on Drew,” Smith-Njigba said. “Drew, he’s doing whatever back there. Rolls out … his eyes are always downfield trying to make a play.”
The moment was one of many that embodied an odd afternoon for the Seahawks on the eve of their bye week. Perhaps none did a better job of that than Tory Horton and his batted kickoff in the waning moments .
With 2:04 to play and Seattle clinging to a one-score lead, Horton kept Matt Gay’s kickoff from going out of bounds. Rashid Shaheed picked up the loose ball to put the two-minute warning in motion.
Essentially, the Raiders lost a timeout, and Seattle ran out the clock more easily.
“I knew they were going to try to kick it out, so I just tried to make an athletic play to jump up and try to keep it in play and kind of field it,” Horton said. “I wish I caught it with one hand, but that’s a pretty hard catch to do with the ball like that.
“I was so happy that (Rashid) recognized the ball was in play and picked it up after I told him, and just happy that we got it under two minutes.”
Coach Mike Macdonald appreciated Horton’s heads-up play, but he could have done without some of Seattle’s gaffes.
Lock, who played turnover-free football in his first three games filling in for injured starter Sam Darnold, coughed up the ball on Seattle’s second offensive play.
While being sacked by Folorunso Fatukasi and Taron Johnson, Lock tried to shovel the ball for an incomplete pass. However, it was ruled a fumble. Las Vegas recovered and took a 7-0 lead on a 10-yard scramble by rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza, who made his first career NFL start.
Then, with 12:17 remaining in the fourth quarter and the Seahawks on the precipice of taking an 18-point lead, Lock fumbled again at the Raiders’ 12-yard line when his hand unexpectedly hit running back Zach Charbonnet during a pass attempt, jarring it loose for a Las Vegas recovery.
Otherwise, Lock was brilliant, completing 14 of 17 passes for a season-high 240 yards and two touchdown passes.
In addition to his heave to Smith-Njigba, Lock unleashed his inner Fran Tarkenton for Seattle’s first touchdown. On third-and-15 at the Las Vegas 34, Lock dropped back, scrambled left, avoided a sack, planted his left foot just shy of the line of scrimmage and — while falling out of bounds — uncorked a textbook throw to Cooper Kupp in the back of the Raiders’ end zone.
“I call him ‘The Locksmith,’” cornerback Devon Witherspoon said of Lock, “because it seems like he’s got all the answers to the damn coverages.”
Though Lock did his best impression of Pablo Sanchez from the Backyard Football video game, Seattle’s defensive dominance in the second half more than compensated for a sluggish opening 30 minutes.
Las Vegas out-possessed the Seahawks 19:15 to 10:45 in the first half, then struggled mightily the rest of the way. The Raiders went three-and-out on five of their six second-half drives and mustered just 27 yards of total offense.
“That’s who we are,” edge rusher Derick Hall, who had one of Seattle’s six sacks of Mendoza, said. “That’s what we’re about: coming in, making adjustments, really just trying to go out and play our style of ball.”
That entailed the Seahawks running the ball twice as frequently as they passed it, while milking precious second-half minutes off the clock. In his third game back from tearing his ACL, Charbonnet logged a season-high 20 carries for 94 yards, and rookie Jadarian Price chipped in nine rushes for 36 yards and a touchdown.
Charbonnet, at 6 feet 1, 220 pounds, is known more for his power than pace and proved difficult to bring down in the open field. He continues to show few, if any, signs that he’s limited by his knee injury.
“I think it’s a lot of training I put in,” Charbonnet said. “I put in a lot of hours; even two days after the Super Bowl, I got straight to work. So, it’s just the work paying off.”
Seattle’s rushing success came at a price, though. Right tackle Abe Lucas went down in the second quarter with an ankle injury, making him the third of five projected starters on the Seahawks’ offensive line to go down over the last month. Left tackle Charles Cross (ankle) and left guard Quenton Nelson (knee) were ruled out before Sunday.
The timing of Seattle’s bye couldn’t be more convenient. A whopping 15 players were listed on the latest injury report, including linchpins like defensive lineman Leonard Williams. Lock has continued to play through injuries to his right (throwing) elbow and oblique, and he was limited to attempting passes only during Thursday’s practice for a second consecutive week.
Standout nickelback Nick Emmanwori told The Athletic that he reaggravated a shoulder injury from a few weeks ago on a hit of Mendoza in the second half, which led to briefly leaving the game. The impending time off will be welcomed by Emmanwori, who also missed Seattle’s season opener while recovering from offseason ankle surgery.
“We got the Niners after the bye,” Emmanwori said. “So, big matchup, important that we get a whole week off. Our bodies will be fully rested for that game. A long stretch of games.”
Ten weeks into Seattle’s Super Bowl title defense, it hasn’t been as clean as a season ago. Thanks to consecutive wins, though, the Seahawks find themselves with a 6-4 record yet still trailing the San Francisco 49ers — who improved to 8-1 on Sunday — by 2 1/2 games in the NFC West.
With seven games remaining, Seattle is still on the outside looking in with respect to the NFC playoff picture. The Seahawks remain in eighth place and will have to pass one of the four NFC North teams ahead of them.
Effective Sunday afternoon, though, Seattle’s focus is on nursing back to health after sliding by the Raiders in an unorthodox manner.
“The bye week’s going to be great for us to rest and recover and get a lot of guys back,” Smith-Njigba said. “So, just using this time wisely. For me, it’s playoff football. We want every single game.”

full_text:
One of the 49ers' biggest issues this season has been their struggles to get to the quarterback. Brian Rothmuller / Icon Sportswire via Getty Images
The San Francisco 49ers gobbled up yards, scored from great distances and finished with the most points, 46, they’ve had this season.
But as massive as their offensive explosion was in Sunday’s 46-40 win over the Dallas Cowboys, it wasn’t enough to mask a tepid pass rush and leaky pass coverage, including from top cornerback Deommodore Lenoir, who was picked apart by quarterback Dak Prescott and his receivers for three touchdowns.
The Cowboys trailed by as much as 19 points in the second half and practically abandoned their running game. That’s usually a red-meat situation for defensive linemen — an opportunity to tee off on a quarterback and pad pass-rush stats. But despite 51 pass attempts by Prescott, the 49ers sacked him just once — when he ran out of bounds for no gain on the Cowboys’ final scoring drive.
Otherwise, he had plenty of time to find wideouts George Pickens, CeeDee Lamb and Ryan Flournoy, who combined for 288 receiving yards and five touchdowns. Prescott’s 343 passing yards were a season high, and Dallas’ 439 yards are the most the 49ers have surrendered this season. Last year’s injury-depleted unit — no Fred Warner, Nick Bosa or Mykel Williams, among others — gave up 440 yards in a Week 17 win over the Chicago Bears.
“Any time you get 40 dropped on you, you’re going to be upset, right?” Warner said Sunday. “That’s far from our standard. But you’ve got to go back, you’ve got to look at the tape and see exactly why that was the case. You’ve got to remove emotion from the equation and look hard at the tape.”
The out-of-bounds sack on Prescott was hardly impressive, and it was the 49ers’ first since Oct. 19.
Last week’s sack-less performance against the Las Vegas Raiders was easy to explain away. After all, DeForest Buckner was playing his first game with the 49ers after his trade from Indianapolis, and Bosa had just returned from a six-week calf injury. Meanwhile, then-Raiders quarterback Kirk Cousins didn’t want to get hit and got rid of the ball quickly.
But Sunday’s pass rush was no better, which contributed to San Francisco’s worst pass-coverage outing of the season.
After the game, 49ers coach Kyle Shanahan noted that neither Lenoir, who hurt his foot against the Raiders, nor fellow starter Renardo Green, who’s dealing with a back issue, practiced in full in the run-up to Sunday’s game. And for the second straight week, Green had to leave in the fourth quarter, which sent rookie Ephesians Prysock onto the field. He was immediately picked on by the Cowboys, who scored touchdowns on every fourth-quarter drive except their final desperation possession when they got the ball with nine seconds remaining.
Afterward, Shanahan defended Lenoir and Green.
“I know we can do better than that,” he said. “But I also give a ton of props to Demo and Renardo. Those guys were hurt, they weren’t able to practice all week. They got out there on Friday but didn’t do any full-speed stuff; it was all walk-through-type stuff. So for those guys to miss all week and battle and go against guys like (the Cowboys’ receivers), I respect the s— out of them.”
Lenoir said he wouldn’t use his injury as an excuse.
“I’ve got to play better,” he said. “They pay me to make plays, and I’ve got to finish on the ball. What happened today can’t happen.”
The 49ers didn’t need sacks against the Raiders because they were resourceful in other ways, including five second-half takeaways.
They had their chances Sunday, too. It looked as if Dre Greenlaw had an opportunity for a pick six in the second quarter, but he dropped the would-be interception. A few plays later, Prescott connected with Pickens on a 39-yard catch-and-run touchdown.
Then, in the third quarter, Warner appeared to get his sixth punch-out forced fumble of the season when he dislodged the ball from running back Javonte Williams, and Green fell on it. But a Cowboy came away with the ball after the scrum, and the 49ers didn’t challenge the play. Dallas scored a field goal on the drive.
“Somehow a guy on their team was walking away with the ball,” Shanahan said, adding his spotters in the coach’s booth couldn’t see a clear recovery. “So we were afraid we wouldn’t (win the challenge) for that reason.”
The 49ers did have one takeaway, Malik Mustapha’s interception at San Francisco’s 10-yard line late in the third quarter. But even that had an asterisk, considering Prescott’s overthrow to Lamb came on fourth down. Allowing the ball to sail out of bounds would have saved the 49ers 30 yards.
The team’s biggest midseason issue is its pass rush and the fact Bosa has no sacks this season. He had excellent pressure on the throw Greenlaw nearly picked off, but that was the exception Sunday. He seemed to be picking his way through the Cowboys’ pass protection for most of the afternoon and hasn’t looked like himself in the two games he’s played after his injury. Buckner, meanwhile, is technically the 49ers’ sacks leader with four, but those came when he was in Indianapolis.
“It didn’t seem like we got there enough, especially at the end when they were coming back,” Shanahan said. “It seems like we got gassed. I could tell how tired we were.”
Usually, when an offense gains 584 yards and scores 46 points, it means the starters on both sides of the ball are watching comfortably from the sideline in the fourth quarter. On Sunday, however, Warner and a few others played all 76 defensive snaps.
And their current stretch doesn’t get any easier. The team flew from Dallas to Colorado Springs on Sunday evening so it can get used to playing at altitude for the upcoming game in Mexico City. That’s where they’ll meet the 7-2 — and suddenly revitalized — Minnesota Vikings. After that, they have a home game against the Seattle Seahawks.
“Obviously, we’ve got to be better,” Warner said. “Great win. We’ve got to win by any fashion. So there’s going to be games where the offense carries us — they carried us today — and we’re going to have to make sure we have our best performance this upcoming week.”

full_text:
Brock Purdy threw touchdowns of 74, 66 and 11 yards on Sunday, but his favorite play was his block on Deebo Samuel's 70-yard TD run. Jerome Miron / Imagn Images
ARLINGTON, Texas — The play of the season wasn’t even Brock Purdy’s favorite play of the day.
The 49ers quarterback was scrambling, looking for a first down on third-and-8, then stopped on a dime like an elite running back and hit Christian McCaffrey in stride for a 74-yard touchdown … yeah, that was cool.
But the play on which he sprinted downfield to block for Deebo Samuel’s 70-yard touchdown on a reverse, well … Purdy was giddy after the 46-40 win over the Dallas Cowboys .
“I thought it was pretty good,” Purdy said. “Everyone was celebrating. I was like, ‘Hey, Deebo! Dude, me and (left tackle) Trent (Williams)!’ Hopefully there’s a sick picture out there. I was pulling with Trent. Dude, it was sweet.
“I could be the next (fullback Kyle) Juszczyk.”
Yes, a quarterback who just led his 8-1 team to 584 yards of offense and six touchdowns hopes to be like the fullback. If that doesn’t sum up the team’s franchise quarterback and leader, nothing does.
His toughness was on full display Sunday as he took some big hits but never wavered. Whether passing, running or blocking, Purdy never let the Cowboys off the hook.
“It just shows how tough he is,” coach Kyle Shanahan said. “And there were a couple times it seemed like he was hurt and never told me that anything was wrong. He took some hits in that game, hung in there and kept making big plays.”
Shanahan did not see Purdy sprinting downfield to block for Samuel. He’s glad he didn’t.
“Our coaching point on that is just get out of the way,” Shanahan said. “It usually doesn’t work well … but he did a good job of overcoming coaching.”
Williams started chasing after Purdy when he saw the quarterback take off to block.
“If Brock was upfield blocking, that means there’s a lot of green grass, and you’re trying to get Deebo to the end zone,” Williams said. “So, I just kicked it into gear and just went and found somebody.”
Purdy cut in line in front of Samuel and, alongside receiver Jordan Watkins, actually got a piece of two Cowboys defenders, as Tom Brady practically yelped in the broadcast booth. It wasn’t quite Ronnie “Sunshine” Bass decleating defenders to clear the way for Jerry “Rev” Harris’ state-title-winning touchdown in “Remember the Titans,” but Samuel appreciated it.
SFvsDAL on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/3RwQ4dNchJ
— NFL (@NFL) November 15, 2026
“Just to see Brock laying it on the line for his brother just shows what type of team we have,” Samuel said.
Purdy’s idol, Juszczyk, also loved it.
“The highest compliment I can give anyone on the team is that they are a football player, and Brock is the epitome of that,” he said. “Whatever he’s asked to do, he’s going to go do it.”
And getting knocked down doesn’t bother Purdy. The QB was sacked five times and laid out a bunch more, including on a violent sandwich hit from two Cowboys after he got rid of the ball.
“It never seems to faze him,” Juszczyk said. “And he does a good job, even when he does get sacked, he gets back close to the line of scrimmage. Kudos to him to stay in it and keep firing.”
Purdy is even firing it when he’s planning to run the ball, like on the 74-yard pass to McCaffrey. He escaped the pocket going to his right and …
“I was 100 percent running,” Purdy said. “I’m always trying to keep my eyes down the field when I’m scrambling and seeing if guys can feel me and see me and try to get into a space. But then there’s a point where I have to use my legs, and I was going to do that when all of a sudden, I just felt Christian pop.”
It was like he and McCaffrey were 5 years old again.
“It really is backyard football at that point,” McCaffrey said. “I think we’ve all played it as kids, drawing up a play on your hand, and it never happens. You ever tell a 5-year-old to run a post route, and he just runs a corner or something else, but he’s open? That was kind of what that was.
“Brock never surrenders and just keeps the play alive, and that’s a big deal.”
McCaffrey started the play blocking on a Cowboys blitz, and Shanahan was shocked he got out in front of Purdy. He said he can’t wait to watch the film.
“Christian was unbelievable on it,” Shanahan said. “I have no idea how Christian was blocking the blitz in the A-gap and ended up where he was. So I’m excited to see it on the plane.”
Purdy would hit McCaffrey for a second touchdown pass, again to beat a Cowboys blitz. Thirty-seven-year-old linebacker Von Miller was one-on-one with McCaffrey, and he chased him for 66 yards. Right until the huge turnout of 49ers fans started cheering again.
Purdy finished 22 of 28 for 389 yards and three touchdowns passing. He also ran twice for 21 yards, once pump-faking a throw to freeze defenders and the other time pretending to make an option pitch before he turned the corner.
The 49ers became the first team since the 2000 “Greatest Show on Turf” Rams to have three touchdowns of at least 65 yards in the same game, per TruMedia. Purdy completed all four of his pass attempts on scrambles for 135 yards, tying Patrick Mahomes and Josh Allen for the most in a game since 2018, per Next Gen Stats.
“I promise, he is the MVP of our league,” Niners linebacker Fred Warner said.
According to DraftKings, Purdy was third in MVP odds (+400) after Sunday’s games ended, behind Allen (+310) and Joe Burrow (+105), who posted his fifth consecutive game with four-plus combined passing and rushing touchdowns on Sunday night against the Steelers.
Purdy’s supporting cast wasn’t bad either. McCaffrey finished with three touchdowns, Samuel had two and rookie Kaelon Black trampled two Cowboys on his scoring run. New bestie Keenan Allen had five catches, and the 49ers averaged 9.4 yards per play, the most by any team over the past two seasons.
The 49ers’ defense couldn’t cover George Pickens or get any pressure on Dak Prescott, but that’s OK.
“The offense can score as many points as we want, and then the defense only needs one stop,” right tackle Colton McKivitz said, smiling. “So they did their job at the end. There are going to be games where the defense bails us out. Right now, we can all just enjoy the quarterback.
“Brock running down to make a block was pretty awesome.”

title: Carson Beck Debut Reveals Cardinals' Big-Picture Problem
full_text:
GLENDALE — It's hours after action at State Farm Stadium concluded, and the Arizona Cardinals' roof is no longer open. The once sun-filled top of the stadium now sits capped with stadium lights illuminating the field where the Los Angeles Rams handed Carson Beck a 34-6 loss in his debut.
It's a perfect representation for how the Cardinals' season has quickly turned. A win last week in Seattle would have pushed Arizona to 4-5 on the year, keeping them alive in the playoff hunt and injecting a massive boost of hope in a year that wasn't expected to yield anything close.
Yet including today, the Cardinals' last two losses now sink them to 3-7 on the season. Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur knows what's at stake to finish these last seven games — and what isn't.
"We got what we've got right now," LaFleur told reporters post-game, as injuries have plagued Arizona's roster.
"It is what it is, and I told the guys there's no magic wand. There's no magic savior. We have seven more weeks of a massive evaluation to see how this roster's going to look. I put it on front street for the guys. It's shared accountability. It's collective."
Beck was the lone bright spot for Arizona on a day where practically nothing went their way, and that speaks volumes on Arizona's biggest issues.
"All in all, for the amount of plays and what we asked him to do, I was impressed with what we asked," LaFleur said of Beck. The third-round pick completed 11-of-18 passes for 108 yards and two interceptions.
" ... It's just a collection of errors on offense. All you ask these guys to do is do their job and I thought he did his job."
The box score doesn't show, but Beck looked competent and in control — something Cardinals fans have been clamoring for. Beck pushed the ball to all three levels of the defense and was massively held back by his teammates.
Beck's arrival to the field was met with a harsh reality — that even if he was their best player on the field tonight, the Cardinals have so many other holes to fill across the roster.
Beck was sacked five times by Los Angeles' defense. The Cardinals rushed for just 34 yards tonight on 11 carries. While Trey McBride paced Arizona in receiving, Beck's crew of scout-team pass-catchers had drops in key moments through the first two quarters before things got out of hand.
Defensively, the Cardinals again didn't stop a team from reaching 30 points. Week 10 marked the seventh time in the last nine weeks where Arizona allowed a team to reach that coveted benchmark. Their performance today was capped by allowing the Rams to get possession with 12:15 left in the fourth quarter... and couldn't muster a single stop before the clock hit zero.
Collectively , the Cardinals can't get anything going on both sides of the ball. That's been a familiar tune for much of the regular season.
The issue isn't Beck playing well. It's that the Cardinals are trying to solve the most important position in sports, and their rookie quarterback played considerably well with absolutely no help around him, and nothing to show for it.
"We have seven more weeks and like I said, we're going to take it one week at a time, but it's going to be a great evaluation over these next seven weeks to see what we've got and see how we're going to build this thing," a clearly frustrated LaFleur added post-game.
Whether Beck is a building block for LaFleur and the Cardinals in the future still remains to be seen. That's a question that will be answered in due time.
However, Beck's performance offered a clear reality check: While injuries have thrown this season sideways, the Cardinals' overall philosophy on team-building and lack of depth again has been exposed.
And that's not something that can be fixed in free agency — or a single draft class. Getting key players back healthy will be needed, though this was a similar drum beat we heard prior to the start of last season.
The Cardinals can't afford to equate health for progress. Their third-round rookie quarterback made that clear tonight in his debut.
Donnie Druin is the Publisher for Arizona Cardinals and Phoenix Suns On SI. Donnie moved to Arizona in 2012 and has been with the company since 2018. In college he won "Best Sports Column" in the state of Arizona for his section and has previously provided coverage for the Pittsburgh Steelers and Arizona State Sun Devils. Follow Donnie on Twitter @DonnieDruin for more news, updates, analysis and more!

Should have been Beck from week 3, would loved to have seen him operate with a healthy team around him. This is a terrible way to try to evaluate QB play for potential future with the franchise

Bidwill needs to come out of hiding and speak to the media about this abomination of a franchise. Takes some ownership Mr. Owner

title: Carson Beck's Cardinals Debut: The Good, Bad And Ugly
full_text:
GLENDALE — Carson Beck's debut for the Arizona Cardinals drew plenty of hype, attention and chatter ahead of Week 10's matchup against the Los Angeles Rams.
Eyes in the desert were glued to action at State Farm Stadium to see what the rookie quarterback could muster in spite of a truly underwhelming cast around him and a Rams defense that holds two of the league's best pass rushers.
Those eyes either turned their televisions off or hit the exits by the middle of the third quarter.
The Cardinals' 34-6 defeat to Los Angeles was eye-opening for a few reasons — Arizona ran just 34 offensive plays. Beck turned the ball over twice. Glimmers of hope were eradicated by halftime.
Yet it's not all bad in the desert, as Beck's box score doesn't tell the entire story of what happened.
That sounds incredibly odd given the score and Beck's 108 passing yards with no touchdowns and two turnovers, but the reality is Beck operated at a high level given the horrid circumstances handed to him — which we'll touch on later.
Beck spread the ball around effectively through short, intermediate and deep passes while proving himself as a mobile presence in the pocket. Drops by numerous wideouts truly killed any chances of sustaining momentum after the second drive.
Tape doesn't lie. While Beck clearly has room for improvement, he was the furthest reason as to why the Cardinals pack their bags as losers from State Farm Stadium. Pound for pound, he delivered on his end.
Beck wasn't completely off the mark for a majority of passes, though the ones that were missed weren't pretty.
After his first interception wasn't close to falling on his shoulders, Beck's second pick of the day was an unfortunate mix of a poor throw and great play by Rams linebacker Wesley Bailey — who peeled off his own receiver to undercut the ball.
WESLEY BAILEY RIPPED IT AWAY FOR HIS FIRST NFL INTERCEPTION 😤 📺 @NFLonCBS | #RamsHouse pic.twitter.com/upvqsq5djk
Beck's eyes were central the whole time, tipping Bailey to the middle and unfortunately for Arizona, that gamble paid off.
The other throw was a big missed opportunity deep downfield, where Zay Jones was streaking open. Beck floated the ball a bit too much, forcing Jones to adjust inside (rather than placing the ball ahead or outside) and ultimately the pass fell incomplete.
This was Beck's first taste of legitimate NFL action, and there does need to be some patience with the rookie quarterback in terms of growth and acclimation to the speed and timing of the game. Still, those are the two top passes he'd love to have back.
The Cardinals trotted out a patchwork offensive line, practice squad receivers and a depleted running back room against one of the league's fiercest defensive fronts. It was a recipe for disaster that no chef could stop.
Beck, as an individual, played up to par given expectations. The same can't be said for the rest of the offense, or his defense that has now allowed 30 or more points in seven of the last nine weeks.
Beck was sacked five times on the day. Arizona's 34 offensive plays matches the amount of yards they had on the ground. The Cardinals went 0-6 on third down and had just one drive of five or more plays after the first quarter. Numerous drops from players stalled any potential scoring drives.
Beck had an ugly supporting cast around him, to say the least.

title: 4 Big Instant Reactions After Cardinals' Frustrating Loss vs Rams
full_text:
In some ways, a new era started for the Arizona Cardinals; in some ways it did not.
Rookie quarterback Carson Beck notched his first start in a 34-6 loss to the Los Angeles Rams — an unfortunate scoreline that is nothing new for Arizona.
Starting on a positive note, the rookie signal-caller finished his much-anticipated debut going 11-for-18 through the air for 108 yards and two interceptions. On paper, those numbers are pretty porous. However, this is one of those cases where the tape did not reflect the stats.
Starting with the interceptions, Beck's first pick was not his fault. It was a great pass to an open wideout that bounced off the receiver's hands and into the hands of Rams safety Kamren Kinchens. The second interception was a great catch by Rams linebacker Wesley Bailey while Beck was targeting Cardinals running back Tyler Allgeier.
Sure, Beck could have looked to throw elsewhere. But Bailey made an amazing play, so it's hard to fault Beck that much.
Another reason Beck was better than his numbers? Many of his completions weren't simple dink and dunks. There is a time and place to go short in the NFL, but often, rookie quarterbacks avoid big plays and check the ball down. That wasn't the case, as Beck pushed the ball downfield more than Cardinals fans are used to, including a 31-yard strike (23 being air yards before the reception) to wideout Devin Duvernay.
Did Beck look like the next Kurt Warner for Arizona? No, but there were still plenty of positives against a tough Rams defense.
With both teams going into this matchup with their star receivers out, it seemed like a big day for the tight ends. That was the case for the Rams, as Los Angeles tight ends Davis Allen and Tyler Higbee both caught touchdown passes against the Cardinals' defense.
Meanwhile, for Arizona, Trey McBride had only 37 yards and no touchdowns on the day. This was McBride's second-lowest receiving output of the season, with his lowest being 31 yards in Week 4.
Now, to be fair, I am not blaming McBride at all. However, this falls on the coaching staff. Head coach Mike LaFleur knew that the top Cardinals receiver, Michael Wilson , would be out for this game. Having McBride be so limited is a coaching error by LaFleur.
Arizona's defense started this game on a fantastic note. Through the first quarter and most of the second, the Cardinals defense looked like a Super Bowl-caliber unit. They held the Rams to field goals, stuffed the run, and intercepted Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford.
This all changed before the second half. The game looked like it would be a 10-3 lead for Los Angeles going into the half. However, after a Beck interception with 43 seconds left in the half, the Rams scored another touchdown to go up 17-3. The defense then spiraled from there.
In the second half, the Rams added another 17 points to reach 34 total. Stafford looked completely comfortable in the second half, which was the opposite of how he looked in the first half. While I had the Rams winning, it was unfortunate, given how bad their defense looked after such a promising start.
While another loss is to be expected with the number of injuries Arizona has, the lack of incomplete halves is a trend that needs to stop. In most games this season, it seems like the Cardinals are either bad, to the point of nothing working in either the first or second half.
While it is never fun to call for someone's job, the world of football is tough, and I think Arizona's coaches and front office have seen enough to move on from defensive coordinator Nick Rallis , especially after this bad defensive outing. Offensive coordinator Nathaniel Hackett is also not safe, and he could get let go, as the Cardinals offense put up back-to-back bad offensive games.
Overall, another ugly division loss, which is nothing new for Arizona. After the past two weeks of playing NFC West teams, they play an AFC West team next week as they travel to Kansas City to face the Chiefs.

title: Evaluating Carson Beck's Cardinals Debut: How Rookie QB Actually Played
full_text:
GLENDALE — Arizona Cardinals rookie quarterback Carson Beck took the field for his NFL debut on Sunday.
It was anything but ideal.
After an enticing opening two drives, the Cardinals' offense stalled in major fashion en route to a 34-6 Los Angeles Rams victory at State Farm Stadium.
Beck finished the day with 11/18 passing for 108 yards and two interceptions with zero touchdowns and a 38.4 passer rating.
The box score didn't look pretty, but Beck's overall performance yields more optimism than some want to give after a massively disappointing score:
All in all, Beck had a fairly promising performance on Sunday. The odds felt like they were always going to be stacked against him given the circumstances entering his first NFL start.
As fate would have it, the talented Rams defense would hold Arizona to minimal damage. Beck's offensive line failed him with five sacks on the day and no rushing game to balance things out. His receivers (minus Trey McBride) were incredibly disappointing and ended a few potential scoring drives with drops.
Beck showed a willingness to push the ball downfield and looked composed in his first taste of action against one of the best defensive fronts he'll see in his lifetime thanks to Aaron Donald and Myles Garrett. Mistakes were made, though expected from an inexperienced quarterback such as Beck.
A loss never feels good. A blowout to a divisional rival sprinkles salt in the wound. Two interceptions, on the surface, is anything but ideal.
Still, Beck showed some promising flashes, and the hope is the Cardinals will build from there.

title: Three Last-Minute Bold Predictions for Cardinals-Rams
full_text:
The Carson Beck era starts for the Arizona Cardinals as they face the Los Angeles Rams. This is a huge game for the Cardinals as their rookie quarterback will make his long-awaited debut.
Los Angeles themselves have been on a winning streak and recently welcomed back Myles Garrett to the mix.
So with a red-hot Rams team coming into town, what out-of-the-ordinary things could happen in this game?
This Sunday's quarterback duel is a tale as old as time  the veteran versus the rookie. It may seem odd that Beck, in his first game, will have a better game than MVP and Super Bowl Winner Matthew Stafford. However, Stafford did not play his best in his first game against Arizona's defense this year.
While his numbers look solid, Stafford missed some key throws that cost Los Angeles a Week six loss to the Cardinals. For Beck, at times, when NFL quarterbacks get their first game, they can throw opposing defenses off their game.
Another way that Beck could have a better game is on the ground. Beck does have some mobility. So head coach Mike LaFleur could dial up some option plays for Beck.
Now, even though I believe Beck will have the better game stat wise, I do think Stafford and the Rams ger the win. However, Beck outplaying Stafford, even in a loss will be a huge morale win for the rookie signal caller for Arizona.
Even though I think Los Angeles will come out victorious, I also think the Cardinals will lead at halftime. So far, leading early hasn't been something Arizona has done this year. In most of their games, they are trailing early.
However, things do bode well for the Cardinals being up early. For starters, with Beck getting his first start, he could come out of the gate firing on all cylinders. The dream for every athlete is to play in the NFL, and this is Beck's first time playing in a regular-season game.
Additionally, Arizona defensive coordinator Nick Rallis's unit played this Rams offense very tough in Week 6, holding the team to 16 points. Starting this game, Rallis could carry over much of the great defensive scheming from the last couple of quarters against Los Angeles. Ultimately, I do think Rams head coach Sean McVay gets things going in the second half and wins, but leading early against a divisional rival could be a big morale boost for this team.
Unfortunately, both teams are dealing with a lot of injuries at receiver. On Arizona's side, star wideout Michael Wilson is out for the year after an injury he suffered last week. On the Rams' side, Puka Nacua is on IR and Davante Adams is out for a couple of weeks.
With both teams depleted at that position, it could be a big day for both teams' tight ends. Cardinals tight end Trey McBride could have 100-plus yards. For Los Angeles, they also have some good tight ends on their rosters.
Both organizations like to use tight end-heavy packages in their offense. This game could easily be a tight-end show for both clubs. Also, rookie quarterbacks often target tight ends, so Beck could target McBride often in this game.
Overall, despite the loss, I believe Arizona will compete closely against Los Angeles. Beck makes some good plays in his first start and gets this new era off to a decent start.

title: Elijah Higgins Extension Screams 1 Big Thing for Cardinals
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals officially announced Elijah Higgins' extension, keeping their tight end room headlined by Trey McBride intact for the foreseeable future.
Higgins opened some eyes with the deal, as his three-year extension is reportedly worth up to $26.8 million. The new contract keeps him in Arizona through 2029.
McBride being awarded a historic extension two offseasons ago could have deterred the Cardinals from really shelling out money to a TE2. While details are still emerging of the actual deal, Higgins' deal is fairly eye-opening for a backup at a non-premium position.
Arizona's financial commitment to Higgins does further highlight one big thing, however.
When Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur first took the job in Arizona, the team's offense was heavily expected to be a predominantly tight end-focused attack thanks to his recent experience with the Los Angeles Rams, who led the NFL in 13 (one running back, three tight ends) personnel.
Thus far, that's been the case.
Even without top blocking tight end Tip Reiman due to injury, the Cardinals' 27% usage of 13 personnel is tied for second-highest in the league.
"There is more responsibility put upon us whether we are in 12, 11 or 13," Higgins said earlier this year. "We are involved in the run game, point of attack, pass pro, and obviously out running routes. Compared to the last three years we have so much more responsibility as a tight end unit. It's a cool thing."
Higgins is the 11th-graded Pro Football Focus tight end this season by their metrics.
Arizona's rushing attack is lacking this season, though that could change if/when Reiman returns this season. The Cardinals' passing attack has been quite impressive with 13 personnel.
“I’m guessing if you broke that down by the down and distance — obviously third down being when you’re in 11 [personnel] a little bit more for obvious reasons (there's) not as much of a threat of run," LaFleur said on why the Cardinals are successful with so many tight ends on the field,
"You’re going to get- not that our tight ends are slow but we’re going to get our receivers out there and try to space out the field. In some aspects, (we’ve) been okay on third down, but in other aspects had more opportunities for growth and for first downs, if you will.
"I’d say that’s kind of mainly it. First and second down, you get a little bit more structured defenses, if you will. I thought the guys have done a good job understanding the space, getting the ball in their hands and being productive in that facet.”

title: Trey McBride Earns New Cardinals Honor
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals have finally made Trey McBride a captain.
Amid the plethora of injuries, the Cardinals are placing the coveted "C" on McBride's chest for the second half of the season according to head coach Mike LaFleur.
That’s Captain Trey McBride to you now 🫡 pic.twitter.com/URdC5P8UF5
The Cardinals, sitting at 3-6, are now moving into the second half of the season hoping to rescue their season.
“He earned it,” LaFleur said on McBride getting the nod (h/t Arizona Sports).
“I think there’s two things about him. One, every single day he puts in the work, and the guys see that. The way he plays on Sunday, it’s how he practices, too. Maybe not as much (expletive)-talking, but nonetheless, he practices the right way.
"Then the second thing that is awesome about any leader, any person in general, he is himself. He’s not trying to be anyone that he’s not, and he just loves this game, he loves that locker room and he loves doing what he can do for this organization.”
McBride, a staple in the Cardinals' organization since emerging as their starter years ago, looks to usher in a new era of Arizona football as Carson Beck gets the nod.
"Of course. Obviously, he's the best player on our offense and one of the best in the league, if not the best. He just carries himself the right way, does the right things, comes in the building (and) does the right things. You all have seen him. When he gets out on that field, he's a 'dawg' and he wants the football," Beck said of having McBride.
"Obviously, we try to get it to him in any way possible. Just leaning on him — we were talking after practice and walked through everything that we have in the script and whatnot. How he sees things, how he sees the defense, different options on his routes and how he can run certain things against certain coverages. Just making sure we're on the same page because that's one guy that I haven't really gone with as much. Watching him — he makes a ton of plays, and you definitely want the ball in that guy's hands. Just walking through that stuff, really leaning on him about how he sees it and making sure we're on the same page."

title: Myles Garrett Headlines Official Cardinals-Rams Week 10 Injury Report
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals and Los Angeles Rams officially have their injury reports for Week 10's clash at State Farm Stadium.
The Cardinals are without three players entering Sunday, as Zach Carter (still on IR), Hjalte Froholdt and Jon Gaines II have all been ruled out.
Arizona has Hunter Long (IR), Roy Lopez, Max Melton, Darius Robinson, Jayden Williams and Andrew Wingard questionable.
For the Rams, just Steve Avila and Terrance Ferguson are officially down as of now. Five players in Davis Allen, Joe Cardona, Myles Garrett, Kam Curl and Trent McDuffie are questionable.

“You look at their defense just as a whole, they’re super talented. They have talent across the board from the defensive line to the linebackers to the back end with corners and defensive backs as well," he said.
"Then you (see) what they do with their scheme and the way they’re able to mix up their coverages, hide certain things, disguise their blitzes, and disguise their coverages on run downs and on third down as well. Then you get in the red zone and (there are) different looks as well. What they’re able to do on defense, it causes problems for offenses and it’s definitely going to be a challenge for us. I think the biggest thing is watching the film, seeing what we want to do, and then ultimately trying to go out there and execute our plan.”

title: Game-by-Game Arizona Cardinals Predictions for the Rest of the 2026 Season
full_text:
After a brutal stretch of games to start the 2026 season, the Arizona Cardinals' second half of the season features some more winnable matchups.
With eight games left, their opponents' combined record is 32-36-1. With an easier schedule, how can this team wrap up what has been, so far, not a great year?
While the Cardinals upset the Rams in SoFi Stadium, I predict they'll lose here at home. With all the injuries both teams are facing in their receiving corps, this has a high chance of being more of a defensive game.
Since neither offense is going to be at full power, the question remains: which team has the better defense?
That team is Los Angeles. The Rams have one of the best defensive duos with edge rusher Myles Garrett and defensive tackle Aaron Donald. Garrett is coming off of an amazing performance against the Washington Commanders.
In that game, Garrett had three sacks and three tackles for loss. Against a shaky offensive line, the Rams' high-powered defensive line is enough to secure the win against Arizona in rookie quarterback Carson Beck's first start.
Yes, miracles can happen in the NFL, and I am predicting one here as the Cardinals go into Arrowhead to knock off the dynastic Chiefs. While Kansas City does have a lot of high-impact offensive players, such as quarterback Patrick Mahomes , tight end Travis Kelce, and running back Kenneth Walker, they have had some poor offensive outings this season.
In Arizona's wins this year, it's been because their defense has played well. While it's an inconsistent unit, they do have their good games. The Chiefs have struggled dealing with pressure this year, as shown in their losses to the Seattle Seahawks and the Denver Broncos. The Cardinals' defensive line is one of the best parts of their defense. If they keep the pressure on Mahomes, that could bode well for a win.
Now, even if Arizona's defense gets some pressure and sacks on Mahomes, he has shown he can still make big plays in a short amount of time. This is where quarterback Beck's strengths come in. In the preseason, Beck was great at getting the ball out and keeping the offense in a rhythm. This could be just enough for Arizona to edge out a huge win this year.
After beating Kansas City and barely losing to Los Angeles, the Cardinals suffer a big home loss. The main reason is that the last time Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels faced this Arizona defense, he was very efficient in both the air and on the ground.
During Week 4 of the 2024 season, Daniels passed for 233 yards, ran for 47 yards, and threw and rushed for touchdowns to help Washington get a big win.
Additionally, the Commanders have rookie linebacker Sonny Styles. Styles has had a great rookie year for Washington, especially in coverage. In the NFL, linebackers usually cover tight ends, so Styles could take away some potential big plays from Cardinals tight end Trey McBride.
The Cardinals finish playing the NFC East in what could be one of the ugliest games of the entire NFL season. Arizona and Philadelphia have each had horrid losses and ugly moments this year. It comes down to the better offense, which goes to the Cardinals. This is because it seems that whether it's Tanner McKee or Joe Milton at quarterback for the Eagles, they can not move the ball.
While Beck has yet to play in an NFL regular-season game, if he can translate his preseason success to the regular season, it could be enough for a very sloppy game. Also, it seems like in this century, Arizona has had Philadelphia's number whenever the Cardinals host.
After Arizona's bye week, I expect a huge win against the Jets. While the Jets offense has some good rookie playmakers, enough for them to put up a respectable 23 points, New York's defense is a mess.
Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur could scheme up some great plays, especially in the pass game. The Jets' secondary has been their biggest weakness this season, so Beck could have the best game of his career to help Arizona win.
This is a very weird game, as the Saints have looked very hot and cold this season. One week, it looks like they could win the NFC South; the next, it looks like they could be picking top five in the draft. However, I do think New Orleans gets the edge because their offense is more electric.
With Cardinals wideout Michael Wilson done for the year, the Cardinals' receiving room isn't in the best shape. Meanwhile, the Saints have Chris Olave, a great wideout, and rookie receiver Jordyn Tyson returns to the state where he played college football.
Additionally, New Orleans quarterback Tyler Shough has shown some good growth as a passer in his second year. Now, Arizona could get this win down south, as the Saints' defense has been pretty porous this year. However, in a close game, I think the Cardinals lose their last road game of the season.
Arizona finishes up the AFC West in a game that, while not inspiring much confidence in their defense, could be a fun shootout that goes Las Vegas' way. This will be a battle of the rookie quarterbacks, with Fernando Mendoza leading the Raiders and Beck leading the Cardinals. It is a rematch of the College Football Championship, where Mendoza was victorious.
I believe Las Vegas takes this because Mendoza is a better quarterback than Beck. While I do think Beck is a fine player, the Raiders took Mendoza number one for a reason. With Las Vegas's defense being poor, Beck could have some great moments this game. However, Mendoza's clutchness shows up for the Raiders as they win on a last-second field goal in Glendale.
Well, after an exciting game, Arizona plummets to earth as they get destroyed by San Francisco. For starters, head coach Kyle Shanahan and quarterback Brock Purdy are too much for this Cardinals defense to handle.
There is also a high chance the 49ers are fighting for the NFC West or the NFC's No. 1 seed. Sometimes, during Week 18, teams rest their starters, but that is very unlikely for San Francisco.
Overall, I predict the Cardinals win three out of their final eight games, with some close losses. This will make their end-of-season record 6-11. Beck and the offense could provide some fun moments, but the Cardinals still have much work to do, especially on defense, which should be the team's main focus after the 2026 season is complete.

title: Are Falcons Checking Out? Three-Game Skid Puts Atlanta at a Crossroads
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons’ losing streak has reached three .
And from what’s been on display, there’s not much reason to believe they’re capable of a turnaround.
As the season spirals, running back Bijan Robinson posed a question after Sunday’s 35-13 home loss to the Kansas City Chiefs : “Is this how we want to go about the rest of the season with this product, or are we going to change? Are we going to strain for each other, go out there and play for each other no matter the situation?”
The Falcons (3-7) may verbally answer with what sounds good to the ear of fans, who showered them with boo birds in Mercedes-Benz Stadium on Sunday.
But the on-field play tells another story.
Especially with a cloud hanging over the franchise’s future as tanking talks get louder after the Falcons became trade deadline sellers in exchange for draft picks last week.
“I don’t think you have to worry about the fight of this football team,” head coach Kevin Stefanski told reporters in Sunday’s postgame press conference when asked how to keep his team from checking out.
“Our guys understand what’s in front of us.”
Atlanta moved its star free safety and team captain Jessie Bates III to the Jacksonville Jaguars and starting center Ryan Neuzil to the Baltimore Ravens .
Entering the week, Tankathon has Atlanta slated for the No. 8 overall pick in the 2027 NFL Draft.
The pick may hold up or even rise with Minnesota and Detroit as the next two games. More than half of the season is gone, and Atlanta is looking like one of the worst teams in the NFL through Week 10.
“Nobody feels bad or cares about how the Atlanta Falcons feel except for us. And we can make a change to the narrative,” said Falcons cornerback A.J. Terrell Jr. “We still got the season in front of us, and we can either take advantage of that or plummet.”
Through the struggles, Atlanta has a saving grace: NFC South bedlam.
The Falcons are currently in the division’s fourth and final spot, with the Carolina Panthers leading the way with a 4-5 record.
Again, welcome to the NFC South, where you can compete for the division crown and a draft pick simultaneously.
“You’re always going to have a chance as long as there are games left on the schedule in the NFC South,” said Corey Levin, the newly appointed starting center for the Falcons .
American football will get a break from the uninspiring product the Falcons have put on the field in recent weeks. They’re on a bye for Week 11.
Then the gauntlet continues at the Minnesota Vikings and former Falcons quarterback Kirk Cousins on Nov. 29, kicking off Atlanta’s final seven regular season games.
“The biggest thing for us is to stay together,” Robinson said. “I think the teams that start to lose a lot later in the season are the teams that drift apart and go amongst themselves.”
Can the Falcons reverse course in the next month and a half and ultimately land a playoff spot?
But Stefanski’s and the players’ optimism has yet to translate into results, leaving the Falcons with seven games to prove their words carry weight.
