title: Falcons Winners and Losers: Atlanta's Offense Disappears in Loss to Chiefs
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons suffered another frustrating loss, falling 35-13 to the Kansas City Chiefs on Sunday. The offense struggled to find any consistency; the passing game never developed a rhythm, and the defense gave Patrick Mahomes too many opportunities to make explosive plays.
There were a few individual bright spots, particularly among Atlanta's young defensive players, but this was another performance that gave a clear indication the team was thinking more about the 2027 NFL Draft than they are about winning the NFC South.
Here are the winners and losers from Sunday's loss.
Hellams deserves credit for stepping into a much larger role following the trade of Jessie Bates . Replacing a veteran safety and team leader is not an easy assignment, but Hellams showed he was capable of handling the opportunity.
He finished with 10 total tackles, including six solo tackles and four assists, leading the way in the secondary. He was active around the football and helped make several stops against the Chiefs.
There will naturally be growing pains with Bates no longer in Atlanta, but Hellams provided some encouraging signs in his expanded role.
A bright spot for Atlanta's future
The rookie linebacker duo continued to show why Falcons fans should be excited about their development.
Perkins finished with five tackles, including four solo tackles and one assist. Daniels contributed seven tackles, with two solo tackles and five assists.
Both players were flying around the football and showed good energy throughout the afternoon.
With Divine Deablo missing another week, this was valuable experience for two young linebackers who could have significant roles moving forward. Their development is one of the few positives Atlanta can take away from this game.
Moody provided some stability after recently taking over for Nick Folk .
He finished the afternoon perfect on all three kicking attempts, converting two field goals from 28 and 38 yards and making his lone extra point.
He accounted for seven of Atlanta's 13 points and didn't leave any points on the field.
Moody also executed a picture-perfect onside kick; the first successful onside kick this season.
you won’t see an onside kick prettier than this. pic.twitter.com/1oSTxR1Hq0
While the Falcons have much bigger problems to address, Moody did exactly what was expected of him. After making a midseason change at kicker, getting a reliable performance is encouraging.
There are legitimate questions about Tommy Rees' offensive approach following Sunday's performance.
Atlanta struggled to establish any consistency, and the play sequencing was questionable at times. One of the biggest concerns continues to be the lack of involvement for Bijan Robinson.
Robinson finished with 71 rushing yards on 16 carries and added six receiving yards on four catches. He averaged 4.4 yards per carry, yet Atlanta struggled to consistently build its offense around him.
Another concerning trend is the Falcons' approach on third down.
There seems to be a lack of trust in the traditional dropback passing game, particularly when Atlanta knows opposing defenses are going to bring pressure. The Chiefs were able to create problems with their blitz packages, and the Falcons didn't consistently have answers.
Rees needs to find ways to get the football out quicker, create easier opportunities for Penix and put his playmakers in better positions.
The talent is there. The offensive execution and playcalling need to improve.
This was a particularly rough afternoon for the veteran left tackle.
Matthews was flagged three times, although the official play by play identifies two holding penalties and one false start. Those mistakes repeatedly put Atlanta behind the chains.
The holding penalties were particularly damaging because they erased positive plays and forced the offense into difficult situations.
For a veteran who has been one of Atlanta's most dependable offensive linemen for years, this was a performance he'd like to forget.
Another frustrating afternoon
Penix finished with 23 completions on 43 attempts for 286 yards, with the majority of those yards in garbage time, zero touchdowns, and an interception. He also rushed four times for 29 yards.
Atlanta finished with 370 yards, but most of them came once the game was well out of reach. They converted only five of 16 third downs. Their first four drives were three-and-outs.
Penix never seemed to find a consistent rhythm. There were flashes, including some productive connections with Drake London and Jahan Dotson, but they weren't enough to sustain drives.
He doesn't deserve all the blame. The offensive line, playcalling and overall offensive execution all contributed to the struggles.
However, Atlanta needs more from its quarterback if it wants to compete consistently.
The continued lack of involvement for Pitts is becoming increasingly difficult to understand.
He finished Sunday's game with four catches for 50 yards on four targets, without a touchdown. He had two catches for nine yards in the first half, and his third catch came with the Falcons down 35-13, and he promptly fumbled.
Those numbers are particularly disappointing considering how much the coaching staff has emphasized getting him involved in the offense.
Offensive coordinator Tommy Rees has previously acknowledged that the Falcons are better when Pitts is involved. However, that philosophy hasn't translated into consistent production this season.
Pitts has the athletic ability to create mismatches against linebackers and safeties. Yet Atlanta continues to struggle to make him a meaningful part of the passing attack.
At some point, the coaching staff has to figure out how to get one of its most talented offensive weapons involved.
This deserves its own category because the Falcons' secondary had a difficult afternoon against Patrick Mahomes.
Mahomes finished with 22 completions on 35 attempts for 348 yards, five touchdowns and zero interceptions, posting a 135.5 passer rating.
Kansas City consistently found opportunities downfield, finishing with 453 total yards and five passing touchdowns.
Terrell recorded five tackles, while Henderson finished with two. However, the tackle totals don't tell the entire story.
There were multiple explosive plays that exposed Atlanta's coverage, including a 50-yard completion to Rashee Rice with Henderson involved in the coverage and a 39-yard touchdown to Cyrus Allen.
The Chiefs also connected on a 43-yard touchdown to Ashton Armstrong late in the fourth quarter.
For Terrell, who is the 11th highest-paid cornerback in the NFL, these are the types of performances that raise questions about the return on investment.
For Henderson, the timing is notable. He recently received a significant two-year contract extension after stepping into a starting role and showing improvement. Atlanta needs that version of Henderson consistently, not performances where opposing quarterbacks can repeatedly attack the secondary.
Losing Jessie Bates certainly doesn't make things easier, but the remaining defensive backs have to do a better job limiting explosive plays.
Mahomes was far too comfortable against this defense, and the coverage issues were a major reason why Kansas City was able to pull away.
There weren't many positives from Sunday's loss. Hellams, Perkins, and Daniels showed encouraging signs, and Moody delivered a perfect performance. However, the offensive struggles, questionable playcalling, and secondary issues continue to raise serious concerns about where this Falcons team is headed.
The Falcons have the week off before they face Kirk Cousins and the Minnesota Vikings (7-2) on Sunday, November 29th in Minnesota.

title: 5 Brutal Takeaways From Atlanta Falcons Loss to Kansas City Chiefs
full_text:
ATLANTA – The Atlanta Falcons lost their third straight game, and the fifth of their last six, on Sunday. They fell to the Chiefs 35-13, marking the third double-digit loss.
The Falcons had a start to forget on offense, surrendering four consecutive three-and-outs to begin the game, marking their worst start in 26 years. Michael Penix Jr. faced pressure on several dropbacks and had a few misfires that put the Falcons behind the chains early. The offense faced third-down distances of 10, 10, 17, and 4 yards.
But the biggest issue was that Bijan Robinson only touched the ball three times over those four possessions. Unsurprisingly, the star running back snapped the drought on the fifth drive with a 17-yard rush that set up the Falcons’ first points of the game.
The Falcons seemed to find some rhythm on that possession, but they quickly went back to another three-and-out, their fifth of the first half. Robinson finished the half with only eight touches and fewer than 20 carries for the fifth time in the last six games (all ended in a loss).
The second half didn’t go much differently, and the Falcons’ drives ended in a punt, turnover on downs, punt, and punt before finally finding the end zone down 28-3 with 8:15 left.
Penix never got comfortable, and he and offensive coordinator Tommy Rees are struggling to find success. Since his outstanding performance against the 49ers, the offense has averaged a dreadful 10.0 points per game.
Fans voiced their displeasure with the team, showering the offense with boos.
"They put in their hard-earned work every single week to try to make it to these games, and it's our job to make it count for them," running back Bijan Robinson said of the fans. "So yeah, when they boo us, we deserve it."
Atlanta was 5-of-16 on third down and only scored one touchdown on five red zone trips.
With the Falcons’ offense struggling to find any semblance of rhythm, the defense was forced into some unfortunate possessions. They started slowly, too, allowing an easy touchdown drive to begin the game, but locked the Chiefs up for much of the game.
The defense just didn’t get any help, and eventually Patrick Mahomes broke through again. After that opening drive score, both of his subsequent touchdown throws came after shortcomings from another unit: the first on an offside negated a field goal and the second after a failed fourth-down conversion at midfield.
Mahomes’ fourth touchdown came in the fourth quarter, with the game firmly in hand and the Falcons’ defense reeling. The fifth came on a scramble drill.
The Falcons held the Chiefs' rushing attack (without Kenneth Walker III) to 122 yards, but Mahomes would finish with 348 yards and five touchdowns – the first time he hit that scoring mark since 2022.
The rookie linebacker was making plays all over the field on Sunday. He finished with five tackles and a tackle for loss, but he was effective in both coverage and as a pass rusher. Perkins delivered big hits and was constantly finding himself around the football.
He has taken full advantage of Divine Deablo’s absence and is pushing for the staff to find ways to keep him on the field once the veteran is back healthy.
Michael Penix Jr. continued to struggle when the defense applied pressure. He was sacked three times and kept accelerating his progressions to check down and avoid getting hit. Even without a blitz, the Chiefs sent simulated pressure that still got Penix off his spot and sped him up. He struggled for most of the game, completing 23-of-43 passes for 286 yards (most of which came with the game out of reach) and an interception.
Until he can find his way under pressure, the Falcons’ offense will keep struggling.
A week after 12 penalties crushed the Falcons in Madrid, some ill-timed infractions came back to bite them in Atlanta. They committed nine penalties for 65 yards, but seven came on offense, and both defensive penalties extended drives that ended in touchdowns.
The worst of which was an offsides penalty that turned a field goal try into a touchdown at the end of the first half. Kansas City took a 14-3 lead into the locker room instead of 10-3, and received the ball to start the second half.
Jawaan Taylor and Jake Matthews were both flagged several times for false starts or holds that snuffed out offensive possessions.
"When you're playing good football teams, you have to be at your best," Kevin Stefanski said. "And we were not at our best."
But beyond the penalties, the Falcons turned the ball over twice in the fourth quarter. For the second week in a row, the Falcons could not get out of their own way.
Corey Levin took over for Ryan Neuzil at center and had one bad snap exchange that ended in a fumble (Penix jumped on it), but it snuffed out a potential touchdown opportunity. The offensive line did not have its best day, allowing three sacks and rushing for 100 yards.
New kicker Jake Moody connected on both field-goal attempts from 28 and 38 yards, but he nailed an onside kick in the fourth quarter to give the Falcons new life. He put the football right in the outstretched arms of Chris Blair, who toe-tapped on the sideline to steal a possession. That play capped a strong afternoon for the Falcons’ special teams.
Tommy Rees also made his first appearance on the sideline instead of in the booth this season. He was seen sitting with Penix during defensive possessions, but the offensive issues persisted, and his unit finished with five three-and-outs.
DeMarcco Hellams stepped in for recently traded Jessie Bates III at safety and was a big winner in this game. His first start since 2023 was outstanding, and he finished with a game-high 11 tackles.
The Falcons lost the fifth of their last six games heading into their bye week, and the schedule gets no easier after next Sunday. Atlanta will face the Vikings, Lions, and Browns before it finally eases up a bit, with winnable games against the Commanders and NFC South opponents to end the season.
At 3-7, any hope of their first winning season since 2017 feels bleak, but they are still alive in the woeful NFC South. They trail the first-place Panthers by one win, don’t hold the tiebreaker, but are still unbelievably alive in that race.
Both the players and Stefanski were confident after the game that they won't lose the locker room amid this skid, but the bye week will be a welcome sight for this team.
Garrett Chapman is a sports broadcaster, writer, and content creator based in Atlanta. He has several years of experience covering the Atlanta sports scene, college football, Georgia high school football, recruiting for 24/7 Sports, and the NFL. You can also hear him on Sports Radio 92.9 The Game.

title: FalconsSI Staff Unanimous in Falcons vs. Chiefs Predictions
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons are looking to get back on track in Week 10, but they face a difficult challenge with Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs coming to Mercedes-Benz Stadium.
Atlanta has lost four of its last five games and is coming off a disappointing performance against the Cincinnati Bengals in Madrid. Now, the Falcons will have to find a way to slow down another talented quarterback while dealing with significant changes to their own roster.
Kansas City will enter the matchup without running back Kenneth Walker III , which could make things more manageable for Atlanta’s struggling defense. However, Mahomes and Travis Kelce remain major threats, and the Chiefs have plenty of weapons to exploit the Falcons’ defensive weaknesses and deficiencies.
How will the game play out? The FalconsSI staff delivers its weekly predictions.
The Falcons have had some frustrating games this year, suffering through two weeks of Cooper Rush and a monsoon in Tampa, for example. But last week in Madrid was different. The Cincinnati Bengals simply showed the Falcons aren't good enough this year.
Their defense has been patched together with duct tape and one-year contracts, and it simply couldn't hold up against Joe Burrow, Ja'Marr Chase, and Tee Higgins. General manager Ian Cunningham saw the same thing we did, and rather than deluding himself into thinking 3-6 in a weak NFC South was good enough, he sold at the trade deadline.
Now Patrick Mahomes and Travis Kelce come to Mercedes-Benz Stadium, and the Falcons are without All-Pro safety Jessie Bates III after trading him to the Jaguars. Mahomes and the Chiefs aren't as explosive as the Bengals, but, well, they're still Mahomes and the Chiefs... and they're better on defense.
We'll see if Michael Penix Jr. and the offense can play well enough to take another step towards feeling good about Penix in 2027, but the Falcons are staring 3-7 in the face.
Prediction: Chiefs 31, Falcons 17
The notion of the Falcons playing up to the competition is fading away.
Plus, there’s a belief that Atlanta is now playing for draft positioning instead of ending its playoff drought.
The Chiefs present too many issues for the Falcons. We all know what Patrick Mahomes can do in the passing attack. And we all watched the Atlanta secondary struggle with Bengals playmakers in Madrid. With Kenneth Walker III out, that may soften the blow against the Falcons’ dwindling run defense .
Offensively, Atlanta is looking pretty “eh.” Michael Penix Jr. has gotten off of his heater and must prove himself as the franchise quarterback against one of the top pass defenses in the league. Additionally, Kansas City is top-10 at stopping the run and will likely stack boxes to stonewall Bijan Robinson as the Falcons deal with the key loss of powerback Brian Robinson Jr.
Atlanta is looking at a third consecutive loss on the road to the 2027 NFL Draft.
Prediction: Chiefs 34, Falcons 21
The Falcons have lost four of their last five, and the road to snapping that skid will run through the Kansas City Chiefs. The perennial contenders will be without Kenneth Walker, but Patrick Mahomes and Travis Kelce are still willing and able to run wild on a reeling Falcons defense that just moved Jessie Bates.
On offense, Corey Levin will be taking over at center , and he'll have a pretty difficult challenge opposite him.
This should be a tight game, but I'm not sure the Falcons can overcome this team opposite them right now.
Prediction: Chiefs 20, Falcons 17
Expects a closer game with Walker sidelined, but Mahomes will ultimately make the difference.
Atlanta’s defense has continued to struggle, and the departure of Bates doesn’t provide much confidence that things will improve against Kansas City’s passing attack.
The Falcons also face questions offensively with a new starting center stepping into the lineup midway through the season. That transition could create additional problems against a talented Chiefs defense.
Atlanta remains competitive, but Kansas City will pull away late to secure the victory.
Prediction: Chiefs 23, Falcons 16
Despite being only a half game back from first place in the division, it really seems like the clock is ticking on the Falcons’ season. The performances in recent weeks and the trades the Falcons made at the deadline make this game feel like a “crap or get off the pot” moment for this team.
There is hope, though. The Chiefs are good, but the Falcons have beaten better teams this year (which sounds crazy given they’ve only won three games). The blueprint for beating the Chiefs is pretty straightforward: stop the run.
The issue is, the Falcons have struggled to do that, especially against inside runs, and the Chiefs are an inside-running team. If they can pull it off, the Falcons’ pass defense matches up well against the Chiefs’ passing offense on paper (even without Jessie Bates).
On the other side of the ball, the Chiefs’ defense has been solid, but I think they have a real weakness in the secondary with the injury to their rookie Mansoor Delane. To exploit it, though, the Falcons will need to get the run game going. Their passing offense has been pretty ineffective when the ground game stalls.
This is a game the Falcons can win... but whether they will is a different story.
Prediction: Chiefs 24, Falcons 16
Despite differences in the projected final scores, all five contributors are picking Kansas City to win in Week 10.
The absence of Kenneth Walker could give Atlanta an opportunity to make this a more competitive matchup, but Mahomes remains the biggest difference-maker heading into Sunday.
For the Falcons, the challenge will be finding a way to slow down Kansas City’s passing attack while getting enough production from Penix and the offense.
Atlanta needs a win to stop its recent slide, but the consensus among our staff is that the Chiefs will leave Mercedes-Benz Stadium with another victory.
Kickoff is set for 1:00 p.m. EST at Mercedes-Benz Stadium and will be shown on CBS.

title: Falcons Beleaguered Defense Catches a Break vs. Chiefs
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons received some significant injury news ahead of their Week 10 matchup against the Kansas City Chiefs. Star running back Kenneth Walker III has been ruled out for Sunday’s game with a groin injury, giving Atlanta’s defense a major break heading into one of its toughest matchups of the season.
NFL insider Jordan Schultz first reported the news Saturday, saying Walker would not suit up against the Falcons. Schultz also noted the injury isn't considered a long-term concern, but Kansas City is playing it safe with its star running back.
Walker has been one of the NFL's most productive running backs this season.
Through eight games, he has rushed for 872 yards and seven touchdowns while averaging an impressive 5.5 yards per carry. His 109 rushing yards per game lead the NFL, and he currently ranks second in total rushing yards behind Atlanta’s Bijan Robinson.
Losing that kind of production is a major blow for Kansas City, but it is a good opportunity for a struggling Falcons run defense that will no longer have to prepare for one of the league’s most dangerous ball carriers.
Without their leading running back, Kansas City will likely turn to rookie Emmett Johnson to handle an expanded workload.
The Falcons' run defense began the season as one of its strengths, but it has been pushed around in recent weeks , including 324 yards in a loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.
Johnson has shown some promise in limited opportunities, recording 111 rushing yards and a touchdown on 26 carries. He has also contributed in the passing game, totaling 237 receiving yards and another touchdown on 14 receptions.
While Johnson can certainly make plays, replacing a back who has averaged 109 rushing yards per game is a significant challenge.
For Atlanta, this creates an opportunity to put more attention on Patrick Mahomes and the Chiefs’ passing attack. The Falcons can potentially be more aggressive defensively without having to account for Walker’s ability to consistently break off explosive runs and control the ground game.
That does not mean Kansas City suddenly becomes an easy matchup. Mahomes remains one of the NFL’s most dangerous quarterbacks, and the Chiefs have plenty of weapons that can create problems for Atlanta’s defense.
However, losing Walker takes away a major component of Kansas City’s offensive identity.
The Falcons have their own injury concerns heading into Sunday, but this is unquestionably encouraging news for Atlanta. Facing a Chiefs offense without the NFL’s second leading rusher is a considerably different challenge than preparing for one with Walker in the backfield.
Atlanta still has to take advantage of the opportunity, but the latest injury news gives the Falcons a major break heading into Sunday’s showdown.

title: Jessie Bates III Recalls ‘Teary-Eyed’ Falcons Goodbye after Trade to Jaguars
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons may not have enjoyed the on-field success that Jessie Bates III may have hoped for.
But the franchise is dear in the star free safety’s heart after spending 3.5 seasons in Flowery Branch.
The All-Pro selections and his momentum-swinging defensive plays, including his ball-hawking interceptions and patented rendition of the “Peanut Punch,” come secondary to the impact he and the franchise had on each other as he heads to the Jacksonville Jaguars via trade .
“You spend somewhere four years; you create relationships, you create bonds that’ll last a lifetime,” Bates told Juston Lewis of the Jacksonville-Times Union .
“There are people over there from the staff, the players, the janitors, the cafeteria people – those are my people. I would see those people every single day, and they did a lot for me. So there’s so much appreciation and love for those guys and girls over there.”
Bates was the first move Atlanta made as sellers in this year’s trade deadline .
On Monday, the Falcons moved the nine-year NFL veteran to Jacksonville for a 2027 NFL Draft second-round pick and a 2028 fifth-rounder.
It marked the end of an era for one of Atlanta’s fan favorites who withstood three different coaches, no playoff appearances, and a world of “what-ifs.”
Bates had become a staple for the Falcons, having been named a team captain and sharing a locker with potential franchise quarterback Michael Penix Jr.
Now he leaves behind the foundation he’s built for a fresh start for a Super Bowl contender.
“It was tough,” Bates said when asked about the moment he departed the Falcons facility. “When I left that building, there were teary eyes from myself and coaches, trainers, equipment guys – a lot of love there. I take pride in not just being a great football player, but just being a great person, being a great light in the building.”
The rationale behind the Bates-to-Jags trade was that the Falcons looked as though they weren’t going to re-sign the safety as he entered unrestricted free agency following the season. At 29, Bates’ age was a factor in the decision, as the Falcons look to start a youth movement and build through the draft .
The Bates move predated the Falcons getting another draft pick for starting center Ryan Neuzil . He was traded on Tuesday to the Baltimore Ravens for guard Andrew Vorhees on an expiring deal and a conditional 2028 sixth-round pick.
On Friday, the Falcons inked younger players to multiyear deals, defensive end Cameron Thomas (three years, $33 million) and cornerback CJ Henderson (two years, $20 million) .
Fans will have to wait to see Bates' debut for the Jaguars. Head coach Liam Coen said Bates will not play against the 1-7 Titans, with no bye week a factor. The Jaguars have already had their bye, but the Falcons haven't. His decision gives Bates the week off that he didn't get with the Falcons.
Meanwhile, the Falcons (3-6) will make their first post-Bates appearance when the Kansas City Chiefs (6-2) come to town for an NFL Week 10 clash. DeMarcco Hellams is expected to step into the free safety role. The Falcons enter their bye week after facing the Chiefs.
Kickoff is also at 1 p.m. and will be aired on CBS.

title: Falcons' Biggest Defensive Problem Is Becoming Impossible to Ignore
full_text:
ATLANTA – The Atlanta Falcons are coming off the fourth loss in five games, and they just traded away their best defender , Jessie Bates III. A once-dominant run defense is reeling, having allowed 98 yards or more in each of those games.
Not to say the Falcons have always struggled against the run, because they haven’t.
In the first four weeks, they allowed 193 combined yards (2.7 yards per carry) and were the NFL’s best run defense by a wide margin. Then, Derrick Henry and the Ravens ran wild in Week 5, piling up 208 yards on the ground. From there, it snowballed, and the Falcons have been the league’s third-worst team since that overtime loss.
And the defensive issues haven’t stopped there.
The Falcons were eighth in defensive EPA, second in defensive success rate, and leading the league in quarterback pressure rates over those first four weeks. But like the run defense, those numbers have plummeted to 22nd, 30th, and 21st in the games since.
Injuries to Za’Darius Smith, Samson Ebukam, and Divine Deablo in the front seven have hurt, as have the absences of C.J. Henderson and A.J. Terrell Jr. on the back end. But Falcons defensive coordinator Jeff Ulbrich was the first to take ownership of the sharp regression, saying the team has been playing well below expectations.
“That's the 100% truth, and I think everybody is taking that upon themselves,” Ulbrich said Wednesday. “I do feel fortunate that we have a group of a bunch of thumb pointers, where [it’s], ‘What can I do more?’ I feel like we have that collectively.”
But these issues start on the ground, the proclaimed identity of this Falcons’ defense.
“We're just not playing it well enough, so that's me, from a scheme perspective, making sure that we're getting guys in the right spaces to be successful,” he said. “At times, we've done that and didn't play well enough. There are times we didn't do that (scheme-wise), and it wasn’t on the players; it was 100% on coaching.
“We all have to do more and do better in regard to defending the run.”
The numbers have been scary, but the defensive coordinator insisted there is no ‘panic’ within the locker room about getting back on track, but there might be if these issues continue on into Sunday. The Kansas City Chiefs are coming to town, and there is no room for error in a game like this.
A unit typically known for its future Hall of Fame quarterback Patrick Mahomes is now feared for what it can do on the ground. Kenneth Walker III (872) ranks second only to Bijan Robinson (880) in rushing yards and threatens to continue the Falcons' run-defense slide.
Ulbrich said stopping a back like this is going to “take all 11.” Walker can get downhill quickly and create havoc at the second level if defenders don’t stick to their run fits or tackle well.
“That's where we have to be at our best. And it's a unique challenge in that way because there's not a whole lot of backs like him,” he explained. “On top of all that, he has gas. He has real finishing speed, and he's a guy that can hit the home run at any time. There's a reason I think he's the first- or second-most efficient runner in the league right now. It’s going to be a great challenge.”
Walker will be the next big challenge for the Falcons, but stopping a back like this is what they want to be known for. Doing it consistently has eluded them in recent weeks.
“I've never been a part of a great defense that didn't defend the run well,” Ulbrich said. “That has to become part of who we are. That has to become part of our identity. And right now it is not.”
The 3-6 Falcons still have time to rediscover the defensive identity that made them one of the NFL's best units early in the season. Those opportunities are running out.
With the bye week coming after Sunday's matchup, the Falcons desperately need to respond against Walker and the Chiefs. If they can't, their season could slip further out of reach, and they have one glaring issue to blame.

title: Falcons Sign Redeemed CB to 2-Year Contract Extension
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons are rewarding one of their biggest defensive surprises this season, agreeing to a two-year contract extension with cornerback C.J. Henderson. The deal is worth up to $20 million with $11 million guaranteed, according to Ian Rapoport , tying the team financially to Henderson for next season with a club option in 2028.
Henderson was the second of two extensions announced by the Falcons on Friday. Edge rusher Cameron Thomas got a three-year deal worth up to $33 million as well.
Henderson stepped into a starting outside cornerback role after A.J. Terrell suffered an injury in Week 2 and has taken full advantage of the opportunity.
What initially appeared to be a temporary replacement assignment has turned into a breakout season for the veteran defensive back, who has established himself as an important piece of Atlanta’s secondary. He was officially moved ahead of Mike Hughes on the depth chart this week.
The two-year extension gives Henderson additional security while allowing the Falcons to retain a player who has become increasingly valuable to their defense. PFF has him as the No. 22-ranked cornerback in the NFL, the highest of any Falcons player.
Through eight games, Henderson has recorded 41 total tackles, 32 solo tackles, nine passes defended, and one forced fumble. His nine pass breakups are already a career high, surpassing his previous best of six, which he recorded during the 2020 and 2022 seasons.
His production has been particularly impressive considering the circumstances surrounding his expanded role. Henderson entered the season competing for opportunities in Atlanta’s secondary, but Terrell’s injury created an opening that he has not relinquished.
The 28-year-old has demonstrated the ability to handle consistent responsibilities on the outside while providing the Falcons with another dependable option in coverage. His performance has also helped Atlanta navigate an important injury in its defensive backfield without having to completely overhaul its secondary.
Henderson’s emergence is especially notable given his NFL journey. The Jacksonville Jaguars selected him ninth overall in the 2020 NFL Draft out of Florida. He spent the first part of his career in Jacksonville before moving to the Carolina Panthers, where he played three seasons.
After appearing in just four games with Atlanta last season, Henderson has found a much larger opportunity in 2026. He entered the year with 33 career starts and has continued to build on that experience with an expanded role.
For general manager Ian Cunningham and the Falcons, extending Henderson represents an investment in a player who has earned a larger place in the team’s defensive plans.
Henderson has earned a starting spot at one of the outside corners, which could push Avieon Terrell inside to nickel. Billy Bowman Jr. hasn't been able to stay healthy long enough to solidify a spot there, and Sydney Brown is a depth piece forced to play starting minutes.
The extension also provides some continuity for a secondary that has dealt with personnel changes throughout the season.
Henderson arrived in Atlanta looking for an opportunity to reestablish himself in the NFL. He delivered the best statistical season of his career and earned a two-year extension from the Falcons.

title: Falcons Edge Cameron Thomas Gets Significant Contract Extension
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons are rewarding one of their biggest defensive surprises, agreeing to a three-year contract extension with edge rusher Cameron Thomas worth up to $33 million, according to the team.
The agreement keeps Thomas under contract with the Falcons through the 2029 season. Equity Sports CEO Chris Cabott, Falcons general manager Ian Cunningham, and senior vice president Bryce Johnston finalized the deal Thursday night.
For Thomas, the extension represents a significant career turnaround after spending several seasons searching for consistency and an opportunity to establish himself in the NFL.
A third-round pick by the Arizona Cardinals in 2022, Thomas initially struggled to find his footing in the league. He recorded three sacks as a rookie but managed just 19 tackles and no sacks in 15 appearances during his second season.
His career took another turn in 2024 when Arizona traded him to the Kansas City Chiefs. However, his opportunity in Kansas City never developed, as he appeared in just four games before eventually joining the Cleveland Browns.
Cleveland provided Thomas with an opportunity to rebuild his career. He appeared in five games with the Browns in 2024, recording 10 tackles and one sack.
Thomas returned to Cleveland for the 2025 season and played in all 17 games. He finished with 27 tackles and 2.5 sacks, establishing career highs in several defensive categories and demonstrating his ability to contribute as part of an NFL defensive rotation.
That production caught Atlanta’s attention.
The Falcons signed Thomas to a one-year contract in March 2026 , giving him another opportunity to prove he could become a consistent contributor. The move has turned into a significant success for Cunningham and Atlanta’s front office.
Through nine games in the 2026 season, Thomas has recorded 25 tackles, two sacks, one forced fumble and one pass deflection. He has also generated 25 quarterback pressures, according to Pro Football Focus.
His emergence has been particularly important for a Falcons defense looking to maintain consistent pressure on opposing quarterbacks. Thomas has provided another productive option along the defensive front while demonstrating the versatility to contribute against the run and pass.
Now, Atlanta is making sure he remains part of its plans.
The three-year extension worth up to $33 million is a substantial reward for a player who joined the organization on a one-year deal just months ago.
Thomas has gone from struggling to find a consistent role in Kansas City to becoming a starting-caliber contributor in Atlanta. The Falcons clearly believe his best football is still ahead of him, and the new agreement gives him an opportunity to continue building on his breakout through the 2029 season.

title: Falcons Trade Deadline Moves Tell One Story, Atlanta’s Leaders Tell Another
full_text:
After dropping to 3-6 and becoming trade-deadline sellers, the resounding narrative has been that the Atlanta Falcons are mailing it in on the 2026 season and building for the future.
That’s not the case, says Bijan Robinson .
“I know people outside of here think that we’re just plummeting the season,” Robinson told reporters on Wednesday. “Nah man, we’re focusing on this week, going to take it one game at a time, and go from there. Try to make a push; that’s where we’re at right now.”
Robinson said head coach Kevin Stefanski met with the Falcons’ leadership committee to ensure players remained on the same page and weren’t moping after the team’s trade-deadline moves. The running back said the committee took Stefanski’s message to heart and described the atmosphere inside Atlanta’s locker room as “positive.”
On Monday, a day after the 34-17 Madrid debacle against the Cincinnati Bengals , Atlanta made shocking moves to trade safety Jessie Bates III after four years with the team. Center Ryan Neuzil was moved on Tuesday in a buzzer-beating deal to the Baltimore Ravens.
For Bates, Atlanta got a 2027 NFL Draft second-round pick and a 2028 fifth-rounder. In exchange for Neuzil, Atlanta received guard Andrew Vorhees and a 2028 sixth-round pick.
“We’re trying to win regardless, man,” Robinson said. “We understand that we got to make some moves, but it doesn’t [change] the fact that we’re still trying to get to where we want to get to in the season.”
Losing four of its last five, the Falcons look to be on a downward trend.
“I truly believe that we have the team and the guys that are going to rally and flip the script,” said quarterback Michael Penix Jr . “We got a lot of guys that care. Not just sitting here, sulking like, ‘We’re at 3-6 right now.’ We have to focus on what’s in front of us.”
But the fact of the matter is the Falcons are very much still in play for the NFC South divisional title, winning which would advance the franchise to the NFL playoffs for the first time since the 2017-2018 season.
Entering Week 10, Atlanta is a half game back from No. 1 in the NFC South, trailing the Carolina Panthers (3-5), New Orleans Saints (3-5), and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers (3-6) in that order.
“We’re still in it,” Penix said. “We got an eight-game season left, and we really want to win all eight.”
But welcome to the NFC South, where you can simultaneously compete for the division crown and draft positioning. If the season ended today, the Falcons would have the 10th overall pick and pick Georgia linebacker Chris Cole, according to Tankathon .
The absurdity of taking a linebacker at No. 10 notwithstanding, the Falcons find themselves balancing two competing timelines: a front office making moves with the future in mind and a locker room still fighting for the present. Whether intentional or not, Atlanta’s trade-deadline decisions suggest a different direction from the one its players envision.
“That’s in no way a focus for me and us,” Stefanski said of Atlanta’s current draft standing. “We talk about long-term, short-term, but that’s not really a focus for us.”
Atlanta’s coming weeks are unrelenting.
This Sunday, Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs (6-2) come to town. Then is the bye week.
Afterward, Atlanta will head to the Minnesota Vikings on Nov. 29 for the “Kirk Cousins Bowl,” then return home to face the Detroit Lions.
Whether the Falcons can turn their belief into wins remains to be seen. But with the front office already looking toward the future, the remaining schedule will test just how much this team has left to play for.
Falcons-Chiefs kicks off at 1 p.m. at Mercedes-Benz Stadium. CBS will air the game.
Sign up for our free Atlanta Falcons newsletter and follow us and 30,000 Falcons fans on Facebook and X for the latest news!
Gerald Thomas, III, is a national award-winning reporter contributing to Atlanta Falcons On SI. He has several years of writing and editorial experience, including covering college athletics under the USA TODAY umbrella.

title: These 4 Ravens Youngsters Must Take The Leap vs Chargers Monday Night
full_text:
The Ravens cannot lose to the Chargers Monday night.
Correction: the Ravens certainly could manage to lose to a previously-winless outfit at home on Monday night, they just can’t expect anything else they do this season to matter if that happens. Given their propensity to choke away games and with just three wins in their last 12 home games and having dropped four in a row in primetime at M&T Bank Stadium, there is certainly reason for concern.
The gravity of the situation weighed on rookie head coach Jesse Minter, who continues to look overmatched, and delivered strange messaging about Lamar Jackson’s thumb surgery . And who seemed to want to embrace being more of a bad cop, but he probably just doesn’t have it in him and he’s been thoroughly runover by a veteran roster to this point, begging questions about him and rookie offensive coordinator Declan Doyle.
Minter hinted at changes in terms of playing time and roles, and, well, after failing to acknowledge the franchise’s sweeping and overarching roster failures at the trade deadline, stripping underperforming players of their role is about all Minter can do. And that must be happening at critical position groups on both sides of the ball, and a path must be created for more youngsters to make a bigger impact.
“I'm excited for us to sort of re-establish our identity,” Minter said last week. “[With] lineup changes, I think those are all individual basis. But there's certain things that we have to have really high standards for. So, we'll see how it all shakes out."
Let’s hope is shakes out with these young players getting more of an opportunity to impact the football game, starting now.
Feels like a long time ago that he was getting as much pre-season hype as any rookie in the NFL. Oh, it was constant . Keep in mind, the third-round pick was going against one of the most pathetic secondaries in the NFL in practice – no matter how heavily failing general manager Eric DeCosta over-drafted the DBs or overpaid them. So there’s that.
And the Ravens faced some preseason defenses that weren’t doing much. But we all know DeCosta’s track record drafting receivers is abysmal, which is why he’s talked about the need to keep swinging. With Jacoby Brissett at quarterback now, the ability to push the ball deep down the seam is there and Lane has clearly always been crafted to do most of his early damage in the slot. It’s time to see if they can unlock his kid a little bit and give him something positive to take into the offseason.
Injuries to him and to the QBs have sapped that early momentum.
No one stands to gain more than him from Brissett’s arrival. He has some of the attributed Trey McBride had in Arizona and McBride rewrote the NFL history books for TEs with Brissett. He’s back from his hand injury for a few weeks now, and needs to be unleashed from the slot, too. Play action deep shots , go routes, double moves.
This offense is utterly pathetic, it lacks any lack or verve outside of Zay Flowers and this fifth-round pick has some acceleration in his game. He should he unleashed against the Chargers linebackers and a secondary that is without All Pro hybrid defender Derwin James.
The coaching staff loves to hype him, but he’s had to play second-fiddle to $60M alleged-closer Trey Hendrickson ( a bust so far no matter how the Ravens want to couch it ) but he needs to get a real chance to rush from the inside and the outside. Especially if Henrickson is going to have his right hand wrapped up like crazy.
He’s tied for first on the team with 3.5 sacks – with injured Tavius Robinson – and has shown an ability to twist in the A Gap and make things happen. The Chargers interior offensive line is the dregs of the NFL and has been for years. Can we get him unleashed a little bit here in a creative manner?
If the Ravens are going to persists on running $19.3M corner Marlon Humphrey against top outside receivers, only to get shredded, then close up shop. He should have been a slot corner years ago; he can’t win outside and there is reason to think Justin Herbert has hit rock bottom for the Chargers and can only get better from here .
Tampa needs to get a chance to show what he can do. He’s healthy, which has been a real problem, and has the length and levers and profile to fit these zone concepts maybe more than some others who have played in front of him. The Chargers do not have a pass catcher with 300 yards or two touchdowns; seems like the perfect time to make this switch and start riding this kid after hyping him up as some kind of draft steal to the local media for years.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: Jacoby Brissett Will Improve  Ravens Offense In These 3 Critical Areas
full_text:
Jacoby Brissett will give the Ravens an opportunity to operate a downfield passing game in ways they never could under Snoop Huntley.
As much as people in Owings Mills have pretended that Huntley is something he’s not, the reality is the scope of Baltimore’s passing game has crumbled when he has had to step in for Lamar Jackson over the years. And there is every reason to believe Jackson is not throwing another pass this season , and maybe never again in Baltimore. And therefore any hopes they have of mustering even a pedestrian pass game rest with the ability to keep Brissett upright; and with this offensive line, that’s going to be no small task .
Having to drop into a new locker room to try to save a season with coaches and players you do not know and in a system that is fairly foreign is a lot to ask anyone. Let alone someone about to turn 34 without great mobility who was just demoted to third-string in Arizona. But that’s where Brissett and the Ravens find themselves.
Brissett will absolutely improve their ability to facilitate certain parts of this offseason, and give them a fighting chance to try to find out what youngsters like Ja’Kobi Lane  and Matthew Hibner and Josh Cuevas can do catching the football .
He’s a gamer, and he won’t go down without a fight.
“I've been super impressed by him,” rookie offensive coordinator Declan Doyle said, “just being able to work with him as he's picking up our offense very quickly, and also being able to provide a little bit of stability to the situation. But really excited about him being here and helping us."
Here’s where Brissett can help the Ravens the most:
Two of the core principles Doyle wanted to emphasize here have fallen totally by the wayside. The under-center running and passing game have washed away with Jackson not finishing a football game since Week 3 and the offensive line is once again one of the worst in the NFL. And with Huntley and then undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano thrust into duty, the play action pass game has faded away, too.
Brissett will lean into that heavily, and it should become more of a staple again.
Since Week 4, the Ravens have attempted just 38 play action passes, that’s 25th in the NFL. Those passes have averaged just 5.9 yards/attempt, that’s, frankly, pathetic and ranks 28th in the NFL since Week 4. And Ravens quarterbacks have completed just 55% of their play-action passes in that span, also 28th in the NFL.
All we heard all spring and summer long was that Doyle was a “genius” because his nascent playbook was loaded with “explosive” plays. This offense is desperate for them now, and getting Zay Flowers going again.
“He's been awesome,” Brissett said Doyle. “What he's thinking as far as the play structure and then obviously how we're attacking the defense, he's very vocal about it. I think that cleans up the communication. I know what he's thinking."
Brissett threw to tight ends more than any QB in the NFL during his two years in Arizona. More even than Jackson. He did it 33% of the time and helped dynamic TE Trey McBride take his game to historic levels . He doesn’t have that guy here, but it’s hard to think that Hibner, with the ability to win with some straight-line speed and a double move won’t become a favorite target if the Ravens do the right thing.
Getting Mark Andrews off the field and out of the way is the only thing to do with his mobility a detriment. They need to get these young TEs in the slot and get them running seam routes that Brissett loves to chuck downfield. Hibner was averaging 9.0 YAC/catch with Jackson in a very limited sample.
If Doyle wants to keep running 11 personnel and then wondering why he can’t run or throw the ball in the second half of games, then maybe he’s just over his head. Lane is even a Joker TE of sorts in the seam.
Brissett is going to throw it 20 yards or more downfield about 10 percent of the time and one of every three attempts with the Cardinals went at least 15 yards downfield – on par with league averages. He has a far bigger arm than Huntley. He isn’t afraid to throw it out of his own endzone.
He will force defenses to respect that and show it early in games to keep them honest in ways we just haven’t seen since Jackson hurt his ankle in early October. He also loves throwing crossers – Brissett had a 113.5 rating on those routes in Arizona – and that’s Flowers specialty coming across the face of the defense. Brissett also excels on outs – 79% completions and 103.9 rating with the Cardinals – and Flowers has been targeted on those routes more than any other.
"We all know he can throw the ball," Flowers said. "He can spin it. But he's just been connecting with us, telling us how he feels about a route, where we should be [and] talking to 'D-Hen' about certain things coming out of the backfield. So, he's just letting his experience show."
Flowers shouldn’t be getting shutout in the boxscore anymore.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: The Ravens Defense Hasn't Had a True Playmaker For Years. And It's Only Getting Worse
full_text:
The Ravens defense hasn’t ever really made a big play in the postseason through Lamar Jackson’s entire career.
Almost like that’s how they were built and hardwired. Because, well, they are .
You cannot go this long with reasonable questions being asked about which players will step up and get the sack or force the fumble or pick off the pass that cements a quality win over an elite opponent with any regularity and not have a fundamental problem. In fact, as much as folks in Owings Mills want to talk about their “culture” as if it’s some winning beacon as they constantly focus on their past and not their present, the reality of their “culture” is overpaid defensive players who don’t deliver , and are especially bad blowing leads and handling the fourth quarter and it spans over four coordinators, now, and two head coaches.
The modern game will come down to a handful of plays, over the course of three hours, in which your blue-chip guys have to be better than theirs. Especially on the defensive side of the ball with every rule change and point of emphasis implemented to incentivize scoring. And for all of Lamar Jackson’s unique brilliance, it still has not been enough to overcome a defense hardwired for failure, to the point that even much-hyper rookie head coach and veteran defensive coordinator Jesse Minter has been no match for it.
Hall of Fame quarterback Kurt Warner, who has watched plenty of Ravens film over years, sees a lot of what I see – not enough go-to guys in the biggest moments who can impact the quarterback, or the football in flight, to put games away. And with $160M put into the defense alone this year, and with Minter’s arrival supposedly a panacea, and with him fully expected to take the defense’s most talented player, Kyle Hamilton, to another level ( it's been just the opposite) , there is reason for concern about the state of affairs.
“It really comes down to can you make the game-changing play?” Warner explained when sizing up this defense. “Can you force a fumble? Can you create, you know, a sack early on in the downs where somebody gets behind the sticks?  A sack, fumble, whatever those things are. That, to me is where the game really skews defensively, because it's hard to just play every down defense in this NFL … “And so that's really what this game comes down to so often on the defensive side is can we create negative plays?"
Instead of the above, the Ravens have the most lifeless and listless second-half defense in the NFL. Everybody shrinks, and no one makes the big play.
They do not have a second-half interception this season despite being throw as much as team in football. Their “closer” Trey Hendrickson (guaranteed a massive $60M for two seasons) hasn’t shown up in the fourth quarter all season and has five total passers in that quarter this season. (Most of general manager Eric DeCosta’s big moves have backfired, massively, and this one is unlikely to age well, either ). They rank 26th in pressure rate in the fourth quarter as a team.
Sadly, that’s become Ravens Football. On defense, that’s how you Play Like A Raven, and Minter has only made it worse.
Only four teams have produced fewer takeaways than the Ravens (who have just nine). No one on this teams has even four sacks – a year ago no one had over five for the season – and Tavius Robinson remains tied for the team lead with 3.5 and he went on season-ending IR weeks ago. Middle linebacker Roquan Smith is paid $20M a year and provides no big plays or momentum-changing hits anymore (he hasn’t for years), and their entire group of defensive backs have combined for zero interceptions all season (Hamilton got his playing linebacker.
Minter’s defense with the Chargers was top three in interceptions per passing attempts his two years there, but it remains the dregs in Baltimore. And there is no reason to expect that to change anytime soon, even if he gets Smith off the field in dime packages and benches $19M corner Marlon Humphrey like he should . Can Minter coach a team and call a defense at the same time, or should Anthony Weaver take over? They have major evaluation issues and roster-construction issues that go well beyond all the assistant coaches and coordinators who have been fired the past four years.
“It is kind of amazing that this has been an issue for the Ravens for years,” Warner said, “and you just say, ‘How does it continue to be an issue with either the same guys, or new guys and with new coaches.' It's hard to put your finger on.”
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: Four Storylines For Ravens' Primetime Matchup vs. Chargers
full_text:
Coming off a much-needed mini-bye after having last played on Nov. 5, the Baltimore Ravens will be at home again and looking to snap a four-game losing streak in Week 10 for their fourth straight game against an AFC opponent when they take on the Los Angeles Chargers on Monday night at M&T Bank Stadium.
Going up against the only team in the league without a win and needing to bounce back from getting shellacked in primetime, the Ravens currently have the worst record in the AFC North at 4-5 but have a golden opportunity to get back to .500 with a win.
There are several intriguing storylines surrounding this matchup between these two teams that entered the season with Super Bowl aspirations. Here are the top four.
The 11-year veteran will be the Ravens' fourth different starting quarterback this season after being acquired via trade nearly 10 days ago. He's already beaten the Chargers once this year in the season opener, when he led the Arizona Cardinals to a 26-14 upset win in which he went  27-of-37 for 277 passing yards and a touchdown with no interceptions and a passer rating of 103.1. Brissett compared learning offensive coordinator Declan Doyle's scheme to a "crash course," but both he and the team are confident in his ability to comprehend and operate it at a high level .
"I would just say, [I'm] very, very impressed with how fast he's learned what we're doing," head coach Jesse Minter said. "I don't sit in every offensive meeting, but just the fact that the work that he put in over the weekend and the work that he put in kind of leading up to Wednesday [because] practice didn't operate at any sort of different level for having a guy that literally just got here."
As for how Brissett's presence under center will elevate the offense, he doesn't pose a threat with his legs like two-time MVP Lamar Jackson or even Pro Bowl backup Tyler Huntley. However, his passing ability is second only to Jackson's among Ravens quarterbacks this season, which will help get both the running and passing game back on track. He'll be able to get the ball in the hands of the playmakers through the air accurately in space, and the Chargers won't be able to load the box to slow down star running back Derrick Henry nearly as much as the Ravens' last four opponents did.
Coming out of what was essentially a mini-bye, Minter all but vowed that there would be some pivotal changes to both the personnel deployment and overall approach that the Ravens have had on the side of the ball that is supposed to be his expertise but has given up an average of nearly 35 points in their last three games. While he wouldn't get into specifics about which players could have their playing time reduced or increased, he reiterated that their top priority remains the same.
"I probably take as much pride of not giving up explosives as any defensive coach in the league, and obviously that's not showing up," Minter said. "It's all lip service right now. That's really, to me, major concern No. 1 from a defensive standpoint is limiting the explosive plays.
"If somebody goes on an 18-play drive and scores a touchdown on us, tip your hat and find different ways to get them off rhythm. But the one play, getting behind a coverage or whatever, those are the plays we have to eliminate."
When it comes to players who should have their roles on defense reduced or changed, four-time Pro Bowl cornerback Marlon Humphrey is at the top of that list. Having him predominantly play on the outside this season has made him a big-play magnet. Minter might consider playing him more in the slot, where he's had his best seasons, or continue rotating him with fellow veteran Chidobe Awuzie and third-year pro T.J. Tampa. Other players who've shown they're deserving more playing time on that side of the ball are veteran safety K'Von Wallace and undrafted rookie outside linebacker Ethan Burke.
The only roster, coaching staff and organization as a whole that the Ravens' first-year head coach is more familiar with than his own is the one he'll be going up against on Monday night. He spent the previous two seasons as the Chargers' defensive coordinator, where he went up against two-time Pro Bowl quarterback Justin Herbert every day in practice and masked the deficiencies of the defensive personnel by amplifying their strengths. His history with Los Angeles head coach Jim Harbaugh goes back even further, as the two won a national championship together at the University of Michigan in 2023.
To call this matchup one between familiar foes is an understatement to say the least but with extra prep time off a mini bye and desperately needing to snap this current losing skid, Minter was likely imparting as much of his knowledge of how to attack his former team on his assistants since their last game ended.
"You're going against somebody you care a lot about, which sometimes makes it even more competitive," Minter said. "I know how Jim feels about it, I'm sure. So, I'm excited about the challenge. I think after the game it's great to be able to catch up and say hey to a bunch of those guys. But obviously, [there's] major, major focus on our team, our players [and] getting our team ready to play at a high level. [I'm] excited to play in primetime in front of our fans and give them something to cheer about."
Staying on the topic of the Ravens Flock, it's been a season and a half since the team last won a nationally televised game at M&T Bank Stadium. They've not only lost their last four primetime games on their home turf, but each loss has been more embarrassing than the last, from getting steamrolled by the Detroit Lions for 224 yards in Week 3 last year to getting routed by the Cincinnati Bengals last Thanksgiving and allowing the eventual AFC champion New England Patriots to rally from an 11-point fourth-quarter deficit in Week 16 last year.
Their first crack at redemption this season couldn't have gone any worse, as they were blown out by the Jacksonville Jaguars in their last game, but they were also being led by a hobbled, undrafted rookie free agent at quarterback , making his first career start. With a more experienced and capable starting quarterback in Brissett, going up against what has been the worst team in the league by virtue of their winless record and what they've shown on tape, there's no reason that the Ravens fans in attendance shouldn't go home with their heads held high after a victory for the first time since the 2024 Wildcard round. In that game, they ran the Pittsburgh Steelers out of two and held them to under 20 points for the second time that season.
Josh is a writer for Baltimore Ravens On SI focusing primarily on original content and reporting. He provides analysis, breakdowns, profiles, and reports on important news and transactions from and about the Ravens. His professional resume as a sports reporter includes covering local events, teams, and athletes in his hometown of Anchorage, Alaska for Anchorage Daily News. His coverage on the Ravens and other NFL teams has been featured on Heavy.com/sports, Maryland Sports Blog and most recently Baltimore Beatdown from 2021 until 2025.

title: Don't Blame Mark Andrews For His Brutal 2026 Season; Blame Eric DeCosta
full_text:
Don’t blame Mark Andrews for the Baltimore Ravens having some of the worst tight-end production in the NFL. It’s really not his fault.
He’s been in decline for three years and obvious signs of athletic regression were there throughout the 2024 season – let alone last year when general manager Eric DeCosta made one of the more impetuous decisions in modern franchise history and gave Andrews money earmarked for 25-year-old Isaiah Likely when that youngster rightfully preferred to wait to hit the market at that point before opting whether to come back to Baltimore.
Don’t blame Andrews for merely continuing down a path the entire NFL knew he was on when DeCosta couldn’t get more than a very late-round draft pick for him after the 2024 season ended with Andrews dropping a critical two-point conversion in Buffalo that only hit him in both hands. Don’t blame him for taking the money when DeCosta offered it; if you were on the other side of someone playing favorites and giving you that kind of $35M handout, darn right you’d take it too.
Don’t blame him for taking the field when overmatched puppet coaches and coordinators continue to run him out on there way more than anyone should, because, well, when you are among the 10-highest paid at your position and the GM has all the power in the building , that’s how it goes. Don’t blame him when he’s back here in 2027, because the contract is virtually untradeable and he’s guaranteed another $5M next year regardless (multiple salary cap gurus have suggested he’ll be on this roster next year because of the terrible contract).
Please try to keep all of that in mind while you consider whether or not to boo one of the better pass catchers in franchise history when he continues to jump offsides a bunch (because he will and he’s doing it more than any non-offensive lineman in the NFL). And when he drops passes, because that’s been going on for years and his drop-rate leads all NFL tight ends (12%, most of any TE with 20 targets). And none of this has anything to do with the injuries to Lamar Jackson.
Those boos should be saved for the decision makers who have repeatedly built bloated and lopsided losing rosters with players who have now been DeCosta-ed (blowing a double-digit lead in the second half of games they lose) 17 times since he took over as GM in 2019, runaway leaders in the NFL.
He’s merely a symptom of the disease in Owings Mills. He’s not the cause. And all of this will get worse.
Andrews is the only veteran TE on the roster after impact blocker Dyrham Smythe was lost for the season on IR and Nick Vannett has toggled between the practice squad. And Baltimore’s tight end production has been abysmal.
The Ravens rank 18th in the NFL with 450 total yards from their tight ends. They have amassed three total touchdowns. They have been nonfactors in the redzone and especially in the second half of games, as the scope of this offseason shrinks once rookie coordinator Declan Doyle rips through his early-game script.
They rank 20th at 9.4 yards per catch and 27th in YAC at 4.2/reception. Much of that is due to the fact that Andrews cannot sprint to separate or high-point the ball anymore. His catch radius ain’t what it used to be, nor are his hands. He should have been benched a good month ago as we suggested, but there’s obviously politics involved in that.
Andrews averages an improbable 2.0 of YAC/catch for the second straight year, that is 37th (dead last among all qualified TEs) this season. He is 31st in Expected Pointed Added/Target among TEs (-0.10) and 50th in yards/route (4.56). None of that will improve in the second half as weather becomes an issue and his body absorbs more hits.
The Ravens best be prepared to run rookie Matthew Hibner and Josh Cuevas out there more than ever before, and hope they can deliver. With journeyman Jacoby Brissett taking over at quarterback, he loves pushing the ball downfield to tight ends on seam routes and no one attempted a higher percentage of passes to tight ends than Brissett the past two seasons . The fewer to Andrews, the better.
Oh, as for Likely, well, he's having an All-Pro season for the Giants despite shaky QB play and he’s making slightly less than what DeCosta bestowed on the aged tight end he preferred. But you can’t blame Andrews for that, either.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: The Ravens Won't Win Anything Until They Get Legit Outside Receivers
Top 4 Reasons The Chargers Could Upset The Ravens Monday Night
full_text:
Monday night is a must-win game for the Baltimore Ravens if they want any chance to pretend to be a playoff team.
A win over the winless Chargers isn’t going to provide some huge boost, mind you, and reaching the postseason will remain a stretch given the realities of this roster (it’s just not very good) and this coaching staff (overmatched thus far, by and large ). But a loss would be nothing short of damning, it would beg real questions about the present and future of this failing franchise and could perhaps further grease the path for two-time MVP quarterback Lamar Jackson to decide to ply his trade elsewhere in 2027.
The Chargers have absolutely been the worst team in the NFL, they have earned that 0-8 record and they seem to have absolutely nothing going for them in any aspect of play, and particularly on offense. Traveling across the country on Monday night is probably not their preference right about now. But don’t think for one minute they can’t win this football game, and, believe it or not, they have several things working in their favor above and beyond the fact that Jacoby Brissett will become the fourth quarterback to start a game for the Ravens this season when he takes over in the huddle in Week 9.
Here are the top reasons why the Chargers could pull this off:
Minter looks horribly out of his depth so far, even messaging information about Jackson’s injuries has been a struggle and having his notes out on Monday to hint at lineup changes isn’t much of a bad cop routine. His veteran roster has walked all over him and his young assistants and he’s facing his mentor, in Jim Harbaugh, who knows his psyche and basically created him. The Chargers have nothing to lose and years of practicing against Minter’s defense in college and the NFL means Harbaugh knows a lot of buttons to push.
No one on Minter's staff exudes any real confidence – defensive coordinator Anthony Weaver has become exceptional at suggesting false confidence – they lack leaders and playmakers on both sides of the ball and expecting them to emerge now under extreme duress in a “can’t-lose game,” strikes me as problematic. Minter has been unable to inspire them to this point and they are incredibly weak, mentally, coming off four straight losses.
Minter was asked about trying to coach and call plays at the same time this week, as he should have been. But he seems shaken, and I don't fancy him against his mentor ( major coaching changes should be on the table now, as longtime Raiders exec Amy Trask suggested to us on "The Daily Flock").
This team is 3-9 in its last 12 at home and their choke gene is even more active at home than on the road. They are incredibly adept at getting DeCosta-ed – (blowing a 10-point lead in the second half to lose) at home, and no lead is safe … Oh and they also aren’t built to play from behind having to turn to yet another QB with a 30-year-old offensive coordinator, Declan Doyle, who has struggled to concoct anything that woks in the second half of games.
The front office is acting in a desperate and panicky mode and general manager Eric DeCosta really only builds choking rosters without many players who show up in the clutch. All of this bleeds into the locker room and the bloated payroll and it's an ugly concoction. And then instead of actual introspection, they throw around hollow words like "culture" and mythologize their past. Yuck.
It's like they are built to self-destruct by executives who really only know how to self -destruct from an Ozzie Newsome personnel family tree that has yet to product a single success as a GM.
Baltimore has lost four straight home prime time games, and the Ravens are going to be expected to discard with the worst team in football. Says here that won’t exactly bring out the best in them by a long shot. Collectively, they have a knack for coming up small, and all the weight is on them. Chargers season is already over.
Justin Herbert is not the worst QB in the NFL. He isn’t.
But that's how he's played this far.
Hall of Fame QB Kurt Warner laid out why he believes the star is struggling so mightily and much of it is how he is being asked to read the field with “pure progressions.” At some point Herbert is going to start ignoring his charlatan coordinator, Mike McDaniel, and do what he wants, how he wants. And Harbaugh is going to start getting on the headset and overruling things or taking over play calling himself.
Wouldn’t be surprised at all if that starts Monday night, whether it gets out publicly or not. Something has to change, sitting in Week 10 with 6 touchdown passes and 11 picks is probably rock bottom (QB rating of 75, and after that there is nowhere to go but up. Herbert knows Minter’s tendencies and defaults as well as anyone – certainly better than McDaniel – and I suspect he exhibits more autonomy against his old coach.
The Chargers got a look at Brissett in Week 1,  when the Cardinals pulled off an upset that no longer looks like an upset. Moving to a new team midseason is brutal – and doing it with a team fighting for its season at 4-5, is even tougher. The Chargers don’t miss Minter as much as they miss having a remotely competent offense that can run or pass the football.
Defensively, the Chargers are better than the Ravens.
They are far superior in the redzone (11th) and on third-down (8th) and have allowed a lower opposing passer rating for the season, too. The Chargers are also superior to the Ravens in points allowed per drive. Given just how pathetic both of these offensive lines are, there is the potential for big plays to be made on defense, but the relative lack of mobility from Brissett, in comparison to Herbert, could end up being a considerable factor in this game and we expect Herbert’s legs to be a big part of the game plan.
Sad as it is to say, given Minter’s pedigree and how highly the Ravens touted him, the Chargers have the edge on defense and a considerable edge at kicker and that might be enough to win a tight game. They are certainly overdue.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: Ravens Coach Jesse Minter Continues Bizarre Handling Of Lamar Jackson's Status
full_text:
Almost everything about the job of being the Ravens head coach, and replacing John Harbaugh, who was a mainstay with the organization, has been awkward for Jesse Minter.
And even among that backdrop, the rookie coach (and seriously struggling defensive coordinator ) has seemed most uncomfortable messaging about two significant injuries for two-time MVP quarterback Lamar Jackson. Minter chose to call a high-ankle sprain that kept Jackson out for nearly a month a “day-to-day” situation for nearly three weeks, and he was very guarded in revealing anything about Jackson’s thumb injury early this week. Then the team put out an oddly worded statement in Minter’s name Friday addressing Jackson’s injury to some degree and calling in a 6-to-10-week recovery.
Everything about Jackson is always a massive national story, especially his injuries and especially when NFL “insiders” have made a cottage industry out of suggesting Jackson will be back on wildly inaccurate and overly ambitious timelines for years . Minter’s handling of Jackson’s earlier issues already struck many as puzzling and on Saturday he continued the strange rhetorical games when he declined to speak as to when Jackson’s thumb surgery was conducted – which would provide critical context for team’s timeline for his recovery.
It’s one thing to expect the least for a team with four straight losses that has been as bad as any in the history of the franchise - the first to fail to score 14 points in four straight games and the second to allow 33 points or more in three straight ( begging major questions of this staff) . But the exchanges about Jackson’s injury are getting a little surreal for not even 10 games into Minter’s tenure here..
To put out a statement in a coach’s name that goes to lengths not to reveal when the procedure in question took place was always going to require further questioning from the media. When it came on Saturday, here’s what Minter had to say about why they released the statement:
“Really just to kind of get it out there of what happened, again less speculation of timelines and what happened and things like that,” Minter suggested. “Lamar [and I are very much on the same page with the whole thing. Leave it at that."
Of course, Minter was then asked directly when the surgery took place:
"The surgery happened, and the timeline is the timeline," he said, which will only heighten a climate where even more speculation takes place.
Jackson was almost certain to never throw a pass again for the Ravens this season from the moment he suffered the major thumb injury on his first snap of Week 8 – his first game back from the high-ankle sprain. That seems even more clear now, with the offense in disarray (good luck to new starter Jacoby Brissett), the offensive line among the worst in football and the Ravens unable to run the football or protect their quarterbacks (three got hurt in rapid succession in that Buffalo game ).
Jackson will decide whether he wants to stay in Baltimore or not his offseason, with no guaranteed money on his 2027 and a bevy of carefully-curated poison pills he negotiated in his favor – an $84M cap hit, a no-trade clause and a no-tag clause among them. It’s led many to believe he will request another trade early this offseason – including the negotiating expert who helped him broker his last contract -  and he will command over $70M a year on whatever structure he prefers no matter where he plays.
In the meantime, the rampant guessing about everything regarding Jackson will only increase in what is shaping up to be surely yet another lost season for the Ravens .
