title: Film Room: Why Broncos Coveted Daiyan Henley—and Could Pursue Him Again
full_text:
In a surprising twist, the Denver Broncos are not acquiring linebacker Daiyan Henley from the Los Angeles Chargers, after all. The trade was nullified due to Henley failing the Broncos' physical on Wednesday night.
Denver had originally sent a 2027 fourth-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick to their division rivals in exchange for their outstanding coverage linebacker, but a knee issue got in the way of the deal being finalized. Denver tried to renegotiate with the Chargers after Henley's visit and physical, but they couldn't agree on terms in the long run.
Henley would have been the best coverage linebacker the Broncos have had in at least the last five seasons, and he would have fit a major need for this defense. His ability to match and mirror against tight ends and running backs in the passing game is fantastic, and he has the range and length to be a high-quality tackler at the second level.
I dove through the first five games of the season to see exactly what the Broncos were targeting. While Henley may not be Fred Warner over the middle of the field, Denver could have gotten a high-quality player that they could extend as a building-block piece for the future.
Let’s get into the tape, because Henley is in a contract year, so if the Chargers don't find a way to re-sign him, the Broncos could very well circle back in 2027 free agency.
Henley has 77th% arm length at 33". This is great use of that length in the run game. His size as a tackler could be an issue, though pic.twitter.com/PtTdt0CO8x
Henley (jersey No. 0) isn’t just a great coverage linebacker. He is an exceptional tackler because he has incredibly long arms and uses sound technique. Those long arms also do a great job to keep blockers at bay and allow him to make plays in the running game.
He uses his length really well to shed blockers at the point of attack, and has enough speed to shoot gaps and chase down ball carriers with relative ease. His technique to wrap up and drag players to the ground is very good, and he doesn’t miss a lot of tackles when he gets home.
When Henley uses his length to shed blocks, its really fun to watch. Good upper body strength on this rep, too. pic.twitter.com/RBVIreP6U8
There are several examples of Henley using his length to his advantage, but he also shows great lateral agility and athleticism to keep himself clean at the second level. His speed and sideline-to-sideline range flash all over his tape, and he can bring some power when he gets a head of steam.
Check out this rep against Denver. He identifies Jaylen Waddle on a reverse, then sprints to the sideline and obliterates Nate Adkins before making the tackle. That’s an incredible play to catch up to Waddle, who is one of the most explosive players in the league.
Henley's range and athleticism is awesome on this rep. That's Jaylen Waddle who he chases down. Not to mention blowing up Nate Adkins before he makes the tackle. pic.twitter.com/FhV3dRZfGW
Speaking of speed and athleticism, Henley is fast enough to cover any running back out of the backfield or tight end over the middle of the field. He is a fluid mover in space, understands route combinations and leverage, and has great feel for zone coverage.
Watch this man coverage rep against the Broncos. Denver likes to use running back RJ Harvey on wheel routes because he is incredibly explosive in space.
Henley presses down, then mirrors Harvey along the sideline, going stride-for-stride in phase. This is a high-quality rep against an upstart receiving back.
This is a fantastic coverage rep for Henley. Harvey runs the wheel, and Henley is step for step going up the sideline. pic.twitter.com/k0BxkZK3ek
Even though Henley has gotten beat more often than he has in the past, his ability to diagnose and react is still very good, and he knows when to pass receivers off to the next zone and stay within his assignment. He had a couple of bad reps against the Buffalo Bills, but those were mostly miscommunication issues between him and his teammates.
When communication is clear, Henley’s zone coverage is among the best in the league. He does a great job of getting depth and flattening to the route, staying underneath the receiver, and keeping his eyes on the quarterback to try to make plays on the ball.
Like this rep against the Arizona Cardinals, who tested him against Trey McBride working vertically up the sideline. Henley’s positioning is textbook on this rep, as he passes McBride off to the next zone but keeps climbing the sideline.
Solid zone coverage rep against Trey McBride. Stays under the route and in phase before passing off and getting depth on the boundary. pic.twitter.com/2N8WRVZQp8
Despite having great length, Henley is undersized for the position (6-foot-0, 225 pounds), and it really shows as a run defender when he has to take on blockers at the point of attack. He doesn’t have the mass or the power to stack and shed blockers, and he tends to get washed out of the play when blockers get attached.
Listed at 225, Henley's size can be an issue if blockers get attached. This isn't as bad as it looks, but you can see him getting pushed around. pic.twitter.com/WWcfRhtpLP
Even though he mitigates this issue with his athleticism, there are too many examples of Henley getting bullied in the running game. It was an issue with him at Washington State, and it hasn’t gotten better as his career has gone on.
Going back to the Denver game, watch left guard Ben Powers blast Henley off the ball and drive him downfield. Henley’s length can’t and won’t save him every play.
This is a Ben Powers tweet. Henley gets bullied. pic.twitter.com/IYT8AmvWr7
Those size concerns also translate to his lackluster blitzing ability. The Chargers didn’t ask him to blitz a lot, but when he did, the results weren’t pretty. For some reason, the Chargers would also ask him to come off the edge as a pass rusher on occasion, and those results were even worse.
This is the best blitz rep I've seen from Henley so far, and im through 3 and a half games. it's not a strong suit of his game. pic.twitter.com/oW4LFotvvf
There’s a lot to like about Henley’s game, and he would have been a fantastic addition to an already loaded Broncos defense. I have 25 additional Henley clips on my X feed to check out, with multiple examples of what we discussed here.
Henley is certainly a starting-caliber player in this league, but with Alex Singleton and Justin Strnad playing quality football in their own right, the Broncos wouldn't have needed Henley to play every down . The Broncos might have been able to hide Henley's deficiencies in the run game and focus on his coverage versatility as a dime linebacker.
Again, though, Henley is in the last year of his rookie contract, so it wouldn’t surprise me to see the Broncos make a run at him as a free agent next offseason. And that's why we moved forward with publishing this film breakdown.

title: Evaluating Lions Internal, External Options to Replace Aidan Hutchinson
full_text:
The Detroit Lions are preparing for the worst regarding the future of defensive end Aidan Hutchinson.
On Sunday, the star defender went down with a non-contact knee injury after leaping in the air to celebrate a sack on New England Patriots quarterback Drake Maye. He didn't return to the game, and reports across the league are indicating that the team is preparing to be without him for the remainder of the season.
Hutchinson leaves big shoes to fill in Detroit's defense. Through nine games Hutchinson ranked second on the Lions in sacks with six and is among the NFL leaders in pressures with 52 pressures.
The trade deadline was Tuesday, meaning any additions the Lions want to make to account for this loss will have to come via their own practice squad, an opposing practice squad or the external free agent market.
Here are 10 possible options for the Lions to replace Hutchinson following his injury.
Moore appears to be the most likely next option as a starter in Detroit's defense. He began the year playing a small role, but injuries to Hutchinson and last week DJ Wonnum have given him extended opportunities that he's made the most of.
All four of Moore's sacks this season have come in the last two weeks. With Hutchinson out now, Moore will likely get more chances to prove he belongs in the mix as opposed to playing a rotational pass-rushing role.
Through nine games, fans have yet to see the 2025 sixth-round pick. Hassanein didn't appear in a game last year, and has been a healthy scratch for each of Detroit's games up to this point.
There was a belief that Hassanein could've gotten an opportunity last week when Wonnum was out, but the Lions elected to go with Anthony Lucas as a call-up instead. Perhaps he's better suited for an opportunity with Hutchinson out now.
As mentioned, Lucas got his first opportunity as a practice squad elevation against the Dolphins in Week 9. He played just 12 snaps, but the Lions' desire to use him instead of Hassanein seems to indicate that they have some confidence in his overall ability.
It's worth noting that Lucas wasn't as flashy in terms of production as a pass-rusher in college, and could be better suited for a role as a big end as opposed to playing the rush-end position.
A Michigan native who has carved out a nice career after playing collegiately at Division II Grand Valley State, Judon has been tied to the Lions at times throughout the last several seasons. Now a free agent, perhaps the Lions finally make the homecoming official for the veteran.
Judon has played in one game this season , that being for the San Francisco 49ers in early October against the Denver Broncos. A four-time Pro Bowl selection who is in his 11th season, Judon has plenty of experience and could provide a burst of energy for the Lions for their stretch run.
However, he's also an aging veteran who started just three games last year and didn't record a sack. After notching 15.5 sacks in 2022, Judon has notched just 9.5 total in over the last four years.
Throughout his career, Reddick has been at his best as a pass-rush specialist. While his production has been declining in recent years, he does have the ability to spark a defense with his athleticism off the edge.
Reddick has remained unsigned throughout the year after appearing in 13 games for the Tampa Bay Buccaneers a season ago. He notched 2.5 sacks last year, and had just one in 10 games for the New York Jets during the previous year.
The Temple product does have some versatility, though, as he can also play the SAM linebacker position. With the injuries Detroit has dealt with at linebacker, Reddick's versatility could be helpful.
Floyd has carved out a nice career over the past decade, with 70 career sacks across stints with five different teams. Floyd has experience in the NFC North having played his first four seasons with the Chicago Bears, and won a Super Bowl with the Los Angeles Rams in the 2021 season.
The veteran doesn't have flashy totals or accolades, as he's never been an All-Pro and has had just two seasons with 10 or more sacks. However, he's been consistent throughout his career, and could be a stabilizing force for Detroit's line.
Injuries have derailed what was a promising career for Bosa, particularly over the past four seasons. A highly touted prospect out of Ohio State, Bosa was the third overall pick by the Chargers in the 2016 Draft and wound up being the Defensive Rookie of the Year.
Bosa made five Pro Bowl appearances throughout his career, but in recent seasons he's struggled with injuries. He was limited to five games in 2022 and four games in 2023, but has played 14 and 15 over the past two years, respectively.
The Ohio State product proved to still have some upside last year with five sacks for the Buffalo Bills, but has gone unsigned. If he's healthy, perhaps he's worthy of an opportunity to see what he still has left in the tank.
BJ Ojulari (Jacksonville Jaguars)
A former second-round pick of the Arizona Cardinals in 2023, Ojulari has showed some promise in his career but injuries have ultimately been too much for him to overcome. He recorded four sacks as a rookie in 2023, but then missed the entire 2024 season and appeared in just eight games last year.
Now with the Jaguars, Ojulari has yet to make his season debut. Perhaps the Lions would be intrigued by some of the flashes of upside he's shown in his career.
Andre Carter II (Los Angeles Chargers)
Carter had a very short stint on the Lions' practice squad last season, as he signed with the team in August before being poached by the Miami Dolphins in November. He hasn't appeared in an NFL game since 2024, but has bounced around the league as a coveted depth option.
The Army product has very limited experience, but could be a solid depth option assuming he'd be familiar with the scheme in Detroit under second-year coordinator Kelvin Sheppard.
Michael Heldman (Kansas City Chiefs)
A Michigan native who went undrafted out of Central Michigan this year, Heldman had a big preseason debut for the New Orleans Saints but would be waived with an injury designation in early September.
He's landed in Kansas City, where he's yet to make his debut. He does have some intriguing athletic tools and was one of the top pass-rushers in college football last year across all levels.
When the Lions were in need of safety depth, Brad Holmes targeted an undrafted safety in Bishop Fitzgerald to add to the active roster. While Heldman wouldn't be the flashiest addition, he would be one that fits the mold of how Holmes has approached these situations in the past.

title: Everything Dan Campbell Said After Detroit Lions Beat Patriots
full_text:
The Detroit Lions defeated the New England Patriots, 35-10, Sunday in Munich, Germany to move to 7-2 on the season.
Here is everything head coach Dan Campbell said following the win during his postgame press conference.
"Well, the effort of all of our players, I thought, was outstanding. Man, the energy, the attitude to get ready for this, and I tell you what, just the support that we felt as a team, I know Saint probably just spoke on that, but you could feel that immediately. Especially with his first big play. Our defense takes field; we end up holding the field goal, but then Saint's big catch, man, makes somebody miss. He runs it in. Our guys are running down to help him in the end zone, and you could just hear the crowd erupt. So this has been an unbelievable experience. Been very special because we did feel like this was a home game. We felt like this was our home, and that was important. Everybody's taking unbelievable care of us all week. I mean, just the hospitality has been unbelievable here. So this is icing on the cake."
"Yeah, I got mine two nights ago. I went in and got my victory beer, because I don't know if I'm gonna be able to get it tonight. We've got to get right back on the plane and get ready for next week's game. I'm with you. We're going to enjoy this victory, this meant a lot to us. When you're able to win and be in this environment that we were able to be in, it's one of those things you'll never forget."
"I spoke to him before we left, and he's in good spirits, and he continues to get better every day. I did not get into details of this trip. I just wanted him to know that 'Hey, still thinking about you and just stay the course.' That was really it."
"Very proud. I mentioned that the starting point for all this was going to be energy, you know, our attitude, our energy, and that showed up early. It was there, you could feel it, but our O line D line, we're going to need to be able to establish the run and stop the run to do what we needed to do, and you could feel our O-line running off the football. You run off the football and you get guys on blocks. You put a hat on a hat, Gibbs will do the rest. He'll do the rest. But you could feel it, man. The O-line really showed up today. I was proud of those guys and the defense."
"I'll tell you what, I'm just going to give you the whole experience. Look, there's a number of things in the game, we do the national anthem of both. That was that was pretty cool. There was actually two. It was pretty cool. You know that (the German fans) it's very prideful. I'm not from Germany, but I could feel it. I could feel it, and that's pretty cool. You can feel the sense of pride here. And number two, a song that I know very well in the third quarter, John Denver, Country Roads. I'm like 'Whoa.' I wasn't expecting that, and everybody in the stadium knows it. It blew me away. I'm like 'Wow, okay, that's a that's a little piece of home,' and you know that was — it was cool. It was just very cool.
"Yeah. Nothing new. We'll know more when we get back in the states, but anytime you lose a player of his caliber, type of teammate he is, he's a captain of ours. That doesn't make things easy. But I thought guys stepped up, you know, in his wake and you know showed up for us today and helped us out."
It's what I just mentioned. Anytime you lose a player like that, and you don't know the entirety of it, you know, but knowing Hutch for who he is, you know it's like, he doesn't stay down long, you know that's that. It does, it hurts a little bit, but as far as this game was concerned, our guys stepped up and finished man. We stayed strong. This is the second time this has happened and our guys have responded in a tough situation and didn't bat an eye. We just went back to work and that's not an easy thing to do, but no, certainly you don't want to know that a player like that is down."
"Well, we like them. It's why we acquired them where we did, and I know this, Derrick Moore gets better every game. The more reps he gets, he gets better. It was good to get Wonnum back today. We know what Mac is, you know, Sky can create in there. So can Tyleik, and all those guys, even Levi and Lacy, they bring a different flavor, but they push the pocket. They've got length, but I think the important thing here is, man, we did what we had to do to get out of this game with a win, played really good defense, and I really thought the back end played outstanding. We played some sticky coverage today and bought us a little bit of time. Those other guys, we're improving. We got to go. You know, we got to go. We'll see where Hutch is at, but we've got to step up now. We need some guys to really step up, and if that is the case, fill that void."
I know this, before we started this trip, we talked about it, and it was it's a three game season for us. We came into this, whatever, we played eight games, and now we had three, and it started with going to Germany, going to Munich, and playing New England. That was one. We've got two more, and so those guys know it. We're on a three-game schedule here, and this was the next one. And we're not going to use excuses. We're going to get back on this plane. We're going to go over, and and we're going to get ready for the next opponent, which is Tampa Bay Buccaneers back at home."
"You know, I don't get too much into that necessarily. We acquire players that that we've got a lot of faith in. They're good. They're  good people. They're, listen, that doesn't mean they're perfect. I'm not perfect. But the point is, you know,  they know how to handle their business, and then you just kind of give them a nugget here and there, and show them the way a little bit, and they're great, man. So those guys, they were locked in for this trip. You know, we knew what we had to do for this game, and they'll be ready to get back on this plane, go back to the states, and get ready to play again."
Well, I don't know if it always comes off. He's very driven. He is highly competitive and very driven. When you put him in those situations, just in a setting where we're sitting here and we're talking, he's very easygoing, fun loving, great sense of humor. He's the sunshine, and you would never know or think that anything could rile him up or get him to that that different, that whatever that is, and that shows up. You roll the ball out there and you tell him you're in a one-on-one or it's a competitive setting, and all of a sudden, man, that the animal comes out and and that's he he's been blessed by God, but he's made the most of what God's given him too. I mean, he really shows up and and does everything he can do with that ability."

title: 6 Winners, 1 Loser From Lions Win Over Patriots
full_text:
On Sunday, the Detroit Lions were the first team playing, squaring off at 9:30 a.m. EST with the New England Patriots in Munich, Germany. After both teams scored on their opening drives, there was an air of anticipation for a high-scoring game.
Instead, both teams lost star players on the same play, with Drake Maye and Aidan Hutchinson each suffering lower body injuries. With the Lions squaring off against a backup quarterback, they quickly ran out to a 21-3 lead at half and did not look back, winning 35-10.
Here is who won the day and gave Lions fans a stress-free Sunday.
As is the case with Gibbs, any time he sets a mark that is “first since Barry Sanders,” it is a good day. This time, it was Gibbs’s 93 rushing yards at half being the most since Barry Sanders in a 1994 game.
Gibbs’s footprints were all over the game, with 171 total yards at half, with a touchdown that he set up with a long reception among his multiple plays. On his first touch of the second half, Gibbs crossed 175 yards from scrimmage.
Gibbs added another touchdown in the fourth quarter, rushing in from 26 yards out. He showcased excellence patience, weaving into the end zone and following his blockers for the final ten yards. It pushed the back over 150 yards rushing on the day and 250 yards from scrimmage.
With seven minutes to play, his day, alongside the starters, was over with the Lions up by 25 points. Gibbs did all of his damage in 3 1/2 quarters of action.
Amon-Ra St. Brown had a very happy homecoming, with the wide receiver recording his first touchdown since September on the opening drive of the game. The All-Pro had an uncharacteristic 56-yard catch and run touchdown as opposed to his normal redzone damage.
The good day continued, with St. Brown recording a second touchdown on the game in the third quarter with a strong catch-and-run for 28 yards, powering through a pile for the last five yards. St. Brown finished at 98 yards in his return home.
McCreary had a tough matchup with AJ Brown on Sunday, and performed admirably. The star receiver was held to two catches for 27 yards through three quarters before leaving with injury, with his best catch coming against Khalil Dorsey.
Meanwhile, McCreary recorded his first interception as a Lion and his first since Week 1 in 2025. It set up the Lions for what should have been a scoring drive to end the first half before a turnover on the goal line.
McNeill continued his strong season, jumping up to 6.5 sacks as the midpoint of the season nears. The NC State product is putting up numbers not seen since Ndamukong Suh in 2011, as pointed out on the broadcast.
McNeill nearly had three other sacks on the day as well, getting close on a flea flicker and then flushing Tommy DeVito into DJ Wonnum’s arms for a sack, before flushing DeVito from the pocket on the second play of the fourth quarter.
Upon Aidan Hutchinson’s injury, the fellow Michigan product Moore was the next man up. Moore responded with his third and fourth career sack in two weeks. On the first, Moore benefitted, taking down DeVito after DJ Wonnum pressured the quarterback towards Moore.
Moore got close to another sack on New England’s sole touchdown for the game, and then got home for his second sack, outright speeding by his lineman to take down DeVito hard.
It is not a stretch to say that this has been a tumultuous week for the Boston College product. The left guard was held out of the Miami game for disciplinary reasons, with head coach Dan Campbell saying that it is on the lineman to respond.
The former Lions’ sixth-round pick responded with a strong game, as he and Penei Sewell had a massive push the entire game, leading to Gibbs’s massive 153 yards on the ground. On Gibbs’s first touchdown, Mahogany had moved the defensive tackle five yards left of his starting spot on the dive.
Mahogany earned the nod over Sewell in the winners category after the franchise tackle was whistled for a hold in the second half.
Hutchinson had a short day in Germany , with the star player getting injured following a sack of Drake Maye. The Michigan product’s sack celebration has faced some concerns in the past regarding how dangerous stress towards his knees is in his jump and landing.
That caught up to the EDGE on Sunday, with his landing instantly buckling his right knee and forcing him out of the game in subpar field conditions. It has been a point of criticism from fans in the past, and it was proven right, with the Lions suffering a humiliating injury in a celebration similar to what happened to Stephen Tulloch in 2014.
Postgame reports indicate that Hutchinson is expected to miss the remainder of the season with a significant knee injury.
Sports writer since 2022. Emmett Matasovsky started covering the Detroit Lions in 2025. He has extensive experience covering Michigan State Spartans athletics, including MSU basketball and football. Has demonstrated passionate, in-depth coverage of college athletics.

title: Report: Lions to Lose Aidan Hutchinson for Season
full_text:
The Detroit Lions are celebrating a big win over the New England Patriots in Munich, Germany. But the emotions have been altered by an injury to one of their stars.
On Sunday, defensive end Aidan Hutchinson went down with a knee injury after jumping into the air celebrating a first quarter sack of New England Patriots quarterback Drake Maye. Hutchinson did not return to the game, and fans immediately feared the worst.
While Lions head coach Dan Campbell did not immediately have an update during his postgame press conference, reports from NFL insiders indicate that Hutchinson is believed to have suffered a serious injury that will keep him out for the remainder of the season.
"Lions star DE Aidan Hutchinson suffered a significant knee injury," reported The Ringer's Tom Pelissero. "Imaging in Munich confirmed the injury to Hutchinson, whose right knee buckled as he celebrated a sack against the Patriots. He's out for the season."
NFL Network's Ian Rapoport added, "There does not appear to be hope that Hutchinson returns this season."
The injury to Hutchinson is a devastating blow for the Lions, who will be without one of the NFL's best pass-rushers. Even as they currently sit in first-place in the NFC North as winners of five straight with a 7-2 record, it makes the future somewhat gloomy given how impactful he is to the defense.
In Hutchinson's absence, the Lions will likely rely more on 2026 second-round pick Derrick Moore . After playing a small role earlier in the year, Moore has had two sacks apiece in each of the last two games including Sunday's win over the Patriots.
D.J. Wonnum is the other starter opposite of Hutchinson, while Tyler Lacy, Eric O'Neill and Ahmed Hassanein are other options on the EDGE. When Wonnum missed last week's game, Detroit also utilized undrafted rookie Anthony Lucas as a practice squad elevation.
With this news, Hutchinson has now suffered a season-ending injury for the second time in three seasons. In 2024, he was playing at an elite level before suffering a significant leg injury in the team's fifth game of the year.
Hutchinson has six sacks this season and 49 for his career through his first four seasons. Drafted second overall in the 2022 NFL Draft, the Michigan product has quickly asserted himself among the game's best at his position.
Last year, Hutchinson bounced back from the previous year's injury to have a career-best year. He logged 14.5 sacks, which earned him Second Team All-Pro honors. He also inked a four-year contract extension worth $180 million in October of last year.

title: Dan Campbell Addresses Aidan Hutchinson Injury: ‘Hurts a Little Bit’
full_text:
The Detroit Lions (and their fans) took over Germany's Allianz Arena on Sunday morning. They controlled the international clash from start to finish, easily dispatching the reigning AFC champion New England Patriots, 35-10.
Yet, Detroit couldn't fully celebrate the Week 10 victory, a fifth straight win for Dan Campbell's squad. The reason why: Aidan Hutchinson, the team's star EDGE rusher , suffered an apparent knee injury on the first series of the game.
It came following a third-and-goal sack of Patriots quarterback Drake Maye by Hutchinson. The sack forced New England to settle for a field goal on the drive and led to Maye missing the rest of the game.
While the play shifted the momentum in favor of the Lions, it also cost them Hutchinson for the remainder of the contest. The University of Michigan product proceeded to hurt himself while celebrating the sack; he jumped in the air and upon coming down, landed awkwardly on his right leg.
In the immediate aftermath of the injury, Hutchinson was ruled questionable to return. Yet, he never played another down Sunday and was eventually downgraded to out.
After the game, Campbell didn't have an update regarding the injury. But, he did express it “hurts a little bit” to lose the pass-rusher.
“We’ll know more when we get back in the states,” Campbell said of Hutchinson. “But any time you lose a player of his caliber, the type of teammate he is, he's a captain of ours, that doesn't make things easy. But, I thought guys stepped up in his wake, and showed up for us today and helped us out.”
Entering the Week 10 affair, Hutchinson was the highest-graded EDGE defender in the NFL, with a Pro Football Focus overall grade of 91.7. Plus, he had generated 50 total pressures, the second-most among 110 qualified EDGE defenders.
Additionally, his sack Sunday was his seventh of the 2026 campaign and the 53rd of his five-year NFL career.
Consequently, if the Lions have to play without him for any significant period of time, it'd be a brutal blow to defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard's unit .
Hutchinson last missed a significant portion of a season in 2024, when he suffered a broken left tibia and fibula in a Week 6 contest against the Dallas Cowboys. The ailment cost him the remainder of the aforementioned season.
He bounced back from that major setback, though, and recorded a 16-sack, 100-pressure campaign in 2025. It earned him a 91.7 overall mark from PFF.

title: Key Takeaways From Detroit Lions 35-10 Victory Against Patriots
full_text:
The Detroit Lions entered their Week 10 contest as a slight favorite against the defending AFC champion New England Patriots.
Detroit's defense was seeking to continue its solid play, as the unit has turned around its fortunes over the course of the past four games.
The defensive roster has aimed to be part of the reason the team continues to stack wins this season.
“That's good. I'm going to make sure I tell Tyleik (Williams) I appreciate him listening in meetings because that's something we actually that I've been saying from Week 1, just a trend here. And I'm not ignorant to it, I'm not arrogant," said defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard. "We have a high prolific offense here. Been afforded that for years now, top five offense. And that's what the talks are, that's what it's about. So just tell those guys, let's make sure that we're the reason why we are doing things, why we are moving forward as a team and an organization and not.
"So, that's been a theme since training camp and guys have taken heed to it. Tyleik is a big reason why we are doing things right right now. He doesn't show up glaringly on the stat sheet like Alim McNeill, Aidan Hutchinson do, but his impact to our defense and to the team's success is tremendous.”
Detroit was able to advance its record to 7-2 after 60 minutes of action, but the key story will be the injury suffered to one of Sheppard's best defensive linemen.
Here are the key takeaways from the Lions' 35-10 victory.
After winning the opening coin toss, the Lions elected to defer.
New England was able to march 60 yards on 11-plays during their opening offensive possession. Mike Vrabel's squad had to settle for a 33-yard field-goal after Aidan Hutchinson sacked Drake Maye.
Unfortunately, the former first-round celebrated by jumping in the air and immediately went down, clutching his right leg. He was evaluated in the medical tent immediately after the Patriots took an early 3-0 lead.
Maye also left the game after the first possession with an ankle injury. He was officially ruled out, just before the start of the fourth quarter.
WHYYYYY pic.twitter.com/xotIPn9yTN
Amon-Ra St. Brown welcomed the return to Germany more than most, as he spent summers traveling abroad with his family.
Prior to the game, his father expressed he wanted his son to score three touchdowns this week, as St. Brown had not recorded a receiving touchdown since Week 3 against the New York Jets.
The former fourth-round pick was expected to have a big game and immediately found the end zone.
On Detroit's opening offensive possession, Goff found the sixth-year wideout on a 56-yard touchdown reception.
He later secured a 28-yard touchdown grab with the help of teammates to eventually find his way over the goal line.
After the Lions extended their lead to 28-3 in the third-quarter, the team executed a human centipede touchdown celebration.
To the house!!! Roar pic.twitter.com/AHLtLeaQS3
Detroit was able to firmly grab hold of momentum in Sunday's game with back-to-back scoring drives, as they followed St. Brown's touchdown with a 97-yard march that ended with a connection from Goff to Isaac TeSlaa.
After stopping the Patriots yet again, the Lions looked to be moving but Goff threw an ill-fated pass in the direction of St. Brown that was picked off by Christian Gonzalez. However, the defense was able to get a three-and-out.
On the ensuing drive, the Lions turned it over to Jahmyr Gibbs. The Alabama product touched the ball on six of the team's seven plays, including a 50-yard reception and a five-yard touchdown to put the Lions up 21-3.
In the first half, Gibbs notched 17 total touches with 171 scrimmage yards and a touchdown, with the 171 scrimmage yards being the most in a first half of an international game in NFL history.
After allowing the field goal on the opening drive, the Lions' defense swarmed the Patriots. With Maye ruled out, Detroit tormented Tommy DeVito for the remainder of the first half. Devito was sacked twice, once by Derrick Moore and once by Alim McNeill.
With less than a minute to go in the first half, the Patriots looked to be driving. However, Devito was picked off by Roger McCreary who returned the ball 22 yards to New England's 42-yard line. It was McCreary's first interception as a Lion.
Detroit drove deep into New England territory with a first-and-goal at the 5-yard line. However, disaster struck as a second-down pass to Sam LaPorta was broken up, then Patriots safety Kevin Byard III stepped in front of a pass intended for Jameson Williams to deny the Lions points with an interception.
Detroit's offense was dominant all afternoon. A Gibbs touchdown run of 28-yards early in the fourth quarter, that extended the lead to 35-10, highlighted just how dominant the run game can be.
Left tacke Penei Sewell pulled to the right quickly and blocked a Patriots defender, clearing the way for the speedy running back to find his way into the end zone for the second time in the game.
Gibbs is the first NFL player to produce 150 or more rushing yards, two or more rushing touchdowns and 95 or more receiving yards in a game since Priest Holmes accomplished that feat back in 2002. He's only the fifth player in league history to do so.

title: Aidan Hutchinson Leaves Lions Game After Celebration Injury
full_text:
Detroit Lions defensive end Aidan Hutchinson left Sunday's game against the New England Patriots after the first series.
He walked off the field under his own power and went to the blue medical tent on the sideline after appearing to suffer a lower leg injury. After some evaluation in the medical tent, Hutchinson limped to the locker room alongside a trainer as shown on the TV broadcast.
He went down after celebrating his sixth sack of the season, when he took down Patriots quarterback Drake Maye on a third-down to force a field goal.
Hutchinson was initially ruled questionable to return with a knee injury and was downgraded to out in the third quarter. Maye also went to the locker room accompanied by Patriots trainers. Maye was replaced by backup Tommy Devito.
After getting Maye to the ground, Hutchinson ran and celebrated by jumping into the air. Upon his landing, Hutchinson went to the ground grabbing at his right leg.
Hutchinson is a massive part of Detroit's defense, as he has emerged as one of the NFL's best young pass-rushers in his fourth NFL season. His sixth sack put him past Alim McNeill for the team lead, and his overall presence has helped the defense notch 28 total sacks as a team, as of the first quarter Sunday.
WHYYYYY pic.twitter.com/xotIPn9yTN
Detroit drafted Hutchinson second overall in the 2022 NFL Draft, and he has proven to be exactly what the team has needed. Sunday's first quarter sack was the 49th of his career. Hutchinson is coming off a career-best 14.5 sacks in 2025, which earned him Second Team All-Pro honors.
The Michigan product has also had to deal with some adversity, as he suffered a broken leg that ended his season after five games during the 2024 campaign. However, he bounced back nicely with his season in 2025, and was rewarded midway through it with a four-year, $180 million contract extension with $141 million in guaranteed money.
The Patriots finished their drive with a field goal from Andy Borregales to take a 3-0 lead. Detroit would answer back quickly, though, as Jared Goff connected with Amon-Ra St. Brown for a 56-yard touchdown to give Detroit an early lead.

title: Setting Lions Fans Expectations For Amon-Ra St. Brown Against Patriots
full_text:
The Detroit Lions are set for a special game Sunday against the New England Patriots.
For the first time since 2015, the Lions will be playing a game on international soil. After their first two international trips were to London, they will be playing against the Patriots Sunday at Allianz Arena in Munich, Germany.
It will be an especially special game for one specific Lion, that being wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown. The fifth-year wideout has ties to the region, as his mother Miriam was born in Germany. He has recently hosted football camps in the region during the offseason as well.
With how impactful he is for the Lions and how much the game means to him, many believe the wideout will be set up to have a big game. Even though he's listed as questionable with a rib injury after being limited in practice, the expectation is that he will in fact play Sunday.
Sports Betting Dime's Drew Ellis believes St. Brown will have a big showing and will get into the end zone at some point in Sunday's game. The USC product to score a touchdown at any point in Sunday's game is the Week 10 best bet.
St. Brown declared during a media session this week that he plans to have a special celebration lined up in the event that he scores a touchdown.
"Most of these Lions picks I decide a day or two before based on matchups, but this is one I’ve known I was going to pick for a long time," Ellis told Lions OnSI. "This game in Germany is special, especially for Amon-Ra St. Brown, who has family roots in the country. The German flag adorns his helmet each week. ASB always has some touchdown celebrations in mind and I 100% believe he has had something special planned for this game."
St. Brown has been on something of a quiet streak as of late, as he hasn't reached the end zone since Week 3 against the New York Jets. That was his fifth touchdown of the season, as he scored two each in the Lions' first two games.
With the stakes of playing a game in an area so close to his heart, Ellis believes St. Brown will get the job done and reach the end zone.
"He hasn’t scored in his last five games, so he’s definitely due and I think the team knows how important this game is for him," Ellis said. "I fully expect ASB to reach the end zone and have another memorable celebration for the German crowd."

title: Expert Predictions For Detroit Lions Matchup With New England Patriots
full_text:
The Detroit Lions will seek their fifth consecutive victory when they take on the New England Patriots Sunday morning in Munich, Germany.
The Patriots, sitting at 5-4 and in second place in the AFC East, are coming off a 45-27 defeat at the hands of the Green Bay Packers. Meanwhile, Detroit prevailed against the Miami Dolphins in Week 9, 19-9.
Without further ado, here are the predictions from the Detroit Lions On SI staff for the Lions' Week 10 matchup with New England.
The Detroit Lions come into Sunday's early morning showdown winners of four games in a row with the chance to win over an international crowd. After enjoying the festivities in Munich, the Lions are taking on a Patriots team that has been up-and-down but has all the talent to make another postseason run.
The key for Detroit will be more consistency defensively. They've been solid in recent weeks since the Week 6 bye, and they face another mistake prone quarterback in Drake Maye. I think the Lions could position themselves to generate multiple takeaways, which would make life much easier for their own offense. Detroit jumps out to a big lead thanks to Amon-Ra St. Brown and Jahmyr Gibbs, and the Patriots aren't able to generate a rally soon enough leading to a big win.
The Detroit Lions have a solid shot to capture their fifth consecutive win Sunday morning in Munich, Germany.
The New England Patriots’ offense, led by the interception-prone Drake Maye under center, has been far from a prolific unit so far this season. In fact, it's averaged a pedestrian 23.4 points per game through the season's first nine weeks.
Plus, New England could be down its top two backs in the Week 10 contest. TreVeyon Henderson has already been ruled out with an undisclosed neurological issue. Meanwhile, Rhamondre Stevenson is listed as questionable with a knee injury.
Additionally, on the opposite side of the ball, the Patriots will be without cornerback Carlton Davis for the international clash. Subsequently, Jared Goff has a chance to exploit New England's secondary, and I believe that Amon-Ra St. Brown, a citizen of both the United States and Germany, has a prime opportunity to deliver a memorable performance.
I believe that St. Brown will come through with multiple big-time catches and play an integral part in the Week 10 victory for Detroit.
Amon-Ra St. Brown figures to be the star of the show when the Lions face the Patriots in Germany.
Detroit's offense has not been lighting up the scoreboard as of late, but the Patriots defense is coming off of a poor performance against the Packers. Christian Gonzalez was made to look quite pedestrian against both Christian Watson and Matthew Golden.
Drake Maye is a turnover machine, and if the Lions' defense can force a couple of ill-advised tosses, they could find themselves securing multiple interceptions this week.
The crowd should heavily favor the Lions this week, making the game feel like a home game.
Dan Campbell's squad gives the crowd plenty to cheer about this week.
The Lions and Dolphins have traveled to Munich to partake in the International Series for the NFL. This is a return to Amon-Ra St. Brown’s home country in an obvious storyline matchup.
The Patriots have been a turnover machine in their first half of the season, as they have yet to play a clean game. The Lions have been able to drive down the field, but have been stuck settling for field goals in the red zone.
It likely will not be the cleanest game with two teams that have traveled across the globe, and it is hard to see either team living up to some preseason expectations. With obvious questions about the Patriots’ strength, considering their losses to fellow NFC North teams, I will side with the Lions.
Amon-Ra St. Brown adds a touchdown to unveil his unique plan and the Lions survive with a win, as Jahmyr Gibbs gets his season back on track with 125 yards from scrimmage.

title: Snaps, Studs, Duds and Defining Stats From Packers’ Horrific Loss to Vikings
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers were exposed as paper tigers by the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday. Again.
Two months after the Packers were buried under a fourth-quarter avalanche against the Vikings, they were buried under a first-half avalanche in the rematch. Five minutes into the third quarter, the score was 20-0.
Game over. Drive home safely.
Here’s our weekly look at the snaps, some important stats and some studs and duds from a pivotal loss.
The Packers played 55 snaps on offense.
Quarterbacks: Jordan Love played 52 snaps before being saved from a further beating for the final three snaps, which went to Tyrod Taylor.
Love was 17-of-27 passing for 220 yards. He would have fallen short of 200 passing yards if not for a ball that went through the hands of tight end Tucker Kraft and safety Harrison Smith and into the hands of Savion Williams. Another 59 yards were lost on sacks.
The Vikings had Love seeing blitzes and pressures when there were neither. From a clean pocket, he was a woeful 6-of-13, including a red-zone interception in the direction of Kraft.
Running backs: As expected given the pressure-packed nature of the Vikings’ defense, Chris Brooks went from injured reserve to playing a unit-high 26 snaps. He was about the only player who performed well in protection. Kaleb Johnson and MarShawn Lloyd got 14 snaps apiece.
Kaleb Johnson with some burst to beat the defender and then gains some yards after contact. pic.twitter.com/vcO4zNLOHB
When Johnson was in the game, he got the rock. He was effective, too, with 10 carries for 42 yards. In the first half, he made something out of nothing. In the second half, there was some actual running room and his no-nonsense approach took advantage. By our count, 40 yards came after contact.
If you’re looking for some optimism, a one-two punch of Josh Jacobs and Johnson could be effective.
Receivers: Christian Watson (47) and Matthew Golden (46), as usual, led the way, with Savion Williams (20) retaining his role as the No. 3 receiver.
Watson has been on a heater for most of the season but the Vikings threw him on ice. He caught three passes for 37 yards. Golden was shut out until late in the first half and led the way with five catches for 70 yards; PFF charged him with two drops and he was 0-for-2 in contested-catch situations.
Returner/receiver Skyy Moore returned after missing five games with an ankle injury, only to suffer another ankle injury. So, he was limited to three-kick return snaps and zero on offense. Bo Melton also exited with an injury after zero snaps on offense and 10 on special teams. So, J. Michael Sturdivant played nine snaps as the default No. 4. He scored a 32-yard touchdown but fumbled on a kickoff return.
Tight ends: Tucker Kraft played all but three snaps. With Josh Whyle sent to injured reserve, Mark Redman played 21 snaps, Jonnu Smith played three and Drake Dabney played three.
For the second consecutive game, Kraft caught one pass. Redman was strong in the run game but his fumble handed the Vikings a quick 3-0 lead. Added together, the Vikings’ tight ends without T.J. Hockenson dominated the positional matchup.
Offensive line: The No. 1 line went the distance. The grouping of left tackle Jordan Morgan, left guard Laken Tomlinson, center John Williams, right guard Travis Glover and right tackle Anthony Belton was the team’s sixth starting unit. The team’s highest-paid blocker, Aaron Banks, played just three snaps on special teams.
Which of the safety blitzers should be picked up? How about neither. pic.twitter.com/reFvQUdXQH
It was a ghastly performance. Williams gave up two sacks; Sean Rhyan might return for the Rams game. Tomlinson, who was shifted back to his “natural position” of left guard, had his worst game since joining the team. Morgan played better after giving up a sack early in the game; Myles Garrett is next.
Mekhi Becton played three snaps as an extra tight end. He gave up one sack and one pressure.
The Packers played 69 snaps on defense.
Defensive tackles: Karl Brooks and Devonte Wyatt played 42 snaps apiece. They were followed by Chris McClellan with 32, Jordon Riley with 28 and Anthony Campbell with 25.
Brooks had one sack; the pressure almost created an interception. Wyatt had just one assisted tackle and one pressure. The Packers aren’t getting nearly enough bang for their buck with him.
Edges: Lukas Van Ness, who was questionable with a back injury, played a unit-high 37 snaps as part of a typically balanced approach. Brenton Cox played 35, followed by Barryn Sorrell and Dani Dennis-Sutton with 34 apiece. Sorrell’s workload was bolstered by another 19 on special teams.
Van Ness was probably the Packers’ best player in the game. He had 1.5 sacks; the half-sack was shared with Sorrell.
Linebackers: With Zaire Franklin missing another game with a shin injury, so it was up to Isaiah McDuffie (every snap) and Ty’Ron Hopper (all but one snap) to hold down the fort.
Franklin did some work pregame, which would signal that he’s on track to return next week against the Rams. Getting Franklin back on defense will allow McDuffie and Hopper to play more on special teams. McDuffie, a special-teams captain, played only three snaps in the kicking game. Speaking of special teams, Nick Niemann played a team-high 23 snaps and Kristian Welch played 20.
McDuffie led the team with nine tackles and Hopper had seven and one pass deflection. They tackled physically but didn’t make any plays.
Cornerbacks: Brandon Cisse suffered an injured rib when he bounced off Myles Price on his third-and-23 touchdown catch, so his day was limited to just 14 snaps. Keisean Nixon went the distance and Carrington Valentine replaced Cisse and played 55 snaps.
Kamal Hadden played two snaps on defense and gave up a long third-down completion on third-and-15 that the Vikings turned into a touchdown to lead 17-0. Benjamin St-Juste is a total afterthought on defense, though he did play 12 snaps on special teams.
Nixon was excellent. He gave up three completions for 20 yards and broke up two passes. Valentine gave up four completions for 33 yards. His physicality really stood out.
Safeties: Xavier McKinney and Evan Williams played every snap. Javon Bullard, who didn’t practice on Wednesday and Thursday and was questionable, played 36 snaps in the slot. Kitan Oladapo didn’t play on defense but logged 17 on special teams.
McKinney grabbed his NFL-leading sixth interception. Williams has been a stud for most of the season but not so much against Minnesota. He wasn’t bad – he’s a menace as a blitzer – but missed a tackle on the Vikings’ clinching touchdown.
RB Kaleb Johnson: Johnson carried the ball five times for 35 yards in the second half. Sure, the Vikings probably didn’t care about the run game at that point, but he ran hard and with a purpose. He had to play one snap of pass protection and stopped the Vikings’ blitzer in his tracks.
S Javon Bullard: The Vikings put Justin Jefferson in the slot at times, and he beat Javon Bullard for a pair of first downs, but Bullard also destroyed a couple receiver screens and pressured the passer with his blitzes.
Edge Lukas Van Ness: Van Ness, as mentioned above, was probably the Packers’ best player. PFF credited him with a team-high four pressures, giving him a dozen over the last three games. He’s had to lead the group without Micah Parsons. With Parsons coming back, Van Ness might get better chances to get after the passer. With six sacks in 10 games, he’s got a chance to get to 10.
CB Keisean Nixon: Justin Jefferson finally had some production, catching nine passes for 74 yards following his reunion with Kirk Cousins. However, according to PFF, Nixon allowed 1-of-3 passing for 8 yards, including a second-and-goal breakup that helped hold the Vikings to a field goal.
Geez. pic.twitter.com/0OAW1qD6oY
The offensive line: From Jordan Morgan getting thrown into the back of Jordan Love’s legs early in the game to the nonstop stream of pass rushers getting in the…

title: Packers Report Card: Grades From Another Beatdown Against Vikings
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The grades are in and, as you’d suspect, they resemble my marks in high school geometry. OK, jokes aside, even I was not as bad as the Packers were in Sunday’s game against the Minnesota Vikings.
In what was billed as a showdown between two of the top teams in the NFC, the Vikings dismantled the Packers in every perceivable fashion.
Arguably the best play of the game for Green Bay’s offense was one that probably should never have happened. Jordan Love threw a ball down the middle of the field for Tucker Kraft in the third quarter that bounced off his hands, off a defender’s hands, and into the arms of Savion Williams. The play was good for 25 yards, and could only be chalked up to sheer dumb luck.
That’s basically all the Packers had on Sunday. Here are our grades from a dreadful performance.
The success of this game was going to be on the shoulders of Green Bay’s offensive line. If the Packers could protect Jordan Love, the offense would have an opportunity against Minnesota’s secondary to put up some points.
If they couldn’t, it was going to be a long day for the offense. The score was 20-0 in favor of the Vikings in the middle of the third quarter. Jordan Love was sacked eight times in the first two-and-a-half quarters as the Vikings built an insurmountable lead.
When Love was pressured, he was snowed under. When he wasn’t, it was almost as if he was anticipating pressure. He sailed the ball over Tucker Kraft’s head on an interception that came as he was fading away from the throw. Even if Kraft is at fault for cutting off his route, Love’s process was bad on the play.
Love was actually better under pressure (11-of-14) than from a clean pocket (6-of-13 with his one touchdown and one interception). It’s just that the frequency of the pressure – 62.9 percent, according to Pro Football Focus – either led to sacks or simply made him uneasy on most dropbacks.
The Vikings defense pressured Jordan Love on 21 of 35 dropbacks (60.0%) and sacked him 8 times. Love faced a career-high pressure rate despite averaging 2.33 seconds to throw, his second-quickest time in a game. @MINvsGB | #Skol
“I think to your point, you take some hits in the game, things like that. As a quarterback, that’s the job,” Love said of the interception, when he acted as if pressure was coming when he actually had a strong pocket.
“You’ve got to be able to stay in there and trust the guys are going to get the job done around you and still be able to deliver. So, I’ll never make an excuse for that. You’ve got to be able to sit in the pocket and just trust what’s going on around you. And we didn’t do that on that play.”
Tyrod Taylor entered the game because of the lopsided nature of the score.
Love and Co. had very few answers for Brian Flores. They showed little interest in a quick passing game that likely needs to be employed against a defense like Minnesota’s. Instead, they tried their bombs-away offense but never had time to find any shots down the field.
They did find a little success in the second half when they switched to a no-huddle offense, but it was too late by then.
Christian Watson and Matthew Golden, who caught 17-of-18 targets for 335 yards last week, caught 8-of-13 for 107 yards vs. Minnesota. PFF charged Golden with two drops. Kraft had one catch for a second consecutive week.
Green Bay’s offense goes by Jordan Love and their passing game. They went nowhere on Sunday.
Perhaps the Packers have found something with Kaleb Johnson leading the way in their backfield? Green Bay’s bar to clear in the run game is incredibly low, but Johnson looked decisive on his runs and was averaging 4.2 yards per carry before the game got out of hand.
Of course, part of the reason the game got out of hand was the Packers’ need to be one-dimensional because of the scoreboard and their inability to consistently rely on their run game.
Josh Jacobs will likely take his role as starting running back when he returns from his finger injury, perhaps as soon as next week against the Rams or perhaps the following week. In the meantime, Johnson needs to be the one who is the bell cow, if such a thing exists for the 2026 Packers.
The good was that the Packers sacked Kirk Cousins three times and picked him off once. They held him to 207 yards on 21 completions. The bad? They gave up three huge third-down conversions that were at least 12 yards in length.
One was a 38-yard touchdown to Myles Price to give the Vikings a 10-0 lead in the first quarter.
The final one was a third-and-12 in which Minnesota was set up in a formation that made a receiver screen feel inevitable. Cousins got the ball to Justin Jefferson quickly and Jefferson did the rest, picking up a back-breaking first down. The Vikings would score a touchdown four plays later to put the game on ice.
Those plays were the difference between a competitive fourth quarter and a blowout.
Aaron Jones found his way into the end zone and did a Lambeau leap, which gave the Vikings a 27-10 lead against his former team in the fourth quarter.
Jones and Jordan Mason were solid if unspectacular for most of the game. Green Bay’s defense was good enough but did not make any significant plays against the run, either.
The final numbers were fine. The Packers gave up 106 yards on 27 carries to Minnesota’s running back tandem. They gave up 129 rushing yards total. That was not awful, but certainly not good enough.
Trey Smack missed another field goal. This one was from 53 yards and never had much of a chance. He’s missed nine kicks this year, which leads the league. The Packers are going to continue to ride the wave of a rookie kicker, but should they?
Ultimately, the loss of points did not matter on Sunday because the Packers’ offense could not do anything against Minnesota’s stingy defense, but it could matter in other games that play out this season.
The return game did little after Skyy Moore dropped out of the game with an ankle injury. J. Michael Sturdivant gave the ball away on a kick return in the fourth quarter. Meanwhile, Minnesota’s coverage was excellent and their kicker was automatic.
The third phase of the game was a decisive victory in Minnesota’s favor.
A lot of discussion is going to surround Matt LaFleur’s decision to give the Vikings an extra down in the first quarter. Minnesota was facing a third-and-8 when it was flagged for a facemask penalty. LaFleur’s options were to back the Vikings up 15 yards or allow them to kick a field goal from Green Bay’s 23.
LaFleur opted for a third-and-23 that put the Vikings back at the 38. Minnesota scored a touchdown on the next play.
From here, LaFleur made the right decision. Points are going to be at a premium against Minnesota’s defense, and Green Bay’s defense had played well up to that point. A sack would knock Minnesota out of field-goal range. An incompletion would have made the field goal harder to make.
Yes, the result was bad. The process, however, was good. A criticism of LaFleur is that he’s often too conservative. In that case, he’s coaching aggressively. Green Bay failing to execute in that situation falls on the players, not the coach.
“You got to roll the dice there and, certainly, that was a pivotal play in the game,” LaFleur said. “We can’t get beat in third-and-23. The odds of that are very, very low and they made us pay.”
The rest of the game? That’s fair to question. LaFleur did not seem interested in getting the ball out of his quarterback’s hands quickly as he was snowed under by Minnesota’s pressure packages.
“We’ve got to have better concepts to be able to get those balls out quicker,” Love said as part of a long answer about the pressure.
LaFleur and his offense found a little bit of rhythm in the second half by using some no huddle, but it was far too late by the time they made that adjustment.
Defensively, Jonathan Gannon’s defense did well to limit the damage from four takeaways to just three field goals but also didn’t take advantage of the Vikings playing…

title: Blame the Organization for Butt Whoopin’ Packers Were Handed by Vikings
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – It takes every player on the field for a play to succeed.
It takes every player on the 53-man roster – heck, it takes all 70 on the team – to win a game.
It takes an entire organization to win a championship. Or not having a chance to win a championship.
The Green Bay Packers got sacked by the rival Minnesota Vikings on Sunday. All week, the players and coaches talked about how playing at Lambeau Field would help with the communication necessary to deal with the Vikings’ pressure packages. The Packers had a veteran offensive line, unlike the first game, and should have been prepared after getting blown out in the opener.
All of that was nonsense. Complete and utter garbage.
“That was a butt-whoppin’,” coach Matt LaFleur said to kick off his introductory remarks.
Yeah, it would be easy to blame the offensive line for missing blocks. It would be easy to blame LaFleur for expecting that game plan to win against that defense. It would be easy to blame quarterback Jordan Love for being skittish in the pocket.
And all those things would be true.
The reason for the loss, however, starts at the top with general manager Brian Gutekunst.
It’s Gutekunst’s complete and total mismanagement of the offense that has the team in its current predicament.
It was Gutekunst who used a first-round pick on left tackle Jordan Morgan in 2024, only to stunt his growth by having him play other positions for two seasons. It was Gutekunst who gave the bank to left guard Aaron Banks in 2025 for no good reason . It was Gutekunst who released Elgton Jenkins after shifting him to center following the signing of Banks. It was Gutekunst who drafted Anthony Belton in the second round in 2025. It was Gutekunst, realizing the errors in his ways, who went to a rummage sale to find Laken Tomlinson, Kevin Zeitler and Mekhi Becton when his offensive line got crushed to start the season.
In 2019, which was LaFleur’s first season as coach, the offensive line consisted of left tackle David Bakhtiari, left guard Elgton Jenkins, center Corey Linsley, right guard Billy Turner and right tackle Bryan Bulaga. That team reached the NFC Championship Game.
On Sunday, the line was Morgan at left tackle, Tomlinson at left guard, John Williams at center, Travis Glover at right guard and Belton at right tackle. It was the team’s sixth starting combination this season. With mediocre blocking, musical chairs and a lack of continuity, Green Bay has one foot on thin ice and another foot on a banana peel in the playoff race.
The Packers should have five big-ticket investments driving the line with Morgan at left tackle, Banks at center, Sean Rhyan at center, Belton at right guard and Zach Bako-Bewele at right tackle. Banks, Rhyan and Bako-Bewele were given big contracts to sign/re-sign in free agency and Morgan and Belton are premium draft picks.
It’s not Gutekunst’s fault, obviously, that Bako-Bewele is out with a major knee injury for the second consecutive year, but there is practically no evidence that any of the four other starters he selected are good enough to be playing for a championship contender.
Which is perhaps why the Vikings for the second time this season showed the world that the Packers aren’t really championship contenders.
On Sunday, Banks essentially was a healthy scratch other than a few snaps on special teams. Imagine that – the ninth-highest-paid guard in the NFL isn’t good enough to start on a team with a porous offensive line.
The Packers like the 34-year-old Tomlinson so much that they moved Banks to right guard. It’s a position he didn’t play at Notre Dame and hasn’t played in the NFL.
“We were going to shuffle up the O-line a little bit,” LaFleur explained after the game. “I think Laken’s been doing a pretty good job and we put him back to his natural position, and we were going to let Banks compete at the right guard. He doesn’t have a ton of time on task at that position, so we went the way we did tonight.”
Banks should be a bedrock on the line, a reliable pass protector and power blocker. Instead, he couldn’t even unseat Travis Glover, who had missed the last four games with a knee injury, to be a starter at right guard on Sunday. At left guard, he is behind Tomlinson, a past-his-prime lineman grabbed off a practice squad.
During a feeding-frenzy game against the Vikings, Banks was a $77 million backup.
Offensive lines need to be powering teams into the playoffs. This offensive line is powering the team into a ditch.
At this point, LaFleur and his coaches seem to be in the chucking-crap-at-a-wall-and-seeing-what-sticks phase of the season.
That’s not what championship teams do.
Things should improve once Rhyan returns to the lineup, potentially against the Rams following the make-believe bye week. However, it’s not as if Rhyan as the ninth-highest-paid center in the league was playing like he was the ninth-best center at the time of his ankle injury at Detroit.
The personnel problems have been exacerbated by the clown show of learning before every game which five blockers will play the five positions. Continuity seems like a punch line to a joke rather than a plan on the offensive line.
And to top it all off, LaFleur and Love seemed to be expecting the blockers to perform like Fordham’s famous Seven Blocks of Granite line, which included Vince Lombardi, rather than the Five Blocks of Swiss. To summarize the first half: Love dropped back to pass, the receivers ran downfield routes and Love got sacked.
Love was sacked five times in the first half, which tied for the most for any full game in the LaFleur era. The sack total swelled to eight through two-and-a-half quarters, tied for the most allowed by any team this season.
It was almost as if the Packers didn’t watch the success the Bills had with a quick passing game during their convincing win on Monday night at Minnesota last week.
“It’s obviously a bad decision, because our quarterback was getting abused just like he did in the first game,” LaFleur said. “We had called some of that early on, and it really wasn’t successful until the second half.”
Finally, the Packers pivoted and they almost got back in the game, which led to this remarkable combination of stats, with Love throwing quick (either by design or by necessity) and still getting pressure at a staggering level.
The Vikings defense pressured Jordan Love on 21 of 35 dropbacks (60.0%) and sacked him 8 times. Love faced a career-high pressure rate despite averaging 2.33 seconds to throw, his second-quickest time in a game. @MINvsGB | #Skol
“I think we had some success in the second half jumping the ball, doing some things, but I think to your point, when you’re facing a defense that’s pressuring that way, you’ve got to be able to get the ball out quick and have those answers and find the holes in the defense,” Love said.
Love noted the complexity and challenges of dealing with the Vikings' defensive front but also said the Vikings didn’t do anything they hadn’t seen on film during the week of prep. So, in other words, the linemen were not prepared mentally and overmatched physically.
“It’s missed opportunities, that’s all it is,” Love said, “and the conversations are what can we do better? What plays can we do better to get the ball out? Obviously, whatever we were calling right there was not working.”
No, it was not. Which begs the question of now what?
The players are the players and the coaches are the coaches. Help is not on the way. Gutekunst picked the blockers. LaFleur picked Luke Butkus to coach them.
Ultimately, Gutekunst handed LaFleur a pile of chicken feathers. With seven games remaining, starting with Myles Garrett, Aaron Donald and the Rams next week, and a daunting road ahead just to squeak into the playoffs, it’ll be up to LaFleur and Love to turn them into something other than the chicken crap the Packers drowned in on Sunday.
From an ugly defeat, @JacobWestendorf has his weekly winners and losers for the Packers. ⬇️…

title: Good, Bad and Interesting Following Packers’ Pivotal, Pitiful Loss to Vikings
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers were trounced by the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday, just like they were trounced at the end of the season-opening game.
Combined, the Packers gave up 49 consecutive points – the final 29 in Week 1 and the first 20 in Week 10 – and lost 30-10. By the end of the game, only purple-clad Vikings fans chanting “Skol” were left at Lambeau Field.
Here is the good, the bad and the interesting following a pivotal loss.
Xavier McKinney’s sixth interception: About the only thing that went right in the first half was McKinney’s toe-tapping interception. Vikings receiver Tai Felton put both hands on top of his helmet, seemingly in disbelief.
The interception was McKinney’s sixth of the season, tops in the league.
“We did all right. We still lost, though, so it don’t really matter,” McKinney said. “It’s a team game. So regardless of what we did out there defensively, we’re still a team and the team lost.”
Carrington Valentine’s physicality: Valentine has never been renowned for his physical play. However, forced into action with Brandon Cisse’s rib injury that he sustained on Minnesota’s first touchdown drive, he helped stuff a perimeter run on his first play and then, after the Packers cut the margin to 20-7, he helped ruin a receiver screen to Justin Jefferson on third down. Early in the fourth quarter, he made an excellent tackle at the catch point against Jefferson.
Kaleb Johnson: The Packers might have a real running back with Johnson, who had 10 carries for 42 yards through three quarters. When there was nowhere to run, he broke a tackle or fought for something. When there was a hole to run, he stepped in the gas to get to the second level. By our count, he broke four tackles and had 40 yards after contact.
A little more wiggle or a second gear would be ideal, obviously, but he’s the best the Packers have without Josh Jacobs.
Speaking of Jacobs, he will push to play against the Rams. A backfield of Jacobs and Johnson would have some potential.
NFC North championship hopes: One picture says a thousand words.
Lions jump to the top! 🦁 What a race we've got going on in the NFC North 👀 pic.twitter.com/D8hhZdrecX
With the loss, the Packers are two games behind the other three teams in the loss column. Really, with the tiebreaker, they are three games behind the Vikings.
Pass protection: Trailing 10-0, Jordan Love was sacked on second down by defensive tackle Levi Drake Rodriguez and on third down by former Packers linebacker Eric Wilson. At that point, Love in four series had completed four passes and been sacked three times, and the run game had 19 yards on eight carries.
Left tackle Jordan Morgan gave up one of the sacks vs. Dallas Turner; more on that in a moment. On the next series, Mekhi Becton came in as an extra tight end alongside Morgan, presumably to help keep Turner at bay. Instead, Becton might not have laid a finger on Turner, who hit Love just as he completed a checkdown.
Late in the half, after Xavier McKinney’s interception, the Packers gained two first downs. With the ball near midfield, they had a chance to cut into a 17-0 deficit. Instead, Turner and Kyle Van Noy combined to sack Love on second down and Van Noy had a sack on third down.
Due in part to the blocking, the Packers had 57 yards at halftime with a 2.2-yard average. The high-powered passing attack averaged 2.0 yards per dropback, with Love’s seven completions offset by five sacks.
The adjustments, namely no-huddle offense, were too little and obviously too late.
“I think we had some success in the second half jumping the ball, doing some things, but I think to your point, when you’re facing a defense that’s pressuring that way, you’ve got to be able to get the ball out quick and have those answers and find the holes in the defense,” Love said.
“Because, obviously, there is holes out there when they’re bringing the pressure. It’s definitely something we’ll look at and how we can be better because you don’t stand a chance sometimes when you’re getting pressure and the routes are still developing. It’s definitely something we’ll look at.”
Love wound up being sacked eight times. The Packers hadn’t allowed more than five sacks during the Matt LaFleur era. It was their most allowed since the 2012 season at Seattle.
“Yeah, it wasn’t great,” he said of the pass protection. “It wasn’t good enough up front, weren’t good enough at getting the ball out and, when you do those things, you’re going to take some hits. Obviously, we know what this defense brings and they’re going to bring pressure and things like that, and I don’t think we were good enough against it tonight.”
Jordan Love had one of the fastest time to throws of the season, and it didn't matter. The Vikings still posted the second-highest pressure rate of any defense in a game this season. pic.twitter.com/gTazXhoFWh
First-drive fumble: Green Bay’s first drive ended after two plays when backup tight end Mark Redman was stripped by Andrew Van Ginkel. The miscue gave the Vikings a gift-wrapped field goal to take a 3-0 lead.
The Packers knew they had to win the turnover battle; the Vikings were 6-0 when they had won it this season. Green Bay lost 4-1 and got smoked.
“Yeah, they can’t happen,” LaFleur said. “Started off, second play of the game, we fumble the football and set them up. That’s giving them three points. I thought all in all, our defense did a pretty good job responding to those difficult situations, but you can’t give up the ball, whether you’re deep in your own territory or you’re in scoring position to put points on the board.
“We knew points were probably going to be at a premium. That’s one of the best defenses if not the best defense in the National Football League right now, and you can’t take yourself out of those opportunities.”
Smack and line strike again: Green Bay’s second drive ended on the other side of the field. On third-and-7 after two horrendously blocked running plays, Dallas Turner ran over left tackle Jordan Morgan to sack Jordan Love. Trey Smack, who missed twice from 55 yards to the north end during pregame, was wide right from 53.
Tight ends: With T.J. Hockenson inactive, the Vikings’ tight ends entered the game with a combined eight catches. The Packers entered the game with Tucker Kraft.
Advantage, Green Bay, right? Not so much. Gavin Bartholomew caught three passes for 36 yards and one touchdown. Kraft caught 1-of-4 targets for 19 yards.
Aaron Banks: The Packers gave Aaron Banks a four-year, $77 million contract in free agency last offseason. The $19.25 million average ranks ninth at the position. Due to a litany of lower-body injuries, Banks has started only three games this season – and finished only one of those.
He was limited participation at all three practices this week with knee and hip injuries but not on the final injury report. So, the only way to look at it was Banks was benched for Travis Glover. Indeed, LaFleur said after the game the decision was to put Laken Tomlinson back at his “natural position,” left guard, and to have Banks “compete” at right guard, which is not his natural position.
Offensive line: The Packers’ starting line had Laken Tomlinson shifting back to left guard and Travis Glover returning to the starting lineup at right guard after missing a couple games with the knee injury he played through at Detroit.
That means Aaron Banks was a backup after starting the last two games.
Only the coaches know whether Glover was the starter at right guard, plain and simple, or if he got the call because Kevin Zeitler was injured. Zeitler was limited participation at practice on Wednesday with an ankle injury. He must have suffered a triceps injury during Thursday’s practice, because he was limited on Thursday, did not practice on Friday and inactive for the game.
