title: Packers Winners and Losers in Loss to Vikings Starts With Pass Protection
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers entered Sunday’s game against the Minnesota Vikings needing a win to have any realistic shot of winning the NFC North. A loss would drop them to 6-4, with two of those losses coming against Minnesota. A win would tie them in the standings with the Vikings and allow them to keep pace with the Detroit Lions and Chicago Bears.
Green Bay’s offense was rolling coming into the game as they piled up 45 points against New England’s defense last week and essentially named their score.
The problem this week was they were facing Brian Flores’ defense.
A bigger problem was facing Flores and falling behind 17-0 in the first half. That’s a death sentence for any offense, let alone one who cannot protect its quarterback.
The Packers added 10 points to pull within 20-10, but gave up a touchdown to Gavin Bartholomew with 8:29 left in the fourth quarter. The game was decided there if it was not already.
As a result, the list of losers is long and distinguished as the Packers were beaten up on their home field.
The biggest culprit of Green Bay’s Week 1 loss to the Minnesota Vikings was the inability to protect Jordan Love.
The biggest culprit of Green Bay’s Week 10 loss to the Minnesota Vikings was the inability to protect Jordan Love. Love was under siege in the first half, and appeared to be rattled at different points even when he was not under pressure. He was pressured on 71 percent of his drop backs in the first half.
Green Bay’s offense threatened giving up more sacks than they had pass completions in the first half. That number ultimately ended at five sacks to seven completions.  Yes, Minnesota’s defense is good, but good defenses are the type that the Packers are going to have to knock off in order to achieve their goals. There was reason for hope after last week’s drubbing of the New England Patriots that the Packers could be set up better to withstand the pressure that Flores and his defense brings continuously.
It didn’t matter. Love was under siege whether Flores rushed four, or if he brought pressure. The run game was not any better. There were so many unblocked defenders in both phases of the offense.
The Packers tried to play with multiple tight ends, six offensive linemen, or leave the running back in for protection purposes. None of it really mattered. Minnesota’s defense has won every matchup they’ve had this year, and this matchup was a win by total knockout.
Jordan Love’s 18 dropbacks in the first half went accordingly.  He completed seven passes. Matthew Golden had two drops. Love threw an interception and was sacked five times.
Following last week’s destruction of the New England Patriots, Love had catapulted himself into the MVP conversation, if one can exist before the month of December.
Sunday’s performance by Love and the rest of the offense should quiet those discussions for the foreseeable future. Maybe it’s not fair, but great quarterbacks are asked to elevate those around them.
Yes, Love was under pressure a bunch on Sunday. That was the expectation coming into the game even if the Packers had a good plan for what the Vikings wanted to do on defense. What Love could not afford to do is leave points on the field. He did just that in the first half when he threw an interception to Harrison Smith after the Packers had crossed into the red zone.
Love’s pass sailed or Kraft was unable to get to the ball. Regardless, Love looked like he was anticipating pressure that never came.
It’s a fine line to follow, but Love could have been better on Sunday too.
Is Tucker Kraft healthy? Are there worse questions that need to be asked? Kraft has not looked like himself for most of the season, and struggled again on Sunday. With the Packers deep in Minnesota territory, Jordan Love loaded up trying to find Tucker Kraft near the goal line. A catch would have given the Packers a first-and-goal. Love’s throw sailed, but Kraft also looked slow and not explosive on the route.
He finished the game with one catch for 19 yards.
Kraft has rarely looked like the tight end who was going to threaten for an All Pro honor last season before injuring his knee.
Will he ever look like that player this season? That remains to be seen, but he certainly did not look like he was anywhere close to that guy on Sunday.
Remember when the Packers briefly held a 25-10 lead against Minnesota in the first game of the season? That lead was short lived because Matt LaFleur took a field goal off the board to try and step on the Vikings’ throat.
The Packers would fail on fourth down and turn the ball over back to Minnesota’s offense. From that point forward, Green Bay was outscored 29-0 by the Vikings. That drubbing continued on Sunday. The Packers were unable to stop the bleeding. Minnesota’s run extended to 49-0 with a 20-0 lead they built in the third quarter.
The Packers have gotten drilled by this team ever since that fateful decision in Minnesota. Why would there be any confidence a potential third meeting in the postseason, on the road, be any different?
Mark Redman was brought to Green Bay to be a blocker. On Green Bay’s first possession, however, he was asked to be a receiver. Redman does not have many opportunities as a pass catcher. He had just two catches on the year coming into Sunday’s game.
His first catch since Week 4 ended in disaster. Redman caught the ball, but was immediately met by Andrew Van Ginkel, who knocked the ball out of Redman’s hands. The forced fumble was recovered by the Vikings, setting them up deep in Green Bay territory. Redman’s mistake cost the Packers three points in the first quarter after the defense stood tall.
Those are the types of mistakes that lose games as the calendar turns to November and December. Redman was fortunate his mistake only cost the Packers three instead of seven.
Trey Smack had his bounce back last week against the New England Patriots where he made all seven of his kicks with relative ease.
The hope from Green Bay was that would carry over into a big division game against Minnesota, but it was not to be.
Smack lined up to kick a 53-yard field goal after Jordan Morgan was smoked by Dallas Turner for a sack on third-and-9 on Green Bay’s second series of the game.
The operation was good, but Smack’s kick was wide to the right. That was his sixth missed field goal of the season and ninth overall. In the first quarter the Packers had gifted the Vikings a field goal and missed one of their own.
The bigger the game is, the slimmer the margin for error becomes. That margin becomes even thinner against a Minnesota defense that has been elite all season. The Packers simply cannot afford to leave points on the field. Smack has left too many of them with 21 points already left on the field this season.
The Packers did not have much to cheer for on Sunday, but Xavier McKinney continued his playmaking ways against Kirk Cousins. The Vikings were threatening to extend their 17-0 lead in the first half when Cousins loaded up a deep ball for Tai Felton down the left sideline.
McKinney tracked the ball from the center of the field and raced to the sideline making an impressive catch with his fingertips. It was probably the best catch of the day by a Packer regardless of the side of the ball they play on.
6th INTERCEPTION FOR XAVIER McKINNEY! 📺: FOX pic.twitter.com/WJ31qNmgQE
McKinney’s pick was his sixth of the year. He had eight in his first season in Green Bay, and may challenge for the top of the league.
The Packers offense had so little going against Minnesota’s stingy defense on Sunday. They trailed 20-0 in the third quarter with Jordan Love getting snowed under by Minnesota’s rush.
On October 10, J. Michael Sturdivant had what he thought was his first touchdown reception of his career, but it was taken away due to a pass interference penalty.
No penalty was stopping Sturdivant this time. He found an ocean’s worth of room in the middle of Minnesota’s defense. Love had enough time to rip the ball to…

title: Vikings Beat Packers, Sack Green Bay in NFC North Standings
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Minnesota Vikings made an emphatic statement on Sunday at Lambeau Field. They are Super Bowl contenders because of their rampaging defense and addition of Kirk Cousins. The Green Bay Packers made a statement of their own.
They aren’t good enough to compete in the powerhouse NFC North.
The Vikings dominated the Packers for almost the full 60 minutes to beat the Packers 30-10.
Minnesota’s ferocious front pillaged Green Bay’s porous offensive line, with Jordan Love absorbing an appalling eight sacks and at times seeing pressure when there was none. The Packers turned it over four times – a horrendous interception by Love when he wasn’t pressured, a wayward shotgun snap that Love couldn’t reach, a fumble by backup tight end Mark Redman and a fumble by kickoff returner J. Michael Sturdivant.
Love watched the final 4 minutes from the sideline. He was 17-of-27 for 220 yards, but the eight sacks cut the net total to 161 yards. He was pressured on 54 percent of his dropbacks, according to the early numbers from Pro Football Focus.
The sacks tell the story. The division standing show the reality.
The Lions, who beat New England in Germany, are 7-2. The Bears, enjoying their bye week, are 7-2. The Vikings, who had lost two in a row but traded for Kirk Cousins this week, are 7-2.
The Packers are 6-4. They are two games behind everyone in the loss column and even further behind the Vikings because of the head-to-head tiebreaker.
The Packers cut a 20-0 deficit to 20-10, but the Vikings had the killer answer with a 75-yard touchdown drive midway through the fourth quarter that not only meant seven points but devoured almost 7 minutes off the clock.
The absolutely killer play was third-and-12. The Vikings had four receivers to the left and an empty backfield. It seemed obvious where the ball was going. Indeed, it was a quick pass to Justin Jefferson, who used those other receivers for an escort for a 16-yard gain.
That set up third-and-1 at the 20. A couple years ago, Packers coach Matt LaFleur dialed up a touchdown pass to Luke Musgrave by having Jordan Love fake a pass to the left, fake a pass to the right and then hit the tight end over the middle. On this play, Kirk Cousins faked a pass to the left, faked a pass to the right and hit tight end Gavin Bartholomew over the middle. He caught the pass at the 15, stiff-armed Evan Williams to the turf and scored to make it 27-10 with 8:29 to play.
J. Michael Sturdivant fumbled away the ensuing kickoff, and some of the fans started heading for the exits before Will Reichard’s field goal extended the margin to 30-10.
At the 2-minute warning, only the fans in purple remained in the stands.
The Packers trailed 17-0 late in the first half but had a chance to double up at the end of the second quarter and the start of the third quarter.
Instead, the offensive line implosion continued. The half ended with Jordan Love taking back-to-back sacks and the second half started with John Williams’ shotgun snap being so far to Love’s left that he didn’t even get a finger on the ball. The Vikings recovered the bouncing ball but the defense, thanks to Keisean Nixon’s second-down deflection and Lukas Van Ness’ third-down sack, held the damage to three points.
Still, it was 20-0 with 10:02 left in the third quarter.
Finally, the Packers got going – though some good fortune. On third-and-20, Love fired one over the middle to Tucker Kraft. The ball went through Kraft’s hands and Harrison Smith’s hands before being caught by Savion Williams for a first down. Then, on fourth-and-11, Love hit Matthew Golden at the sideline for 12. On the next play, Love hit J. Michael Sturdivant for a 32-yard touchdown.
Suddenly, despite giving up two more sacks on the drive, the Packers had some life – and there was some life in Lambeau – with a 20-7 margin with 5:37 left in the third quarter.
The Packers had some real life after forcing a three-and-out. With the Packers going no-huddle, Love completed passes to Christian Watson, Tucker Kraft, Matthew Golden and Watson to get into scoring range. However, on third-and-10, nobody blocked either of safety blitzers, Josh Metellus and Theo Jackson, and Love’s all-arm pass to J. Michael Sturdivant landed short of its destination. Trey Smack’s 40-yard field goal cut the margin to 20-10 with 19 seconds left in the quarter.
The Viking struck first. After Green Bay forced a three-and-out to start the game, it faced a second-and-10 from its 5. Jordan Love connected with backup tight end Mark Redman in the flat, but he had the ball punched loose immediately by star edge Andrew Van Ginkel, who recovered at Green Bay’s 10.
The defense did well to limit the damage. On second-and-15, Barryn Sorrell beat Lukas Van Ness in a race to the quarterback to sack Kirk Cousins. One play later, Will Reichard kicked a 34-yard field goal.
The Packers got into scoring position on the ensuing drive, but Dallas Turner destroyed left tackle Jordan Morgan, with Morgan and Turner combining to take down Love for a sack. Trey Smack’s 53-yard field-goal attempt was wide right.
Set up with a short field, the Vikings struck again. On third-and-8, safety Evan Williams blitzed and clobbered Cousins to force an incomplete pass. A flag was thrown for a facemask on the Vikings. Coach Matt LaFleur could have the Vikings kick a 41-yard field goal or push the Vikings back for 15 yards. LaFleur took the penalty and the Vikings made him pay the highest price imaginable.
Cousins ripped one up the seam to Myles Price, who bounced off Brandon Cisse at the 12 and strolled into end zone. Cisse was shaken up – he eventually walked to the locker room with a rib injury and did not return – and the Vikings led 10-0 with 2:46 left in the quarter.
Green Bay got into the red zone on the next possession, meaning a matchup between Jordan Love and the Vikings’ top-ranked red zone defense. The Vikings won. Love felt pressure that really didn’t exist and threw one off his back foot to Tucker Kraft up the seam. The pass went right to safety Harrison Smith for Green Bay’s second turnover.
After an exchange of punts – Love was sacked on second and third down – the Vikings took advantage of another short field to drive 55 yards for a touchdown and a 17-0 lead.
The Packers appeared to have made a game-changing play when Karl Brooks took down Kirk Cousins, who threw a boneheaded interception to Lukas Van Ness. However, Cousins was correctly ruled down, so Brooks got the most inconsequential sack imaginable. That’s because on third-and-15, Cousins went deep to Tai Felton for a 24-yard completion to the 1. Aaron Jones scored on the next play.
Incredibly, the Vikings – who were playing without top tight end T.J. Hockenson, No. 2 receiver Jordan Addison and No. 3 receiver Jauan Jennings – led 17-0, even with the defense having held Justin Jefferson to one catch for 13 yards.
The Packers went three-and-out on the next drive. Matthew Golden, coming off a huge game against New England, dropped a pass on second down and couldn’t make a diving catch at the sideline on third down. Through five possessions, the Packers had 38 yards and averaged 1.9 yards per play.
With a speck of life late in the first half following Xavier McKinney’s interception, Love completed two passes for first downs to Matthew Golden before he was sacked on back-to-back plays. The Packers punted, with Love having completed seven passes and getting sacked five times.
The half ended with the Packers getting booed off the field.

title: Officiating, Roughing the Passer And More Make-or-Break Packers-Vikings Factors
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Remember the roughing-the-passer problem early in the season for the Green Bay Packers?
It’s still a problem, and it could be a huge factor for Sunday’s game against the Minnesota Vikings.
Including one by Dani Dennis-Sutton last week, the Packers have been deemed guilty of nine roughing-the-passer penalties this season. That’s more than double the next three teams – Carolina, Cleveland and Kansas City are next with four – and four more than the rest of the NFC North teams combined.
Meanwhile, Jordan Love has not drawn a roughing foul. So, the Packers are minus-9. Only one other team is even minus-3.
Minnesota, on the other hand, has been flagged twice for roughing despite applying more hits on the quarterback than any other defense.
The NFL reconfigured officiating crews because of nationwide flight problems this week. The new referee is Clete Blakeman. According to NFL Ref Stats, Blakeman’s crew is No. 1 in defensive penalties, No. 1 in defensive penalties that resulted in first downs and tied for No. 1 in roughing-the-passer penalties.
#MINvsGB officiating crew cheat sheet update Clete Blakeman assigned as the referee & fellow head ref Alex Kemp is on his crew for Sunday's game also This will already be the #Packers third game w' Alex Kemp involved in 2026, which is rare for any team to have same official… pic.twitter.com/RE0WwC4UM8
While the Packers apparently are cheap-shot artists, the Vikings play with halos.
According to NFL Penalties, the Vikings’ defense has been penalized a league-low nine times this season. Nine – as many total penalties as Green Bay’s roughing-the-passer count. Minnesota has not been flagged for pass interference or defensive holding.
Here are four more critical factors.
The way to stymie the Vikings’ powerhouse defense is to run the football. It’s the one sort-of weakness on one of the best defenses of the era.
The last three games, the Vikings gave up 154 rushing yards against the Colts, 230 rushing yards against the Vikings and 134 rushing yards last week against the Bills. They allowed only 3.0 yards per carry against Buffalo but Buffalo eventually wore them down to hog the ball for 43 minutes.
Can the Packers run the football, of course, is the million-dollar question. They had a breakout game last week against New England, but was that a sign of real progress or a mirage? That they will attack a defense without premier linebacker Blake Cashman will help.
The Vikings blitz the quarterback at a historic level. Against most defenses, the concern is limited to third down. Against Minnesota, the concern is on every down. It’s so extreme that the Vikings blitz 80.0 percent of the time on first-and-10.
Jordan Love is good against the blitz. Of 29 qualifying passers, Love is ninth with a 109.8 passer rating against the blitz, according to Sumer Sports. He is No. 1 in passing yards by a relative mile – he has 932 passing yards, almost 200 yards more than No. 2 Drake Maye – and trails only Brock Purdy with nine touchdowns.
“His anticipation to see space and just trust his receivers and get the ball into wherever area that’s supposed to be has been pretty awesome,” offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich said this week.
“Whether that’s layering a ball, giving it some time or throwing it on a line, it’s been pretty impressive to watch just that. And again, we’ve talked about it, he’s calm, doesn’t get rattled, so he’s just a special player when it comes to like, he can just handle those things and it’s been fun to watch.”
Flores will not be scared of Love. At all.
In Week 1, Love dropped back to pass 46 times. He was blitzed on 40 – or 87.0 percent. OK, that was in Minneapolis with a makeshift offensive line. So, what about last year at Lambeau Field? Love was blitzed on 20-of-24 dropbacks, or 83.3 percent.
The ability to protect Love will, obviously, be critical. When given time, Love is the game’s best big-play quarterback. On passes thrown 20-plus yards downfield, he’s tied for third with 23 completions and is first by a wide margin with 826 yards. On the other hand, the Vikings have allowed only eight completions on deep passes; only four teams have given up fewer.
Green Bay, for all fireworks from last week, has been fairly mediocre on offense this season. It’s a modest 12th with 24.0 points per game. That’s disappointing production given all the turnovers provided by the defense. A big reason why is Green Bay is 19th in the red zone and 22nd in goal-to-go situations.
Minnesota’s defense is elite. The Vikings are first in both areas, giving up touchdowns 26.3 percent of the time in the red zone and at just a 40.0 percent clip in goal-to-go.
“They are very good, and on top of that you see very minimal snaps down in the red area,” Packers coach Matt LaFleur said. “They’ve done a really good job. This is one of the top-ranked, if not the top-ranked defense in the National Football League. They’re just really stout. They do a great job. What they do such a great job of is just getting you behind the sticks, so you’ve got to stay on schedule versus this group.”
The Vikings made a huge move at quarterback by acquiring Kirk Cousins.
“The way he threw the football this week, it's a really cool thing to see,” Vikings coach Kevin O’Connell said.
The arrival of Cousins is practically a two-for-one. Justin Jefferson is one of the best receivers in the league, if not the best. He is only 54th in the league with 31 receptions and 38th with 393 yards, though, because of the quarterback problems the Vikings hope they solved.
“He understands how the defenses play, especially covering me,” Jefferson told reporters this week. “And he understands, just like he said the other day, the plays that we have called that are kind of my plays, and he understands that the timing and the windows to throw those type of plays, but he also doesn't force those type of plays to me and he just lets the game come to him.”
Cousins remains a big-time quarterback. Surrounded by a less-than-stellar supporting cast with the Raiders, he is 11th in passer rating, fifth in yards and second in touchdowns.
The key will be applying pressure. He’s never exactly been fleet of food, and Father Time and the impact of the torn Achilles sustained at Lambeau Field in 2023 hasn’t made him any faster.
Cousins ranks 22nd with an under-pressure passer rating of 49.5. From a clean pocket, it’s 118.9.
“He’s a really good quarterback, and he’s still playing at a high level,” coach Matt LaFleur said. “Just watching how he gets the ball out of his hands – I buzzed all of his touchdowns from earlier this year, and he’s still got it, man. He’s still got the arm strength. I think he looks better than he did maybe in his time in Atlanta, to be honest with you.
“I think some of that is time away from that injury that he had playing here and I just think he’s playing at a high level. He can process really, really fast. Certainly, he’s got a ton of experience, so it’s hard to fool a guy like that.”

title: For Packers, Rivalry Showdown vs. Vikings Is Most Important Game of Season
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers have entered the NFL playoffs as the No. 7 seed each of the last three seasons. It’s a death sentence if the goal is to win the Super Bowl and not just reach the postseason.
That’s what makes Sunday’s game against the Minnesota Vikings arguably the biggest game of their season.
The Packers have won five of their last six games and are coming off easily their best performance of the season, a dominant blowout of the defending AFC champion Patriots in New England last week. For all of their efforts, though, they are still in last place in the NFC North. And while their 6-3 record is good enough to have them in the midseason playoff bracket , it’s as the dreaded No. 7 seed.
The seventh seed has to open the playoffs on the road against the No. 2 seed. With an upset win, like the Packers had at Dallas in 2023, the reward is a road game at the No. 1 seed. In other words, the No. 7 seed needs to beat the top two teams in the conference just to get to go back on the road for the conference championship game.
The difference is especially acute this year because of the haves- and have-nots reality of the NFC. There are eight teams with winning records in the NFC. Four are from the NFC North and three are from the NFC West. All four of the NFC North teams have six or seven wins.
“I don’t really worry about other teams,” coach Matt LaFleur said this week. “It’s just how can we help our team improve on a daily basis? But it’s not surprising to me. I knew this. All the teams in this division are really strong, and I knew it was going to be a challenge. But I think when you go through challenges, and if you can come through it on top, then you’re going to be more calloused and be better for it.”
The more battle-tested, the better, for the Packers.
As it stands, the No. 7 seed would open the playoffs at the Chicago Bears. The Packers wouldn’t be scared of that matchup, given how well they played in pummeling their rivals at Lambeau earlier in the season. But the Bears might be the most complete team in the NFC. They haven’t lost a game started and finished by Caleb Williams and they made the biggest move of the trade deadline by acquiring defensive tackle Jeffrey Simmons.
The No. 6 seed would open the playoffs at the New York Giants, who are 5-3-1 and lead the NFC East due in part to playing by far the easiest schedule in the league so far. Their quarterback is J.J. McCarthy and they just lost at home to the Commanders.
The No. 5 seed would open the playoffs at the Carolina Panthers, who are 3-6 and lead the heinous NFC South with a 3-5 record.
Who would you rather play in the wild-card round? Williams and the Bears, McCarthy and the Giants or Bryce Young and the Panthers?
That’s why this game is so vital for the Packers.
With a win, the Packers would be 7-3 and (sort of) ahead of the Vikings, who would be 6-3. The alternative is being 6-4 and two games behind the Vikings in the loss column.
With a win, the Packers would be 5-3 in conference games and 2-2 in division games, which are key tiebreakers. With a loss, they’d be 4-4 in the conference and 1-3 in the division – including a sweep at the hand of the Vikings.
With a win, the Packers would maintain their one-game lead over the Seattle Seahawks and Los Angeles Rams in the race for the final playoff spot. With a loss, depending on the outcome of the other games, they’d be tied. On Sunday, the Seahawks will play at the Raiders and the Rams will play at the Cardinals.
“I feel extremely in confident in this team. We’re extremely confident in one another,” safety Javon Bullard said. “We got to keep rallying off these wins, man. We know we in a tough-ass division; like you said, the North keeps winning, man. But I think we got the best division in football right now, and it’s a true testament to everybody in this division. Like it’s going to come down to the wire. And why not us is the question. We got another NFC North opponent coming in here, and we got to find a way with the dub.”
This might not be a must-win game but it’s pretty darned close. There just is no margin for error. Not with the power of the NFC North and the NFC West. Not with the Packers’ remaining strength of schedule being the second-toughest in the league. Now with the blown opportunities at Minnesota and Detroit putting them behind the 8-ball in the standings and tiebreakers.
Added together, a win would be a big step toward getting out of the seventh-seed sinkhole. A loss would put them on thin ice in the playoff race.
“Why not us?” Bullard said. “I think we’ve showcased what we can do. We’ve beaten some of the better teams in the league and I think, honestly, we just got to keep putting it on tape. Keep showing the world that the Packers aint’ going nowhere. And I think – I got to stop saying I think – I know we got the players in here to do so and I know we have the coaching staff to do so and as long we keep trusting and believing in each other, I think sky’s the limit.”

title: Five Bold Predictions for Second Half of Packers’ Season and Playoffs
full_text:
The Green Bay Packers are halfway through the season, and will take on the Minnesota Vikings as a jumping-off point for how the rest of their season could play out.
With a win, the Packers would be tied with Minnesota in the loss column and avoid losing what could be a crucial tiebreaker in the NFC North playoff picture.
A loss would keep the Packers in the basement of the NFC North, and will essentially put them three games behind Minnesota by virtue of the tiebreaker the Vikings would own over them.
The month of December is no cakewalk, either, with a home date against Josh Allen’s Buffalo Bills, and a Christmas Day showdown against the Chicago Bears. The Packers will earn whatever comes to them for the rest of the season.
With nine weeks down and nine weeks to go and the calendar having turned to November, here are some bold predictions from our crystal ball for the rest of the Packers’ season.
The Packers are only able to move the ball on offense one way. That’s Jordan Love carrying out an aerial assault on opposing defenses. Their run game is virtually nonexistent, and Green Bay’s top two receivers have done their part to help Love find his way to the top of the NFL in passing yards.
Can it continue? The answer is yes. The Packers are going to be playing in big games down the stretch, which will require Love to play well for them to win. Since our season forecast has the Packers winning six of their last eight games, the bet here is he will continue to play well.
As a result, Love will end up leading the league in passing yards, edging out Cincinnati’s Joe Burrow, who enters Week 10 with a slight advantage in yards per game.
In that scenario, Love would be an MVP finalist, but we think he loses out to Buffalo’s Josh Allen at least in some part due to Allen’s team finishing with a better record than Green Bay.
The Packers have not had two receivers top 1,000 yards in the same season since Jordy Nelson and Randall Cobb accomplished that in 2014. The 2014 offense was one of the best the Packers fielded under the stewardship of Aaron Rodgers and Mike McCarhty. They rode that group all the way to the NFC Championship Game.
This year, Matthew Golden and Christian Watson have both been top-tier targets for Jordan Love. They’re both pushing 1,000 yards already, with Watson leading the way with 879.
Now, the question is whether they will set the NFL record for most yards by a duo . Detroit had Herman Moore and Brett Perriman reach the record of 3,174 yards in 1995, when it was a 16=game season.
Throw in an asterisk if you’d like, but Watson and Golden are on pace for 3,139 receiving yards. Can they find an extra 36 yards somewhere? The bet here is yes. The Packers are going to have to continue throwing the ball to sustain any semblance of success on offense.
“Those guys have been making play after play,” Love said this week. “MG, when he first got here last year, was making a lot of plays. Obviously, the situation we had, we had a lot of depth in the room (and) he wasn’t getting a lot of those opps. Christian’s been making play after play since he’s been here. He’s been getting better and better each year. It comes down to I know these guys are going to make the plays.
“It just is us seeing it all as one, being on the same page with how we’re seeing routes, how we’re seeing the coverages that teams want to play against us, and then me putting the ball in a great spot and them making those plays. I know we’re more than capable of doing it every play.”
As long as Watson and Golden are healthy for all 17 games, we’re betting they break the record held by the Lions’ crew.
The Packers are just one game out of first place in the NFC North in the loss column, and they’ve already knocked off the Chicago Bears with a 31-7 drubbing at Lambeau Field.
The Bears did not have two massive pieces for that game. Jeffery Simmons was in Tennessee and Caleb Williams was nursing a hamstring injury.
Chicago has not lost a game that Williams has started and finished this season, and their defense has looked formidable in the two-game sample following Simmons’ addition to their defensive line.
The bet here is that both teams will have the same record going into a Christmas Day showdown at Soldier Field, which will have NFL executives licking their chops.
The Packers have lost the last two games at Soldier Field, including a disastrous ending in the postseason last year. This year, they’ll give their fanbase a big lump of coal on Christmas, as the Bears will knock off the Packers, giving them the inside track to winning the NFC North.
Much like last year, a loss against Chicago will prove to be the difference between winning the NFC North and having to go on the road in the postseason.
This time, things will be different. The Packers will enter the playoffs with the fifth seed of the NFC playoffs and knock off a Tampa Bay team that is only in the postseason by virtue of playing in the worst division in the conference.
A big day from Jordan Love and Christian Watson vs. the Buccaneers will send them on a short flight back to Chicago, where they will meet Williams and the Bears again.
This time, however, the Packers are the ones who emerge victorious, avenging their Christmas Day loss to Chicago. Jordan Love will have another big day against Chicago, with Matthew Golden setting up a game-winning field goal by rookie Trey Smack, which splits the middle of the uprights.
That win in the divisional round will put the Packers just one game away from the Super Bowl.
Matt LaFleur and Kyle Shanahan have met three times in the postseason as head coaches, and Shanahan’s teams won all three.
In the 2019 NFC Championship Game, Raheem Mostert ran around, over and through Green Bay’s defense en route to a 37-20 victory that was not as close as the final score would indicate.
Two years later, the Packers were the No. 1 seed with everything lined up for a Super Bowl run. Za’Darius Smith and Jaire Alexander returned from long-term injuries for this game against a San Francisco team that was in the postseason but not as good as that year’s Packers team, which felt destined to give Aaron Rodgers a second title.
It was not to be. Poor offense and disastrous special teams wasted an otherwise strong defensive effort, and Rodgers never played another postseason game for the Packers.
In 2023, Jordan Love had the upstart Packers in position to upset the No. 1-seeded 49ers in the divisional round but they fell just short due in part to a missed field goal.
This time, the Packers will travel back to San Francisco in search of their first trip to the Super Bowl since winning Super Bowl XLV to cap the 2010 season.
This place, however, is a house of horrors for Green Bay, and Brock Purdy will get the best of Green Bay’s defense late. A late touchdown pass to George Kittle in the middle of the end zone with minimal time left will break the Packers’ hearts and send the 49ers to the Super Bowl.

title: Saturday’s Packers Roster Moves: Two Key Additions, Two Critical Non-Moves
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers activated two key cogs to their offense on Saturday, making them available for Sunday’s huge NFC North game against the Minnesota Vikings.
Here’s a look at the Packers’ roster moves, starting with the two roster moves that were not made that send a strong and important signal.
After missing the first two days of the practice week due to a back injury, starting edge and top pass rusher Lukas Van Ness returned to practice on Friday and was listed as questionable.
Backs can be tricky, but Van Ness must be fine. Otherwise, the Packers would have added Arron Mosby or Nyjalik Kelly to an edge group with a limited depth chart of Van Ness, Barryn Sorrell, Brenton Cox and Dani Dennis-Sutton.
“I’m doing good, thank you,” said Van Ness, who leads the team in sacks . “It felt good to get back on the grass today.”
Mosby has been elevated three times; the next time the Packers want him to play in a game, they’ll have to sign him to the 53-man roster. Kelly, an undrafted rookie who had a strong training camp, still is awaiting his NFL debut.
“I think both those guys have done an outstanding job,” coach Matt LaFleur said on Friday. “Obviously, Mosby has played more ball than Nyjalik. But in the event we had to pivot and go that route, we’d feel comfortable with that.
Among the players who were questionable on Friday’s injury report were safeties Javon Bullard and Xavier McKinney. The Packers have only four safeties on the roster – starter Evan Williams and backup Kitan Oladapo being the others – but they did not pull up John Saunders from the practice squad.
Even though he missed the first two practices of the week, Bullard declared he would play .
“We been able to battle adversity,” Bullard said. “That was really our focal point going through offseason, man. Finishing and just battling, withstanding adversity, because you don’t know when adversity is going to hit. It’s going to hit at some point for everybody in this league – every team in this league, every player in this league.
“So, you got to withstand those storms and really just fight battles. Chin up and chest out. And I think this team has done that. We’ve weathered a lot of storms. We’ve weathered a lot of misfortunes with things like that. I think this team is one of the best, if not the best in the league, and we just got to continue to put that on tape.
Just in time to face the blitz-happy Vikings, the Packers regained the services of Chris Brooks, their top pass-protecting back. He just competed his second week of practice.
“Oh, yeah,” coach Matt LaFleur said of the perfect timing for Brooks’ return. “You’ve got to do a great job in all phases in terms of in the run game and in the pass game versus this unit.”
Brooks carried the ball seven times for 29 yards, a 4.1-yard average with a long run of 14, during the Week 1 game against the Vikings. He had a 27-yard run in Week 4 against the Buccaneers but sustained an ankle injury in that game. He missed the last five games and just completed his second week of practice.
There is an interesting dynamic in Green Bay’s backfield for this game. One, Josh Jacobs is out following last year’s broken finger. Two, Kaleb Johnson had a breakout game in Jacobs’ absence last week. His 68 rushing yards was the most by any Packers player this year and beat their season average. Three, given the Vikings’ propensity for blitzing on any down and any situation, Brooks would seem to be a necessity to have on the field as often as possible.
“I think he ripped off a couple nice runs in that game the first time we played him,” LaFleur said of Brooks. “And I think the running game, especially the later you go in the season, the more important it is. As the weather turns, especially at home, you better be able to run the football.”
Skyy Moore, who leads the team with a 16.0-yard average on punt returns and a 27.5-yard average on kickoff returns, will make his return after missing the last four games with an ankle injury. He returned to practice this week.
Moore had a 63-yard punt return against the Jets in Week 2. That’s as many yards as his replacements, Coleman Owen and Matthew Golden, combined the last seven games.
“Yeah, yeah, for sure,” he said when asked if it was disappointing to be sidelined after emerging as a threat on offense as well as special teams. “Just being away from the guys, when they go to practice and I'm just on the sideline and everything, I'm just happy to be back around and moving around out there.”
Moore’s ability to provide a first down’s worth of field position as a returner and perhaps contribute in the slot as a runner or receiver should make him an immediate asset.
“It would be huge” to get him back, quarterback Jordan Love said this week. “We’ve definitely been down a couple guys and I think guys have stepped up, but Skyy, just to have him in the receiver room, but also special teams – he’s been such a great returner for us – it’ll definitely be huge to get him back and I’m grateful that we’re able to get him back this week. I’m excited to have him out there.”
The additions of Moore and Brooks meant the Packers needed to create two roster spots.
Not surprisingly, one of them was releasing receiver/returner Coleman Owen, who had been promoted from the practice squad to take Moore’s role on special teams.
In four games, Owen averaged 9.0 yards on four punt returns, with a long of 16 in his debut against Dallas. He fielded all 10 punts cleanly. Owen returned kickoffs in one game, the Thursday night matchup against Carolina. He fumbled his first opportunity and finished the night with a 26.3-yard average on four returns.
“There weren’t as many opportunities just based on the flow of the games we've been playing,” Moore said. “But I think he stepped in and did a great job. You know, came in, caught all the punts confidently and he followed his training. I felt like he did a great job.”
Tight end Josh Whyle suffered a concussion in the Carolina games and has not practiced the last two weeks. The Packers added a tight end, Kenny Fletcher Jr., to the practice squad this week, which seemed like a signal that Whyle might have a prolonged absence.
Without Josh Whyle, the Packers for a second consecutive week elevated Drake Dabney from the practice squad. He played six snaps on special teams against New England.
The #Vikings have elevated TE Devin Culp and WR Jeshaun Jones to the active roster for tomorrow's game. Culp has changed jersey numbers from 48 to 83. pic.twitter.com/OU2Al6Oh0J
The Vikings elevated tight end Devin Culp to help offset the injury that will sideline T.J. Hockenson. Interestingly, with starter Jordan Addison questionable and Jauan Jennings out, they also elevated a receiver.

title: 4 Key Quotes From C.J. Stroud After Texans' Week 10 Loss to Browns
full_text:
The Houston Texans dropped a critical Week 10 game against the Cleveland Browns this weekend in a 24-27 road loss that now drops this team to a gloomy 3-6 record through 10 weeks of action.
And after the events of the Texans' loss , we got to hear a bit from quarterback C.J. Stroud and some of his thoughts from the loss; about what went wrong, what needs to be fixed, and how he feels about this team moving forward.
With that in mind, let's take a look at four of the most important quotes from Stroud following their Week 10 loss to Cleveland:
The Texans' offense took a nosedive in terms of their production and efficiency once jumping from the first half to the second, to the point where C.J. Stroud combined for less than 25 passing yards after halftime.
As to what Stroud saw throughout that second-half collapse, the Texans simply couldn't adjust to the Browns' pressure and their ability to get "sticky in coverage."
“They just started pressuring and getting sticky in coverage," Stroud said. "We really didn’t adjust to it. We gotta do a better job coming out in the second half and finding ways to move the ball and get points.”
A major issue the Texans fell into within this loss was their excessive penalties , as they incurred 13 total flags for 112 yards; some of their worst results when it comes to limiting penalties all season long.
Stroud sees a clear need for the team to adjust from their shortcomings and lack of discipline in this game, but also has the faith that the Texans can make the necessary changes to get back on track.
“We gotta play better as players. There’s a lot of things where we don’t need the penalty. We’ll take if you get beat just let the guy go on special teams, or the false starts, we gotta fix that," Stroud said.
"I don’t know all the other penalties we had but those are the main ones that I thought affected the game. I have the utmost hope and faith in Tae [Ersery] and whatever happened on special teams, the guys getting it fixed. The time is now. We gotta be moreurgent because time is running out.”
Stroud said he felt it was difficult to adjust to the Browns' defense coming out of the half. But exactly why was it such a struggle for the Texans this week to make the necessary tweaks for better results offensively?
One aspect that Stroud highlighted was the lack of different route concepts the Texans were running, along with the main idea of simply finding a way to come out with a win––no matter what.
“Honestly I don’t know. We gotta find ways to protect it, because guys are open on the back end. That’s what I think a lot of teams will do. They’ll just pressure and try to say, ‘you gotta make a big play," Stroud said.
"I think we gotta be able to not just run two to three routes, widen our route tree, and just run by people sometimes, and do it more often. Gotta find ways to win tough games. This is November. It’s playoff time already. We put ourselves in position to win. No matter how it looks, we gotta find a way to win the game.”
The Texans fell into some of their flaws from last season in this one, particularly as it relates to their production on early downs, and how that bled into their production on third downs. Houston finished the day converting on just three of 12 third-down opportunities, while the Browns converted on 7-15.
Was that the most frustrating part of the loss for Stroud? In his mind, the end result of a loss stings just as bad as the little things that didn't go right throughout the course of Sunday.
“I mean it’s frustrating losing at the end of the day. We’ve had a lot of close games and we haven’t found a way to win those games. That’s the tough part I believe," Stroud said.
"At the end of the day, I gotta look myself in the mirror. I had the third down to Dalton [Schultz] that I missed a little high. If we stay on the field right there, we burn some more of their timeouts and burn some more clock. That’s an impact play that I could’ve made that I gotta be better. I think with all of our tape, we just got some messy stuff that we gotta clean up. Gotta do it quick. Quick turnaround.”

title: Texans' Biggest Winners and Losers From Week 10 Loss vs. Browns
full_text:
The Houston Texans fell in a humbling loss to the Cleveland Browns on the road in Week 10 , 24-27, that now puts them in a tough 3-6 hole to climb out of for the remainder of the season.
And in the midst of the Texans' sixth loss of the season ( also against a familiar face in Deshaun Watson ), there were a handful of winners and losers to account for on Houston's side of the equation; some guys that kept this game within reach until the final drive, while others made this one a bigger uphill climb than it should've been.
With that in mind, let's break down a batch of three of the Texans' biggest winners and losers from their latest Week 10 loss to Cleveland:
In a game (and especially a second half) where the Texans' offense wasn't the most consistent unit we've seen them be this season, Nico Collins rose to the occasion for one of his best performances of the year so far.
Collins found his way to a team-high nine receptions and 94 yards on a staggering 16 targets for the day, along with hauling in one of C.J. Stroud's three touchdown passes. It was his first game of the season eclipsing even 10 targets, and marked only his second performance of the year where he saw over 90 receiving yards.
CJ Stroud into a tight window to Nico Collins for 6! HOUvsCLE on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/gZg6uDeOlt
The Texans made it a clear focus to get Collins involved as a focal point in the passing game, and he delivered on those opportunities when they came. If only Houston could've continued that trend further into the second half, the results of this game could look a whole lot different.
This was yet another game for DeMeco Ryans where his group fell into some of the same holes that they have throughout the first half of the season: they continued to look like one of the most penalized and undisciplined teams in the NFL, while also suffering from an inexcusable collapse on the defensive side in the second half.
The Texans incurred 13 penalties throughout the day. The Cleveland offense put together 20 unanswered points between the second and third quarters. The game was unofficially sealed on their final defensive drive of the day after back-to-back plays resulting in a 15-yard penalty and a 30-yard explosive from Harold Fannin Jr.
It's starting to feel like Groundhog Day for the Texans as they continue to suffer from the same lapses week after week, despite having the talent around the roster to be a playoff threat. And at its core, Houston's coaching deserves just as big of a chunk of the blame––if not more––than the performance on the field.
Throughout the 2026 campaign, the Texans have not been the team they once were last season when it comes to the turnover battle. Through 10 weeks of the 2025 season, Houston had found their way to 15 total turnovers––much higher than their nine total takeaways across the same stretch of time this year.
However, the Texans were able to find their way to a takeaway on Deshaun Watson because of Pro Bowl safety Calen Bullock finally coming alive for his second interception on the season, which came at a pivotal moment in the fourth quarter that could've changed the tides just a bit, though the offense couldn't deliver on the opportunity.
Calen Bullock comes up with a big INT for the Texans! HOUvsCLE on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/Yg6htXWLnV
Bullock will have to keep the momentum flowing by continuing to have a nose for interceptions as the ball-hawk we know he's capable of being moving forward. With a Thursday night date against Daniel Jones and the Indianapolis Colts, there could be a perfect opportunity on the horizon to do just that.
One of the Texans' two most pivotal penalties of the game happened to come from their final offensive drive, where fourth-round rookie Febechi Nwaiwu, in his first-ever NFL start, incurred a brutal holding call to turn what would've been a first-down gain on fourth down into a drastically different fourth and 20––essentially ending the game.
It's a tough break for Nwaiwu in his big opportunity of this weekend, especially considering he performed well throughout the game, all things considered. Through the first half, Nwaiwu allowed zero pressures in the 12 pass protection snaps he had on Mason Graham and Maliek Collins.
However, those costly mistakes in terms of penalties continue to hurt the Texans in a big way week after week, especially on the offensive line. This weekend against the Browns turned out to be no different, and that blemish on Nwaiwu's otherwise solid day stings after the fact.
Jalen Pitre was showing up for the Texans many times throughout the day as the hard-hitting, impactful defender that this group needs him to be to rise to their true ceiling as a defense.
He finished with six tackles— five of them coming solo— along with a tackle for loss and a pass defended. It tied Pitre's second-highest tackle count in a game on the season and marked only the second game of the year where he recorded both a tackle for loss and a pass defended.
For the Texans' defense to be at their best, Pitre needs to be on the field making plays. And while this defense still proved to suffer from some of the same shortcomings they have all season long, it's hard to imagine how things would look if Pitre were still out due to injury as he was earlier in the year.
What might've been a more game-changing penalty than Nwaiwu's holding call in the fourth was Kamari Lassiter's unnecessary roughness call on the final defensive drive before it; one that turned a Deshaun Watson incompletion on second and long into a 15-yard gain, then quickly became a Quinshon Judkins game-sealing touchdown.
Kamari Lassiter has had some terrible calls against him this year pic.twitter.com/WrGwzAH3ls
The results of the call could certainly be debated––and it seemed like DeMeco Ryans didn't exactly see the official's point of view during his postgame comments––but the flag is yet another blemish on what's been an underwhelming season for the Texans' No. 2 corner, and turned the tides in a big way this game.
Lassiter is now up to eight flags on the season, which comes out to the second-most among all defenders in the NFL; far too many for the Texans' Pro Bowler.

title: What Texans' DeMeco Ryans Said After Frustrating Week 10 Loss to Browns
full_text:
The Houston Texans dropped a pivotal Week 10 road matchup against the Cleveland Browns for a 24-27 loss, now dropping this team to a less-than-ideal 3-6 record after nine games on the season.
And after the game, we got to hear from DeMeco Ryans and some of his thoughts from the Texans' sixth loss of the season, explaining what went wrong this weekend, and what will need to be fixed moving forward for Houston to get their playoff aspirations back on track.
Let's sort through seven of the most notable quotes from Ryans' post-game presser:
Of the biggest takeaways that Ryan gathered from the Texans' loss to open his presser, their 13 team penalties remained a key reason as to attribute the end result to–– as has been the story many times before this season .
"Yeah, it goes back to we can't hurt ourselves when you have 13 penalties, especially there late in the game. We need to move the football, and we get penalties on special teams, penalties offensively, penalties on defense. All three phases had critical penalties that hurt us."
Texans cornerback Kamari Lassiter was called for a pivotal, controversial unnecessary roughness penalty during the Browns' final offensive drive of the game. When DeMeco Ryans was asked about the said call, he didn't seem to fully agree with the call on the field.
"I saw Kamari going up for the football. Nothing was intentional there by Kamari. He's going up for the football, and I have to look at it and see how that is a penalty on him."
Kamari Lassiter has had some terrible calls against him this year pic.twitter.com/WrGwzAH3ls
When it comes to what Ryan saw on the Browns' game-sealing touchdown run from Quinshon Judkins, he was keen on the defense's need to be better tackling.
"Yeah, we're trying to stop him right there. We got to play better run defense, got to tackle better. We got to stop it better, play better, run defense, be stout there, and get get a stop."
Quinshon Judkins gives the Browns the lead with 53 seconds to go! HOUvsCLE on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/lxgi0XZEWS
The Texans' second half was a totally different feeling than the first on both sides of the ball.
What was the difference for the Texans and their momentum? Ryan highlighted the Browns' ability to get the ball out fast, Houston's excessive penalties, and the disparity of third downs that turned the tides in the second half of action.
"Yeah, they got the ball out quick. They hit an explosive on us earlier in the game. They hit an explosive. We can be better there with how we played."
"And, you know, overall, they started to get the ball out quicker and make some plays. Deshaun made some plays running around on the edge. But the game, to me, really came down to the penalties, right? Thirteen penalties. Then it came down to third down, right? We only converted, I think, three third downs, and they were seven of 15."
"So some of those third-and-medium plays that they were able to convert and stay on the field, we didn't get stops, and vice versa. Our offense didn't convert enough third downs to stay on the field to really get drives sustained and keep the ball moving. So that's where the game kind of tilted in their favor."
Despite a poor second half from C.J. Stroud and the Texans' passing offense, Ryans still saw some positives from his performance thanks to his ability to make plays under pressure.
"Yeah, I thought C.J. still made some plays, even with the pressure that was on him. I thought he was still able to move around in the pocket and scramble and run to get a first down a couple times. And, you know, he kept plays alive even though there was a lot of pressure."
"He didn't take a lot of sacks. So I'm still happy with how he played and happy with the decisions that he was able to make."
The Texans have a quick four-day turnaround before they're tasked with their upcoming matchup vs. the Indianapolis Colts .
As to how Ryan’s is going to prepare his group for the task ahead, moving on quickly remains the main idea.
"Hey, you got to move on quickly. We can't dwell on this. We know the issues that we have. We look at it, starting with everybody looking at themselves first and seeing where we can be better, and we move on. Got a good coached team coming in on Thursday night."

title: 3 Biggest Texans Takeaways From Costly Week 10 Loss vs. Browns
full_text:
The Houston Texans have fallen in yet another embarrassing loss this weekend against the Cleveland Browns on the road , 24-27, that drops them to a 3-6 record through 10 weeks, and puts them in a steep hole to climb out of moving forward for the rest of the season.
Let's break down three of the biggest takeaways from the Texans' defeat in Cleveland, and what it might mean for their hopes moving forward:
There's no better way to describe the Texans' offensive performance in this game than being quite literally a tale of two halves.
Houston started this game firing on all cylinders offensively. C.J. Stroud had completed 15 of 19 passes for 190 yards and two touchdowns. The Texans had stormed out to a 17-0 lead until about two minutes to go in the first half, then the Browns chipped in for another 10 points.
But in the second half, things fell off a cliff. Stroud went on to log just 21 more passing yards. The offense couldn't gain any momentum through the air, and a Woody Marks injury in the third quarter halted any momentum on the ground. Houston went on to be outscored 7-17, and punted on six of their final eight drives.
A total offensive collapse for the Texans. Consistency continues to be hard to find, and it was the biggest reason why they've now fallen to their sixth loss of the season.
After a week against the LA Chargers where the Texans' penalty issues seemed to turn a corner, this group could not put together a repeat performance. Instead, they had one of their most undisciplined days of the season so far.
13 penalties. 112 yards allowed. Some of those calls––particularly the game-shifting unnecessary roughness call on Kamari Lassiter on the final Browns drive in the fourth––may have been questionable. Others, such as holding calls on the offensive line to the likes of Aireontae Ersery and Febechi Nwaiwu, were inexecutable.
The main idea remains that the Texans continue to shoot themselves in the foot by incurring so many flags on a weekly basis––and until their collective discipline turns around in the right direction, it'll continue to be the case.
The result stings even worse knowing that Cleveland entered this week as the most penalized team in the NFL, and left this game with just two flags for 47 yards. The Browns simply came into this game more prepared than the Texans , and it showed up in a big way through their penalty numbers.
The Texans had already been forced to dig out of an 0-4 hole to start the season after many mistakes haunted them through the first four weeks. And after two avoidable losses to the New York Giants in Week 7 and now the Browns in Week 10, it's going to be even tougher to imagine Houston can make the strides necessary for a late run to the postseason.
Houston sits 2.5 games back of the seventh seed in the AFC, currently held by a Browns team that now claims the head-to-head tiebreaker over the Texans. The sixth-seeded Cincinnati Bengals also hold a head-to-head tiebreaker.
For the Texans to guarantee a spot in the postseason at this point, it may rely on them to win out for the final eight games on the schedule, which comes as a result of many avoidable mistakes in games like this against the Browns and at home against the Giants.
Houston needs to claim a win in the next two games on their schedule: on a short week against the Indianapolis Colts and the Lamar Jackson-less Baltimore Ravens the week after. Two winnable games on paper, but as we've seen just this week, seeing this team take advantage of those matchups on the schedule is a whole lot easier said than done.

title: Texans Facing RB Shortage vs. Browns With David Montgomery Out
full_text:
The Houston Texans are right around the corner from their Week 10 matchup against the Cleveland Browns .
And it's shaping up to look like another shorthanded day for the Texans when it comes to their backfield.
According to an update from the Texans, running back David Montgomery has been ruled out for Sunday with a groin injury.
Houston Texans Week 10 Injury Report Updates: RB David Montgomery (groin) and CB Jaylin Smith (hamstring) will not travel with the team to Cleveland and have been ruled out for Week 10 at the Browns. T Braden Smith has been added to the Week 10 Injury Report with an illness… https://t.co/aqvEigvHGz
Montgomery has been out with the same groin injury since Week 5 against the Tennessee Titans, and was seemingly trending up for a chance to play this week.
He was a full participant in practice on Friday after being limited the day before, and was previously listed as questionable to play against Cleveland.
However, it turns out the Texans will be cautious surrounding their veteran running back's availability for this weekend, and hold him out of the action. And as a result, this Houston offense will be rolling into Week 10 with a pretty slim running back room, all things considered.
Without any reported practice squad elevations for this weekend, the Texans will be heading into Week 10 with just two running backs on the active roster: Woody Marks and Emari Demercado.
The Texans did have three running backs on the roster earlier this week, which did provide an extra sense of depth and security in the position. However, following their decision to sign wide receiver Nikko Remigio , the team also decided to cut ties with veteran Dare Ogunbowale.
Ogunbowale had been on the roster dating back to Week 4's game against the Dallas Cowboys in an effort to add depth within the backfield and some special teams prowess. However, as Montgomery was trending up and the running back room was looking healthier, the Texans decided to let him go earlier this week.
But Montgomery won't be ready to play this week, and will instead be targeting his return for Week 11 on Thursday night against the Indianapolis Colts––which means the Texans’ running back depth (or lack thereof) will be tested in Cleveland for this weekend.
Since Montgomery has been out of the lineup for the Texans, the offense has primarily relied on Woody Marks to handle the bulk of the work in the backfield throughout.
Dating back to Week 5, Marks is averaging 16.8 rushing attempts per game for 63.5 yards, paired with an average of two receptions for 16.0 yards.
Perhaps the Texans could sprinkle in a bit of Demercado this time around in order to take some of the weight and heavy workload off of Marks' shoulders with a quick turnaround for Thursday’s game. However, for the majority of carries, you can expect them to be in the hands of Marks.
And against a matchup like the Browns' rushing defense, there's a chance that Marks could expose some of their holes that have popped up frequently this season. Cleveland currently ranks 27th in the NFL for rushing yards allowed (1,175) and 28th in yards allowed per rushing attempt (4.7).
Kickoff against the Browns lands at 12 p.m. CT, where a victory would make for their fourth on the season, as well as make for their first back-to-back win of the season.

title: Texans' Jadeveon Clowney Embracing Next Man Up Mentality Amid Injuries
full_text:
The Houston Texans are entering their Week 10 matchup against the Cleveland Browns a little more banged up than usual.
And that's especially so as it relates to their edge rusher unit. Not only has Danielle Hunter already been ruled out for Sunday's action due to a hamstring injury, but Will Anderson Jr. has also been listed as questionable with a knee injury after not participating in team practice on Friday.
Of course, being without one of those two studs on the front seven–– let alone both of them–– is a huge loss for the Texans and their overall ceiling on the defensive side of the ball.
Houston's pass-rush is really the engine that makes their defense go on a week-to-week basis. And for as up and down as this unit has been over the course of this season, losing any of their Pro Bowl talents for a near-must-win game against Cleveland is a less-than-ideal outcome.
However, in the wake of those injuries to the Texans' defense, veteran edge rusher Jadeveon Clowney doesn't seem to be too phased. And in fact, he seems ready to go for what should be an increased role for him on the team's road trip to Cleveland.
"It's the National Football League. It happens. Next man up mentality," Clowney said of the Texans' injuries, via Aaron Wilson of KPRC2 . "That's why you go and prepare like a starter, no matter what role you're in. You just prepare, and make sure you're ready when your number is called."
Throughout the first half of the Texans' season, Clowney hasn't seen the most snaps on a week-to-week basis. He's averaging only a 36.5% snap share on the defense, and hasn't seen a game in which that number has eclipsed 50%.
But that's been a result seen with the combination of Anderson and Hunter on the field, each seeing around 70% of the defensive snaps coming their way.
Without one of those pieces, or perhaps even both, Clowney––one of the league's best DE3s––immediately slots into a starting role, and does so coming fresh off his best performance of the season so far.
Against the Los Angeles Chargers , Clowney was one of three defensive linemen to total a pair of sacks on the day, and did so on just 24 total snaps.
On Sunday, that snap count could be double what it was this past weekend. And against Clowney's former team in Cleveland, paired with the fact that he'll be going up against his former quarterback from Houston in Deshaun Watson , the stage could be set for a strong performance on his behalf.
"I'm looking forward to it, man. Next game on the schedule is a big one for us," Clowney said of facing the Browns. "Trying to get two wins back-to-back. Haven't had that all season, so I'm looking forward to that."
The Texans will reveal closer to kickoff on Sunday afternoon whether or not Anderson will be there to accompany Clowney on the defensive line. Regardless of whether or not he's a part of the equation, though, expect Clowney's next-man-up mentality to remain the same.

title: Texans' 3 Biggest Keys to Victory vs. Browns in Week 10 Matchup
full_text:
The Houston Texans have a pivotal Week 10 game on the horizon against the Cleveland Browns , where a win would take them just one game away from getting back to a .500 record, and put them one step closer to clawing back into the AFC playoff picture.
However, taking home a win in this week's road trip against Cleveland is shaping up to be a task a bit easier said than done. Not only is this Browns team a surprising 5-4 through the first half of the season, but the Texans are heading into this game with multiple key injuries to account for.
That means for Houston, they'll have to hone in on a select few keys to victory in a select few areas of the game in order to secure that much-needed win, and continue building momentum before their short week of preparation for Week 11.
With that in mind, let's break down the Texans' three biggest keys to victory in this weekend's matchup against the Browns:
The Browns' passing defense could make things a bit tougher for the Texans through the air, especially with a talent like cornerback Denzel Ward likely locking down his side of the field . But where Houston could expose Cleveland's defense is within the run game.
Cleveland's run defense through the first half of the season has not been the most consistent. They rank 27th in opposing rushing yards allowed and 28th in rushing yards per attempt. On six occasions this season, the Browns have alllowed over 125 opposing rushing yards, and they're 2-4 in those same games.
If the Texans can lean on Woody Marks––and maybe even David Montgomery if he's deemed available for Sunday––for a strong showing, even without a fully healthy offensive line, that's an easy route for Houston to gain a leg up on an otherwise solid Browns defense.
The Texans were finally able to tweak some of their penalty issues in their latest matchup against the Los Angeles Chargers. Houston incurred just six penalties for 36 yards in Week 9, which was a much better result than the past few weeks in which this team had shot up towards the top of the league in total flags and yards given up from penalties.
However, that success in the penalty category has to continue moving in the right direction for the Texans in the second half of the season. Especially in a game like this where Houston will be without multiple key starters, the margin for error becomes a bit thinner than usual.
So for the Texans' offensive line in particular , limit the holds, the false starts, and the illegal shifts, and Houston can take advantage of a team in the Browns who have also struggled when it comes to penalties––as they currently lead the NFL in total penalties called against them with 82 (over nine per game).
The Texans will be without Danielle Hunter for the first time of his tenure in Houston this Sunday, as he's been ruled out with a hamstring injury that was seemingly suffered earlier this week in practice.
There's no doubt his loss is a big hit to the Texans' pass rush. However, being without Hunter only increases the responsibilities someone like All-Pro edge rusher and current NFL sack leader Will Anderson has on Sunday to make the job a bit more difficult for Deshaun Watson and the Browns offense.
The only problem? Anderson's status is also in question for Sunday. He's been listed as questionable due to an ankle injury suffered in Thursday's practice, and had left him as a DNP for the following day.
For one, the Texans need to hope that Anderson is good to give it a go against the Browns. If he's out, the task gets even tougher for this defense and their overall pass rush. But if Anderson is indeed healthy, he has to bring his A-game for a Defensive Player of the Year-level performance to keep this unit afloat.

title: Texans Need This Veteran to Step Up With Danielle Hunter Out vs. Browns
full_text:
The Houston Texans are officially without Danielle Hunter this weekend against the Cleveland Browns.
After Hunter had been deemed a limited participant in the Texans' team practice on Thursday with a hamstring injury, to then turn to a DNP one day later, the decision was quickly made for Houston to sit out their veteran pass rusher for Week 10.
Houston #Texans Friday Injury Report & Game Status Report for Week 10 at the Cleveland Browns: pic.twitter.com/qrw9og0Fa0
There's no doubt that losing Hunter is a significant loss for the Texans–– no matter how long the timeline for his absence is.
Hunter has been a massive part of the Texans' pass-rush success since he arrived back in 2024. This season, he's been active in each of Houston's eight games to this point, recording 19 tackles, three TFLs, four sacks, and a forced fumble.
In fact, Hunter has yet to miss a single game for the Texans throughout his two years in the building. He's had a perfect 17-game attendance in both 2024 and 2025, and was on pace to do the same again this year after being active for all eight games before.
But this week against the Browns, the Texans will have to improvise without Hunter as a piece of their defensive puzzle. And keeping that in mind, it means one key veteran on Houston's defensive line will need to step up for a big game in his place–– which is none other than Jadeveon Clowney.
Throughout the Texans' season so far, we've seen Clowney established in his role as the third defensive end on Houston's front; a valuable rotational piece operating behind Anderson and Hunter for depth and pass-rushing prowess in the stints that either of them are resting on the sidelines.
And it's a role that Clowney has performed rather solidly in. Through the six games he's been healthy for, Clowney has put together 12 tackles, four TFLs, and 3.5 sacks despite playing in just 37% of Houston's defensive snaps.
That 37% snap share is the lowest that Clowney has seen on any team throughout his entire career . He's being used less often than ever, but still remaining a potent contributor off the edge who can get to the quarterback and be a stout run-stopper.
However, when someone as pivotal as Hunter is taken completely out of the equation due to a hamstring injury, the role for Clowney quickly shifts into one that is way more important than before.
Clowney becomes the clear starter right next to Will Anderson (so long as he's also healthy), and his snap count likely jumps to around 70% of the Texans' reps on the defensive side; a similar count to what Hunter sees when he's on the field.
That means Clowney will be on the field for twice as much as he is on a week-to-week basis, and his abilities as a stout pass-rusher and run defender become even more vital than they were before as the Texans' third defensive end. More snaps mean more down-to-down responsibilities.
The Texans have a lot of talented players on their defense, yet their depth off the edge isn't nearly as strong when Hunter is out of the equation.
That puts the challenge on Clowney's shoulders to step up and be a worthwhile complement to Anderson Jr. throughout the day in Cleveland as someone who can limit the Browns' ground game, and getting a handful of pressures sent in on Deshaun Watson in the process.
While losing Hunter undoubtedly stings for the Texans over any stretch of time, having an experienced and productive depth piece behind him in Clowney might make the absence a bit easier to stomach.
Time will tell if Clowney will be able to excel in his expanded role this weekend against the Browns. But if he can, the road to a second straight victory for Houston becomes a whole lot easier to imagine.
