title: Colts Keeping Jonathan Taylor Could Pay Major Dividends for Young Core
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts have undergone significant changes over the past several weeks, with several established veterans departing as the organization begins looking toward its future. While those moves have created opportunities for younger players to step into larger roles, they've also left the locker room without some of the veteran voices that have carried the team through the last decade.
One player who remains, however, is Jonathan Taylor.
The Colts faced considerable uncertainty surrounding Taylor's future ahead of the NFL trade deadline , with the possibility of moving their star running back generating plenty of discussion. Ultimately, Indianapolis elected to keep him , providing some much-needed continuity for a roster that has experienced considerable turnover.
Taylor's value to the organization has never been difficult to recognize on the football field. He's one of the NFL's most productive running backs and remains a central part of what Indianapolis wants to accomplish offensively. But following the departures of players like Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner, his importance to the organization extends well beyond his production.
Now one of, if not the most established, veterans remaining, Taylor has an opportunity to help guide a younger generation of Colts players.
And judging by the way some of those players already speak about him, his influence is being felt already.
Perhaps the best indication of Taylor's importance came following Indianapolis' 24-22 victory over the Miami Dolphins on Sunday.
Rookie linebacker CJ Allen, who has been working his way into a larger defensive role, was asked about Taylor's influence on the organization. His response offered an interesting glimpse into how much the veteran running back means to some of the younger players in Indianapolis.
"When I see JT play, he just inspires me because I know how hard he works," Allen said, then directing admiration towards Taylor for how much he appreciates the example that he sets.
"When I see JT play, he just inspires me because I know how hard he works" CJ Allen explains what Jonathan Taylor means to him and the Colts. 🎤: @AKinkhabwala pic.twitter.com/OutLrKVlS8
Allen explained that he pays attention to the running back's daily routine, including the way he approaches his preparation and gets his work done around the facility.
That distinction is important.
Taylor has already established himself as one of the league's premier players, earning All-Pro recognition and becoming one of the most productive running backs in franchise history. For a young player entering the NFL, having the opportunity to observe how someone at that level operates on a daily basis can provide a valuable example of what it takes to succeed professionally.
Allen is still early in his development, and the Colts are hoping he can eventually become a foundational piece of their defense. Having someone like Taylor around to demonstrate the importance of consistency, preparation and professionalism can only help that process.
The same sentiment was reflected by another Colts rookie, running back Seth McGowan.
McGowan, who has begun carving out a role behind Taylor in the Indianapolis backfield, made it clear just how much he appreciates having the veteran around, especially after all the trade speculation.
"I remember praying that he didn't leave just because I love playing with him so much," McGowan said. "He's become like a big brother to me."
"I remember praying that he didn't leave just because I love playing with him so much." #Colts running back Seth McGowan shared with Sports Director @ACwishtv how much he appreciates Jonathan Taylor's leadership: pic.twitter.com/DPlAV7ucyQ
For a rookie trying to establish himself in the NFL, having a player like Taylor in the same position room is an opportunity not many players get. McGowan has been able to learn alongside one of the best backs in football while beginning to establish his own identity within the offense.
The two have also developed a productive partnership on the field. Against Miami, Taylor and McGowan combined for 160 rushing yards, with Taylor leading the way with 83 yards and McGowan adding 77 yards and a touchdown.
Their relationship is another example of how Taylor's presence can benefit the organization beyond what he contributes individually.
Indianapolis is still evaluating what it has in McGowan and several other young players . Having an established veteran who can help them navigate the challenges of an NFL season provides a valuable resource as those players continue to develop.
Taylor's importance to the locker room has become even more apparent following the organization's recent roster restructuring.
The departures of Nelson, Buckner and other established players have changed the makeup of the Colts' locker room and leadership group considerably. While Indianapolis still has experienced players capable of providing that leadership, Taylor is perhaps the most important presence remaining.
Taylor acknowledged as much following the trade deadline, recognizing that those who remained needed to take greater responsibility for helping the younger players.
"We have to go out there and we've got to try to rally these guys," Taylor said, via ESPN's Stephen Holder. "But we also got to make sure that we're doing our things on and off the field the right way to show and set an example for the rest of the guys in the locker room."
Taylor has not necessarily been known as one of the most vocal leaders in Indianapolis, but leadership looks different for everyone.
Sometimes, the most effective way to lead is through example.
That's what makes Allen's comments particularly encouraging. Taylor doesn't need to be the loudest voice in the room. His actions are already providing an example for those around him.
Taylor's experience also gives younger players someone to turn to as they encounter the challenges that come with establishing themselves professionally. Whether it's navigating the demands of an NFL schedule, handling adversity or understanding the preparation required to compete at the highest level, Taylor has experienced just about everything the league can throw at him.
For a Colts team that is going to need significant contributions from its younger players moving forward, having that kind of presence around the building is important.
There is still plenty of uncertainty surrounding the direction of the Colts organization, particularly with the team undergoing significant changes and looking toward a different future.
Developing younger players will be one of the most important parts of that process. Indianapolis needs to determine which players can become long-term building blocks, and giving them opportunities to learn and grow will be essential.
Keeping Taylor provides the Colts with an established veteran who can help make that transition easier.
Allen and McGowan are two particularly encouraging examples. Both are beginning to find their footing in Indianapolis, and both have already expressed how much they value having Taylor around.
Those relationships could become increasingly important as the Colts continue evaluating their younger talent and determining what the next version of the roster will look like.
There is also something to be said for the continuity Taylor provides. With so many familiar faces no longer in the building, retaining someone who understands the organization and has spent his entire NFL career in Indianapolis gives the younger players another connection to the team's past.
Of course, Taylor's presence alone isn't going to guarantee that the Colts develop into a competitive team. Indianapolis still needs to make the right decisions with its roster, staff and overall direction.

title: Game Balls from the Colts' Historic Victory Over the Miami Dolphins
full_text:
Historic? Yes, that is a perfectly apt descriptor for the Indianapolis Colts ' victory over the now 1-8 Miami Dolphins.
Given the context provided by ESPN's Stephen Holder , that is one way to describe the Colts' 24-22 win over the hapless Dolphins .
According to ESPN Research: The Colts are the first team in the Super Bowl Era (since 1966) to win a game despite being outgained, losing the turnover battle and committing 10 more penalties than their opponent (13 to 3). This is a Dolphins statistic.
Despite the overall level of play at Lucas Oil Stadium on Sunday, there were some players that stood out for their positive contributions in the winning effort.
Seth McGowan and Jonathan Taylor each have a case for the offensive game ball, but considering Taylor's fumble and McGowan's touchdown, I decided to bestow the hallowed honor upon the impressive rookie.
McGowan finished the game with 12 carries for 77 yards and a touchdown, good for 6.4 yards per carry.
Shane Steichen's post-game comments outlined how highly the Colts think of the seventh-round rookie, "Yeah, it's been great - he's seeing it really well, he's so explosive going through the line of scrimmage - when he sees it, he goes and gets it - but yeah, he just runs so hard and physical."
McGowan has seen his workload significantly increase since he received his first NFL carry in week 2 against Kansas City. On Sunday, McGowan's 12 carries were a career high, alongside a career-best 77 yards rushing.
The rookie's versatility and explosivity on kickoff also drew positive postgame comments from the head coach: "He's awesome, I mean, he's so physical, he cares so much, he puts in so much hard work, and so to have that versatility as a returner and a runner is awesome for our football team."
For years after the departure of Zack Moss,  Indianapolis has searched for a compatible backfield partner for Jonathan Taylor. As the Colts enter an uncertain future beyond the 2026 season, their backfield seems to have found a semblance of stability.
If all of CJ Allen's highlight plays had held up on Sunday, there would have been several voices in Colts' nation comparing the rookie's performance to another #53 who played linebacker in Indianapolis.
Despite having an interception erased by a Kenneth Harris' illegal contact penalty, Allen's presence left an indelible mark on Sunday's contest. The Georgia product finished the game with a team-leading 9 total tackles, 2 tackles for loss, a sack, and a pass defense.
It was the most impressive performance of the young rookie's career, which only spans three starts of significant playing time.
"Yeah, he's flying around - I mean, he's making a ton of plays, he's wearing the green dot [and] getting that experience in there is awesome for him - I'm really excited for his growth and his development right now," said Shane Steichen after Allen's stat sheet stuffing Sunday.
After an impressive first start filled with a few routine learning moments, the young linebacker continues to make strides every week.
His progress will be one to continuously monitor as the season dawdles along. Allen is beginning to show why he should be considered a foundational piece for the next regime to build the next winning Colts defense with.
Justin Walley also made a tremendous case to take home the game ball with his performance on Sunday. The young corner bounced back from a knee injury that had sidelined him for the last two weeks to put together a sterling performance for a secondary that desperately needed it. When healthy, Walley looks to have settled in as another bright spot on a struggling Colts' defense.
Spencer Shrader has been a revelation for a Colts team that is looking for small victories anywhere they can find them.
Against the Dolphins, Shrader finished the game 1-1 on his field goal attempt. His 51-yard boot amounted to the difference in the two-point win.
Each extra point, no longer the automatic conversion they used to be, ended up carrying its weight in the close win as well.
On the year, Shrader is 8-9 from 50+ yards, with a long of 59. After a close competition throughout training camp in which he was consistently pegged as the underdog, Shrader has given Indianapolis reason to consider a high-round RFA tender in the offseason.

title: Winners and Losers from Colts' Win Against Dolphins: Young Roster Provides Hope
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts got a much-needed win against the Miami Dolphins in Week 10, effectively ending their five-game losing streak and putting them at 3-7 on the season, but it wasn't all pretty.
Indy's young core remains the lone bright spot from this dark season, and their efforts against the Dolphins suggest that their rebuild's immediate future may not be as bleak as we'd previously assumed it'd be.
With that being said, follow along as I break down the Indianapolis Colts' biggest winners and losers from their Week 10 win over Miami.
The rookie linebacker has continued to look like the guy the Colts' envisioned he'd become .
In his third start, and second as the green dot of Lou Anarumo's defense, Allen led the Colts in tackles and was overall a play-making menace.
Allen had nine tackles, two tackles for loss, one sack, one pass break-up, and a would-be interception that was negated by defensive pass interference from a teammate agains the Dolphins.
Indianapolis Colts' CJ Allen Reacts to Big Performance in 24-22 Win Over Miami Dolphins pic.twitter.com/TQURFEuZJw
The Colts may just have a budding star at linebacker after all.
The Colts were incredibly high on their third-round pick from 2025, cornerback Justin Walley, but a season-ending injury during the preseason forced us to wait another calendar year until we can see if his early impressions would translate to gamedays.
Walley's regular-season debut got off to a rocky start, but he has since found his footing, and the Colts have established a building block for the future.
After missing the past two weeks with a knee injury, Walley returned to the gridiron in a massive way .
Against the Dolphins, Walley logged five tackles, two tackles for loss, two pass break-ups, and a forced-fumble sack that was scooped up by Colts' defensive lineman Adetomiwa Adebawore for the score.
Walley may not be the Kenny Moore II carbon-copy that many assumed he'd become, but he's certainly showcased a playstyle that warrants comparisons.
The Colts' seventh-round pick from the 2026 NFL Draft has slowly but surely began to find his footing as an NFL running back.
At first, Seth McGowan's efforts suggested nothing more than being a breather for star running back Jonathan Taylor, but as of recent, he's earned his keep as a regular rotational back.
Part of the reason the Colts aren't leaning on Taylor more is due to the fact their season is already lost. They don't want to waste Taylor's health, so McGowan has gotten more of an opportunity as we enter the back half of the 2026 regular season.
And with that opportunity, McGowan has thrived.
Against the Miami Dolphins, Seth McGowan notched his second career rushing touchdown in back-to-back weeks. He totaled 77 rushing yards on just 12 carries (6.4 yards per carry) and now looks like the ideal change-of-pace back the Colts have been looking to pair with Jonathan Taylor since Zack Moss left ahead of the 2024-25 season.
The Colts' veteran wide receiver did not have a performance for the ages, though he was the team's leading receiver in a much-needed win.
Laquon Treadwell led all Colts' passcatchers with three receptions for 24 receiving yards and one touchdown against the Miami Dolphins.
Treadwell touchdown ‼️ 📺CBS pic.twitter.com/BXenWAeS28
What's so special about this statline?
Treadwell is a ten-year veteran who made an active roster for the time since in seven years ahead of the 2026 regular-season. He'd carved out a special teams role with the Colts before earning a spot in the offense's wide receiver rotation, and now he's serving as Shane Steichen's top option for the foreseeable future.
Treadwell scored his first touchdown since 2021 against the Dolphins, and although that likely won't matter as far as the Colts' future plans goes, this is an awesome story that deserves any praise that may comes its way.
The Indianapolis Colts beat the Miami Dolphins despite Daniel Jones' 41.5 passer rating, the worst passer rating in a win in his career and the worst in any game of his Colts career, according to Next Gen Stats .
Through the air, Jones went 11-22 (50%) for 108 passing yards, 1 passing touchdown, and threw two interceptions.
Per NFL Pro Insights, his 41.5 passer rating was the second-worst by a Colts starting quarterback in a win since 2000, only ahead of his current backup Anthony Richardson's 39.0 passer rating in a Week 3, 2024 win against the Bears.
Jones now leads the league with 12 interceptions, yet head coach Shane Steichen said that he'll remain the team's starting quarterback for the Colts' Week 11 divisional matchup against the Houston Texans on Thursday Night Football.
Despite the Colts parting ways with their only two starting-caliber wide receivers in the week leading up to their Week 10 matchup against the Miami Dolphins, tight end Tyler Warren failed to step up as the team's de facto WR1 .
With Alec Pierce out indefinitely with a re-aggravated heel injury, the Colts' dreadful passing game opened the door for Warren to benefit from, yet the second-year tight end left the Week 10 win with just three targets to show for.
Warren totaled just one receiving yard on two receptions against the Dolphins, which goes to show just how anemic the Colts' passing game has become.
Naturally, they've started to lean on the running back duo of Jonathan Taylor and Seth McGowan, but the end result of their passing games leaves much to be desired.
Tyler Warren will likely be part of the Colts' rebuilding plans as he still has two years left on his rookie contract, as well as a fifth-year option waiting in the wings, and he'll need to step up sooner than later as the 2026 season nears its conclusion.
Yes, the Colts ultimately won the game, but it was hardly because of anything Shane Steichen did .
The Colts played hard, which could be viewed as a positive for Steichen, but it more so feels like the new wave of players are playing for eachother more than anything else.
Steichen's unjustified, steadfast belief in Daniel Jones remains his biggest blunder , but his team is also playing with far less discipline than they showed earlier in the year.
The Colts managed to stay afloat at 2-2 through the season's first four weeks, and a big reason for that is because they averaged a league-low four penalties per game.
Ever since, though, they've played far more reckless. Since Week 4, the Colts have averaged 8.5 penalties per game, and their most extreme example of such regression comes from their Week 10 win against the Miami Dolphins.
Against the Dolphins, the Colts committed 13 penalties, which is the most in a single game under head coach Shane Steichen.
Some of this can be attributed to the Colts turning to their young rostered players after losing several longtime veterans via the trade deadline, but it's still up to Steichen to get the best out of them.
Noah Compton is the Publisher of Indianapolis Colts On SI. Noah is from the Indy area and has been covering the Colts since 2022, including stops at FanSided, The Blue Stable, and SBNation.

title: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly From the Colts’ Fortunate Win Over the Dolphins
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts got back in the win column on Sunday with a 24-22 win over the one-win Miami Dolphins, but it wasn't a convincing performance.
The Colts found a way to get the job done, though there were plenty of reasons to be encouraged, concerned and downright frustrated with what unfolded against Miami. Here's a closer look at the good, the bad and the ugly from the Colts' most recent outing.
If there was anything for the Colts offense to be excited about, it’s their run game. Jonathan Taylor and Seth McGowan teamed up to rush for 160 yards and a touchdown between them.
Beyond what the stats say, both McGowan and Taylor ripped off several long runs to move the sticks and keep the Colts’ offense on the field. McGowan especially came in clutch, picking up the yardage needed at the end of the game to ice it and give the Colts their first win on US soil since September.
On a day where the passing game was close to inept, having a dominant ground game to lean into certainly played a massive role in the Colts returning to winning ways.
Defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo was itching to get Justin Walley back on the field after missing the last two games with an injury, and his performance against Miami showed exactly why the Colts view Walley as such an important player for them.
Back in his slot cornerback role, Walley finished with five tackles, two tackles for loss, a pass breakup and a sack-fumble which resulted in a defensive touchdown for Indianapolis, the highlight of the day for the Colts.
In addition to strong coverage and the splash play on a nickel blitz, Walley made some strong tackles flying up the field in run defense. His energy and execution helped fuel a very respectable defensive performance.
Walley wasn’t the only young defensive player to make an impact.
CJ Allen put together his third excellent game in a row, setting the tone with his physicality in the run game and nearly coming away with two interceptions in pass coverage while also recording a sack. Bryce Boettcher, the Colts’ other rookie linebacker, also flew around the field, finishing with seven tackles.
CJ ALLEN INCOMING 📺 CBS pic.twitter.com/7wGDIa7aCO
On the back end, AJ Haulcy flashed some of his potential with some solid work in coverage. Up front, Jaylahn Tuimoloau continued his fine stretch of play, getting after the quarterback and coming up with a huge batted pass late in the game.
It’s becoming more and more clear every week that the Colts may not be super competitive in the near future, but they do have a plethora of exciting pieces to develop and build around moving forward.
Tyler Warren’s sophomore slump continued on Sunday. Even though the Dolphins have had trouble defending the tight end in the passing game this season, Warren was silenced.
Miami held Warren to just two catches for only a yard. Warren finished with more rushing yards than receiving due to a three-yard carry in the first half to move the chains.
The Colts were certainly hoping to see more out of their tight end, especially with the team trading away their most reliable wide receivers earlier in the week. But Warren didn’t answer the call.
The Colts finished with a season-high 13 penalties for 83 yards, their most fouls in a game under head coach Shane Steichen. Those numbers are staggering, and it’s honestly somewhat surprising that Indianapolis managed to sneak away with a win.
One unit in particular wasn’t more susceptible than the others.
Injuries on the offensive line, combined with a brand new bunch of receivers, made it difficult for the offense to remain in sync. Defensively, pass interference and defensive holding penalties extended Dolphin drives far too frequently. Even special teams lacked discipline, as block-in-the-back fouls negated excellent returns.
Without question, the Colts will have no chance of turning their season around down the stretch if they continue to shoot themselves in the foot.
While the Colts ultimately did get the win, which is most important, head coach Shane Steichen deserves plenty of criticism for how the game played out.
As Steichen says on a regular basis, it’s his responsibility to get the team ready to go win a football game. The penalties, lack of a cohesive passing game and poor execution to see the game out late against a one-win team whose starting quarterback was making his NFL debut were all evidence that Steichen fell significantly short of adequately preparing his team to play.
Had Steichen and the Colts found a way to lose to Miami, the fourth-year head coach would almost certainly be out of work in the next 24 hours.
Recently, Sauce Gardner has been on the receiving end of some slightly unfair criticism revolving around the trade the Colts made for the All-Pro cornerback at last year’s trade deadline. Unfortunately, on Sunday, Gardner didn’t do much to quiet those complaints.
Gardner only allowed two catches for 20 yards, but didn’t force any incompletions and was flagged multiple times, including a defensive pass interference foul on a third-and-14, which gifted the Dolphins a first down.
It wasn’t all bad, but it wasn't very good either. To make things worse, Gardner left the game in the second half with a calf injury, the third injury to that body part since he arrived in Indianapolis at last year’s trade deadline. Overall, just a day to wipe from the memory if you’re the 25-year-old cornerback.
Indianapolis’ offensive line hasn’t looked the same since trading Quenton Nelson. That included against the Dolphins, but for different reasons.
Injuries to several starters piled up and forced the Colts to do some serious reshuffling up front. Right tackle Jalen Travis was ruled out, forcing right guard Matt Goncalves to kick outside to tackle. During the first quarter, left tackle Bernhard Raimann suffered a concussion and did not return, meaning Luke Tenuta had to man down the blindside for Daniel Jones.
The only players who remained in their typical positions were center Tanor Bortolini and left guard Jalen Farmer. Both held their own, but the Colts certainly may have had more offensive success had their line been at full strength.
Simply put, the passing game without established receiving options is borderline pathetic to watch.
The most productive pass catcher for the Colts, Tyler Warren, was nearly invisible all day long. Drops and poor throws from Daniel Jones significantly restricted any success through the air. Jones finished 11-for-22 for 108 yards, a touchdown pass and two interceptions.
It was clear, even with better weapons , that Jones has struggled mightily this season. Asking him to try and turn his form around with a worse situation around him than a few weeks ago simply isn’t fair, nor will it produce results.
Either way, the Colts have a lot of thinking to do regarding their passing game if they want to see some improvements down the stretch.

title: Biggest Takeaway From Colts' Win Against Dolphins: Perhaps Daniel Jones is Ideal Bridge Option After All
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts entered their Week 10 matchup against the Miami Dolphins on a five-game losing streak.
After four quarters of back-and-forth dysfunction, the Colts came out on top to earn their third victory of the season. It required a matchup against a first-time starter at quarterback for a one-win team, but the new-look Colts needed this confidence boost as they turn to their future.
Nothing has changed as far as the Colts' 2026-27 season is concerned, though their efforts in Week 10 has provided something to look forward to as the end of their previous era is slowly but surely weeded out.
The decision to keep rolling with Daniel Jones as the starting quarterback makes zero sense, but there's reason to believe he'd be the Colts' best option as far as a bridge quarterback for the next regime's first season goes.
Follow along as I break down my biggest takeaway from the Colts' win in question.
The Indianapolis Colts declined to trade starting quarterback Daniel Jones at the deadline despite interest because they wanted to provide the next general manager the opportunity to either roll with Jones as the bridge quarterback for 2027-28, or make him a June 1st cut designation.
The latter would save the Colts ~$38 million in cap space for 2027-28, though it would have to be accounted for after the fact, whether that be solely for 2028 or via a prorated payout in the years following.
Regardless, the notion of keeping Jones around seems nonsensical.
Head coach Shane Steichen will undoubtedly prefer to roll with Jones if he's given the opportunity to right the ship in 2027, but there's almost no reason to believe that the Colts quarterback will provide a steady hand in furthering the development of the future.
Here's how Daniel Jones has fared over the last four weeks:
1. 13-22 (59.1%) 108 pass yards, 1 INT 2. 19-28 (67.9%) 144 pass yards, 1 TD, 2 INTs 3. 20-34 (58.8%) 180 pass yards, 1 TD, 1 INT 4. 11-22 (50%) 108 pass yards, 1 TD, 2 INTs
Jones wasn't much better prior to this stretch, but he still warranted benching considerations , and this four-game performance proves that he cannot get the job done.
I would be remiss not to acknowledge his league-worst supporting cast, at least regarding the wide receiver position, but plenty of other quarterbacks in similar, if not worse, situations have managed to play better.
Shane Steichen has remained steadfast in his belief that Jones is the best option for the 2026-27 Colts, and he explained what goes into his weekly process of determining whether or not a change is needed following the team's Week 10 win against the Dolphins.
"I think I take everything into account," Steichen explained. "I always go back and look at the film and make sure, 'on this play, was it his fault or someone else's fault?' There's a lot that goes into it. Obviously, the biggest thing is taking care of the football moving forward."
This is the sixth straight week that Steichen has said Jones needs to clean up his ball security, yet we've not seen results.
And because I no longer can make sense of Steichen's refusal to entertain a quarterback change, the only way I can justify the Colts keeping Jones around to be their bridge option is due to the fact he may just be the best possible tank commander.
Indianapolis would still owe Jones mid-tier QB money in this hypothetical, which would be an overpay if he continued to play as he has in 2026.
However, that may just be the best course of action.
As a friendly reminder, the Colts are without their 2027 first-round pick, so any chances of finding their face of the franchise are slim to none as far as this upcoming draft goes. However, they still have their own 2028 first-round pick, therefore all eyes are set on the 2028 NFL Draft.
The Colts will likely be one of the league's worst teams next season, but they can't just throw games a la Paul Crewe in their pursuit of a top draft selection.
Openly tanking is not just frowned upon in the NFL; it's the biggest possible rules violation.
But if the Colts convince the league that they're honorably tanking with a proven quarterback, then no harm, no foul.
This is mostly a tongue-in-cheek proposal, but then again, Jones has played so poorly in 2026 that this outcome is not ridiculous.
The Colts' 2027-28 offense will largely feature the same personnel; therefore, it's fair to envision a reality where a Jones-led operation nets similar results.
Ideally, the new era will bring inspiration to whichever version of the new-look Colts we get, thus giving us a stronger floor than what we're seeing this season, but we'd need an unforeseen turnaround before we can envision a Jones-led Colts offense being anything other than dysfunctional.
Noah Compton is the Publisher of Indianapolis Colts On SI. Noah is from the Indy area and has been covering the Colts since 2022, including stops at FanSided, The Blue Stable, and SBNation.

title: Colts vs. Dolphins Best Bets: Feed JT and Cash In
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts have a legitimate chance to finally get back in the win column Sunday, and I think we have an even better chance to make some money off the game plan they’ll need to use.
Indianapolis is 2-7 and riding a five-game losing streak, while the Miami Dolphins come to Lucas Oil Stadium at 1-7. Call it a Toilet Bowl, but ugly football can still give us some clean betting angles.
We’re 16-9 on Colts-specific best bets this season, and this week feels pretty straightforward.
Indianapolis doesn’t have many proven answers left, which means Shane Steichen should be putting the ball in Jonathan Taylor’s hands as often as possible.
Run the rock and make Kyle McCord beat you.
Here are my three best bets for Week 10.
I’m going right back to Taylor.
He probably should have gotten his get-right touchdown last week. Taylor ran six yards down to the Dallas 2-yard line, lost his shoe, and had to come out before Seth McGowan scored his first NFL touchdown on the next snap.
Taylor has gone two straight games without scoring, with his last touchdown coming in Week 7 against Minnesota. He still enters Sunday with eight rushing scores this season.
Forget the trade rumors. Taylor is still here, and with how limited this offense has become, there aren’t many other options near the goal line.
One play could cash this line.
Dulin caught one pass last week, but it went 55 yards for a touchdown against Dallas. With Downs and Allen gone, those opportunities should become more available.
The Colts have to manufacture yards somehow when defenses load up against Taylor. Dulin’s speed makes him an obvious candidate for screens, shot plays and anything designed to create a chunk gain.
At 14.5 yards, I’m betting he gets at least one opportunity and makes it count.
This one is simple: I’m betting on the first-time starter making a mistake.
McCord will make his first NFL regular-season start Sunday and throw his first official pass against Indianapolis. The Colts have only two interceptions this season, so I understand the hesitation.
But the young defensive front showed life against Dallas, including Laiatu Latu’s strip-sack of Dak Prescott. If Indianapolis can create pressure and force McCord into obvious passing situations, there should be an opportunity for this secondary to finally make a play on the football.
First NFL start, on the road, against a defense that showed some juice last week. I’ll take my chances on one mistake.
Good luck and bet responsibly.
Game odds refresh periodically and are subject to change. If you or someone you know has a gambling problem and wants help, call 1-800-GAMBLER.

title: 3 Things Colts Must Do Against Dolphins to Snap Their Five-Game Skid
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts have lost five straight, but Sunday might be their best chance in weeks to finally stop the bleeding.
Miami comes to Lucas Oil Stadium at 1-7, and with Malik Willis on injured reserve, the Dolphins are turning to Kyle McCord for his first NFL start. For a Colts team sitting at 2-7, this is absolutely a game they should believe they can win.
But with this offense as depleted as it is, Indianapolis needs to keep things simple.
Daniel Jones is left with a thin group of proven weapons. The path to victory is pretty straightforward: lean on the stars who are still here and make the rookie quarterback uncomfortable.
Here are my three keys to a Colts victory in Week 10.
After all the trade deadline chaos, Jonathan Taylor is still here. Now, let him remind this league just who he is.
Taylor enters Sunday with 656 rushing yards and eight touchdowns on 161 carries. If Indianapolis establishes him early, this entire offense changes.
If Taylor dictates the game, the Colts can stay ahead of the sticks, control the clock, and avoid forcing Jones to carry this barren passing game.
This isn't complicated. Run the damn ball.
McCord is in line to make the first regular-season start of his NFL career after Miami placed Willis on injured reserve with a groin injury.
The Colts don't have an elite pass rush, but this is exactly the kind of matchup where their young defensive ends need to step up. Show pressure, disguise coverage, and force McCord to make decisions before he gets comfortable.
We've seen defensive minds like Bill Belichick and Mike Vrabel make life miserable for inexperienced quarterbacks. Indianapolis needs to bring that same aggressive mentality Sunday.
You cannot let McCord settle in.
The Colts want to run the ball all afternoon, but eventually there will be a third-and-long where Jones has no choice but to throw it.
That's where Tyler Warren is going to have to be the dominant physical force he is.
With Allen and Downs gone, Warren is clearly the most dangerous receiving option left. He has 38 catches for 275 yards and two touchdowns on 53 targets this season, plus another score on the ground.
Miami knows that, too. The Dolphins can crowd the middle, bracket Warren, and force someone else to beat them.
It might not matter. Warren has to win through contact, create after the catch, and make the handful of plays this offense simply cannot get from anywhere else right now.
Miami is averaging just 15.8 points per game, 31st in the NFL. Indianapolis does not need to be perfect.
Feed Taylor, make McCord uncomfortable, and let Warren be the difference-maker. If Indianapolis sticks to that formula, there's no reason this five-game losing streak can't end Sunday.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: 3 Storylines to Watch in Colts Week 10 Clash with Dolphins
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts will return to Lucas Oil Stadium this weekend looking to put an end to a difficult stretch of football. After beginning the season with a 2-2 record, Indianapolis has dropped five consecutive games and finds itself in a lost season, where the focus has shifted from a playoff pursuit to evaluating the future.
The Colts have undergone significant changes over the past several weeks, both on and off the field. Sunday's matchup presents an opportunity to start moving in a different direction, but Indianapolis will need a much more complete performance to take advantage of the opportunity.
Miami arrives in Indianapolis having experienced plenty of its own struggles this season. At 1-7, the Dolphins are equally desperate to find some momentum, setting up an important matchup for two teams that desperately need a positive result.
Here are three storylines to watch as the Colts prepare to host the Dolphins in Week 10.
The Colts traded away their two most productive wide receivers in Keenan Allen and Josh Downs at Tuesday's deadline, leaving behind a receiving corps that looks drastically different.
While the organization added to its draft capital, it also left a substantial void in its passing attack that needs to be filled.
The two receivers combined for 73 receptions, 705 receiving yards and two touchdowns. They also accounted for 67% of the Colts' targets, 70% of their receptions and 61% of their receiving yards from the wide receiver position. Replacing that level of production will be a considerable challenge for an offense that has already struggled to find consistency.
With Alec Pierce still on injured reserve, Indianapolis' wide receiver room consists of Laquon Treadwell, Ashton Dulin, Anthony Gould, Deion Burks and Nick Westbrook-Ikhine. The five of them have combined for 49 targets, 27 catches, 375 yards and one touchdown. Needless to say, the group lacks consistent production.
Gould and Burks are two younger players who could also benefit from the increased opportunities. Head coach Shane Steichen shared that Gould will take on a larger role in the slot following Downs' departure, while Burks will rotate in.
Tyler Warren will also need to be a regular feature of the passing attack. The second-year tight end has already established himself as one of Jones' more reliable targets, leading the team with 38 receptions for 275 yards.
With fewer established options available at wide receiver, Warren could see an even greater share of the offensive workload moving forward. Still, he can't do it all himself, and at least one wide out will have to take the bull by the horns.
Ultimately, the Colts need several players to take advantage of opportunities that simply weren't available to them before the trade deadline. Sunday's matchup against Miami will provide an early indication of whether Indianapolis has enough depth and versatility to remain competitive offensively with its reshuffled receiving corps.
The Dolphins placed starting quarterback Malik Willis on injured reserve with a groin injury, meaning second-year quarterback Kyle McCord will step into the starting role.
The change under center presents an opportunity for a struggling Colts defense to regain some confidence. Indianapolis has struggled to consistently get off the field, ranking near the bottom of the league in several defensive categories. Perhaps more importantly, they've struggled to create turnovers, ranking 31st in the NFL with 5 total takeaways, though it has produced three in the last two games.
McCord has yet to attempt a pass in a regular-season NFL game, making it difficult to know exactly what to expect from the young quarterback. He does bring a live arm and has experience operating in high-pressure situations dating back to his college career, which included stops at Ohio State and Syracuse. However, making a first NFL start on the road presents an entirely different challenge, particularly against a defense that should be hungry to make his afternoon uncomfortable.
Rushing the passer will be key. The Colts will need to find ways to generate consistent pressure. Defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo has several young players who could make an impact in this matchup, including Laiatu Latu, Adetomiwa Adebawore and rookie Caden Curry. Creating difficult passing situations and forcing McCord to make quick decisions should be among the priorities for Indianapolis, as speeding up his internal clock will help generate turnover opportunities for the back end.
Of course, the Colts cannot afford to overlook Miami's other offensive weapons. The Dolphins still have a capable running game and will likely look to establish it early to take some pressure off their quarterback. Indianapolis will need to contain the run and force Miami into obvious passing situations rather than allowing the offense to dictate the game on the ground.
How successful the Colts are in frustrating McCord will have a direct impact on the outcome of the game. Fail to do so, and Miami may sneak away with a victory.
Turnovers have become one of the most significant problems for the Colts this season, and Daniel Jones has been at the center of those struggles.
Jones has struggled mightily protecting the football, with his mistakes putting additional pressure on an offense that has already had difficulty finding the end zone. He enters Week 10 with 10 interceptions through nine games, giving him one of the highest totals among NFL quarterbacks.
Even more concerning is the frequency with which those mistakes have occurred. Jones has thrown an interception in eight of his nine appearances this season, including each of his last four games. He has also thrown just six touchdown passes during that span, leaving Indianapolis deprived of the efficiency Jones showed he could operate at a season ago.
Giving the opposing offense additional possessions will made an already struggling defense's job even more difficult, while the offense has frequently been forced to overcome mistakes that could have been avoided.
There are certainly some circumstances working against Jones. The Colts have dealt with injuries throughout their offensive lineup and have a huge question mark at the wide receiver position. Allen and Downs were important parts of the passing game, particularly in providing Jones with reliable options underneath and in the middle of the field. Adjusting to an entirely different group of receivers could create some communication and timing issues early on.
However, that makes protecting the football even more important. Jones does not need to force difficult throws or attempt to manufacture big plays on every possession. Indianapolis still has Jonathan Taylor available in the backfield, and the Colts should look to lean on their running game to take some pressure off of Jones. Taking what the defense gives him, avoiding unnecessary risks and being willing to throw the football away when necessary would represent an important step in the right direction.

title: 3 Matchups That Will Test Just How Bad the Colts Really Are
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts are back home Sunday for a matchup that, if we’re being honest, isn’t exactly must-watch TV.
Indianapolis is 2-7 and riding a five-game losing streak, while Miami enters at 1-7. But beneath the surface, there are a few battles that could bring some life to this game.
More than anything, this feels like a litmus test for how bad this Colts team really is. If Indianapolis struggles against this Miami team, things are really, REALLY bad.
Here are three matchups I’m watching closely.
After all the trade deadline chaos, Jonathan Taylor can finally put the noise behind him and get back to playing football.
Taylor has 656 rushing yards and eight touchdowns, but he has managed just 69 rushing yards over the last two games. I think some of that had to do with everything transpiring around him and this organization.
This feels like the perfect get-right spot.
Miami is allowing 111.8 rushing yards per game, and the Dolphins just lost defensive tackle Zach Sieler for the season with a torn biceps. This game pretty much comes down to whether the Colts can run the rock against a Miami front that suddenly looks much more vulnerable.
If Taylor gets rolling early, Indianapolis should control this game.
Normally, I would call this a get-right game for Daniel Jones, too. The problem is the front office just stripped away almost every proven weapon he had.
Josh Downs is in Kansas City, and Keenan Allen is in San Francisco. Tyler Warren is now the centerpiece of the passing game, while Laquon Treadwell and Ashton Dulin are being asked to do more.
Now, Jones hasn’t been good. He has thrown for 1,722 yards, six touchdowns and 10 interceptions, and he still hasn’t looked like the same quarterback he was before the Achilles injury ended his 2025 season.
He also made it clear this week that he wasn’t thrilled with the deadline moves. But what are you going to do?
Miami only has 12 sacks this season, with Chop Robinson leading the team at four.
If Jones is going to create anything through the air with this depleted group, he is basically going to have to do it all.
This matchup might tell us the most about Indianapolis’ defense.
Kyle McCord is making his first NFL start Sunday and has never thrown a regular-season pass. For a young Colts defense that looked at least somewhat competent last week, this is about as favorable of a quarterback matchup as you can ask for.
Indianapolis still has Sauce Gardner and Charvarius Ward outside, with Cam Bynum behind them. The Colts rank 17th in passing yards allowed at 224.8 per game.
They should make life miserable for McCord early. If a quarterback making his first NFL start finds consistent success against this secondary, then this unit really is that bad.
The Colts have every opportunity to take control of this game, and frankly, there's no excuse for another lifeless performance. If Indianapolis can't handle a depleted Miami team at home, this season might be even worse than we thought.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Revisiting the Colts' Blockbuster Sauce Gardner Trade One Year Later
full_text:
374 days ago, the Indianapolis Colts made one of the biggest trades in franchise history, surrendering two first-round picks and wide receiver Adonai Mitchell to acquire New York Jets cornerback Sauce Gardner.
The move came with Indianapolis sitting at 7-2 and looking like a legitimate Super Bowl contender. General manager Chris Ballard believed he had an opportunity to acquire one of the NFL's premier young defensive players and address a major weakness in the secondary.
Fast forward 12 months, and the circumstances surrounding that decision look drastically different.
The Colts are 2-7, Ballard is no longer with the organization and Indianapolis has begun accumulating draft capital for its next rebuilding effort. Gardner remains in Indianapolis, but the franchise has yet to see the kind of return it envisioned when making such a substantial investment.
Meanwhile, the Jets have already begun seeing solid returns from the compensation they received for Gardner.
Let's take a look back at the trade and how both sides have fared from it a year later.
The Colts' decision to pursue Gardner made plenty of sense at the time.
Indianapolis was the top team in the AFC, with an explosive offense and a defense that appeared to be one piece away from becoming a legitimate contender. However, injuries and inconsistent play in the secondary had created a weakness that opposing offenses could exploit.
Gardner offered an opportunity to address that problem with one of the league's most accomplished young cornerbacks.
The former No. 4 pick had earned first-team All-Pro honors in each of his first two NFL seasons and was widely regarded as one of the best players at his position.
Indianapolis was acquiring more than just a starting cornerback. It was bringing in a potential defensive cornerstone who had already established himself among the NFL's elite.
That alone helps explain why Ballard was so willing to mortgage the franchise's future to get a deal done.
The Jets received Indianapolis' 2026 and 2027 first-round picks along with Mitchell, who had been selected in the second round of the 2024 NFL Draft. It was an enormous investment for a cornerback, even one with Gardner's pedigree.
Ballard was essentially betting that Indianapolis' championship window was open and that the draft selections would be late enough to justify sacrificing them for an established star.
Unfortunately, the remainder of the 2025 season did not go according to plan.
The Colts won their first game with Gardner, but lost the next seven straight, finishing 8-9. The team that once stood atop of the conference missed the playoffs entirely. Their 2026 first-round selection consequently became the No. 16 overall pick, which the Jets used to select Oregon tight end Kenyon Sadiq.
Had the Colts held onto their pick instead of trading for Gardner, some of the prospects still available at No. 16 for their selection included safety Dillon Thieneman, wide receiver Omar Cooper Jr. (both Indianapolis natives) and a long list of talented edge rushers to improve what was and still remains a weak point for the Colts.
To make things worse for Indianapolis, their 2-7 record means their 2027 selection would be the No. 4 overall pick if the season were to end today. So there's a real possibility Indianapolis acquired an All-Pro cornerback in exchange for a top-20 draft pick, a top-five draft pick and a young wide receiver.
Purely on paper, the total trade package looks ugly for Indianapolis.
While the circumstances surrounding the trade have changed, Gardner remains the centerpiece of Indianapolis' return.
There is no questioning the talent that made him such an attractive acquisition. However, his time with the Colts has been interrupted by injuries and has yet to produce the consistent results expected from a player who commanded two first-round picks.
Gardner appeared in just three games following the trade during the 2025 season before suffering a calf injury that sidelined him for the rest of the year. He returned for the 2026 campaign but experienced another interruption to his availability, limiting the amount of time Indianapolis has had its prized acquisition on the field.
Through eight games this season, Gardner has recorded 26 tackles and seven passes defended without an interception. While those numbers don't tell the entire story of a cornerback's performance, they illustrate the relatively modest statistical production Indianapolis has received so far.
It would be unfair to place the Colts' defensive struggles entirely on Gardner. Indianapolis has dealt with injuries and personnel deficiencies throughout the front seven, and one cornerback cannot single-handedly transform an entire defense, regardless of the price Indianapolis paid to get him.
Nevertheless, the Colts acquired Gardner because they believed he could make a significant difference. His limited availability and inconsistent results have made it difficult to justify the enormous price.
That doesn't mean the investment cannot eventually pay off. Gardner is still young and remains under contract through 2030, giving the Colts plenty of time to see their investment pay off.
But evaluating the trade one year later requires acknowledging that Indianapolis has not yet received the impact it expected.
The other side of this transaction makes the evaluation even more complicated for Indianapolis.
While the Colts have been waiting for Gardner to establish himself as the centerpiece of their secondary, the Jets have begun turning their return package into meaningful pieces for their own roster.
New York used Indianapolis' 2026 first-round selection to draft Sadiq, who has shown flashes of significant potential during his rookie campaign. Through nine games, the Oregon product has recorded 21 receptions (second on team) for 235 yards and a touchdown.
Those numbers aren't necessarily eye-popping, but Sadiq has already demonstrated the receiving ability that made him such an intriguing prospect. His seven-catch, 105-yard performance against Detroit in Week 3 offered a particularly encouraging glimpse of what he could become.
Mitchell has also benefited from the change of scenery.
After struggling to establish himself in Indianapolis, the former second-round pick has received a larger opportunity in New York. He missed four games following a finger procedure but returned to record seven receptions for 142 yards and a touchdown against the Raiders in Week 8.
Through his first four appearances of 2026, Mitchell has logged 265 receiving yards while averaging 16.6 yards per reception, beginning to show the downfield ability that made him so intriguing to the Colts in 2024.
Neither player has established himself as a definitive building block just yet, but both have provided the Jets with meaningful contributions and enough optimism moving forward for New York to believe they won the trade by a landslide.
The most significant asset, however, is still waiting to be realized.
New York has yet to use Indianapolis' 2027 first-round selection, which is likely to wind up being another top-half selection, at worst. The Jets will have a chance to some more top-end talent to their roster.
That gives New York a considerable advantage when evaluating the early returns of the transaction. The organization has already acquired a promising rookie tight end, given a young receiver an opportunity to develop and retained another first-round pick for the upcoming draft.
Indianapolis, meanwhile, has one player to show for the entire package.
Jumping to conclusions on who the trade benefited more would be premature. There's still plenty of time for that equation to change. Gardner has the talent to reestablish his status as an elite cornerback, and his remaining contract gives him an opportunity to provide value well beyond the first year of the deal.
What was once viewed as an aggressive move to help Indianapolis compete for a championship has become a reminder of the risks…

title: 3 Things We Learned From the Jaguars' Beatdown of Titans: Bhayshul Tuten's Role is Clear
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars found another AFC South win in Week 10, this time putting up points in all kinds of different fashions on their way to a 40-23 victory over the Tennessee Titans.
The Jaguars' Week 10 road win was defined by explosive plays and great individual efforts on both sides of the ball, with the likes of Parker Washington, Trevor Lawrence, and Travis Hunter all making game-changing plays to lift the Jaguars to a win.
This is the last time we see this version of the Jaguars before their reinforcements join them for an AFC South title push in the form of Jessie Bates and Jordan Davis. So, what did we learn from the Jaguars this week? We break it down below.
This backfield has been Bhayshul Tuten's each week, and we certainly did not enter Week 10 with the impression that this would change against the Titans. But what we did learn on Sunday was that the Jaguars view the gap between the No. 1 and No. 2 spots in the backfield as one that is growing as the season goes on. This, of course, is because the usage of the Jaguars' top two backs demanded such an observation.
Even with Tuten at less than 100% , the second-year back played 70% of the snaps and had nearly 30 touches. Meanwhile, Chris Rodriguez had four carries and just 10 snaps played, giving him fewer snaps on the day than LeQuint Allen for the first time this season. Tuten has been the No. 1 running back all year long, but the last few weeks while he has been injured have really shown us how wide the gap is on the depth chart.
"Yeah, he played hard, man. He played tough. I think we were very close to breaking a few again," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said after the game about Tuten. "Got to go look at it and see if there was some more opportunities there, but I was very proud of the way that he continues to challenge himself with very little practice preparation throughout the course of the week to come out and give us his best every Sunday these last two weeks of game day. He's not perfect. He's not 100 percent and he continues to play for this team, and I appreciate that."
The Jaguars' pass-rush is the most fascinating debate of the 2026 squad. The Jaguars recorded one sack of Titans quarterback Cam Ward, with Antonio Johnson getting home on a blitz in the second-half. A week earlier against the Baltimore Ravens, the Jaguars also recorded just one sack, this time from linebacker Foyesade Oluokun. Even half of the Jaguars' four sacks against the Colts in Week 8 were from non-defensive linemen, with Oluokun and Jalen Huskey each notching one.
That is to say the Jaguars are getting some results with their pass-rush, but it is not coming in the form of sacks from their top defensive linemen. The Jaguars are seeing pressures make an impact, such as on the Travis Hunter interception, but their defensive line has 9.5 sacks through nine games. Their non-defensive linemen have 6.5. The pass-rush has been unique this season, and nobody likely predicrted the Jaguars' big three on the defensive line would have 6.5 sacks by nearly Thanksgiving.
The Jaguars have made it work to this point. And perhaps the addition of Jordan Davis in some way impacts the rest of the pass rush's productivty. But a mix of scheme and game scripts have called for the Jaguars' pass-rush to have quite the confounding sack production through nine games.
Josh Cameron has been terrific for the Jaguars as a sixth-round rookie . It started with a red-zone touchdown against the Cleveland Browns in Week 1, and it has kept rolling since. Cameron now has three touchdown catches through nine games, which is quite the impressive mark considering his role in the Jaguars' offense. Cameron is not a high-volume route runner for the Jaguars who plays in a lot of three-receiver sets. His role has been more so in 12 and 13 personnel and in the red-zone, yet he has continued to find ways to make an impact as a rotational piece.
The Jaguars are still using Brian Thomas Jr. as a starting receiver , with Thomas seeing more targets Sunday than Cameron did (four to three). With the Jaguars opting not to trade Thomas at the deadline, they were making it clear that they like their receiver room as-is for the 2026 season. Thomas plays in three receiver sets when the Jaguars spread it out, Cameron makes an impact in heavier formations both as a receiver and as a run-blocker.
That is what they should continue to lean on, and next year is the actual appropriate time to start to look at a potential shift. Cameron can make an impact and get valuable experience now, and then the Jaguars can take another look at the makeup of the room after the season. It is very easy to see a scenario where Cameron gets a larger role in his second season after a strong rookie year, a lot like Bhayshul Tuten has done at running back.
John Shipley has been covering the Jacksonville Jaguars as a beat reporter and publisher of Jaguar Report since 2019. Previously, he covered UCF's undefeated season as a beat reporter for NSM.Today, covered high school prep sports in Central Florida, and covered local sports and news for the Palatka Daily News. Follow John Shipley on Twitter at @_john_shipley.

title: Shipley's Dozen: Jaguars Continue to Roll in AFC South, Travis Hunter's Elite Level, and Much More
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are ... pretty dang good!
It felt like the Jaguars played at a C+, B- level against the Tennessee Titans in Week 10, but it still resulted in a 40-23 win on the road. The Jaguars are rolling, and the rest of the AFC is clearly on notice.
We break down the big Week 10 win and the bigger picture with this week's edition of the Shipley's Dozen column. Do not forget, you can read this column each morning after a Jaguars game.
This was the best version of Parker Washington we have ever seen, and not just because of the eye-popping numbers he put up during the first-half. Washington set career numbers in the first two quarters alone before finishing the game with seven catches for 152 yards and a touchdown. For my money, it was the best Washington has ever played for the Jaguars even beyond the numbers, simply because he showed the entire skill-set.
Putting the Titans' highest-paid defensive back in a spin cycle with his route-running? Check. Yards after the catch and toughness? Check. Ability to win in contested situations downfield? Check. Ability to win on the sideline with coordination and athletic ability? Check. Washington was elite on Sunday, and everyone on the field knew it.
How many cornerbacks in the AFC have played as well as Travis Hunter has this season? Hunter recorded his third interception of the season Sunday. He was targeted five times, giving up four catches for ... 13 yards. He has been a playmaker, he has tackled well, and there are simply not many cornerbacks doing the things he is doing every single week at the position. The case for him as an All-Pro are clear, and the only cornerbacks in the AFC who I think have played anywhere near his level are Denzel Ward and Nohl Williams. He has already become one of the best players at his entire position in the NFL, and the Hunter trade continues to pay off for Liam Coen and James Gladstone as a result.
"It was an unbelievable catch. Unbelievable play," Coen said after the game about Hunter's interception. "Critical because we had just turned it over, right? On the interception. Talk about having each other's back. That's what this group does. That's what this group is. Such a special play by obviously a special player.
It was a good week for the Jaguars. In fact, it was a great week. The Jaguars improved on paper more than any other team in the NFL at the very start of the week. Then the locker room responded in the right way in the middle of the week. Then the Jaguars finished it with another 40-point game and a road blowout of an AFC South foe, while seeing their positioning in the AFC South improve due to the Texans losing in Cleveland. The Jaguars sent a message all week , and it has been received loud and clear for all to hear.
"I think this was really just about our team, to be honest. Our team's got a lot of confidence. Our team was damn good without Jessie (Bates III) and Jordan (Davis) and Davon (Godchaux)," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said after the game. "That's how these guys went into the week. Hey, we can beat people. We feel confident every time we walk out on the grass on Sundays and hopefully those guys can only come and add to an already talented, tough team as we get down a stretch that we're trying to go on a run here, you know?"
It should be clear why the Jaguars made the Jordan Davis and Jessie Bates III moves , at least in the short-term. The Jaguars were clearly the better team over the Titans so there was never any real chance of them having to pay for starting backups Matt Dickerson and Rayuan Lane at nose tackle and safety, but if they were playing the Chicago Bears or any other talented team, maybe the Jaguars would not have been as well off.
The Jaguars did not get much of an impact from their interior defensive line Sunday, both against the run and pass. Several times Cam Ward was pressued off the edge but stepped up in the pocket to scramble for yards, while there was not quite the elite run-stuffing effort we are used to seeing from Jacksonville. Add in a few missed tackles in space at the safety spot, and it is very clear where Bates and Davis can help the Jaguars right off the bat.
It is starting to get tougher and tougher to be surprised by rookie sixth-rounder Josh Cameron. Cameron has come up big for the Jaguars time and time again during his debut season, and Sunday may have been his best game. He caught three passes for 67 yards, including a 28-yard shot down the sideline on the opening drive and a 25-yard touchdown to give the Jaguars their first double-digit lead of the game with under 10 minutes left. Add in everything he did as a run-blocker and the Jaguars have quite the find with Cameron.
If there is one thing the Jaguars have gotten from backup center Jonah Monheim last season, it is the ability to step in on a whim and give them good snaps. Monheim has been the backup behind starting center Robert Hainsey since the Jaguars drafted him out of USC in the seventh-round of the 2025 NFL Draft, and they haven't really had to worry about their center depth ever since. This came up again Sunday, with Hainsey leaving in the first-half and Monheim playing well as he played 45% of the offensive snaps.
Monheim stepped in and played well for Hainsey on a few different occasions as a rookie, and the fact he has been so consistent at center should give the Jaguars confidence if Hainsey is out for an extended period of time. There is no update on Hainsey as of this writing, but the Jaguars will survive if they have to start Monheim.
I continue to be impressed by Jaguars safety Antonio Johnson, who looks like he will be a perfect fit next to the rangy Jessie Bates. Johnson is not collecting turnovers at a high clip like he was a year ago, but there is a good case to make that he is playing better now than he has at any other point in his career, and Sunday was another example of it. On a day with great individual performances across the board, Johnson's stood out to me as the most underrated.
Johnson's value to Anthony Campanle's pressure looks and blitz schemes have been clear all season, and he got home once again on a sack of Cam Ward on an important third-down in the second half. But for a defense that had some issues with tackling, Johnson also looked like the team's top player in that category, making several impressive stops in space after the catch. He has been one of their best defenders all season, and Sunday was another example.
I was surprised that we saw barely any Chris Rodriguez Jr. Bhayshul Tuten hasn't been healthy for two weeks now, and he is clearly not running with the same burst that he was even a few weeks ago. Despite that, we have seen Tuten lead the backfield in back-to-back weeks. He was the focal point against the Baltimore Ravens on a short week, while Rodriguez then barely sniffed the field on rushing downs against the Titans. Tuten is clearly hurt, but it is also still very clearly his backfield.
Trevor Lawrence having another stellar game. Lawrence threw three touchdowns, had several huge plays made with his legs, and simply looked like he was on another level tha anything the Titans were throwing at him. The scary thing is that this was all expected. Lawrence’s 352 passing yards were the fourth-most in a single game in his career, and his 120.2 passer rating marked his fourth game this season with a 120-plus rating (tied for the most in the NFL). He also has five games with three or more passing touchdowns, tied for the most in the NFL He is playing like an MVP right now.
James Gladstone. The Jaguars just put up 40 points for the second time in three weeks and this team should be even better moving forward after they added Jessie Bates III and Jordan Davis at the trade deadline. Gladstone has been as aggressive as any general manager in the entire NFL since he was hired, and the fact that the Jaguars can be an even better version of the team we just saw play is a scary thought.…

title: The Jaguars Have a Golden Opportunity to Take AFC South and Run Away With It
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are more than just at top of the AFC South after Week 10. They are all alone, and their neighbors are moving further and further away.
After Sunday's 40-23 win over the Tennessee Titans , the Jaguars are sitting at 7-2 and as one of the best teams in the entire AFC. And thanks to one other key result on Sunday, the Jaguars saw their already-high chances of winning the AFC South for the second-year in a row increase.
It is worth remembering that the Jaguars have never won the AFC South two years in a row. Each time they have won it in recent years, such as 2017 and 2022, they fell on their face afterward. That is why the question all season is whether the Jaguars would prevent themselves from becoming another one-hit wonder after winning the AFC South crown in 2025. So far, they have instead become an AFC powerhouse.
The only real threat to the Jaguars in the AFC South during the Liam Coen era has been the Houston Texans, which is exactly why the Jaguars should be rooting for a Texans loss week in and week out. The Jaguars got exactly their wish with the Texans somehow a 17-0 first-half lead against the Cleveland Browns, losing 27-24 after allowing the Browns to score the game-winning touchdown with 53 seconds left.
According to The Athletic's playoff simulator machine, the Texans now have only a 2% chance to win the AFC South. It is not impossible for the 3-6 Texans to win it, but they are now four games behind a Jaguars team that is now putting up 40 points on the regular. For the Texans to win the AFC South, they would need to win out and then see the Jaguars go 3-5 over their final eight games.
The Jaguars still get to play the Titans again, the Indianapolis Colts, and then winnable games against the New York Giants, Pittsburgh Steelers, Dallas Cowboys, and Washington Commanders, along with an important Week 15 battle with the Texans. That is a schedule the Jaguars should find a few wins in at the very least, but especially so when you consider the way the Jaguars have been playing as of late.
The Jaguars have a +125 point differential this season, best by any team through their first 9 games since the 2021 Bills (+145). It's the second-best point differential through 9 games in franchise history, trailing only the 1999 team that reached the AFC Championship Game… pic.twitter.com/jBPPSHklJh
The Jaguars look like one of the best teams in football; looking like the best team in the AFC South should be what comes at the very minimum. But after the Texans' loss to the Browns, the Jaguars are in a perfect position to run away with the AFC South and secure a top seed in the AFC down the stretch. They have to take care of business in their final three AFC South games later in the season, but their golden opportunity is right there in front of them.
With the Texans still having tough games against the Steelers, Jaguars, and Green Bay Packers, it is looking less and less likely they can go on a run despite a few easier games. But the Jaguars right now look like they have a clear path to another AFC South title, thanks to some help from the Texans along the way.
It isn't over in the AFC South, but Week 10 brought us closer to the end.

title: Game Balls From Jaguars' 40-Burger vs. Titans:  Parker Washington is Leveling Up
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars kept the good times going once again on Sunday, leaving Nashville with an important win over the Tennessee Titans.
The Jaguars were always set to be big favorites against the Titans in Week 10, but that means nothing if you don't finish the job. Finishing the job is exactly what the Jaguars did Sunday, taking the Titans down in a 40-23 win that made it clear they are still quite a bit ahead of the Titans in the AFC South pecking order.
So, who were the Jaguars' best players during their latest big win? We break it down below in this week's game balls.
There were a lot of things to like about Parker Washington's performance against the Titans. Washington had a career-best day in terms of receiving yards, caught a touchdown, and looked every bit the No. 1 receiver who the Jaguars' offense relies on to function. Add in his 50-yard touchdown a week ago, and it is tough to say there are many more explosive playmakers at the receiver position outside of the NFL's elite tier.
Washington finished Sunday with seven catches for 152 yards and a touchdown, giving him the most receiving yards of his career and one of the best outings a Jaguars receiver has had in a game during the Liam Coen era. Washington looks every bit as important to the Jaguars' offense as any player not named Trevor Lawrence, and Week 10 was just the latest example in a near-20 game sample size. Washington looks ready to get paid, and in a big way.
A career day for Parker Washington 👏 🏈 1st Jaguars WR with 145+ Rec yds in a half in the last 11 seasons 🏈 First Jaguars WR with 150+ receiving yards since Week 5 of 2019 🏈 Career-high 6th Rec TD of the season pic.twitter.com/4kifL9RKzK
Washington won at the catch point with ball skills, near the sidelines with coordination and awareness, and after the catch with speed and explosiveness. He can truly do it all as a wide receiver, and that is exactly what he did for the Jaguars on Sunday. The No. 1 wide receiver spot in the Jaguars' offense looks different than other No. 1 spots, and Washington has thrived.
Trevor Lawrence earns consideration after his day, too. Lawrence went 25-of-35 for 352 yards and three touchdowns for a 120.2 passer rating, and he also added 27 yards on four runs. But, as Liam Coen said after the game, Parker Washington was the best player on the field.
I continue to be impressed by what Travis Hunter does for the Jaguars at cornerback, and it does go beyond the big plays he makes in terms of takeaways. It is important to not forget those plays, with Hunter's three interceptions ranking second among AFC cornerbacks. His latest interception might have been his most impressive yet, and it showed exactly why Hunter is considered a blue-chip talent at the cornerback spot.
Hunter did more than just make big plays for the Jaguars in coverage, of course. He also was able to give the Jaguars a physical edge on the perimeter, shutting down several of the Titans' screens and showing off some serious aggressiveness when it came to tackling. Hunter played good football on Sunday once again, and he continues to look like one of the best talents on the entire roster.
Cam Little was 4-of-4 on field goals on Sunday, and he continues to look like a real weapon for the special teams unit. Little made field goals from 46, 48, 36, and 40 on Sunday to ensure the Jaguars never gave up the lead to a Titans team that, to their credit, was fighting for all four quarters. Considering the Jaguars did not build a double-digit lead until there was just under 10- minutes left in the game (which they allowed to be cut to seven points barely a minute later), Little came in clutch for them in what was often a close game.
