title: Raiders Stock Report: Risers & Fallers After Loss to Seahawks
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders entered their Week 10 home matchup against the Seattle Seahawks as a different team than they were last week. After nine games and another loss against a quality opponent that Las Vegas could have competed better against, the trade deadline forced the Raiders' hand.
The Raiders' front office received an offer they could not refuse from the Minnesota Vikings. After using the No. 1 overall pick on Fernando Mendoza, Las Vegas acquired a third-round pick from the Vikings in exchange for Cousins, paving the way for Mendoza's first start.
All eyes were on Las Vegas' rookie in Allegiant Stadium, as the Raiders have long sought a young, talented quarterback with Mendoza's skill set. Those skills have been tucked away on the bench and the practice field this season, up until Sunday, that is.
The Raiders' offense looked competent on Sunday, and they did so early in the game for one of the first times all season. Following a Seahawks turnover, Mendoza led the Raiders on an 11-play, 46-yard touchdown drive, making several plays that wouldn't have been possible previously.
This included an 11-yard touchdown run on third-and-goal that put the Raiders up 7-0 early in the game. Mendoza finished the first half as the team's leading rusher. That literally would never have happened previously.
Offensively, the Raiders played arguably their best first half of the season. Mendoza completed 11 of his 13 first-half passes for 90 yards, leading Las Vegas to a 10-7 lead. The Raiders' offense looked formidable in the first half.
This was the case even when the unit didn't score points. Furthermore, Las Vegas sustained drives significantly better in the first half than it did in recent weeks. It was far from glamorous, but the unit moved the ball better in general.
Las Vegas' defense came to play on Sunday. The unit held the Seahawks to one touchdown in the first half, responding well to the spark their teammates on offense started the game with. Even that touchdown they allowed was a fortunate play for the Seahawks.
The Raiders' defense was one tackle away from holding Seattle scoreless in the first half. After allowing multiple rushers to run for 100 yards in the first half in recent weeks, Las Vegas' defense held the Seahawks to 52 rushing yards in the first half.
Yes, the defense gave up big plays in the second half, but that's after the unit was again left on the field for way too long. In the first half, Las Vegas won the time of possession by nearly nine minutes. Early in the fourth quarter, the Seahawks held the ball for 13 of the second half's first 17 minutes.
Leonard's unit also forced two turnovers, helping keep the team competitive. The unit could have performed better, but today's loss wasn't on the defense .
Both of Las Vegas' safeties made costly mistakes on Sunday. Jeremy Chinn and Treydan Stukes are two of the best defensive backs on the roster. If defenses can successfully complete passes against those two, it is likely to be a long day for the Raiders.
The Raiders have struggled to run the ball long before any of their current running backs were on the roster. Las Vegas has invested heavily in the running back position in each of the last two offseasons. It is unlikely the Raiders whiffed on both players. The reason for the struggles is up front.
The Raiders have changed head coaches, offensive coordinators, running backs, and quarterbacks, yet they struggled to run the ball for the fourth straight season. That was the case on Sunday against the Seahawks , even with Mendoza's runs adding to the total.
The only position group the Raiders have not adequately addressed that impacts their ability to run the ball is the offensive line. Tyler Linderbaum was a solid addition. However, Las Vegas has question marks at every other position on the offensive line.
Kolton Miller has lost a step. Both starting offensive guards are mediocre, at best, regardless of who Las Vegas plays at those positions. DJ Glaze's durability is top-tier, but he still needs further improvement. The Raiders essentially have question marks at three or four offensive line positions.
This has significantly impacted the Raiders' ground game. Through three quarters, Las Vegas had 65 rushing yards. That was not enough to help the Raiders sustain drives in the second half. With four minutes remaining in the fourth quarter, Las Vegas had scored zero points in the second half.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: 3 Instant Reactions to Raiders' Fernando Mendoza's First Start
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders entered their Week 10 matchup against the Seattle Seahawks looking for their first win against a team with a winning record this season. Yet the historical importance of the day did not escape those in attendance.
Of all the issues the Raiders have had in recent seasons, and there have been many, the quarterback position has been the one where Las Vegas has lacked stability the most. The only position with a comparable turnover rate is the head coach position.
Las Vegas' front office addressed both this offseason, hiring Klint Kubiak and Andrew Janocko to lead their revamped offense and drafting Mendoza with the first overall pick. However, through the first half of the season, the trio had yet to work together on the field.
After trading veteran quarterback Kirk Cousins shortly before the trade deadline, that all changed on Sunday. After years of subpar play at the quarterback position, Las Vegas trotted last season's Heisman Trophy winner onto the field. If all goes as planned, he'll be the last for a while.
Las Vegas got off to the perfect start, forcing a turnover on Seattle's first drive. This gave Mendoza a short field on his first drive as a pro. The short field opened up the playbook for Kubiak and Janocko in ways rarely seen this season. It was a methodical, well-planned first drive.
Mendoza and the Raiders' offense marched downfield on an 11-play, 46-yard touchdown drive. Those seven points tied Las Vegas' season-high in first-quarter points, and Mendoza did it on his first drive.  The first drive gave a glimpse of how well the offense can run with Mendoza under center.
Mendoza's mobility and accuracy helped open up Las Vegas' offense directly and indirectly. Mendoza's mobility forced the Seahawks' defense into difficult situations. The possibility of Mendoza moving the pocket or scrambling only made Mendoza's pinpoint accuracy that much more lethal.
For the first time this season, Las Vegas' quarterback put opposing defenses in a similar situation as their own defense in recent weeks. The Raiders' defense has struggled against mobile quarterbacks who throw well on the run or can run well altogether. This time, Las Vegas' opponent had to deal with it.
The Raiders had a chance to score right before halftime but did not. They received the ball first in the second half, and didn't score then either. A score on either drive would have put the Raiders up by multiple possessions. Instead, things went the opposite direction.
Las Vegas did not score a single point in the third quarter and went nearly the entire fourth quarter without scoring. The Raiders followed arguably their best first half of the season against teams with a winning record, with a forgettable second half.
Yes, everyone knows Bowers is one of one. He is undoubtedly the best tight end in the league when healthy. However, things were much more difficult for the Raiders' offense once the Seahawks did not have to worry about him. Bowers missed the second half with an ankle injury.
Las Vegas' offense looked completely out of sorts without Bowers on the field. Not having Bowers on the field changed the flow of the game for the Raiders' offense and, therefore, its defense. Las Vegas' roster is still a work in progress, but they have to figure out how to be productive without Bowers.
That is much easier said than done, especially until the Raiders make additional roster moves in future offseasons. However, for the rest of the 2026 season, Kubiak and Janocko will have to draw up better plays when Bowers is not on the field.
Bowers is a critical part of Las Vegas' offense, but there have to be answers available to the Raiders' coaching staff this season, should he be unavailable.
A loss is a loss, and there are few positives that can come from it. However, the Mendoza got valuable experience on Sunday. The fact that the Raiders kept the game close against a team with a winning record proves they are headed in the right direction.
It was far from pretty, but it was a productive day in the grand scheme of things for Mendoza, Kubiak, and the Raiders.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: Why Win Over Seahawks Could Legitimize Raiders Playoff Aspirations
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders have had a unique season to watch in 2026.
Starting out of the gates hot with a three-game winning streak, everything was looking up for this team. Then a four-game skid followed, and the Raiders currently sit at 4-5 after a win against the New York Jets and a loss to the San Francisco 49ers.
The Raiders are not currently in the playoff picture, but it would only take a few wins for them to enter the conversation. This would be impressive considering it is the first year under Klint Kubiak , with a lack of household names on the roster and a team in its initial rebuilding season.
Las Vegas takes on the reigning Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks this afternoon, a true test for No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza in his first career start. The Seahawks feature one of the NFL's best defenses, so Mendoza would impress the NFL world if he can help them get the win.
Not only would that win get the Raiders to 5-5, but it would also show they have every capability of being a postseason team, despite a rebuild underway.
The Seahawks may not be the force they were last year en route to a Super Bowl victory, but they are still a solid team capable of making the postseason. These are the kinds of teams the Raiders need to beat if they want to have a shot at the playoffs.
While they are still good, there are weaknesses in Seattle. The Seahawks cannot move the ball the same way they did last year (Raiders fans are well aware of why ), and the defense is gettable if the opposing offense finds a rhythm.
The NFL media will be asking whether the Raiders are a legit playoff team if they win this game, which would be an incredible place to be in the middle of November. Raiders fans were rewatching Indiana games from the previous Saturday at this time last year.
The Raiders would sit at 5-5 with a win, and they'd be watching the New England Patriots and Cleveland Browns, hoping for losses so they would have the same record as those teams. There is a chance both those teams lose, considering their opponents, which makes this game that much more important for Las Vegas.
A loss doesn't necessarily knock the Raiders out of contention; they'd still be in the hunt. However, it would more than likely show they aren't ready just yet.
There are no outcomes that would ruin the Raiders' future, so fans shouldn't worry too much about what happens. The upside, however, is too exciting to ignore.
Carter Landis studied journalism at Michigan State University where I graduated in May of 2022. He currently is a sports reporter for a local television station, and is a writer covering the Las Vegas Raiders

title: What Mendoza's Rise to QB1 Means for Kubiak, Raiders Offense
full_text:
After years of subpar play at the quarterback position, the Las Vegas Raiders drafted quarterback Fernando Mendoza with the No. 1 overall pick in this year's draft. The Raiders signed veteran quarterback Kirk Cousins to give Mendoza extra time to develop.
Well, the time has arrived for the Raiders to ensure his development happens on Sundays too, not just during practice. Mendoza brings much of what the Raiders need at quarterback. Now, they hope a half-season of learning from the sideline will pay dividends.
However, just as important as Mendoza starting is the fact that the team is what Mendoza can do for head coach Klint Kubiak and offensive coordinator Andrew Janocko. At 4-5, it was clear that Las Vegas' offense needed more.
Play-action passes are a lot more difficult for defenses to stop when the quarterback is a legitimate threat to leave the pocket or escape an incoming defender. That possibility makes things even more challenging for opposing defenses if the quarterback is an accurate passer.
Cousins was accurate, no doubt. Yet if he did not get the pass off on a play-action pass, it was almost guaranteed to be a sack. Should Mendoza use his legs even marginally, it could open up the play-action pass for the Raiders, which could help them get the ball downfield for more explosive plays.
Imagine a play-action pass where the Raiders' quarterback can be depended upon to make the right read, throw an accurate pass anywhere on the field, or run the ball if nothing is open. You have to imagine it because they have not had a quarterback who can do that in years.
The Raiders' offense has struggled to run the ball for the past three seasons. That will likely be the case even with Mendoza under center for the rest of the season. Las Vegas could still use help at the wide receiver position, and their offensive guard positions are a toss-up on any given Sunday.
Mendoza will go through his growing pains . He will throw interceptions and lose the Raiders a few games as he learns the ropes. The Raiders will need much more than Mendoza to fully turn things around. However, if he plays anywhere close to his potential, Las Vegas is in business.
The unit will still have its issues, but with Mendoza leading the way, Kubiak and offensive coordinator Andrew Janocko no longer have to worry about what throws their quarterback can or cannot make, especially when trying to pass the ball down the field consistently.
With Mendoza at quarterback, Kubiak and the Raiders don't have to throw the whole play away when the quarterback is pressured . They have a quarterback who at least has the potential to run the ball. If Mendoza can successfully use his legs when the time comes, that is another win.
Mendoza's accuracy should get the ball to Las Vegas' pass-catchers. Several of the Raiders' wide receivers have created separation at a high level and have some of the highest win-percentage rates in the league.
They now have a quarterback who can get the ball to receivers before defenses soften up, after shutting down the Raiders' offense for most of the game. The rookie gives Las Vegas a quarterback with a skill set that, on paper, should help the Raiders' play-callers be more successful.
Mendoza should help Las Vegas' offense in ways seen and overlooked. The quarterback touches the ball on every play. In today's NFL, a limited quarterback puts a ceiling on a team. As Mendoza enters the first start of his career, the Raiders' coaching staff simply needs him to do what he does well.
“I think that’s what you want from the coaches you work with and the players you work with, is that there’s no surprises and people are the same all the time,” Kubiak said.
“Obviously, intensity gets notched up, but you want to go see what they’ve done in practice. You want to see how it shows up in the game, and usually it’s those emotionally stable individuals that are able to treat practice and the games the same way.”
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: How Raiders Growing Pains All Part of Promising Plan
full_text:
As the Las Vegas Raiders approach kickoff at Allegiant Stadium against the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks, the growing pains have never been more apparent than in this month-and-a-half stretch.
Las Vegas has played some of the NFL's best teams since early October, losing every game against them while only beating teams with losing records. To face reality, the Raiders are a young group with many flaws hidden by great offensive coaching from head coach and play-caller Klint Kubiak, who faces his former team on Sunday afternoon.
With rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza making his first career start, the growing pains of the 2027 Raiders could continue against a Sam Darnold-less Seahawks team that bolsters the top-ranked defense in the NFL.
These growing pains are frustrating if you're a part of Raider Nation. As a neutral observer, I feel the same way, but this is a part of the process and, as the late Heath Ledger's Joker in The Dark Knight said, "It's all part of the plan." This isn't a sadistic tactic by Kubiak and general manager John Spytek to annoy and gaslight fans; they want to win, and it shows in the effort on the field, but the talent disparity is legit.
Wide receiver, defensive tackle, the secondary, and the offensive line are likely to face a retooling next offseason, but what is important is discovering the young pieces, where they fit, and who the core talents are to maintain. All of those positions lack an elite talent at the moment.
But the mission going forward isn't just to try and tally up a few more wins: it is to evaluate the youth on this roster while working through the growing pains that the players and staff are facing.
There was a learning curve for safety Treydan Stukes after a hot start to his rookie season, but he's begun to find his groove again; rookie cornerbacks Hezekiah Masses and Jermod McCoy have all flashed at some point this season; and right guard Trey Zuhn II has impressed as a starter.
Then there's Mendoza: the golden boy of the franchise. We're finally going to see him in full-time action after the Raiders traded Kirk Cousins back to the Vikings. I'm excited to see the arm talent, mobility, and aggression, if any, from the 2026 No. 1 overall draft pick.
The moral of the story is this: the Raiders are going through the growing pains of a rebuilding organization that is committed and disciplined. However, they're seeing legitimate progress before their eyes. Las Vegas will eventually see it with Mendoza, and if the final product lives up to the hype, special times could arrive in Sin City.

title: What Raiders Defense Must Do To Get Back on Track Against Seattle
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders' defense started the season flying high. The unit showed a remarkable turnaround from last season in its first three games. Then, Las Vegas had a string of games against several of the league's best offenses, and the unit suddenly looked much different.
The talent gap between the opponents the Raiders beat and the teams they lost to couldn't be greater. Las Vegas went from playing the league's worst to the league's best, and won more games in half a season than in all of 2025. Perspective matters, but so does progress.
The conundrum in gauging the Raiders' defense is that in each of their wins, no matter how they looked, the unit made multiple critical plays that won the game or put Las Vegas' offense in an excellent position to do so.
This cannot be discounted, as the Raiders' offense struggled at times in each of their four wins. On the other hand, the unit has had more than a few forgettable performances this season. Across the board, Las Vegas' 4-5 record is accurate for where they stand at this point in the season.
Las Vegas' defense has struggled to get off the field on third down this season, allowing opponents to convert on several critical third-and-long situations. The Raiders' defense has allowed opponents to convert nearly half of their third-down attempts this season.
Through nine games, opposing offenses have gained nearly 30 more first downs against the Raiders' defense than Las Vegas' offense has gained this season. This has naturally left Las Vegas' struggling defense on the field longer than is ideal.
The third-down conversions the unit has allowed have hurt them just as much as their inability to stop the run or the pass for extended periods each week. The unit must correct all three things as soon as possible, as they have been the difference between winning and losing.
“When you’re stacking inconsistent plays, it’s always multiple things. But I’d say fatigue makes cowards of us all. When you’re on the field a long time, mistakes tend to happen more often. We’ll just put it that way," Leonard said earlier this week.
The defense's inability to stop the run, especially in the first half, is another thing the unit has to focus on moving forward. There must be added emphasis on not just stopping the run, but doing so early. If they do so early, it may make teams reconsider running against them.
Las Vegas' cornerbacks were already known to be the unit's weakness. It has been for years. Opposing offenses were always expected to have success through the air against the unit. That is not a surprise.
What is surprising has been the unit's inexplicable first-half performances against the run. There is no way to explain allowing multiple teams to rush for 100 or over 100 yards in the first half alone. Literally any progress against the run, early in games, would be more than the unit has done lately.
Roster-wise, the Raiders' defense is unquestionably an unfinished product. This offseason was the first significant addition of talent. It will likely not be its last. Las Vegas is vulnerable on the interior of its defensive line, but if it can stop the run early, offenses won't be able to attack that weakness.
The Raiders' defense has had its issues this season, most of which were expected when analyzing the roster during the offseason. Yet for a front office that did its due diligence this offseason, the need for development was always a part of the plan for the unit.
Entering the season, the Raiders' defensive needs were largely a gamble the front office knew it was taking. It has not been pretty, but the front office is likely okay with where things stand entering Week 10.
Moving forward, the unit will need all hands on deck to help get things going in the right direction. The roster is what it is right now. It will be up to Leonard and the rest of the coaching staff to find the right buttons to press and plays to call.
“No, all I think about is the guys. I want them to play fast. If anything messes with that, I’m like, ‘Take it out. We won’t do it.’ I want their confidence to be extremely high at all times, so just having conversations in and out with them, and the ultimate vision of what I have we'll get there in time.”
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: 3 Raiders Facing Pressure To Perform Sunday Against Seahawks
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders are looking to get back into the win column, but they'll try to do so against the Seattle Seahawks.
The defending Super Bowl champions haven't been the unstoppable force they were last season en route to a championship, but they are still a team that poses a major threat to the Raiders. Fernando Mendoza battles one of the best defenses in the NFL in his first career start.
For the Raiders to pull off this win, they'll need several players to step up and help Mendoza. Who do they need to have a big game?
Let's break down a few players who they'll need to perform against the Seahawks.
As he gets healthier, Jeanty needs to put up better performances -- especially in Mendoza's first start.
The Raiders will face an elite run defense, and Jeanty hasn't gotten going at all on the ground this season. Las Vegas can't rely on Mike Washington Jr. to carry the rushing attack against this team.
Jeanty was the No. 6 overall pick in 2025, but he hasn't played like it. If there's ever a time for him to turn things around, it's now.
Burford has had some rough moments this season, but he has played better as of late. He faces another tough challenge from the Seahawks' defensive line.
Byron Murphy II is one of the best defensive linemen in the NFL, and Burford will likely see him. If the Raiders want to protect their rookie quarterback and finally break out of their run-game slump, they'll need the interior offensive line, including Burford, to play a nearly flawless game.
The Seahawks have built an identity off winning in the trenches, an area the Raiders have faltered recently. If Las Vegas is going to pull off this home upset, Burford's improved play has to prove to be for real.
The Seahawks have relied on their passing game to score points, so they'll need Chinn to carry a heavy workload on defense.
Jaxon Smith-Njigba is playing like one of the best wide receivers in the NFL, so Chinn must be smart and help his cornerbacks out. He has a 58.9 coverage grade from Pro Football Focus, which is one of the worst marks of his career, and that cannot be the case against this team.
Chinn must be smarter in coverage facing this offense, because if he isn't, they'll get beat downfield and struggle to win the game. A lot rides on Chinn's shoulders.
Carter Landis studied journalism at Michigan State University where I graduated in May of 2022. He currently is a sports reporter for a local television station, and is a writer covering the Las Vegas Raiders

title: Four Losers And Four Winners From Miami's Week 10 Loss
full_text:
The second losing streak of the season reached three games for the Miami Dolphins after they fell against the Indianapolis Colts in a 24-22 thriller (?).
Miami, a team full of rookie talent and an equally young coaching staff, faced off against a Colts team with a gutted roster thanks to multiple trades before the deadline when the organization dumped veteran experience for draft capital. The result is what you'd likely expect: a pretty even contest with plenty of mistakes made by each team.
For the Dolphins, it doesn't get much closer in a loss — literally, they lost by two points. Rookie quarterback Kyle McCord made his NFL debut, but it's clear he wasn't the biggest problem for Miami.
Social media and multiple media outlets, including us, already have credited his performance as being one of the biggest reasons Miami lost this game, and unfortunately for Gonzalez, it's justified.
He might have drilled a 53-yarder in the third quarter, but no one remembers that. Gonzalez missed a pair of field goals — from 47 51 yards out — as well as an extra point after their final touchdown in the fourth quarter. In a game where the Dolphins lost by two points, he was unable to score SEVEN by himself.
This has been a brutal kicker carousel for the Dolphins. Field goals between 40 and 50 yards are becoming automatic for the new wave of kickers in the NFL and college football. For goodness sake, the college football game between Indiana and Minnesota on October 31 featured back-to-back 60-yard field goals. There's no excuse for this to be a recurring issue for Miami.
A player named Malik threw a passing touchdown in this game, except it wasn't the injured quarterback from Liberty. Instead, it was the wide receiver from Virginia who aired the ball out to Jalen Tolbert for a 34-yard score in the second quarter.
Combine that with an efficient day receiving — three targets, three receptions for 50 yards — and Washington showcased his unique versatility to Miami's offense. He and Caleb Douglas combined for 111 receiving yards off six receptions. While the two might not be considered one of the best in football, the wide receiver duo was exactly what McCord needed to count on in his debut.
Entering this game, Indianapolis had one of the worst run defenses in football — 137 yards per game given up, the third-most in the NFL. Despite that, the Dolphins struggled to establish the run from the start, certainly not what McCord wanted to see.
Gordon did all he could with 20 carries and collected 76 yards for his troubles. But Wright? A whopping negative 2 yards on three carries. It feels brutal to say, but he's a magnet for defenders in the backfield. Miami's rookie quarterback managed a better job evading tacklers for 4 yards and a touchdown on the ground.
It's hard to pin this on Wright, but he's technically responsible for injuring backup center Andrew Meyer when he ran into him on a screen pass. Regardless, there needs to be new life in the backfield when Gordon is not in the game, whether it's more snaps for Kaytron Allen or someone else getting an opportunity.
As mentioned earlier, McCord didn't have a running game to fall back on, so it was up to him to move the ball down the field. It wasn't always pretty, but McCord played better than a lot of people thought he would, finishing with 209 yards on 17 completions, along with the aforementioned rushing touchdown.
While he didn't throw an interception, poor ball security led to a fumble when he was sacked by Justin Walley, which turned into a touchdown to start the second half. It was one of those split-second decisions a quarterback has to make — either throw the ball away or hold on and take the sack. In this case, McCord did neither, a fairly common rookie mistake.
But take a step back for a second. McCord still found a way to give the Dolphins an opportunity to win this game by giving Gonzalez two opportunities to do his job. Overall, there's potential for McCord, but it's going to take more than one game to decide whether to let him ride out the season or bring back Willis once he's healthy.
McCord threw to Dulcich a few times in this game. The first was a deep shot in the first quarter that was out of reach. The second was thrown behind him on fourth down after it was tipped at the line of scrimmage, turning the ball over to the Colts. Lastly, an incomplete pass on the two-point attempt to begin the final quarter.
Miami played a clean game of football with three penalties, but one of them was a false start on Dulcich on their opening drive. Considering the struggles of the Colts' defense going into this game (with no exception to tight end coverage), it was disappointing to see Dulcich be this ineffective.
Johnson was an automatic "no thank you" for Daniel Jones when deciding where to throw the football. He was targeted twice in this game, denying a single reception on either opportunity. When he wasn't doing that, he was playing cleanup duty with four tackles, a TFL, and a pass deflection.
However, his highlight for the day was his interception in the third quarter, then returning it 59 yards for a touchdown. Miami was down by 11 before that play, and the Dolphins remained within reach of the lead for the rest of the game. Johnson has been red-hot since the Chiefs loss, allowing less than 25 yards in coverage in all but two games — Detroit (39) and the New York Jets. (127)
Miami's defense was reeling from the loss of Zach Sieler, and it didn't get any better with Zeek Biggers and Jordan Phillips getting hurt as well. Rodriguez had more pressure on his plate to deliver as a result, but aside from one tackle on Jonathan Taylor at the line of scrimmage, he didn't make a noticeable impact.
The Colts, to their credit, found ways to take him out of the play, either targeting opposite sides of the field or sending additional blockers to make him a non-factor. Hopefully, Rodriguez can bounce back against Buffalo on November 22 and return to DROTY status, because with how hurt the defense currently is, it looks grim with Josh Allen and James Cook around the corner.
The season may have started ugly for Chop, but he has slowly turned into one of the best pass rushers Miami has to offer. He did a bit of everything against Indianapolis, with six pressures, five tackles, a sack, and two QB hits. His effectiveness at stopping Jonathan Taylor, considered one of the best backs in football, should not go unnoticed.
Just like that, Robinson has already passed his sack total from last season with eight games to go. If he can bring it home, it'll be one of the best comeback stories for the Dolphins after the way he regressed in 2025. Just like with Rodriguez, Miami will need him to keep it up with matchups against Buffalo, Denver and Chicago on the horizon.

title: Five Instant Overreactions to the Dolphins-Colts Matchup
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins fought back late, but ultimately couldn't pull out a win against the Colts, falling 24 to 22. Let's overreact to this Week 10 matchup, where Miami once again lost in key moments.
The Dolphins’ kicking game was at DEFCON 1 over a month ago, and every week since then has just made things more embarrassing. Zane Gonzalez, who has missed field goals in each of the last two weeks, missed another two today, along with a PAT.
Entering this game, Miami was bottom eight in field goal and extra point percentage, and that only got worse against the Colts. It’s clear that wholesale changes are necessary, but on a week-to-week basis, it might be time to take extreme measures.
At this point, outside of obvious field-goal situations, it might be in Miami’s best interest to try a new strategy, either being more aggressive with fourth down decision-making or playing the field-position game and punting deeper into enemy territory. Their special teams unit has done nothing to inspire confidence, and it may be time to take the ball out of the hands of their kicker.
Two of the coolest highlight plays of the week came courtesy of third-year receiver Malik Washington. Early on, he caught a backwards pass, and lofted the ball down the field right into the hands of Jalen Tolbert for a 34-yard touchdown. Then, he made a stellar one-handed catch on a pass that Kyle McCord floated into the area of several Colts defenders.
Washington’s growth has been one of the few bright spots for Miami’s offense in 2026. His route-running has improved, and with increased opportunity, he’s produced his fair share of standout reps. He should be one of the focal points of Miami’s offense in the weeks (and potentially years) to come, and it’s in Bobby Slowik’s best interest to find ways to get the ball in his hands.
The highlights of individual performances have overshadowed the truth: this group hasn’t been good enough. Yes, Paul, Proctor and Brewer (who missed this game) have all flashed, but neither Jonah Savaiinaea nor Austin Jackson have solidified themselves as unquestioned, and consistency from all five spots has been questionable.
This game, without Brewer, was much of the same. Ollie Gordon had 76 yards on 20 carries , and Kyle McCord faced immediate pressure in crucial situations. Some of that, naturally, falls on the protection-adjustment skills of a backup quarterback and center, but performance hasn’t been nearly good enough.
Miami's interior defensive line bears a significant amount of blame in this one. In their first game without Zach Sieler, the Dolphins allowed 172 rushing yards, with both Jonathan Taylor and Seth McGowan averaging over 5 yards per carry.
The pass rush was slightly better, pressuring Daniel Jones on his two interceptions. However, they only finished the game with one sack. The trio of Kenneth Grant, Jordan Phillips and Zeek Biggers (who left this game early) still have plenty of room to develop, and without their leader, they become easier to exploit.
As has been said after just about every game Miami has played, the rookies stood out in this one. Caleb Douglas made multiple stellar catches, DJ Herman created displacement on a few blocks, and Michael Taaffe and Chris Johnson both recorded interceptions.
For the first time in years, the Dolphins have drafted a class of players that truly look like core contributors for the foreseeable future. This roster was (and largely still is) bereft of talent, but this infusion will pay dividends if they can continue to develop.
Tyler DeSena is currently a journalism student at the University of Central Florida. Prior to joining Dolphins On SI in 2026, DeSena worked with dolphinstalk.com, and created independent social media content on X, YouTube and TikTok.

title: Miami Dolphins Week 10 Instant Takeaways: Dolphins Should Kick Themselves for Missed Opportunity
full_text:
In this season where wins have to hard to come by for the Miami Dolphins, they really let one slip away against the Indianapolis Colts in Week 10.
We might even suggest they should be kicking themselves for not being able to beat a reeling Colts team that's not only bad but was down their top three cornerbacks in the second half.
Kicking themselves ... get it?
If you're among those who believe the Dolphins are tanking, organically or ethically or otherwise, then what happened at Lucas Oil Stadium was perfect because Zane Gonzalez really doesn't fit into the team's long-term plans, so him missing three kicks isn't damaging for the future of the organization.
If the Dolphins are trying to win games as part of establishing a foundation and some belief, then we'll repeat what we said last week, that the Dolphins absolutely need to move on from him.
That's the biggest and most obvious takeaway from this game, which was all about quarterback Kyle McCord and his NFL debut.
As expected, it was an uneven performance by McCord, with some good and some bad.
The good included his touchdown run on a QB keeper and a couple of nice throws, but he also didn't do anything to suggest that Malik Willis is the one who's been the problem on offense.
The biggest negative, of course, was the sack he took that turned into a Colts touchdown when he fumbled. McCord very clearly saw the free blitzer early in the play and wasn't anywhere near quick enough to get away from the pocket and put himself in position to throw the ball away. And at worst, he should have been able to protect the ball even if he needed to take the sack, and that was a clear rookie mistake that showed a lack of awareness.
The bottom line is his performance should have been good enough to help the Dolphins win against a very bad Indy team.
Instead, the Dolphins dropped to 1-8 on the season as they continue to look like a team headed for a top 3 picks at worst and maybe with a shot at the first overall pick.
-- As an indication of how depleted the Colts are, former Dolphins WR Nick Westbrook-Ikhine was signed from the practice squad to the 53-man roster and promptly let the first third-down pass go right through his hands. Later in the game, he was flagged for offensive pass interference and he finished with zero catches.
-- Pretty amazing (and not in a good way) that barely after the CBS analyst says the Dolphins need to avoid pre-snap penalties that Greg Dulcich gets flagged for a false start. Oy. Outside of that, though, the Dolphins played a relatively clean game with three penalties for 30 yards. Indy, on the other hand, was flagged 13 times for 83 yards, including a defensive holding that nullified a pick-six that might have sealed the outcome early in the fourth quarter instead of the Dolphins have a shot at the end.
-- Of course, it would have been nice had the Dolphins bothered to block linebacker C.J. Allen instead of letting him run free on a blitz between Kadyn Proctor and Patrick Paul, though we don't know for sure who's to blame there.
-- One thing that stood out with McCord is he sure got quite a few passes batted down at the line of scrimmage, including the final failed fourth-down attempt. Though it looked like intended receiver Kevin Coleman Jr. was surrounded at the 35-yard line when he needed to get to the Colts 32.
-- McCord banging his thumb on a helmet following through early in the game was  the last thing you wanted to see happen. But that is going to happen with all the penetration the Dolphins offensive line usually allows.
-- This may come as a surprise to some fans, but Dolphins receivers in the first half weren't getting any more open with McCord at QB than they did with Malik Willis.
-- In addition to continuing his strong run as a pass rusher, including a sack with a nice bull rush, Chop Robinson had maybe the best run stop we've ever seen from him against Jonathan Taylor.
-- Already missing Zach Sieler, the Dolphins really didn't need to have Zeek Biggers leave the game with a knee injury. That the run defense struggled probably was not a coincidence. And then to make matters worse, Jordan Phillips suffered an arm injury. Ugh.
-- Big performance by Malik Washington doing a little bit of everything, including his TD pass to Jalen Tolbert off a double pass. First Dolphins TD pass by a non-quarterback since, yes again, Mountaineer Shot, the Matt Haack throw to Jason Sanders against the Eagles in 2019. Great call, nice throw by  Washington.
-- Great catch by Michael Taaffe on his third pick of the season, though someone could point out he cost the Dolphins 6 yards because this was going to be a fourth-down incompletion. It's not very significant in terms of lost yardage, but we hope the Dolphins don't do the same thing if we're talking about 20 or 30 yards.
-- DJ Herman has made a couple of really nice lead blocks already in this game. Also was the recipient of Kyle McCord's first NFL completion.
-- Truly amazing that every time Jaylen Wright gets a carry, there is major penetration from the defensive line and he almost invariably gets hit in the backfield. At this point, it's almost laughable.
-- Zero issue with the Dolphins going for it on fourth-and-2 in the first half ... regardless of the result. It's an evaluation season. Shame a good drive ended without points, but the point remains.
--  Don't know what was better, Chris Johnson's pick-six or the touchdown celebration. And, of course, Gonzalez misses the PAT. Doesn't matter actually because Johnson is going to be a good player for a while and Gonzalez might be gone this week (maybe).
-- Not to take anything away from a great Dolphins defensive series in the fourth quarter, but it’s pretty easy to see why the Colts are 2-7 (2-14 over their last 16).
-- I'm going to go ahead and say it, Dolphins receivers made more good catches for Kyle McCord in this game than they have for Malik Willis all season.
-- Jordyn Brooks was really, really good and it's time to acknowledge that for all the accolades Jacob Rodriguez has been getting for his strong rookie season, he's the best linebacker on the team and probably the best player overall.

title: From Beck to Brady: Trying to Predict Where Dolphins QB Kyle McCord's Debut Will Fall
full_text:
Not sure if you've heard, but first-year quarterback Kyle McCord will make his NFL debut for the Miami Dolphins against the Indianapolis Colts on Sunday.
Of course you knew that, it's been the topic of conversation since the Dolphins placed starter Malik Willis on injured reserve Tuesday with what now is being described as a core muscle injury.
The Dolphins offense struggled for most of the first eight games of the season because of a wide variety of issues and the question is whether McCord can bring some life to it.
This is an exciting time for some fans quick with an evaluation that Willis simply isn't the long-term answer at quarterback for the Dolphins based mostly on the results and what they've seen as Willis' hesitation in the pocket and too-slow decision-making.
It's been a saying for a long time that the backup quarterback often is the most popular player on the team if you don't have a star at the position because the unknown brings hope of something better.
But, of course, the grass isn't always greener ... and if the backup was better than the starter, then maybe he wouldn't be the backup.
That brings us to McCord, who is an unknown as a quarterback can be because he's never played a down in the NFL. Yes, he looked good in Green Bay's preseason finale against Arizona this summer, but that was the preseason and that's nothing like a regular season game because defensive coaches keep things very simple for those games and pull out all the stops for games that count.
McCord is a different type of quarterback than Willis, and maybe he'll be quicker with his decisions and let it rip more freely, and maybe that produces more completions but maybe that also produces more throws into traffic with a bad outcome and maybe an interception or two more.
Head coach Jeff Hafley said he would encourage McCord to be aggressive, but any rookie making his first start is bound to have some hesitation. That's just natural.
The bigger issue for McCord is that the Dolphins supporting cast, which everyone can acknowledge is sub-par, didn't get any better over the past week. On the contrary, McCord now will have to play without starting center Aaron Brewer and rookie wide receiver Chris Bell.
So what do the Dolphins have in Kyle McCord? And what might it first NFL look like?
For some fans, the idea is that maybe he becomes for the Dolphins what Brock Purdy became for the San Francisco 49ers after taking over for the injured Jimmy Garoppolo late in his rookie season — against the Dolphins no less.
We also saw — pretty sure we saw — a reference to another former sixth-round pick taking over for an injured starter in his second season and never let go of the job. You know, Tom Brady?
The other end, of course, is McCord turning into former Dolphins second-round pick John Beck, who flamed out after getting his first NFL start in October 2007.
Beck was a poor 9-for-22 for 106 yards in his first NFL start in a 17-7 loss against the Eagles.
Even Brady's first start was pretty mundane in terms of stat, as he went 13-for-23 for 168 yards with no touchdowns or picks, though it did come in a 44-13 Patriots win against Peyton Manning and the Colts when the defense dominated.
We certainly have no reason to expect that kind of dominance from the Dolphins against the Colts today, even if Peyton Manning isn't playing anymore.
We would suspect, however, that McCord's stat line will look more like that of Brady than that of Beck.
It's a guess as to what McCord actually will look like again because judging his work at Ohio State and Syracuse and in the preseason — his stats were uninspiring last year with Philadelphia and this year with Green Bay before that finale — though he does look the part.
A best guess from here in terms of what his stats will look like would be something like 15-for-27 for 189 yards with one touchdown and one pick.

title: Dolphins Sunday Mailbag: Grant, Uche, Jonah, and More
full_text:
Part 2 of the pre-Colts game Miami Dolphins On SI mailbag:
Hi Alain, with Uche getting huge backing being named a captain, what sort of deal do you expect? This is Grant's chance; should we have high expectations of him finally living up to his draft status? A loss is a win on Sunday considering the Jets have their pick … thoughts? Thanks
Hey Colin, let’s begin with the idea that Josh Uche absolutely deserves a contract extension after the way his season has started, and how he finishes will determine what kind of contract he might get. I don’t know it will be big money regardless, but maybe a second year gets tacked on. As for Grant, yes, this absolutely is a big moment for him because he’s going to get additional snaps and he’s further removed from the foot injury that cost him the start of the season. He needs to show something, period. As far as the game and the draft, the Colts don’t have that extra incentive — if any team were so inclined — to lose because their 2027 first-round pick belongs to the Jets.
From Damian from Pittsburgh:
Hi Mr. P! Greetings from Pittsburgh. Hope all is well, and your holiday plans are coming into focus. Thinking about the OLine, specifically the disappointing right side. Jackson is a lost cause; even setting aside the injuries, he's a below-average RT. Not quite a bust, but way overdrafted. I'm more interested in Jonah, and if he's salvageable. Is he gonna come around? And what if MIA swapped him to LG? Put him between two strong OLineman, and pop Proctor over to the right side (guard or tackle). Thoughts?
Hey Damian, Jackson has been a solid starter for most of his career, though, yes, absolutely overdrafted. With Jonah, no, I would not advocate switching him back to the left side. At some point, he’s got to make it work on his own. The good news with him is he’s definitely better than he was as a rookie, though there still are some holes in his game, particularly in pass protection.
Hi Alain, good to see the Dolphins defense contain Goff and the Lions last week. It made me wonder about your thoughts on Hafley’s defensive philosophy and his tree. My understanding is that he runs a scheme similar to Fangio’s but from what I can tell, he never worked with Vic. Do you have any insights on his defensive influence, and how you feel about his coaching overall at the halfway mark of the season?
Hey Daniel, I’d say overall I’ve been very impressed by Hafley in terms of getting his players ready to play and I like his defensive scheme and how it’s progressed throughout this season. The inspiration for his defense come from the Pete Carroll scheme with the Seattle Seahawks and also from working with Robert Saleh when the two were assistants with the San Francisco 49ers. My only complaint with Hafley is I’d like to see him be a more aggressive in fourth-down decisions, but that’s being picky because I do think he’s off to a very good start.
Hi Alain. Great work as always. Any idea how much a GM considers a draftees age as part of the evaluation process prior to drafting? As a for instance and considering two recently drafted Dolphins players, Chop has played 39 NFL games vs. Jacob’s 8 with Chop being 4 months younger. I appreciate that a longer college career could mean a more developed player coming out and possibly maturity issues but considering wear and tear long term, I would assume if the potential is seen to be there a younger prospect is seen as a big bonus. Thanks again for the fantastic, objective  reporting.
Thanks Lee, appreciate the kind of words. As you indicated, an older prospect logically gives you a more mature, more polished draft pick, while the younger prospect might have a longer shelf life. But the reality is a GM won’t be thinking 8-9 years down the road, so the longevity issue takes a back seat to getting somebody more ready to contribute quickly. So if everything else is equal, particularly in terms of ceiling, a GM likely will go with the older prospect who’s going a better chance to help out right away.
Greetings Alain ! After the Colts started their own rebuild, I thought Miami had a good chance to win. But now the Dolphins have a QB who has never thrown a pass in a real NFL game & in a hostile environment. While they may have traded best their best D-lineman, they still have Sauce Garder & Charvarius Ward vs rookie WRs plus Lou Anarumo, who can confuse a young QB. They still have Jonathan Taylor vs a Miami DL without Zach Sieler. Not to mention a terrible Special Teams unit. As the late, great Dick Enberg used to say, "Oh my!" Do we see a heavy dose of Ollie Gordon ? A lot of check-down passes ? As always, I look forward to both All Dolphins (appreciate the shout-out, doing much better) & Dolphins Collective podcasts plus all the best out there written content on Miami DolphinsonSI.Com.
Thanks Dave, it’s a pretty good assessment of the game you had right there, and a heavy dose of Ollie Gordon II and check-downs absolutely is a logical thing to expect, simply to make Kyle McCord’s NFL debut as simple as possible.
If McCord goes 2-2 and plays well, does Willis return as starter?
Jeff Hafley already has said that Willis will be the starter once he returns, and it’s exactly what Hafley should have said but with the understanding that if McCord lights it up, then he’ll have every right to reconsider that stance. And it’s not going to be about whether the Dolphins win or lose, but rather how McCord performs. But it would have to be a really impressie performance to just shelve Willis like that.
Not a game question, but I read things about Miami’s team needs, I see lots of positions of need but it’s almost as if WR is being considered not a need. This is one of the worst rooms in football, even if Douglas is somewhat OK. Do you think they still need upgrades there, Alain?
Oh, without question. What the Dolphins have at wide receiver is a lot of potential with Douglas, Chris Bell and Kevin Coleman Jr., but only Douglas should be locked in for a big role in 2027, along with Malik Washington. So, yeah, that group still could use some help,  which is why so many fans like the idea of taking Jeremiah Smith if the Dolphins have the chance.

title: Breaking Down the Dolphins Saturday Updates for the Indianapolis Game
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins made the expected moves Saturday ahead of their Week 10 game against the Indianapolis Colts, but they still have an opening to be filled at some point.
The Dolphins announced early Saturday afternoon they had signed kicker Zane Gonzalez to the 53-man roster off the practice squad, along with elevating quarterback Brady Cook and wide receiver Jalen Reagor.
Head coach Jeff Hafley already had indicated earlier this week the team would be signing Gonzalez to the active roster, which was the only way he could kick again for Miami this season after exhausting his three allowed elevations.
The move can be questioned based on Gonzalez missed a field goal each of the past two games, although special teams coordinator Chris Tabor said Thursday the miss against the New England in Week 8 was more about the whole operation than a Gonzalez mistake.
"I think he's a good player," Tabor said. "I think he's a player that, yes, he missed a kick he should have made. We can all agree about that and Zane would too. In my eyes, that's kind of his first miss. I know on stats that it's two, sometimes there's other things that go on. I'm just not really, I'm not a guy that just pushes players away. He's been on the street for six weeks, seven weeks, and this was his third week back, so I think that he's still working to get to where he needs to be, right? I got a lot of confidence in him and we're working hard at getting better. I look forward to watching him kick this weekend. I got a lot of confidence in him, and it's real easy for me."
The signing of Gonzalez put the Dolphins at 52 players on the active roster after the moves this week that saw QB Malik Willis and DT Zach Sieler go on injured reserve, CB Reese Taylor getting waived, and DT Keith Cooper Jr. signed off the Carolina Panthers practice squad.
Cook was on the active roster earlier this season before being waived and re-signed to the practice squad, and he seemed like a logical choice to be re-signed to the 53 if he's going to back up new starter Kyle McCord for the next four games while Willis is on IR. Technically, the Dolphins don't have to make that decision until after Cook has been elevated three times, which woud come after the Week 12 game against the New York Jets.
Reagor being elevated would seem to indicate that wide receiver Chris Bell indeed will be inactive after being listed as doubtful on the final injury report of the week with a knee injury that kept him out of practice Thursday and Friday.
Along with potentially getting snaps at wide receiver, Reagor also becomes an option to return punts and/or kickoffs.
Bell will be joining Jalen Wayne, who was ruled out Friday, on the inactive list. Reagor will join Malik Washington, Caleb Douglas, Kevin Coleman Jr. and Jalen Tolbert on the game-day roster.
Lastly, as expected, the Dolphins didn't activate cornerback Darrell Baker Jr. off PUP and officially was downgraded to out on the injury report.
The Colts' own series of moves was highlighted by defensive end Arden Key being activated off injured reserve. Dolphins fans should remember Key as the player flagged for a roughing penalty on the famous "Facemask Pass" by Ryan Fitzpatrick against the Las Vegas in December 2020.
The Dolphins also signed LB West Weeks off their practice squad to their 53-man roster, and placed  TE Mo Alie-Cox and LB Akeem Davis-Gaither on IR.
Lastly, the Colts elevated LS Jacob Bobenmoyer and WR Quez Watkins to the active roster from the practice squad.

title: Dolphins-Colts Game Preview and Predictions: Can Miami Overcome Injuries?
full_text:
For a change, the Miami Dolphins are given a chance by more than just one or two national media members heading into their Week 10 game against the Indianapolis Colts — and that's despite the injury to starting quarterback Malik Willis.
The Dolphins will go into the game with a 1-7 record but after giving playoff contenders New England and Detroit a battle before losing at Hard Rock Stadium the past two weeks.
That, of course, with quarterback Malik Willis and standout defensive lineman Zach Sieler in the lineup, with both now on injured reserve. The Colts also have their issues, having traded four veterans — Quenton Nelson, DeForrest Buckner, Keenan Allen and Josh Downs — in the midst of a wildly disappointing season that's already seen GM Chris Ballard lose his job.
The Colts did retain star running back Jonathan Taylor and veteran defensive tackle Grove Stewart, who had been rumored to be on the move, and it's not like they're playing for draft position since their 2027 first-round pick belongs to the New York Jets as the result of the Sauce Gardner trade that keeps looking worse every day.
Indianapolis is favored by 3.5 points, according to the Fan Duel Sportsbook .
This is the second consecutive year the teams will face each other, the 2025 meeting coming in the season opener when the Colts humbled the Dolphins, 33-8, in a game that set the stage for Miami's disappointing 7-10 season that produced the regime change and rebuilding project that's going on right now.
That season-opening win was part of a fantastic start for the Colts, who once were 8-2 and very much looking like legit AFC contenders. The bottom then fell out and it hasn't stopped falling out, Indianapolis losing 14 of its past 16 games going back to last November 23.
This is why the Dolphins are being given a chance — even predicted by some — to win the game Sunday despite having a quarterback on his third team in two years ready to play his first real NFL snaps.
The Colts gave Dallas all it could handle last week before losing in overtime, and they may benefit from the uncertainty of their roster being done now that the NFL trade deadline has passed.
From this end, it's just difficult to give the Dolphins the nod here with an unproven quarterback who will have to work with the same subpar supporting cast that's hampered Willis so far this season, and without Aaron Brewer out on top of everyhing.
The Dolphins defense probably will be able to keep the score close, but we'd still call it something like 20-10 for the Colts.

title: The One (Tight End) That Got Away from the Dolphins
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins have looked to build up their tight end room in 2026 and currently feature three rookies at that position.
Against that backdrop, one would think there was more than a little bit of remorse in watching Elijah Higgins sign a contract extension with the Arizona Cardinals on Friday.
The Dolphins haven't often watched a late-round draft pick they cut as a rookie go on to have success with another team, but it's clearly what's happened with Higgins
You remember Elijah Higgins, right? The Dolphins drafted him as a wide receiver out of Stanford in the sixth round of the 2023 draft with the idea of making him a tight end, but ended up cutting him in the moves to the 53-player limit.
The Cardinals claimed him off waivers and he's gone on to make himself a nice career as the backup to starting tight end Trey McBride, sometimes starting in two-tight end sets as well.
The Dolphins kept three tight ends that year — Durham Smythe, rookie free agent Julian Hill and veteran Tyler Kroft. The latter played eight games that season, mostly on special teams, and didn't catch a pass all year.
His would be his final NFL season, and it's pretty obvious by now that the Dolphins messed up by not keeping Higgins instead of Kroft given what we know now.
Clearly, the Dolphins didn't do a great evaluation job on Higgins.
What made it more painful is that the Dolphins had only four draft picks that year, the result of the trades that brought Tyreek Hill, Bradley Chubb and Jalen Ramsey, as well as the tampering violation that cost Miami a first-round pick.
The other three picks that year were CB Cam Smith, RB De'Von Achane and T Ryan Hayes, and obviously only Achane has panned out.
Interestingly, Higgins was drafted after fellow tight end Hunter Long was included in that Ramsey trade that also cost the Dolphins a third-round pick.
The Dolphins went the veteran route at tight end the past two years with Jonnu Smith in 2024 and Darren Waller last year, but now their most grizzled player at the position is Greg Dulcich, who is only 26 and in his fifth NFL season.
Having a lot of youth at the position is fine, and maybe Will Kacmarek, Seydou Traore and Justin Joly all will go from intriguing rookies in 2026 to significant contributions sooner rather than later, but clearly the Dolphins could have used Higgins the past couple of years and into next season.
The case with Higgins is interesting because if you take a look at late-round picks (say, sixth or seventh round) that the Dolphins have cut, it's extraordinarily rare to see somebody go on to succeed with a second team.
That clearly happened with Higgins.

title: Tale of the Tape: How Kyle McCord Compares to Former Dolphins Backup QBs Heading Into Their First Start
full_text:
Ready or not, and the Miami Dolphins believe and hope he is, Kyle McCord is going to make his NFL debut Sunday.
There are some tough circumstances for the first-year player from Syracuse, most notably the absence of center Aaron Brewer to go along with that of IR'ed star running back De'Von Achane.
On the flip side, McCord will be going against an Indianapolis Colts team in the midst of a lost season, with a 2-7 record and four veterans traded away before or at the NFL trade deadline.
In that sense, let's just say the timing is better than if McCord's first start for the Dolphins after arriving as a trade acquisition over the summer had come next Sunday when Miami is scheduled to face the Buffalo Bills at Highmark Stadium.
So how challenging is the task facing McCord, combining his lack of experience — shoot, his lack of any NFL regular season snaps — the team he'll be leading and the opponent? And how does it compare to the other instances over the past 10 years when the Dolphins have had to turn to their backup quarterback because of injuries?
Kyle McCord, 2026, Week 10 — Trade acquisition, first-year player, replacing starter Malik Willis against the 2-7 Indianapolis Colts
Analysis: The supporting cast performance was an issue for Willis when he was in the lineup, and that was before Brewer and WR Chris Bell were sidelined with injuries.
Quinn Ewers, 2025, Week 16 — Rookie seventh-round pick, replacing starter Tua Tagovailoa for 7-8 Dolphins against the 5-9 Cincinnati Bengals, was 20-for-30 for 260 yards with 0 TD, 2 INT and a 66.0 passer rating in a 45-21 loss
Analysis: What made things easier for Ewers was that the Dolphins already had been mathematically eliminated from playoff contention and he had gotten some game action before.
Tyler Huntley, 2024, Week 4 — Veteran free agent signing, replacing backup Skylar Thompson for 1-2 Dolphins against the 0-3 Tennessee Titans, was 14-for-22 for 96 yards with 0 TD, 0 INT and a 73.3 passer rating in a 31-12 loss
Analysis: The tough part for Huntley was that he really wasn't a great scheme fit for Mike McDaniel's offense, though he did have prior starting experience with Baltimore.
Skylar Thompson, 2022, Week 6 — Rookie seventh-round pick, replacing backup Teddy Bridgewater for 3-2 Dolphins against the 4-1 Minnesota Vikings, was 7-for-13 for 89 yards with 0 TD, 0 INT and a 75.5 passer rating before leaving with an injury in a 24-16 loss
Analysis: While the matchup was tough, Thompson basically had played the whole previous game after Teddy Bridgewater's exit after one play.
Teddy Bridgewater, 2022, Week 4 — Veteran free agent signing, replacing starter Tua Tagovailoa for the 3-1 Dolphins against the 2-2 New York Jets, was 0-for-1 before leaving with an injury in a 40-17 loss
Analysis: Bridgewater was in a good position to succeed in this one, even though he fell victim to the NFL's new zealousness about not missing concussion possibilities.
Jacoby Brissett, 2021, Week 3 — Veteran free agent signing, replacing starter Tua Tagovailoa for the 1-1 Dolphins against the 2-0 Las Vegas Raiders, was 32-for-49 for 215 yards with 0 TD, 0 INT and a 74.8 passer rating in a 31-28 overtime loss
Analysis: Brissett had starting experience, but this was against a good opponent.
Ryan Fitzpatrick, 2020, Week 12 — Veteran free agent signing in 2019, replacing starter Tua Tagovailoa for the 6-4 Dolphins against the 0-10 New York Jets, was 24-for-39 for 257 yards, with 2 TD, 0 INT and a 97.9 passer rating in a 20-3 victory
Analysis: Fitzpatrick had started the first six games of the regular season that year before giving way to first-round pick Tua Tagovailoa, so we might even be messing with semantics in calling him a backup here.
Brock Osweiler, 2018, Week 6 — Veteran free agent signing, replacing starter Ryan Tannehill for the 3-2 Dolphins against the 3-1 Chicago Bears, was 28-for-44 for 380 yards, with 3 TD, 2 INT and a 94.9 passer rating in a 31-28 overtime victory
Analysis: Osweiler had 25 career starts before this game, though this was a tough matchup for Miami.
Matt Moore, 2017, Week 8 — Veteran free agent signing in 2011, replacing starter Jay Cutler for the 4-2 Dolphins against the 3-4 Baltimore Ravens, was 25-for-44 for 176 yards, with 0 TD, 2 INT and a 47.2 passer rating in a 40-0 loss
Analysis: Though that Thursday night game turned into a horror show for the Dolphins, Moore was in a good spot beforehand with a lot of starting experience.
Matt Moore, 2016, Week 15 — Veteran free agent signing in 2011, replacing starter Ryan Tannehill for the 8-5 Dolphins against the 4-9 New York Jets, was 12-for-18 for 236 yards, with 4 TD, 1 INT and a 126.2 passer rating in a 34-13 victory
Analysis: This was a great spot for Moore, who had closed out a big overtime win against the Arizona Cardinals the previous week.

title: What Dolphins Teammates and Coaches Said About Kyle McCord Ahead of his First NFL Start
full_text:
The big storyline for the Miami Dolphins for their Week 10 matchup against the Indianapolis Colts obviously will be the NFL debut of quarterback Kyle McCord.
Less than three months after being acquired in a trade with the Green Bay Packers, McCord will start in place of Malik Willis after Willis landed on injured reserve with a core muscle injury.
Naturally, McCord was the big topic of conversation in interviews this week, with teammates and coaches offering their thoughts from different angles, from head coach Jeff Hafley to center Andrew Meyer, who likely will be making his first start of the season as well with Aaron Brewer dealing with a concussion.
"Good. I say that – he's mostly had the look team reps. He's done a good job in the look team reps that he's given us. The developmental periods that we have, I mean, it's why we do it, right? So say he's gotten 10 to 15 reps over the last 10 weeks, it's 100 reps of our plays. So he's done a good job in those periods. But it's going to be a lot different. I mean, him now being the starter and getting the game plan and playing every down and playing with a live rush and going through a real football game. So I'm excited to see what he can do. It opens a great opportunity for him and I'm happy that he'll get his chance."
"I mean, it's kind of the same as – we've had these discussions as we've gone through the year. We lost De’Von (Achane). I know we had the same conversation about, how's the run game change? Everybody that's in this building is in this building because we think they can run our offense and they can run our offense really well. I think there's things that make Malik different and special, like he can use his legs and he's got legit speed that no offense to Kyle, but Kyle doesn't have 23 miles an hour on the GPS in his body. So that's going to change how he approaches the game. But there's things we do in the pass game and the run game that he can handle and he likes doing and he excels at. So it's not going to change all that much. Probably just going to be things that are less running down the field."
"I think the biggest thing when you watch him play, he's a good processor. He sees the field well. He processes information well. He's really good in and out of the huddle. You know the simple things that a quarterback needs to do, he does well. He's a tough kid. I mean, obviously when he was in Philly, he's playing in preseason games at the end, taking a beating. He got up, kept playing, which is obviously impressive. And I think when you just look at the way he carries himself, he's very professional. The guys gravitate around him. Around him, you can see their energy, his energy. He's kind of a quieter guy, but he's got some swag to him, which is obviously important in that position."
"I think he's got good poise. I know we've thrown some different things at him. Apparently last week we probably practiced a lot of twists. But I think he's got good poise. I'm excited to see him. Just like I'm excited to see a lot of guys that have an opportunity this Sunday."
"I think that it helps a lot. I mean obviously we've built a chemistry in there between just the snap exchanges, stuff like that and we have a really good relationship so I think that it's comforting for sure like just knowing like that we've both gotten a lot of snaps together. Knowing that that's who I'm going to be out there with, it's definitely a little comforting."
"Me and Kyle have been building a great chemistry, caught enough balls. Ready to go out there on Sunday and compete."
"I mean, I think that's something that you definitely can hang your hat on. Being at a school like Ohio State and then playing some big games at Syracuse too, I think should give you confidence that you’ve played on a big stage before, you’ve played against some of the top guys in the league right now. So I think the confidence level coming from those games is definitely there."

title: Expanding Myles Price’s Role Will Be in Vikings' Best Interest Moving Forward
full_text:
Week 10 sent the Vikings to Green Bay to face off against the Packers in an important NFC North showdown. It was also an opportunity for the Purple and Gold to rebound after a humbling defeat to the Bills on Monday Night Football.
Several factors weren't working in Minnesota's favor. The Vikings' starting quarterback, Kirk Cousins, arrived through a trade earlier in the week and had less than a week to prepare for the game. Not only that, but two wide receivers—Jordan Addison and Jauan Jennings—missed the game due to injury.
With Addison and Jennings sidelined, second-year WR Myles Price stepped up to help the Vikings achieve a 30-10 victory over their rival . Price caught all four targets for 49 yards and a touchdown while adding one rushing attempt for 12 yards, giving him 61 of Minnesota's 312 offensive yards.
COUSINS TO MYLES PRICE FOR A TD ON 3RD AND 23 MINvsGB on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/jSQvCluTla
Considering how the Vikings' WR depth behind Justin Jefferson has left much to be desired this season, it's in head coach Kevin O'Connell & Co.'s best interest to keep feeding Price the ball moving forward.
Heading into Sunday's game against the Packers, Price had been mostly used on special teams as a return specialist. He had only played 90 offensive snaps in the team's first eight games, and 29 of those came against the Bills last week, finishing with a six-yard catch on four targets.
Price played a season-high 33 offensive snaps on Sunday (four more than in Week 9) and got five touches on those opportunities. It was obvious that Jefferson would lead the wide receivers in snaps, but it was surprising that Tai Felton saw more offensive reps than Price.
Felton played all but 10 offensive snaps for Minnesota, participating in 59 plays. He was targeted more than Price, catching three of five passes for 33 yards. Considering Addison and Jennings were out, it was nice to see Felton step up, even if he was outplayed by Price.
O'Connell may need to re-evaluate his wide receiver room if Cousins develops a rapport with Price. Having him as the fifth wide receiver on the depth chart seems unreasonable if he can be more productive than the players above him. For reference, Addison has finished with 27 or fewer yards in five of his seven appearances, while Jennings has 54 receiving yards on the season.
That doesn't mean Price shouldn't continue as the team's return specialist, but it does mean that he could be ready to do more for Minnesota. The Vikings are used to rostering specialists who can contribute offensively, such as Cordarrelle Patterson and Percy Harvin.
Price may not have the pedigree of Harvin or Patterson, but he seems to rise to the occasion when given opportunities. Against the Packers, he played less than half of the team's offensive snaps, finished second in receiving yards, and found the end zone.
If given more chances, what else could the 24-year-old accomplish with the Vikings? We'll find out on Sunday Night Football in Week 11 against the 49ers, who allowed 343 receiving yards and five TDs on 30 catches in their 46-40 win against the Cowboys over the weekend.

title: 3 Vikings Studs & 2 Duds in Sunday's Dominant Win vs. Packers: Minnesota's Offense is Waking Up
full_text:
The Vikings desperately needed to regroup after an embarrassing loss to the Bills on Monday Night Football. This week would be another challenge for the Purple and Gold: a road trip to play the Packers.
Week 10 felt different. The Vikings looked competent offensively, and the defense did its best to contain the explosive Packers offense. Minnesota looked like the team many fans hoped they would be this season, earning a 30-10 win over their division rival .
Some players were studs in this game, doing a lot to help win the contest. Others struggled to contribute in a positive way, earning a "dud" title for the game against the Packers.
Let's take a look at five notable Minnesota players from Week 10's win against Green Bay.
Welcome back to Minnesota , Kirk Cousins. The veteran quarterback didn't have crazy numbers for the Vikings on Sunday, but he completed 21 of 31 passes for 207 yards, two touchdowns, and one interception.
In their first game with Kirk Cousins, the #Vikings already have their second-highest point total of the season. pic.twitter.com/KLNGNrD5wo
The offense converted half of their third downs after not converting a single one last week against Buffalo. Minnesota's 11 passing first downs helped to win the time of possession and control the pace of the game.
The Vikings have been playing fullback Max Bredeson a lot less since the start of the season, instead looking to tight end Ben Yurosek as an active blocker. Bredeson was once again used lightly in Week 10, even with Minnesota running the ball on half of their 62 offensive plays.
Bredeson was targeted with one pass, but was unable to haul it in. Minnesota might be struggling to find a role for the rookie blocker if he continues to struggle to be effective when given opportunities to make an impact.
Patience has paid off handsomely for rookie safety Jakobe Thomas. After being inactive all season , the third-round pick finally got an opportunity to take the field against Green Bay and made an impact in his small role.
Thomas was credited with two tackles against the Packers, but the most celebrated contribution was a forced fumble on a kick return from J. Michael Sturdivant early in the fourth quarter that was recovered by fellow rookie Jake Golday.
Even the @Vikings ' special teams is forcing turnovers! MINvsGB on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/F8HXXTeFb4
It's great seeing the young guys making plays.
The Vikings' offensive line has struggled this season, and not even starting left tackle Christian Darrisaw is immune to mistakes. Heading into this game, he has been credited with allowing nine quarterback pressures and six sacks while being flagged for three penalties.
Honestly, almost any Minnesota offensive lineman could have been included here due to some protection issues that led to Cousins being sacked three times for a loss of 24 yards. Thankfully, those plays didn't hurt the Vikings too much, but the status quo won't be good enough if the Vikings want to win a Super Bowl.
Wide receivers Jordan Addison and Jauan Jennings were out for this game. Justin Jefferson played well, leading all pass catchers by grabbing nine of 13 targets for 74 yards. However, the team still needed someone to step up.
COUSINS TO MYLES PRICE FOR A TD ON 3RD AND 23 MINvsGB on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/jSQvCluTla
Myles Price made the most of his opportunity, catching all four passes thrown his way for 49 yards and a touchdown. With Cousins at the helm, it will be interesting to see if chemistry continues to develop with Price as the season goes on.
