title: Why Titans Waiving Veteran RB Suggests Nick Singleton May Finally Get Another Go vs. Jaguars
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans' injury report is a full-on laundry list for today's game. Carnell Tate is out on the offensive side of the ball, hampering Cam Ward's pass-catching options, while LBs Anthony Hill Jr. and Cody Barton are missing time for Robert Saleh's defense.
As for the overall outcome of this matchup with the Jacksonville Jaguars, it's difficult to expect fireworks from a Tennessee team that just traded two of their best long-term assets. But games like these, even if the Titans don't pull off the upset, can serve as "see what they got" opportunities.
Rookie RB Nick Singleton has risen to the top of that list today as a result of one personnel move Tennessee made yesterday. The Titans waived veteran back Michael Carter. That may seem like a non-needle-mover on the surface, but this could be significant for Week 10.
Tyjae Spears is questionable once again this week; the backup RB hasn't played since Week 6. Carter had recently spelled Spears' usual complimentary touches due to Singleton not having proven his readiness in limited runs.
Coach Saleh said earlier this month that Singleton is getting better, and now, the guy that had been playing above him is waived. Coincidence? I think not.
Tony Pollard not being moved at the deadline signaled that RB1 duties aren't changing hands anytime soon, but that may have actually been good news for Singleton. A battle for Pollard's second-hand man bodes well for the rookie - particularly well if Spears keeps missing time.
Does Singleton have what it takes to make an impact in this offense? It's impossible to know based on his four carries this season. Again, however, what we should be worried about right now is seeing what players have and who could help take this rebuild to the next level.
If Pollard doesn't resign this coming offseason (Spears is also a free agent), Singleton will likely have first claim to take over the backfield unless the Titans draft another back. Even in that latter case, the now-rookie would have a year under his belt and potentially earn touches anyway.
That futuristic possibility traces back to today's game. If Spears remains sidelined, Singleton should become the Titans' RB2. That doesn't automatically mean he sees a ton of clock, but the stars are aligning for a look his way given the team's trajectory.
Singleton hasn't had a touch in the backfield since October 4, in a loss to the Baltimore Ravens. Another go is overdue, and Titans fans should be excited to see what another month in the lab has done for the rookie.

title: 3 Keys to Titans Pulling Off a Tide-Turning Divisional Upset Over Jaguars
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans enjoyed a bye in Week 9, but will return to the field in Week 10 to face the 6-2 Jacksonville Jaguars at Nissan Stadium.
Sunday's contest against the Jaguars will be Tennessee's first game since the trade deadline, when they dealt long-time starting safety Amani Hooker to the Buffalo Bills. Outside of trading All-Pro defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons to the Chicago Bears, sending Hooker to the Bills was the Titans' biggest in-season move.
After starting the year 1-7 and moving its two best defensive players before the deadline, Tennessee is a sizeable home underdog with Jacksonville coming to town. That said, let's look at three keys for the Titans to pull off the major upset.
Winning the turnover battle may not even be enough for the Titans to beat a possible Super Bowl contender in the Jaguars. Tennessee's offense must play a clean, efficient game from start to finish, as a timely turnover could end up costing them a second win and any chance of a rebirth this year.
Quarterback Cam Ward, who has committed a turnover in each of the last six games , has been a culprit in handing the ball to the other team. The 2025 No. 1 overall pick must cut these mistakes out and keep the Titans competitive on Sunday.
When running back Tony Pollard is carrying the ball at a high level , Tennessee's offense is usually a well-oiled machine. Despite interest from multiple teams, the Titans decided to retain Pollard instead of dealing him at the deadline, as the veteran has been one of the most productive backs in the sport in recent weeks.
Pollard has rushed for over 115 yards and two touchdowns in each of the last two games, and if he continues that hot streak against Jacksonville, it will not only benefit the offense but also the defense by giving them rest and keeping the Jaguars' dynamic offense on the sideline.
Lawrence has been playing at an elite level this season and is a legitimate MVP candidate, so Robert Saleh's defense has their hands full. However, a fantastic way to make any quarterback uncomfortable and shut down a potent offense is to wreak havoc in the backfield.
Tennessee must make Lawrence speed up his progression and feel pressured in the pocket. If the 2021 No. 1 overall pick receives solid protection for most of the afternoon, he'll dice up the Titans' secondary, so the front seven must step up in Week 10.
Dharya Sharma is a sportswriter from Nebraska who has been covering the Tennessee Titans through his website, SharmSports, since 2023. He is also an NFL and NBA writer for The Sporting News and had a previous stop with Sportsnaut. Follow him on X @SharmSports

title: Titans' Overloaded Injury Report May Put an Upset Over Jaguars on Ice in Week 10
full_text:
Carnell Tate missing the Tennessee Titans' Week 8 matchup wasn't enough to derail the offense from their best performance of the season. Even in a loss, Tennessee posted 36 points and ground up some real momentum for the first time in weeks heading into the bye.
But what about Tate and four other major players missing the contest? That isn't even mentioning another questionable designation on, you guessed it, the offensive side of the ball. Robert Saleh's post-bye goal was for this team to come out swinging.
That in itself isn't the issue, but it's hard to really land a hit when you're missing a hand. The Titans, in addition to Tate, will be without LBs Anthony Hill Jr. and Cody Barton, G Peter Skoronski, and P Tommy Townsend. The latter two were sent to the injured reserve list today.
On top of that laundry list, RB Tyjae Spears is once again questionable. Spears hasn't played since October 18, in the Titans' win over the Indianapolis Colts.
This is a team coming apart at the seams at the worst time. One-instance absences - like Tate's in Week 8 - are easier to handle. But the Titans are a 1-7 squad down five starters against the best team in their division.
Forgive our staff for entering tomorrow with a pessimistic mindset , but things simply aren't falling in a positive way for Tennessee. Of course, this doesn't negate the positive draft capital the team acquired at the deadline, nor does it cancel out Ward's progress.
However, it does mean that a Tennessee team down on their luck have caught another bad break.
You'll recall an 0-2 Titans team in a winnable situation on the road watching rookie RG Fernando Carmona Jr. exit vs. the New York Giants. Tennessee lost that game 12-7, and are just now trying to get Carmona back into the swing of things in practice.
LB Cedric Gray missed Week 1 due to a concussion, and has still yet to return to the leading role he held last season. The Titans aren't 1-7 because of injuries, but setbacks like these have arguably led to the team ending up on the wrong side of the five one-score games they've lost.
From that point of view, Week 10's injury report isn't all that surprising. Although, as the season winds down and certain decisions have to be made about this roster prior to an especially important draft, the added pressure from being down impactful talent works against the Titans' rebuilding process.
We'll see how the undermanned team fares tomorrow, but for those hoping for a turnaround-sparking upset, you may want to splash cold water on that optimism ahead of time.

title: Staff Predictions for Titans vs. Jaguars: Tennessee Won't be Blown Out... But a Win is a Different Story
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans are preparing to take the field for the first time in two weeks tomorrow, which means the Titans On SI staff are back in action trying to predict how the contest will go. Unfortunately, we went undefeated in predicting a defeat in Week 8.
Things haven't changed going into Week 10. In spite of improvement from Cam Ward, the only thing the Titans really benefitted from over the break was their added draft capital. Of course, that won't help them when the Jacksonville Jaguars come to town.
Although, none of us expect Tennessee to take this one lying down. Here's the staff's latest round of Titans predictions.
Echoing what my fellow writers will say, I believe the Titans put on a more than fair scoring performance in this one. I expect Cam Ward to continue to improve, even without Carnell Tate ; it's the defense, after trading both Jeffery Simmons and Amani Hooker, that is more likely to falter.
At 6-2 in the hunt for a championship run, Jacksonville is simply leaps and bounds ahead of Tennessee. The two teams are a part of the same process, but the Jags' rebuild could be considered done and over with. The Titans' feels like it will never end.
It's being played in Nashville, and Tennessee nearly took the legs out from under a similarly elite Bengals team just two weeks ago. But I don't see a win here for the home team.
The Titans appear to be overmatched on paper, but as we saw against the Bengals, this is a gritty team that tends to fight more often than not. I think QB Cam Ward has another solid game where the optimism surrounding his future continues to grow, but in the end, the Jaguars prove to be too much to overcome.
I expect QB Trevor Lawrence to have a big day against a depleted Titans defense as the Jaguars pull away late to improve their record to 7-2.
Despite trading away their top defensive players at the deadline, I still think the Titans come out with a fire lit under them at home and keep this game close. If quarterback Cam Ward can build on his promising show in Cincinnati in Week 8, and the defense forces a few turnovers, Tennessee has a shot to pull off the major upset.
However, in the end, Jacksonville is the more complete team with better coaching, and should pull out a narrow victory on the road to continue their quest for the top seed in the AFC.

title: Carnell Tate Was Titans’ Perfect Draft Pick — Where Critics Miss the Mark on Tennessee’s Rebuild
full_text:
The hiring of Robert Saleh this past offseason drew a fair bit of criticism to the Tennessee Titans. A lot of folks were just happy that Brian Callahan was gone, and that Matt Nagy wasn't tabbed as the next man for the job. But when draft night came and went, even Saleh's supporters left confused.
General manager Mike Borgonzi selected Ohio State Buckeye Carnell Tate with the fourth overall pick. In a draft that had been seen as generally weak in the WR area, taking Tate ahead of multiple big-name defenders shocked fans of a franchise that just hired a defense-first coach.
That exact criticism continues to echo today. Just earlier this week, an X post went viral calling out the Titans passing up on three "game changers" to take Tate instead. The post has 3,500 likes and counting, as well as nearly half-a-million views.
Titans had 3 game changers on defense available and took #that pic.twitter.com/Zg9p0bCRie
The Tennesseean gave the pick a C- back in April. NFL's Chad Reuter graded the Titans' first day a more respectable B+, though he still said it was "not because Tate's talent didn't merit it, but because top defenders Arvell Reese and Sonny Styles were still available."
This wasn't the sentiment across the board, but it's safe to say that the Titans' pick wasn't as universally beloved as a number that came before and after it. However, Tate is proven up to this point to be exactly what the aforementioned post said Tennessee missed out on.
Tate leads the Titans in targets (51) and yards (413) through the air. He's about to miss his second game in a row, but an entire contest down didn't dethrone the rookie playmaker. He also received the NFL's Offensive Rookie of the Month honors for October.
Ian Hartitz pointed out after Tate's last showing in Week 7 that he had come down with eight catches on nine contested targets this season. That's an 89% rate, and at the time, was second only to Los Angeles Rams' superstar Puka Nacua.
Tate was taken to build around Cam Ward, and the verdict on the latter still technically remains out. No matter what happens under center for Tennessee, Tate could have done little more (save for maybe better ball control) up to now to validate the Titans selecting him.
Would any one of the defenders taken after Tate have been as good in Tennessee? There's a chance...  but none of those guys have the defensive equivalent of Tate's rookie of the month honor. One of those nods went to LB Anthony Hill Jr., who the Titans took in the second round.
Maybe Tennessee got a few things right this time around, after all.

title: Hughes’ View: Nick Allegretti’s Giants Start Should Change the Commanders’ Center Plan
full_text:
When Lucas Patrick went down with a concussion, rookie Matt Gulbin took over while the Washington Commanders ' original plan at center, Nick Allegretti, stayed on the sideline, a move I thought was odd . Against the Giants, with Patrick still out, the team turned back to Allegretti, who looked good in the process. All five starters on the offensive line played 69 snaps Thursday and surrendered only one sack (four pressures) to the Giants, after giving up five sacks in the first meeting , which ended in a tie.
"I gotta give a lot of love to the Commanders' offensive line." @willcolon66 gives credit to the @Commanders ' big men for their impact on the team's win against the @Giants 🙌 pic.twitter.com/0KWwxUWvzC
After the Rams game, Commanders head coach Dan Quinn said Gulbin entered because he had taken the most reps at center. Allegretti had been spending more time at guard. With Patrick in concussion protocol, Washington named Allegretti the starter before Thursday’s game . The bigger question is why Allegretti wasn't getting more reps at center during the week leading up to the Rams game. The Giants blitzed on 62% of Daniels’ dropbacks in the first meeting, according to Next Gen Stats . Following Thursday’s game, New York head coach John Harbaugh credited the Commanders for staying out of long third downs : "They got in the third-and-short too often. And they weren’t in the third-and-long enough. So, credit them for that." Those shorter situations also gave the Giants fewer obvious passing downs to attack Daniels . The better protection Thursday belongs to the whole line. Allegretti was still at center for every snap. At the very least, Allegretti earned the right to be considered at the position moving forward. Even when Lucas Patrick returns, if he gets the starting job back, Allegretti should still take center reps each week. title: Vernon Davis Q&A: Jayden Daniels, Redskins Homecoming and Life After Football
full_text:
Vernon Davis spent much of his NFL career away from Washington, but that's where his football story began. He grew up in the city, played at Dunbar High School and Maryland, and eventually returned home to finish his career in a Redskins uniform. Between those stops came the sixth overall pick in the 2006 NFL Draft, two Super Bowl appearances, and a championship with Denver. There is plenty of football to talk about, including how much the tight end position has changed, what Davis sees in Jayden Daniels, and what he learned during his years in Washington. But retirement hasn't exactly slowed him down. These days, Davis is acting, producing films, and pursuing an entirely different kind of career. In a Q&A interview with Commanders On SI, Davis answered questions about his NFL career, the modern game, his retirement, and his work in Hollywood. Here is the full exchange, organized by topic.
Philip Hughes : You came into the NFL as the sixth overall pick at a time when taking a tight end that high was unusual. When you watch the position in today's NFL, what has changed the most from the position you entered in 2006? Vernon Davis : When I came into the league in 2006, the tight end position was still viewed primarily as a guy who could block and make plays in the passing game when his number was called. I was fortunate to come in with the mindset that I could do both, but I also knew I was part of a changing position. The biggest difference today is how much the tight end has become a featured weapon in an offense. Teams are moving tight ends around the formation, lining them up in the slot, out wide, in the backfield—basically treating them like oversized receivers who can also block. The athleticism at the position has really taken off. When I watch today’s game, I see tight ends being asked to do things that weren’t as common when I entered the league. They’re creating mismatches against linebackers and safeties, stretching the field vertically and becoming major parts of the passing game. The position has evolved tremendously. That’s something I’m proud to have been a part of. When I was drafted sixth overall, there was a lot of discussion about whether a tight end should go that high. Today, I think people have a much better understanding of the impact an elite, versatile tight end can have on an offense. Philip Hughes : Your combination of size and speed was considered unusual when you entered the league. If a 22-year-old Vernon Davis entered the NFL today, how do you think an offensive coordinator would use him differently? Vernon Davis : I’d be a matchup problem every single week . They’d move me all over the formation and force defenses to decide how they wanted to cover me. If you put a linebacker on me, I’d take advantage of the speed. Put a safety on me, I’d use my size. The goal would be simple: create mismatches and get the ball in my hands. Philip Hughes : We hear so much now about tight ends being "matchup weapons," but the position still requires players to block defensive ends and linebackers. In your mind, what separates a great receiving tight end from a truly complete tight end? Vernon Davis : To me, a great tight end is somebody who can catch the ball and make big plays. But a complete tight end is somebody who can do it all. You’ve got to be willing to put your face in there and block a defensive end, block a linebacker, do the dirty work—even when you know you’re not getting the ball. That’s what separates you. You have to be a football player first. If you can block, catch, run and create mismatches, you’re a complete tight end. Philip Hughes : Which tight ends playing today do you enjoy watching most, and what specifically do you see in their games that you appreciate as someone who played the position? Vernon Davis : I love watching George Kittle. That guy plays with an attitude. He’s physical, he’ll block, he’ll catch the ball, and when he gets it in his hands, he’s looking to make something happen. I see a lot of the things I loved about playing the position in him. I also like Trey McBride. He’s got that toughness and versatility you want in a tight end. He’s not just out there trying to catch passes—he’s willing to do the dirty work, too. As a former tight end, that’s what I appreciate. I like watching guys who play the position like football players, not just big receivers. Philip Hughes : Defenses have become faster and more versatile since you played. Has that made life harder for tight ends, or has the way offenses create mismatches actually made the position more valuable? Vernon Davis : I think it’s made the tight end more valuable. Defenses are faster and more versatile, but that just creates more opportunities for a tight end who can do it all. If you can run, catch, and block, you’re a problem. Every time you line up, the defense has to make a decision—and that’s where you create the mismatch. Philip Hughes : From a tight end's perspective, what can the position provide a quarterback that a wide receiver or running back simply can't? Vernon Davis : I think it’s the versatility. As a tight end, you can help your quarterback in a lot of different ways. You can stay in and block, you can protect him, or you can release and go make a play down the field. And because you’re bigger than a receiver but can still run, you can create some real problems for a defense. When your quarterback knows you can do whatever the play needs, that’s a big advantage.
Philip Hughes : Washington currently has different types of tight ends in Chig Okonkwo, John Bates, Ben Sinnott and Colson Yankoff. How valuable is it for an offense to have tight ends with complementary skill sets instead of asking one player to do everything? Vernon Davis : I think it’s huge. You don’t have to have one guy trying to do everything. You can have a guy who’s really good at blocking, another guy who can go make plays in the passing game, and guys who can do a little bit of both. That gives your offense a lot of flexibility and makes it harder for the defense to know what’s coming. When you have a tight end room like that, everybody has a role, and you can play to each guy’s strengths. Philip Hughes : Okonkwo is an explosive athlete whose ability after the catch is one of the strengths Washington wants to utilize. When you have a tight end with that kind of speed, what are the best ways to create favorable matchups for him? Vernon Davis : You’ve just got to find ways to get him in space . Move him around, put him in the slot, motion him, line him up outside—make the defense figure out who’s going to cover him. Once he catches the ball, just let him do what he does. Get it in his hands and let him make a play. Philip Hughes : Ben Sinnott is now in his third NFL season. Tight end has traditionally been considered one of the more difficult positions to learn. Why can development take longer there, and what tells you that a young tight end is beginning to put everything together? Vernon Davis : It takes time because you’re really learning two positions at once. You’ve got to learn how to block, how to read defenses, how to run routes, and understand the timing with your quarterback. It’s a lot. For me, you know a young tight end is putting it together when the game starts slowing down for him. He’s not thinking about every little thing anymore—he’s just playing. He knows his assignment, he’s confident, and he starts making plays without having to think so much. That’s when you know he’s starting to get it. Philip Hughes : What does playing with two tight ends do to a defense before the snap? From a player's perspective, why can 12 personnel create problems even when neither tight end actually gets the football? Vernon Davis : When you put two tight ends out there, the defense has to think a little more. They’ve got to figure out what you’re doing—are you blocking, are you releasing, are you going in motion? You’re making them make a decision before the ball is…

title: Commanders and Cowboys Are Both Two Games Back. Why Is Dallas Still Second?
full_text:
Dallas scored 40 points Sunday and lost. San Francisco beat the Cowboys 46–40 , dropping them to 4–6. Washington had already done its part with a 24–21 win over the Giants on Thursday. The Commanders got help while they were off, but they’re still third in the NFC East. The difference is winning percentage. The NFL counts a tie as half a win and half a loss , giving Washington the equivalent of 3.5 wins in nine games. That’s a .389 winning percentage. Dallas has four wins in 10 games, or .400. There’s no head-to-head tiebreaker to apply; the Cowboys are still ahead.
Dallas began Sunday a half-game closer to first-place New York than Washington. Now both teams are two games back. That’s the ground the Commanders gained without playing. Dallas hosts Tennessee next Sunday, November 22, at 1 p.m. ET. Washington won’t face Cincinnati until Monday night. If the Cowboys lose, they’ll fall to 4–7 (.364), and the Commanders will move into second place before taking the field. They would still have to keep it. A loss to the Bengals in that scenario would drop Washington to 3–6–1 (.350) and put Dallas back ahead. And if both teams win next week, the Cowboys would remain second by an even thinner margin: .455 to .450. title: Commanders Midseason Report Card: Washington Is Wasting a Plus-Seven Turnover Margin
full_text:
This past Thursday's 24-21 win over the New York Giants gave the Washington Commanders their third victory in an up-and-down year in which they’re plus-seven in turnover margin but haven't been able to string together consecutive wins. In most seasons, we'd already be talking about the draft, but since the NFC East is still up for grabs, the eight games remaining on Washington's schedule still matter. The following grades are from the first nine games. Quarterbacks: B Jayden Daniels has thrown for 1,499 yards with 10 touchdowns, two interceptions, and a 97.1 passer rating in seven games, and has 280 rushing yards and two TDs in 42 rushing attempts. Both picks came against New York, which is precisely why his winning drive mattered: the offense had needed him to make up for possessions he had just given away. The elbow injury cost him two full games. Marcus Mariota threw four touchdown passes without an interception and looked good in relief before he reinjured his knee. Rookie Athan Kaliakmanis played in that game and went 15-of-33 for 186 yards, a touchdown, and an interception in London.
Jayden Daniels had an up and down night but came through late against the Giants. 23/33, 249 passing yards, 3 TD, 2 INT, 28 rushing yards. His late touchdown to Stefon Diggs completed the comeback for Washington. pic.twitter.com/NQZgUbb2Vr
Running backs: C− Washington has 1,051 rushing yards. Daniels has 280 of them. Rachaad White leads the actual running backs with 275 yards on 65 carries. Jacory "Bill" Croskey-Merritt had 239 on 67 before his current trip to injured reserve, and Austin Ekeler has 109 on 33 since returning. White and Ekeler have helped as receivers, but the rushing attack hasn't provided a dependable answer when the offense needs a few extra yards. Blocking and play calls share in that result; the group grade reflects the overall production, not a claim that every short run is the back's fault. Wide receivers: B− Stefon Diggs has six of Washington's 15 passing touchdowns. His 36 catches for 386 yards lead the receivers, and the 32-yard winner against the Giants was his biggest play yet in the Burgundy and Gold. Rookie Antonio Williams has 28 catches for 326 yards and two touchdowns. He played 59 of 69 offensive snaps Thursday, more than any other Washington receiver, and has made a case for a starting role beyond this season . Treylon Burks has made 14 catches for 260 yards. Those contributions became more important when Terry McLaurin tore his patellar tendon and was lost for the season. The group has found answers, though it has not made the passing game consistently dangerous. Tight ends: C Chig Okonkwo has 27 catches for 263 yards but no touchdowns. John Bates contributes in the blocking game, where his five receptions don't tell much of the story. Ben Sinnott had one catch this season before Thursday . He caught four passes for 42 yards and a touchdown against the Giants, giving Daniels another option when the offense needed one. It was the tight ends' most encouraging recent development. One game does not rewrite what the group did over the previous eight. Offensive line: C− The center situation has supplied the clearest snapshot of the season. Lucas Patrick left the Rams game with a concussion. Rookie Matt Gulbin finished it, and Nick Allegretti started against the Giants after playing just two offensive snaps since Week 3. Washington allowed four sacks against Los Angeles. Allegretti played all 69 offensive snaps Thursday. The line gave Daniels much better protection in the rematch, allowing one sack and four pressures, although Brandon Coleman added another false start. Washington has allowed 21 sacks over nine games, with three players taking snaps at center. Sam Cosmi has played above the group’s C− grade. He has allowed just five pressures on 297 pass-blocking snaps. At Washington’s nine-game mark, PFF ranked him fifth among guards in pass-blocking grade—All-Pro-caliber work in that part of the game. The Giants' performance is the standard to build on, but it's not enough by itself to erase the earlier questions about the center plan. Defensive front: B− Odafe Oweh has five sacks, and K'Lavon Chaisson has 3½. Chaisson has also forced three fumbles. The team has 18 sacks and has allowed 934 rushing yards, roughly 104 per game. The run defense gives this grade some weight. Washington held Dallas to 66 rushing yards in Week 2 and Seattle to 44 the following week. Oweh had a sack, forced fumble, and recovery against Indianapolis. Daron Payne added a sack and forced fumble in the first meeting with the Giants. Chaisson has made that kind of play in three different games. The front has given the Commanders more than its sack total alone shows. The interior has changed since those early games. Payne and Javon Kinlaw went on injured reserve after Week 8, putting more on Shy Tuttle and Tim Settle as Jer’Zhan Newton returned from a torn pectoral muscle. Tuttle has two sacks, including one in the five-sack win over Philadelphia. Dorance Armstrong forced a fumble in that game that Charles Omenihu recovered. Five of Washington’s 18 sacks came against the Eagles; the other eight games produced 13 combined. The work against the run and the turnover plays earn the B−. The uneven sack production keeps it from going higher. Linebackers: B Sonny Styles leads Washington with 80 tackles. Frankie Luvu has 55 and two sacks. He recognized the play before the snap , dropped McCarthy for a two-yard loss and forced a punt. Without it, there might not have been a final winning drive. title: Commanders Safety Quan Martin Fined $17,911 for Unflagged Hit vs. Rams
full_text:
The NFL fined Washington Commanders safety Quan Martin $17,911 for a hit on Tutu Atwell that officials did not flag in the 20–13 loss to the Rams . Washington got the third-down stop. Six days later, Martin appeared on the league’s Week 9 fine list for unnecessary roughness, listed as a hit on a defenseless player. The official gamebook places the play at 9:22 of the second quarter. Los Angeles faced third-and-2 at its own 28, and Matthew Stafford went to Atwell over the middle (the play is the second video below in the X embed). The pass fell incomplete, with Martin credited on the play. The Rams punted for the second straight possession. That stop was part of a day when Washington held Los Angeles to 3 of 14 on third down . Luke McCaffrey returned the kick 10 yards to Washington’s 29, and the Commanders moved the chains once before punting it back. Washington led 10–3 at the time.
Then on the next third down, Stafford gets an easy one to his WR. But *doink* its a PBU/drop from Tutu Atwell. pic.twitter.com/yYoNzaYJWi
Had Martin been flagged then, the Rams would have had a first down. Instead, the stop held up in the gamebook, and the fine came later. The NFL reviews every play for potential violations, whether the officials called a penalty or not. Its public list doesn’t spell out what part of Martin’s contact prompted the fine. He can appeal, though the listing doesn’t say whether he will. Former Washington cornerback Emmanuel Forbes also received a fine for a play in that game. The Rams had asked Forbes to do more with Jaylen Watson out before the game. The NFL assessed him $10,839 for a separate second-quarter incident it described as striking, kicking, or kneeing. Officials flagged Forbes at 12:25, giving Washington 15 yards and a first down. title: Commanders Daily: New York Giants Gained 399 Yards but Scored 21. Joe Burrow Is Next
full_text:
The Washington Commanders have held four straight opponents to 23 points or fewer, and Thursday’s 24-21 win over the Giants kept that run going. New York also gained 399 yards , 59 more than Washington, which makes the score a little harder to judge on its own. San Francisco scored 23 against the Commanders, Philadelphia 10 , the Rams 20, and now the Giants 21. That’s an average of 18.5 points over the last four games for Daronte Jones’ defense, but New York had chances to make Thursday’s number much worse. The Giants reached Washington’s red zone four times and scored touchdowns on two of those trips. Through Week 6, opponents had scored touchdowns on 18 of 22 red-zone trips against Washington . In the first quarter, they got to the 15 before the Commanders stopped Cam Skattebo for no gain and J.J. McCarthy threw an incomplete pass on third down. Dominic Zvada missed the ensuing 33-yard field goal wide left. Washington stopped the touchdown, but the missed kick was New York leaving three points on the field. Later, the Giants got back inside the 20, only for Frankie Luvu to punch the ball loose from Malik Nabers at the 16. Jeremy Reaves recovered it, ending another promising New York drive without points.
OUR BALL 📺 #WASvsNYG @nflonprime pic.twitter.com/htMKiTEWHg
Washington also held the Giants to 4-of-12 on third down, including two stops when it couldn't afford to give New York another first down. Jayden Daniels threw interceptions on consecutive fourth-quarter possessions, and the Giants went three-and-out after both . On the second, New York took over at Washington’s 46 with a four-point lead and 2:15 remaining. Skattebo gained seven yards on two runs, but Sonny Styles dropped McCarthy for a two-yard loss on third-and-three. New York punted, giving Daniels the chance he needed to win it. But Isaiah Likely’s nine catches for 127 yards are still on the film, including a 66-yard touchdown on third-and-seven that put New York ahead 21-17. Cincinnati is next, although the Bengals still play Pittsburgh on Sunday night before visiting Washington on November 23. Cincinnati enters this Sunday’s game averaging 30 points, the second most in the NFL , and Joe Burrow has thrown 16 touchdown passes in his last four games. The Commanders have 11 days between games to sort through what worked against New York and what didn’t. They forced a turnover in the red zone and made the late third-down stops they needed Thursday. If Burrow finds the kind of room Likely found, though, Washington may not get away with allowing 399 yards again.

title: Commanders’ Ben Sinnott Had a Career Night on Fewer Snaps. Will the Targets Keep Coming?
full_text:
Coming into this season, the Washington Commanders were hopeful that this was the year tight end Ben Sinnott would break out . Used mainly as a blocker over his first two seasons, he hasn't had the chance to showcase the skill set he displayed while at Kansas State. He entered Thursday night's game against New York with one catch for six yards this season. He finished the game with four catches (on four targets) for 42 yards and a touchdown , setting single-game career highs in catches and yards. The interesting thing is Sinnott did that on 24 offensive snaps, two fewer than he played against the Rams four days earlier. Sinnott played 26 of Washington's 62 snaps (42%) against Los Angeles and was not targeted. The question I've been asking myself since: Why did Jayden Daniels look his way four times Thursday after Washington had barely thrown to him all season? According to RotoWire , Sinnott ran eight routes against the Rams and nine against the Giants. Before Thursday, he’d drawn two targets on 66 routes all season.
Jayden Daniels against a blitzing Abdul Carter? TD to Ben Sinnott #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/UGWVyNTCXK
Sinnott caught a five-yard pass with 11:53 left in the second quarter. Chig Okonkwo was listed as questionable to return with a back injury at 10:23, then returned early in the third quarter. Sinnott got 37 of his 42 yards on two drives that put Washington ahead. Late in the first half, he caught a short pass on second-and-eight and hurdled a defender on his way to a 12-yard gain that brought Washington to the Giants’ 15. Sinnott caught Daniels’ one-yard touchdown pass in traffic on third-and-goal. Washington went into halftime up 10-7. The Giants took a 14-10 lead in the third quarter. On the first play of Washington’s next drive, Daniels hit Sinnott for 24 yards. Antonio Williams finished the drive with a 31-yard touchdown. Despite the back injury, Okonkwo still played 41 snaps and made four catches (on eight targets) for 24 yards. John Bates played 28 snaps, while Colson Yankoff was inactive with a knee injury. Sinnott caught two passes while Okonkwo was out, including the touchdown. His longest catch came after Okonkwo returned. "I got the opportunities tonight," Sinnott said after the game . "I took advantage, and it feels good."
It's good to see the offense finally shine a light on Sinnott; it's that much harder to defend when you can't just assume he's on the field as a blocker. In two-tight-end packages, Commanders offensive coordinator David Blough should give Sinnott a few defined passing-game opportunities on early downs and near the goal line. Blough should continue his approach of giving each tight end their own distinct role , but should also look to take advantage of Sinnott's receiving and after-the-catch ability that, until Thursday night, was going to waste. If Okonkwo is back to his usual workload against Cincinnati, I’ll be watching the snaps he shares with Sinnott. When Washington needs a first down and both tight ends are out there, does Daniels go back to Sinnott? title: Commanders Could Finish Ahead of Giants With the Same Record After Thursday’s Win
full_text:
While the Washington Commanders' win over the New York Giants on Thursday night didn't change the order of the NFC East standings, it did change the conversation. Washington now sits at 3-5-1 and is two games behind the Giants , but a loss would have put them four games back with eight games left, which is virtually impossible to come back from. The good news is the Commanders now own the tie-breaker advantage with New York, something that could factor into things down the stretch.
The two NFC East rivals fought to a 27-27 tie in October , mainly due to gaffes by both teams in overtime, before Washington won the primetime matchup this week. Washington finished the season series 1-0-1, and Jayden Daniels has yet to lose to the Giants since turning pro. By rule, the October tie counts as half a win and half a loss for each team. Head-to-head record is the NFL’s first tiebreaker between two clubs in the same division. If Washington goes 5-3 over its final eight games and New York goes 3-5, both would finish 8-8-1. In a two-team tie, the Commanders would finish ahead of the Giants because they went 1-0-1 against them. Thursday’s win gave Washington that edge, but it still has to erase the two-game gap. That example assumes a two-team tie; a three-team tie involving Dallas would follow the NFL’s separate tiebreaking procedure. Make no mistake: Washington still has to stack wins. After the mini-bye, New York hosts Jacksonville on Sunday, November 22, and the Commanders host Cincinnati the following night. A Giants loss and a Washington win would cut the gap to one game. The teams won’t meet again this season, so the head-to-head edge only matters if the Commanders make up the ground elsewhere. title: Commanders Daily: Washington Was Last in the NFL on Third Down. What Changed Against the Giants?
full_text:
The Washington Commanders entered Thursday's game with the New York Giants dead last in the NFL in third-down efficiency, at 31.13%. Just four days earlier, they had only converted 3-of-12 against the Rams. Commanders head coach Dan Quinn said those stalled drives were keeping Washington from getting enough chances to run the ball. Against the Giants, the Commanders converted 7-of-14 third downs. Quinn went into the game knowing what he wanted: "Sustain some drives, convert some third downs, get into it again, and that'll be an important part of this week for us to do that." All three of Washington’s touchdowns came on third down. Jayden Daniels found Ben Sinnott from the Giants’ 1 with five seconds left before halftime, giving the Commanders a 10-7 lead. In the third quarter, Antonio Williams took a short pass on third-and-one and turned it into a 31-yard touchdown to put Washington back in front. The last one came after Daniels threw interceptions on consecutive possessions, only for the Giants to go three-and-out both times. Facing third-and-four from New York’s 32, Daniels found Stefon Diggs, who made a defender miss and scored with 57 seconds left to give Washington a 24-21 lead.
Jayden Daniels hits Antonio Williams and let's him do the rest! Third and inches turns into a thirty one yard TD for Washington. pic.twitter.com/hrkZ5m6T45
There’s a detail behind those seven conversions worth a closer look. Six came with one yard to go, including Sinnott’s third-and-goal touchdown. Diggs’ score on third-and-four was the only other one. Washington didn’t convert a third down needing five yards or more, so getting into manageable spots on first and second down mattered. A four-yard run and a five-yard catch by Diggs set up Williams’ third-and-one touchdown. Daniels was also sacked just once after the Giants got him five times in the October tie . Nick Allegretti started the game at center with Lucas Patrick out, although the sack totals alone don’t tell us how much of that difference came from the change. Washington ran the ball 33 times Thursday, gaining 105 yards. Daniels accounted for 11 attempts and 28 yards, and the offense still went 0-for-2 on fourth down. That’s a lot to clean up for a team that needed all three touchdowns to beat New York. Cincinnati is coming to town November 23, giving Quinn and offensive coordinator David Blough 11 days to build on what worked. Their next test is whether Washington can still move the chains on third down when it needs more than four yards.
